en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the *Vimānavatthu* in the *Khuddakanikāya*.
Introduction to the Work:
I pay homage to the Lord of Great Compassion, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of all that is to be known, and who teaches through methods that are skillful, profound, and diverse.
I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, honored by the Fully Enlightened One, endowed with true knowledge and conduct, by which people are led out from the world;
it is perfected in virtues such as moral discipline and is established in the paths and fruits.
I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
By the power of whatever merit has arisen from this homage to the Triple Gem,
may I be free from obstacles everywhere.
The merit performed by the deities in various previous births,
distinguished by the attainment of results such as their respective celestial mansions (*vimāna*) and so forth—
this [work] proceeds by way of questions concerning them and by way of answers.
The teaching was delivered by one who has personally witnessed the fruits of karma.
Formerly known as Vasinī, this work called the *Vimānavatthu* was compiled among the *Khuddakanikāya* by the great seers.
Having relied upon this very work, and elucidating the ancient method of the commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) by specifically clarifying the introductory narratives (nidāna) here and there,
I shall set forth a precise determination of the meaning that is perfectly pure, unadulterated, and subtle.
"I shall provide a beautiful commentary on the meaning according to my ability, following the tradition of the Mahāvihāravāsins without deviation.
Listen attentively, O virtuous ones, as I speak it."
In this context, "palaces" (*vimānāni*) refers to the distinguished abodes for the play and residence of the deities. For these are produced by the power of their own well-performed deeds;

because they possess specific dimensions such as one or two *yojanas*, are resplendent with various jewels, and are endowed with diverse colors and shapes, they are called "palaces" (*vimānāni*) due to their preeminent beauty and their being especially worthy of honor. This is the basis of the palaces.
The *Vimānavatthu* (Stories of the Mansions) is so called because it has these [deities] as its cause; it is the teaching proceeding in such a manner as, "Your throne is made of gold," and so forth.

This is merely an illustration, since this teaching proceeds by depending upon the excellence of those deities' physical forms, enjoyments, retinues, and so on, as well as the karma that produced them.
Alternatively, it is so called because, by way of its result (vipāka), it serves as the cause for understanding other types of karma.
It should be understood as the *Vimānavatthu*.
By whom was this spoken? Where was it spoken? When was it spoken? And for what reason was it spoken? It is said:
This *Vimānavatthu* proceeds in two ways—by way of questions and by way of answers. Therein...
The verses of response were spoken by various deities; as for the verses of inquiry, some were spoken by the Blessed One, some by Sakka and others, and some by the elder disciples.

Furthermore, among those [who spoke], it was primarily he who, for one incalculable aeon plus a hundred thousand aeons, had been accumulating the equipment of merit and knowledge for the sake of becoming the foremost disciple of the Blessed Buddha.
Having fulfilled the perfections of a disciple in due course, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—

having reached the pinnacle of the entire knowledge of a disciple’s perfections accompanied by such distinguished qualities as the six direct knowledges and the four analytical insights, standing in the second rank of the chief disciples,
and being established by the Blessed One as the foremost among those possessed of psychic power— spoke these words.
And as for the speaker, first while wandering on a divine journey for the welfare of the world, he asked the deities in the celestial realm; then,
having returned from there to the human world, for the purpose of making manifest to humans the fruit of merit,
he combined the questions and answers into one and reported them to the Blessed One, who then spoke them to the bhikkhus at the request of Sakka.
Although that was spoken by the deities by way of providing an answer, it is indeed the word of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Thus,
having been spoken here and there by the Blessed One and the Elders by way of questions, and by the deities by way of their answers, the compilers of the Dhamma,
who were reciting the Dhamma and Vinaya later on, brought it all together into one.
Thus they were included under the compilation titled *Vimānavatthu*.
This, then, is the brief and general response to the questions such as "By whom was it spoken? and so forth.
In detail, however, regarding the phrase "By whom was it spoken?", [it was spoken] because of the aspiration made at the feet of the Blessed One Anomadassi.
From this point on, the path leading to the arrival of the Great Elder (Mahāthera) must be explained;

however, since that has been detailed here and there in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the scriptures, it should be understood according to the method presented therein. Regarding the specific [questions] such as "Where was it spoken?
and so forth, the answers will follow according to the method for commenting on the meaning of each respective *vimāna*.
Others, however, say: One day, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:

"At present, even though people lack perfection of physical basis or perfection of field, they have nonetheless performed various meritorious deeds through the perfection of their own mental faith and have been reborn in the world of the devas with magnificent success."

“They experience [the results]. What if I, while wandering on a tour of the devas, were to make those deities witnesses, have them speak of the merit they have accumulated and the fruit of merit they have attained according to their realization, and then report that matter to the Blessed One?
In this way, my Teacher would make the fruit of karma directly evident to human beings, like the rising of the full moon in the vault of the sky.”

"By demonstrating that even small deeds, through faith directed toward the field of merit, result in magnificent fruits, he will—taking each particular *vimānavatthu* as the occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*)—deliver a great discourse on the Dhamma.
That shall be for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of many, of gods and humans alike. Having risen from his seat, [he took] a red double-layered cloth...
Having dressed himself in another red upper robe and arranged it over one shoulder, he— resembling a moving peak of an anthill mountain,
anointed with streaks of vermilion all around like flashes of lightning and suffused with the glow of twilight—
approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Having declared his purpose, and being granted permission by the Blessed One, he rose from his seat.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, he entered the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
Emerging from that state, he went at that very moment to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven by means of his power of psychic potency (*iddhi*).
There, in various places, he questioned those various deities regarding the meritorious deeds they had accumulated, and they told him. Then, [he returned] to the world of humans.
Having arrived, he reported all that had occurred there to the Blessed One according to the established procedure, and the Teacher gave his approval.
Thus, taking this as the occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*), he taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled company.
Now, regarding this *Vimānavatthu*, among the three Piṭakas—the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sutta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—...
It is included in the Sutta Piṭaka; within the five Nikāyas—namely, the Dīghanikāya, Majjhimanikāya, Saṃyuttanikāya, Aṅguttaranikāya, and Khuddakanikāya—it is included in the Khuddakanikāya;
and among the nine branches of the teaching (sāsanaṅga)—namely, sutta, geyya, veyyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, itivuttaka, jātaka, abbhutadhamma, and vedalla—it is comprised within the gāthā.
“I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha, two thousand from the monks,
and eighty-four thousand are those doctrines that have been transmitted to me.
Thus, this is a compilation of a few among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma acknowledged by the Keeper of the Dhamma-Treasury.

There are seven chapters: the Chapter on Divisions, the Chapter on the Throne, the Chapter on the Heart-Creeper, the Chapter on the Pāricchattaka Tree, the Chapter on Madder, the Chapter on the Great Chariot, the Chapter on Pāyāsi, and the Chapter on Well-Placed [Actions]. As for the subject matter: in the first chapter there are seventeen subjects;
in the second, eleven; in the third, ten; in the fourth, twelve; in the fifth, fourteen; and in the sixth, ten. In the seventh...
If the eleven intermediate celestial mansions (*antaravimāna*) are not included, there are eighty-five subjects; however, if they are included, there are one hundred and twenty-three subjects.

From the verses, there are one thousand five hundred verses. Among its chapters (*vagga*), the Chapter on Seats (*Pīṭhavagga*) is the first; among the subjects (*vatthu*), the subject of the Golden Seat (*Sovaṇṇapīṭhavatthu*) is the first;
and within that, the verse beginning "A golden seat for you" (*pīṭhaṃ te sovaṇṇamayaṃ*) is the first.
1. The *Itthivimāna*: 1.
The Chapter on Seats (Pīṭhavagga): 1.
The Explanation of the First Seat-Vimāna (Paṭhamapīṭhavimānavaṇṇanā)

In this regard, the origin of this first case is as follows: while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, King Pasenadi of Kosala provided an incomparable gift for seven days to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha;
subsequently, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika provided a corresponding gift for three days.
Likewise, when the great female lay devotee Visākhā gave her great almsgiving, the occurrence of that peerless gift became renowned throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

Then, people here and there raised this discussion: "Is it only by such a relinquishing of vast wealth that a gift becomes more fruitful, or is it also by relinquishing according to one's own means? The monks...
Having heard this, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

"Monks, a gift will not become more fruitful merely through the excellence of the object to be given; rather, it is through the excellence of the clarity of one's mind and the excellence of the field.
Therefore, even a mere handful of broken rice, a mere scrap of cloth, a mere mat of grass and leaves, or even a mere stale myrobalan fruit [given with a pure heart]..."
"Whatever is established upon a person worthy of offerings with a serene mind will be even more fruitful, more radiant, and more far-reaching," he said.
For it was likewise stated by Sakka, the lord of the devas:
"When the mind is serene, there is no such thing as a small offering."
"Whether it be toward the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One, or toward his disciples.
Now, this discourse spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. People gave gifts to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the needy, mendicants, and beggars according to their means;
they set out drinking water in the courtyards of their homes and placed seats at the doorposts.

They set them aside. Now at that time, a certain elder monk who was a wanderer for alms—graceful in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking away, in his bending and stretching, with downcast eyes and perfected in deportment—while wandering for alms, arrived at a certain house as the time drew near. There, a daughter of good family was full of faith.
Having seen the Elder, she was filled with serene confidence and gave rise to profound reverence and esteem.

Experiencing sublime joy and gladness, she led him into her house, paid homage to him with the fivefold prostration, prepared her own seat, spread a smooth yellow cloth over it, and offered it to him.
Then, when the Elder was seated there, she thought: "This is my supreme field of merit."
Thinking, “He has been served,” with a mind full of faith, she served him with food according to her means and fanned him with a fan.
When the Elder had finished his meal, he delivered a Dhamma talk concerning the offering of seats and the giving of food, and then departed.
That woman, reflecting upon her own act of giving and that Dhamma discourse, was continuously filled with rapture.
Having been afflicted by that disease, she gave even that seat to the Elder.
Then, at a later time, being afflicted by another illness, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in size.
She had a retinue of a thousand nymphs, and it was through the power of her gift of the seat that this came to be.
A golden couch, one *yojana* in length, capable of moving through the air with great speed, and shaped like a gabled chamber, appeared;

for this reason it is called a "throne-palace" (*pīṭhavimāna*). Indeed, because a cloth of golden hue had been spread [upon it] as an offering, it became made of gold, manifesting a result corresponding to that deed;
and because of the intensity of the surge of joy, it possessed great speed; and because of the [recipient's] worthiness...

Because it was given according to their own mental inclinations, it followed their respective desires; and due to the excellence of its beauty, it became entirely pleasing and endowed with a preeminent splendor.
Then, on a festival day, when the deities were going to the Nandana Grove for a pleasure excursion by means of their respective divine powers, [the chariot arrived].
As they were going, that goddess— clothed in celestial garments, adorned with celestial ornaments,
and surrounded by a retinue of a thousand nymphs— departed from her own abode, ascended that palanquin-vimāna,
and proceeded to the park with great divine majesty and immense splendor, illuminating all around like the moon or the sun. By him...
And at that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wandering on a tour of the heavens in the manner previously described,
arrived at the Tāvatiṃsa realm and revealed himself not far from that deity. Then, upon seeing him, that deity— her faith and reverence having arisen with great intensity—
immediately descended from her couch, approached the Elder, and paid homage to him by prostrating herself at his five limbs, her ten fingernails shining together in radiance.
She stood there paying homage with her hands joined in *añjali*. Although the Elder, by the power of his knowledge of the destiny of beings according to their deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*),
perceives directly through the penetration of his wisdom the wholesome and unwholesome karma accumulated by her and other beings—
as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit placed in the palm of his hand— nevertheless, immediately upon the rebirth of the deities...
“From where indeed have I passed away to be reborn here, and what wholesome kamma did I perform to obtain this prosperity?”—
with reference to her past existence and the kamma she had accumulated, there generally arises a recollection established by the nature of things (dhammatā),
and through that, knowledge of it exactly as it is arises; therefore, having caused that deity to recount the kamma she had performed:
Desiring to make the fruit of karma manifest to the world with its devas, he said:
“Your magnificent throne is made of gold; it moves with the speed of thought wherever you wish.
Adorned, wearing garlands, and well-robed, you shine like lightning upon the peak of a cloud.”
“By what means do you have such beauty? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those enjoyments arise for you, whatever is dear to the mind?
I ask you this, O goddess of great majesty.”
"What merit did you perform while being a human being?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions? he asked. She replied:
“Delighted, that deity, when questioned by Moggallāna,
answered the question asked, [explaining] the fruit of which kamma this is:
‘When I was a human being among humans, I gave a seat to those who had arrived.’”
I paid homage, performed the añjali-gesture, and gave gifts according to my means.
"Because of that, I have such a complexion; because of that, I prosper here;
and whatever wealth arises for me that is dear to my heart, it comes to pass."
“I declare to you, O monk of great power, that when we were human beings, we performed meritorious deeds;
because of that, our majesty blazes forth in this way, and my complexion shines in all directions.
In this context, *pīṭha* refers to any such thing as a block of wood, a shop-counter, a stool for making offerings, or a seat made of cane.
The specific names such as *masāraka* refer also to seats made of wood and other materials.

For instance, in the phrase “footstool (*pādapīṭha*) or foot-slab (*pādakathalika*),” it refers to a wooden block or similar object suitable for placing the feet; whereas in the phrase “pīṭhasappī” (a cripple), it refers to something graspable by the hand.
Furthermore, in certain regions, by local usage, the word “*pīṭhikā*” refers to a shop. [In the phrase] “*bhūtapīṭhikā*... [it refers to...]
In the phrase “devakulapīṭhikā,” it refers to a bench that serves as a place for making offerings to deities.
In the phrase “bhaddapīṭhaṃ,” it refers to a seat woven with rattan, creepers, and so forth, with reference to which it is said, “he brought a bhaddapīṭha.
And in passages such as “well-arranged beds and benches” or “by one having a bed or a bench made,” it refers to various types such as the *masāraka* (wood-apple wood) and others.

A seat made of wood and so forth. Here, however, it should be understood as a golden celestial mansion (*vimāna*) one *yojana* in extent, fashioned in the shape of a cross-legged posture (*pallaṅka*) and produced through the power of a deity’s merit.
As for the word "those" (*te*), it is the same as the pronoun *ta* found in such passages as: "Those who do not see Nandana do not know happiness."
It occurs in the sense of the singular and plural of the personal pronoun. In such passages as, “Homage to you, O noble steed among men; homage to you, O supreme among men;
homage to you, Buddha, Hero, be it so,” it occurs in the sense of the dative case by virtue of the word *tumha*, meaning “to you.
And in such passages as, “What have you seen? How have you heard? Have you transcended all acquisitions? Have you shattered the taints?”—it occurs in the same way.

In the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). In such passages as “What is your vow? What indeed is your holy life? (*kiṃ te vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ*), it is used in the sense of a possessor (*sāmī-atthe*). Here too, it should be understood in the sense of a possessor.
For the meaning is “your” (*tava*). Regarding the term *sovaṇṇamayaṃ*:
here the word *suvaṇṇa* [is used] in such contexts as “in gold or in ugliness, in the well-gone or the ill-gone,” and “the state of being golden” (*suvaṇṇatā*).
In such passages as “susaratā,” it occurs in the sense of the perfection of skin. In such passages as “the golden [birds] surround the crow,” it refers to the *garuḷa*.
In such passages as “golden-colored, with skin resembling refined gold,” it refers to gold (*jātarūpa*). Here too, it should be understood as referring specifically to gold;
for that is called “gold” because its beautiful color is identical to the color of the Buddhas.

Gold itself is *sovaṇṇaṃ*, just as in the expressions “*vekataṃ vesaman*” and so forth. Furthermore, the word *maya* occurs in the sense of the personal pronoun *asmat* (we) in such passages as “*Anuññātapaṭiññātā, tevijjā mayamasmubho*.
In the passage “*Mayaṃ nissāya hemāya, jātamaṇḍo darī subhā*,” it occurs in the sense of designation (*paññatti*).
In such passages as “*Manomayā pītibhakkhā sayaṃpabhā*,” it occurs in the sense of manifestation (*nibbatti*).
It is called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because it is produced by the mind alone, without any external condition.

In such phrases as, "What if I were to knead clay myself and build a hut made entirely of clay," it has the sense of a transformation (*vikāra*). In such phrases as, "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*) or "consisting of virtue" (*sīlamaya*), it serves merely to complete the meter.
Here too, it should be understood either in the sense of a transformation or as a mere metrical filler. For when [one says], "with gold... [and so forth].

The meaning is “made of gold” (*sovaṇṇamaya*). In that case, the suffix *-maya* should be understood in the sense of a derivative product, as in “a transformation of gold is *sovaṇṇamaya*. It is also appropriate to say it is in the sense of “produced from.
However, when the meaning is “that which is produced by gold is *sovaṇṇa*,” then the suffix *-maya* should be understood merely as a word-filler (*padapūraṇa*), as in “gold itself is *sovaṇṇamaya*.”
“Uḷāraṃ” means excellent, best, or great. Indeed, the word *uḷāra* occurs in the sense of "excellent" in such passages as “He attains a later distinction that is more excellent than the former.
It occurs in the sense of "best" in such passages as “Master Vacchāyana indeed praises the ascetic Gotama with an excellent praise.
And it occurs in the sense of "great" in such passages as “Those of great wealth, of great fame, of gross [form],” and so forth.
And that celestial mansion (*vimāna*) is called "excellent" (*uḷāra*) because it is excellent in the sense of never satiating those who enjoy it for its delightful nature;

it is supreme because it is praised for its universal beauty and so forth; and it is great because of its vast dimensions and high value—it is thus said to be "excellent" (*uḷāra*) by virtue of all three meanings.

"Swift as thought" (*manojavanti*): here, "thought" (*mano*) means consciousness (*citta*). Although the word "mind" (*mano*) is a common term for all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states of consciousness, because it is stated as "swift as mind" (*manojava*), it should be understood by way of a functional consciousness (*kiriyamayacitta*) that occurs toward any object whatsoever.
Therefore, it is "swift as mind" (*manojava*) because its speed is like that of the mind, just as [in the compound] *yathā*.
“Oṭṭhamukha” means exceedingly swift movement. For the mind, due to its rapid transformation, falls upon even a very distant object in a mere instant;
thus the Blessed One said: “Monks, I do not see any other single thing that transforms so rapidly as this mind, monks,” and “It travels far, it wanders alone.”
"Going" means that she goes through the air toward the park from the celestial mansion where that deity dwells.

Regarding the phrase "wherever she desires," here the word *kāma* occurs in the sense of desirable objects such as forms and so forth, as in: "For sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and delightful; they agitate the mind in various forms.
In passages such as "desire is passion, lust is passion," it refers to longing and attachment.

In such passages as “The defilement of sensual desire is clinging to sensual pleasures,” it refers to all forms of greed (*lobha*). In such passages as “One might speak in praise of serving one’s own desires,” it refers to the common ways of the village (*gāmadhamma*).
In such passages as “There are three clansmen here who dwell desiring their own welfare,” it refers to the wish for one’s own benefit.

In such passages as “Dependent on oneself, not dependent on another, free, going wherever one wishes,” it refers to the state of sovereignty (*seribhāva*); and here too, it refers to the state of sovereignty.
Thus it should be understood; therefore, *yenakāmaṃ* means "according to one's own wish," that is, in accordance with the deity’s desire.

*Alaṅkatā* means "with adorned limbs"; the meaning is: her body was embellished with divine ornaments measuring sixty cartloads, consisting of various types such as bracelets and anklets, which were radiant with networks of diverse rays and illuminated by many kinds of jewels. This [term] is used here in the vocative case.

This is the singular number. "Malyadhara" means one who wears garlands, because her hair, hands, and other limbs are beautifully adorned with celestial flowers—such as those from the *kapparukkha*, *pāricchattaka*, and *santānaka* creepers—which are made of highly refined gold and various jewels, and which are radiant and beautiful with masses of shimmering rays flashing forth on all sides.
"Suvattha" refers to those produced by the wish-fulfilling creepers, possessing various distinct colors and qualities, and endowed with perfectly pure, brilliant luster.
By way of divine garments such as the covering of the supreme undergarment (*nivāsanuttariya*), there are beautiful clothes. "You shine" (*obhāsasi*) means you illuminate.
"Like lightning" (*vijjuriva*) means like a flash of lightning. "On the mountain peak of clouds" (*abbhakūṭa*): this accusative case is used in the sense of the locative.
Or, "you shine" (*obhāsasi*) is a word containing a causal meaning, the sense being "you cause to shine" (*obhāsesi*). In this alternative, "on the mountain peak of clouds" (*abbhakūṭa*)...
The instrumental case (upayogavacana) should be understood here in the sense of "instrumentality" (upayoga). This is the meaning:

just as, for example, the peak of a dark cloud, already radiant and colored by the glow of twilight, is further illuminated—shining forth especially brightly—by streaks of lightning flashing out from all sides; even so...
"This celestial mansion, made of perfectly refined gold, resplendent with various jewels,

and naturally luminous— you, adorned with every ornament, have especially illuminated it with the radiance of your own body, which shines forth in every direction, and with the brilliance of your garments and jewelry."

For here, “throne” (*pīṭha*) is the word that is to be demonstrated, while “cloud-peak” (*abbhakūṭa*) is the word used as an illustration. Likewise, “those” (*te*) is the word that is to be demonstrated;

for although it is expressed in the genitive case in relation to this word “throne,” it is expressed in the nominative case in relation to these words: “adorned, wearing garlands, well-clad, you shine.”
It transforms; therefore, it is said, "you. "Like lightning" is an illustrative expression.
"You illuminate" is the demonstration of the relationship between both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison.

For this term "you illuminate" is spoken in the second person (*majjhimapurisa*) with reference to the word "you," whereas with reference to the word "bench," it is spoken in the first person (*paṭhamapurisa*).
It undergoes transformation (*pariṇamati*). Here, the word *ca* should be understood as having been elided (*luttaniddiṭṭha*).
Thus, the phrase “you shine forth wherever you wish” and “like a mass of clouds illuminated by lightning” undergo transformation into the accusative case, despite being in the nominative.
Likewise, the word “throne” (*pīṭha*) is the term to be qualified, while “golden, sublime,” and so forth, are its qualifiers.

But is it not the case that, having said "made of gold," one should not say "excellent" (uḷāra), because gold is superior due to its being a base metal [compared to silver], and because what is intended here is the divine [gold]? No; for there is a specific distinction.
For just as refined gold (*rasaviddha*)—which is superior and perfectly pure—is better than gold fashioned for human use, so too is that produced from a mine [superior].
Then, whatever among divine things is most excellent—just as, among divine gold, there is *cāmīkara*; more excellent than *cāmīkara* is *sātakumbha*; more excellent than *sātakumbha* is *jambunada*;
and more excellent than *jambunada* is *siṅgīsuvaṇṇa*. For that is the most excellent of all. Therefore Sakka, Lord of the Devas, said:
“Freed together with those who were freed—the ancient matted-hair ascetics—completely released along with those who were completely released.”
“The Blessed One, with the color of refined gold, entered Rājagaha.
Therefore, although it was said that it was “made of gold,” it was further described as “exquisite.

Alternatively, this term “exquisite” (*uḷāra*) was not stated solely with reference to its being the most excellent or refined; rather, it was stated also with reference to its greatness. This is the meaning already expressed.
And here, the passage beginning with “a seat” (*pīṭha*) and so forth is a demonstration of the similarity between the fruit [of merit] and its corresponding action.
Therein, by the phrase “made of gold,” he shows the excellence of the material basis of that celestial mansion (*vimāna*); by “magnificent,” he shows the excellence of its supreme splendor;
and by “swift as thought,” he shows the excellence of its movement. By the phrase “it goes wherever it wishes,” he demonstrates the perfection of the seat’s quality through its swift velocity.
Alternatively, by the phrase "made of gold," he shows its excellence; by "magnificent," its vastness and greatness;
by "swift as thought," the greatness of its power; and by "it goes wherever it wishes," he shows the ease of its movement.
Or else, by "made of gold," he shows its beauty and the splendor of its color.
By the word "exalted" (*uḷāra*), he shows its beauty and loveliness; by "swift as thought" (*manojava*), its speed;
and by "it goes wherever it wishes," he shows its unimpeded movement everywhere.

Alternatively, that celestial mansion (*vimāna*) is the natural result of a specific meritorious deed; because that deed was the natural outflow of non-greed (*alobha*), [the mansion likewise possesses these qualities].
It is made of gold; it is sublime due to being an outflow of non-hatred (*adosa*); and it moves with the speed of mind wherever it desires due to being an outflow of non-delusion (*amoha*).
Likewise, because that karma is an outflow of faith (*saddhā*), it is made of gold;

because it is an outflow of wisdom (*paññā*), it is sublime; because it is an outflow of energy (*vīriya*), it has the speed of mind; and because it is an outflow of concentration (*samādhi*), it goes wherever it desires. This is due to being an outflow of both faith and concentration.
It should be understood that it is made of gold; it is "exalted" by virtue of being a manifestation of concentration and wisdom;
it is "swift as thought" by virtue of being a manifestation of concentration and energy; and it "goes wherever it wishes" by virtue of being a manifestation of concentration and mindfulness.

In this context, just as the description of the "throne" and so forth serves to praise the excellence of the deity’s majesty resulting from the fruit of merit through the display of her celestial mansion's perfection, [so too should the chariot be understood].
Thus, the passage beginning with “adorned” (*alaṅkata*) is a praise of the excellence of the fruit of merit by way of demonstrating the perfection of one’s personal being (*attabhāva*).

For just as an ornament of refined gold, even when fashioned by a master craftsman of well-trained skill, shines only when inlaid with various gems that blaze with networks of rays and not when it is plain,
so too does a personal being endowed with all its limbs and beautiful in its fourfold symmetry shine only when well-adorned and embellished.

It shines, not merely [naturally]. Therefore, by the words "adorned" and so forth, he shows her a specific, acquired splendor (*āharima*), while by the word "you shine," he shows that which is unacquired (*anāharima*).
Likewise, by the former he shows an excellence of splendor characterized by a present tense suffix, and by the latter, one characterized by a past tense suffix.
Or alternatively, by the former he shows the perfection of her objects of enjoyment (*upabhogavatthu*), and by the latter—
The perfection of the basis for enjoyment.
Here it is asked: "But is that celestial mansion (vimāna) drawn by yoked draft-animals, or rather, is it drawn by unyoked ones?
Although in the world of the gods there are chariot-vimānas drawn by yoked draft-animals—according to such statements as "a chariot of thoroughbreds yoked by the thousands"—those sons of the gods...
In this way, at the time of performing their tasks, they manifest themselves in the form of vehicles, just as the divine son Erāvaṇa manifests in the form of an elephant during his playtime.
This, however, and other such instances, should be understood as improper modes of conveyance.
If this is so, one might ask: is the air element within that celestial mansion (vimāna) the specific condition for its movement, or is it the external air element?

The term "internal" is to be understood here. For just as when the moon-palace, the sun-palace, and so forth move from one place to another, there exists a great wind-circle produced by the common karma of the beings who depend upon them, which possesses extremely swift speed and propels them along;
there is no such external wind-element that propels them by acting as a pusher. And just as the Wheel-Treasure [proceeds]...
It proceeds by way of the air element arising from within;

for there is no external air element that causes it to proceed by impelling it, as is the case with the moon-palace and so forth, because it proceeds immediately after the words "May the noble Wheel-Treasure proceed," etc., through the power of the mind of a Wheel-turning Monarch. Thus, of that deity...
It should be understood that he goes by means of the air-element dependent upon himself through the power of the mind. Therefore it was said:
"He goes with the speed of thought wherever he desires. 2.
Having thus praised the excellence of that deity’s fruit of merit in the first verse, [the Blessed One now speaks] regarding its cause.
In order to reveal his perfection of merit, the two verses beginning with "By what means do you have such a complexion? were spoken.
Therein, the word *kena* (by what) is used in the sense of censure in such passages as, "What king is he who does not protect the world? What indeed do you think I should say to you?

It is used in the sense of indefiniteness in such passages as, "Whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present... It is used in the sense of inquiry in such passages as, "What indeed [is this] here..."
In such passages as "Wealth is the best thing for a man," it should be understood here as well that [the word *kena*] refers to a question.
Furthermore, in the phrase "by what" (*kenā*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is "for what reason. "Tesaṃ" means "of you.
"Etādiso" means "of this kind," the sense being "as it is seen now. "Vaṇṇo" refers to the word *vaṇṇa*; [as in the passage]: "But when were these, householder, gathered together?"... [and so forth].

In such passages as “the praises of the ascetic Gotama,” it occurs in the sense of *guṇa* (quality). In such passages as “in many ways he speaks the praise of the Buddha, he speaks the praise of the Dhamma, he speaks the praise of the Saṅgha,” it occurs in the sense of *thuti* (praise). In such passages as “Now by what quality (*vaṇṇena*) is one called a ‘fragrance-thief’?
it occurs in the sense of *kāraṇa* (cause/reason). In such passages as “three sizes (*vaṇṇā*) of the bowl,” it occurs in the sense of *pamāṇa* (measure/extent).

In such passages as “There are these four castes, Master Gotama,” it refers to birth (*jāti*). In such passages as “Having manifested the form of a great king of elephants,” it refers to shape (*saṇṭhāna*).
In such passages as “The Blessed One is golden-hued, with very white teeth, and full of energy,” it refers to the color of the skin (*chavivaṇṇa*).
Here too, it should be understood as referring precisely to the color of the skin. This is the meaning here: by what specific kind of merit, acting as the cause, [is this attained]?
"O deity, has such a body-color as this, of such a kind, pervading twelve yojanas, arisen for you?
By what is it successful for you here?"—by what excellence of merit does that sublime fruit of well-performed conduct, which is now being obtained by you in this place, succeed and come to fruition?
"It arises" means it is produced; [it is said] in the sense of its non-interruption.

The meaning is that they occur one after another. "Wealth" (*bhoga*) refers to specific types of property and requisites, such as clothing, ornaments, and so forth, which have received the name "wealth" in the sense of being objects to be enjoyed.
*Ye* is an indefinite designation by way of a general term; *keci* is an indefinite designation that touches upon a particular variety.
By both [terms], there is a comprehensive inclusion, pervading without remainder those kinds of wealth found therein, whether they be superior, more inferior, or otherwise.
For this description is all-inclusive, just like [the expression] "whatever formations there are. "Pleasant to the mind" means they are to be loved by the mind;
the sense is "agreeable to the mind.
And here, by the phrase "such a beauty," the specific qualities previously mentioned are included within the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of that deity.

The perfection of beauty (*vaṇṇasampadā*) has been shown. By the word “possessions” (*bhogā*), the perfection of the qualities of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇasampadā*)—consisting of divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles which serve as the basis for enjoyment and utilization—is indicated.
By the phrase “dear to the mind,” the desirability, loveliness, and attractiveness of those forms and so forth is shown.
By the phrase “is found here,” however, the perfection of divine lifespan, beauty, fame, happiness, and sovereignty is demonstrated. “Whoever... [the rest of the passage follows].
By the phrase "dear to the mind," those qualities mentioned in the Sutta as: "He surpasses other devas in ten respects:
in divine life-span, in divine beauty, in divine happiness, in divine glory, in divine sovereignty, and in divine forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects."
There are ten points. It should be understood that their inclusion here is shown without exception.

"I ask" (pucchāmi) means I pose a question; the meaning is, "I desire to know. Granted, this [is already implied] by the use of the interrogative pronoun *kiṃ* in such passages as: "By what is your complexion so beautiful?
By what do you prosper here? What merit did you perform? By what is your splendor thus blazing?"

It is understood that these three verses were spoken by way of a question because no other purpose was possible. However, the word "I ask" was stated in order to make known the specific nature of this question.
For this question is not, first of all, a "demonstration of the unseen," since there is no state of the Great Elder (Mahāthera) having failed to see such a matter;
nor is it for the "cutting off of doubt," because he has entirely eradicated all uncertainty.

It is not an inquiry for consent (*anumatipucchā*), because it does not proceed in the manner of seeking consent—as in such passages as, "What do you think, O royal prince?"—nor is it an inquiry out of a desire to speak (*kathetukamyatāpucchā*), because the Elder did not question her with the intention that the deity should speak.
Rather, it should be understood specifically as a "corroboration of what has been seen" (*diṭṭhasaṃsandana*). This point was already explained below.
In the *Aṭṭhuppattikathā* (The Discourse on the Occasion), this has already been clarified by the passage beginning with "Even though the Elder... and so forth. The word *taṃ* means "you.

This [pronoun] is dependent both on what precedes and what follows; it should be understood as the accusative singular when dependent on what precedes, but as the dative singular when dependent on what follows.
Regarding the word *devī*, here the term *deva* refers to [the King], as in: "O King, these eighty-four thousand cities, headed by the royal capital Kusāvatī... and so on.
In such passages as, "O King, take delight in this; have regard for life," it is used with reference to conventional deities (*sammutideva*);
whereas in such passages as, "The teaching of that God beyond gods (*devātideva*), the All-Seeing One," it is used with reference to purified deities (*visuddhideva*).
For when the Blessed One’s status as a god beyond gods is stated in relation to purified deities, the status of others is thereby implied. "The Cātumahārājika gods are long-lived..."
In such passages as “possessed of beauty, abounding in happiness,” it refers to gods by way of rebirth. Here too, it should be understood precisely by way of gods by rebirth.
As for the meaning of the word (*padattha*): she plays, sports, and dallies by means of her own merit and psychic power; she delights in the five strands of sensual pleasure;
or else, according to the method stated below, she shines and radiates, and she travels through the air in a celestial mansion (*vimāna*)—thus she is a goddess (*devī*).
“*Tvaṃ devī*” (you, O goddess) is the singular form used for addressing her. *Mahānubhāve* means one of sublime power;
that power of hers has indeed been demonstrated by the two preceding verses.

Regarding the term *manussabhūtā*: here, humans (*manussa*) are so called because of the abundance of mind (*manas*), by virtue of qualities such as mindfulness, heroism, and fitness for the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"With cultivated minds" means having minds endowed with superior qualities. Who, then, are they? They are the distinguished beings dwelling in Jambudīpa. Therefore the Blessed One said:

"Bhikkhus, in three respects the humans of Jambudīpa surpass the humans of Uttarakuru and the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Which three? They are brave, they possess mindfulness, and here there is the living of the holy life.
For it is thus that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Paccekabuddhas, the Chief Disciples, the Great Disciples, the Wheel-turning Monarchs, and others [excel].

And beings of great power arise right here. However, some say that because they possess the same physical form and so forth as those living on the minor islands, the inhabitants of the other great continents were also designated simply as "human beings.
Others, however, say: "Human beings" (*manussa*) are so called because of the abundance of the mind (*manas*) accompanied by greed and its opposites, such as non-greed.

For among those beings who are of human birth, greed and its opposites—non-greed and so forth—are especially prevalent. Due to the prevalence of greed and the like, they fill out the path to the states of misery;
due to the prevalence of non-greed and the like, they fill out the path to the happy destinies and the path leading to Nibbāna.

Therefore, because of the prevalence of the mind accompanied by greed and its opposites—non-greed and so forth—the inhabitants of the four great continents [are distinguished] from the inhabitants of the minor islands.
A particular class of beings is called "human beings" (*manussa*). However, worldly people say they are "humans" because they are the descendants of Manu.

Manu was the first person of the first eon, the founder of the world's social conventions, the one who ordained what is beneficial and harmful for beings, and stood in the place of a father to them; he is the one who is called "Mahāsammata" in the Teaching.
Beings who abide by his instruction and admonition—both directly and through tradition—are called "human beings" (*manussa*) because they are like sons to him.

For that very reason, those youths are also designated as "men" (*manuja*). Those who have become humans, born among humans, or attained the human state are "those who have become human" (*manussabhūta*).

"What merit did he perform? means: what kind of wholesome deed (*sucarita*), known by the name "merit" (*puñña*)—so called because it purifies (*punāti*) and cleanses (*visodheti*) the continuum in which it has arisen, and because it produces the fruit of a state worthy of honor (*pujja*)—did he perform among the various types such as giving and virtue?
The meaning is that he accumulated and brought it to fruition. "Possessing blazing majesty" means having the power of merit shining forth in every respect.
But why is it asked here, "What merit did he do when he was a human being"? Is there no performance of meritorious deeds in other realms of existence? It is not that there is none.
For even in hell, the occurrence of wholesome sense-sphere consciousness can sometimes be found;
how much more so, then, elsewhere! Have we not already said that "this question is for the purpose of correlating what has been seen"? Therefore, the Great Elder—
Having seen that [result] which arose from performing meritorious deeds while remaining in the human state, he asked— seeking the actual fact—

“What merit did you perform as a human being? Alternatively, because in other realms there is either absolute happiness, absolute suffering, or an abundance of suffering, [one does not perform] meritorious deeds there.
The opportunity is not easily obtained because the convergence of conditions, such as reliance upon a true person (sappurisa), is extremely difficult to find.

Even when it occasionally arises, it is neither sublime nor vast due to the aforementioned causes; however, within the human realm, because of the abundance of happiness, the opportunity for performing meritorious deeds and the convergence of conditions such as reliance upon a true person are generally easy to obtain.

Because it is easily accessible. Furthermore, whatever suffering arises therein also serves as a specific supporting condition (*upanissaya*) for the performance of meritorious deeds; for faith has suffering as its supporting condition.
Just as, when a blade is being fashioned with a hammer, its heating exclusively in fire or its moistening with water is not the specific condition for its capacity to perform the act of cutting.
Furthermore, just as water that has been heated to a specific measure is a special condition for that [food],

even so, the state of being exclusively possessed of suffering, the abundance of suffering, and the state of being exclusively possessed of happiness are not special conditions for the performance of merit.
However, when there is the heating of suffering to a specific measure and the cultivation of happiness, the performance of merit gains its supporting condition (*upanissaya*).
When it arises, it does so with great radiance and great expansion, and it is capable of cutting through opposing factors;
therefore, the human state is a distinguished condition for the performance of merit. Hence it was said:
"Having become human, what merit did you perform? The rest is easy to understand.
4. Thus questioned by the Elder, that deity answered the question. To demonstrate this matter, the verse beginning with “That deity, being delighted” was spoken.
By whom, however, was this verse spoken? By the compilers of the Dhamma (the *Dhammasaṅgāhakas*).
Therein, “she” (*sā*) refers to the one previously addressed as “I ask you, O goddess of great power. “Deity” (*devatā*) includes both a son of the gods (*devaputta*) and a Brahmā.

The term *devatā* is also used for a daughter of the gods. For in such passages as, “Then a certain deity, at the end of the night, of surpassing beauty...,” the son of a god is called a “deity” (*devatā*), taking the word to mean simply a “god” (*deva*).
Likewise, in such passages as, “Those seven hundred sublime deities, having emerged from their Brahma-palaces...,” it refers to Brahmas.
"In your exquisite beauty, O deity, you stand there, illuminating all directions like a medicinal herb among the stars"—in such passages as these, it refers to a goddess (*devadhītā*).
Here too, it should be understood as a goddess alone. "With a joyful mind" (*attamanā*) means with a satisfied mind, through rapture and gladness.

"Captivated" (gahitamana): For a consciousness accompanied by rapture and joy, because there is no room for dejection, is as if made one's own and seized by those two. Or, "satisfied" (attamana) means having one's own mind (sakamana).

For a consciousness associated with blameless rapture and joy receives the designation "one's own" (saka), because it brings benefit and happiness to its possessor both now and in the future; the other [type of consciousness] does not.
“By Moggallāna”: because he was the son of a wealthy brahmin of the Moggallāna clan, that great elder was known as “Moggallāna” by way of his clan;
thus, it is “by Moggallāna. “Was asked”: he was asked for the purpose of correlating what had been seen.
The construction is: “That deity, being pleased in mind, answered the question. And her state of being pleased in mind is [expressed by the words] “Even that which is indeed slight... etc.
“Thus, this very deed became the cause for such great divine prosperity. Previously, she had experienced intermittent joy based on the fruit of her own merit;
but now, [thinking], “Even a service rendered to a certain elder has such an exalted fruit, and this one is the foremost disciple of the Buddhas, possessed of sublime virtues and great majesty,”...
"I am able to see him and pay him homage, and he asks me a question connected precisely with the fruit of my own merit"—
thus it arose from two reasons. With such intense joy and gladness having arisen,
she accepted the Elder’s words with her head and, being asked the question, answered it.
"Questions" (pañha) refers to that matter desired to be known; he "expounded" it, that is, he spoke and answered it. But how did he expound it?
"Being asked" (puṭṭhā) means by way of the manner of being asked—that is, in the very manner of having been questioned.

For here, although "questioned" (pucchitā) has already been stated, the subsequent word "being asked" (puṭṭhā) should be seen as a restriction for the sake of a specific meaning. Indeed, when something is already established, its restatement serves to indicate a specific meaning.
It exists. But what is the specific meaning of this term? It is the correspondence of the explanation to the question.
For when the action that serves as the cause is asked about after the fruit of the action has been shown, there is the manifestation of the mutual correspondence between those two.
And it is the explanation, both in its sense and its phrasing, of the manner in which the question was posed.
The response occurred in accordance with the question; thus, in order to indicate this distinction, after saying "the one who asked," it was further stated "the one who was questioned.
Alternatively, by way of qualifying that deity as "the one who asked," the state of having been questioned and the answering of the question [are established].
This is the praise of the cause. This is what is meant: the question is that by which the Elder asks, “By what means do you have such a complexion,” and so forth.
That deity is called “the one questioned” because she has performed the action [that prompted] that question, or because she has explained the cause of that question.
Since she is the one questioned and the performer of the action being questioned, therefore [she provides] the answer.
"Asked. And because one who has been asked has the nature of explaining the action being questioned, he therefore "answered the question.
The phrase "the fruit of which action this is" is a demonstration of the actual form of the meaning expressed by the word "question.
And here the meaning is as follows: this [fruit] is immediately evident to the one asking and to the one being asked.
The "question" is mentioned because one wishes to know the fruit of merit of that specific action; thus, he explained the meritorious deed. 5.
The passage beginning with "I among humans" is the manner of answering the question. Therein, "I" is how the deity identifies herself.
Having said "among humans," she further says "having become human" in order to show that human qualities were present within her at that time.
For one who, being born as a human being, commits such unwholesome acts as the taking of life and, becoming liable to punishment,
undergoes great suffering by receiving corporal penalties such as the severing of hands from kings and others here and there— this person is called a "hell-being among humans.
Another, likewise being born as a human being, through the power of past karma, does not even obtain food or clothing.
Overcome by hunger and thirst, abounding in suffering, and finding no support anywhere, he wanders about;

this is what is called a "human-ghost" (*manussapeta*). Another, though belonging to the human species, lives dependent on others, bearing the burden of others, having broken the bounds of noble conduct or practicing improper behavior, is censured by others, terrified by the fear of death, and dwells in the thickets, abounding in suffering.
One who wanders about without knowing what is beneficial or harmful, intent only on dispelling the sufferings of sleep, hunger, and so forth—
this is called a human-animal (*manussatiracchāna*). But he who knows what is beneficial and harmful for himself, has faith in the fruit of kamma, is endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing,
is compassionate toward all beings, is full of a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), and avoids the unwholesome courses of action while practicing the wholesome courses of action...
By practicing the bases for the performance of merit, one fulfills them; such a person is established in human nature and is called a "human" in the ultimate sense.
This [Bodhisatta] was also like that. Therefore it is said: “among humans, having become human. The meaning is:
those who have attained the human state within the category of beings (sattanikāya) and remain without having abandoned human qualities (manussadhamma).
"Of those who have arrived" (*abbhāgatānaṃ*) means of those who have come toward [the host]; the meaning is "of guests who have arrived. For there are two kinds of guests:

the *atithi* (visitor) and the *abbhāgata* (one who has come). Among them, a guest with whom one is already acquainted is an *atithi*; one with whom no acquaintance has been established is an *abbhāgata*.
An *atithi* is one who has arrived earlier, whether he is an acquaintance or not; an *abbhāgata* is one who presents himself at the time of the meal, having arrived just now.
*Abbhāgata*: one who has arrived unexpectedly. This refers to a guest who has been invited for a meal, or one who has arrived unexpectedly without being invited.

However, this [term] refers to one who is unfamiliar and has just now arrived without an invitation; it is said "to those who have arrived" (*abbhāgatānaṃ*) out of respect, though the plural number is used here.
*Āsana*: that wherein one sits (*āsati*, *nisīdati*) is called a seat (*āsana*). Whatever is suitable for sitting is meant here.
However, a stool (*pīṭha*) was intended; because it was small and insignificant, he called it a "seat" (*āsana*).

"I gave" means: having given rise to joy, thinking, "What has been given by me to this elder will be of great fruit and great benefit," and having faith in both the action and the fruit of the action, I gave it for the sake of that elder’s use; the meaning is that I relinquished it by way of a detached renunciation.
"Abhivādayinti" means she performed an act of salutation; that is, she paid homage to those worthy of offerings by prostrating with the five points of the body.

For, while performing that very act of salutation, she effectively caused the person being saluted to pronounce a blessing—such as "May you be happy," "May you be free from illness"—by the very fact of her paying homage.
"Añjalikaṃ akāsī" means she made the gesture of the *añjali*, radiant with the joining of the ten fingernails.
The meaning is that she performed an act of veneration toward those distinguished by their virtues by supporting them on her head. "According to her power" means according to her strength;

the meaning is that she acted in accordance with the wealth available to her at that time. "She gave gifts" means that by relinquishing objects of giving such as food and drink, and thereby feeding those worthy of offerings, she generated merit consisting of generosity.
And here, "I" indicates the state of connection by showing that the action and its fruit reside within a single continuum;
"having become human beings among humans" indicates the specific continuity that served as the basis for that performance of merit;
and "who had come" indicates both the excellence of the mind [of the recipient] and the excellence of the field for the gift.
This is because it illustrates that [the gift] proceeded without regard for anything whatsoever, such as the recipient.
The phrase, "I gave a seat and gave a gift according to my power," shows the giving of the essence of wealth;
the phrase, "I paid homage and performed the añjali-gesture," shows the giving of the essence of the body.

6. *Tenā* means by that aforementioned merit acting as the cause. *Me*: this word *me* occurs in the sense of the agent (instrumental case) in such passages as “*Kicchena me adhigataṃ, halaṃ dāni pakāsituṃ*” (“It was attained with difficulty by me;

it is now fit to be proclaimed”), meaning “by me. In such passages as “*Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū*” (“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to teach the Dhamma in brief to me”), it occurs in the sense of the recipient (dative case), meaning “to me. In such passages as “*Pubbeva me,*” [it occurs in the sense of the ablative case, meaning “from me”].
In such passages as, “O monks, when I was still a Bodhisatta, not yet fully awakened to supreme enlightenment,” the term occurs in the sense of the genitive (sāmī-attha);

here too it is in the sense of the genitive, meaning “mine. Furthermore, this word *me* should be connected in both ways—as in “by that merit of mine” (*tena me puññena*) and “such as mine” (*me etādiso*).
The rest is exactly as previously explained.
When that deity had thus answered the questions, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna taught the Dhamma in detail.
That teaching was beneficial to that deity and her retinue. Thereupon, the Elder returned to the human world and reported all those events to the Blessed One.
Taking that as the occasion, the Blessed One [spoke] to the assembled company.
He taught the Dhamma. However, it is only the verses that have been included in the collection.
The commentary on the First Seat-Vimāna is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Seat-Vimāna.

The second throne-palace is made of beryl. Its origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and its commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*) should be understood in the same manner as stated for the first. This, however, is the distinction:
it is said that a certain woman living in Sāvatthī, upon seeing an elder who had entered her house for alms, felt a mind of faith and offered him a seat.
Having spread her own seat with a blue cloth over it, she gave it to him.
Because of that, when she was reborn in the world of the gods, a palanquin-palace made of beryl was produced for her. Therefore it is said:
“Your magnificent seat is made of beryl; swift as thought, it goes wherever you desire.”
Adorned with garlands, wearing fine clothes, you shine like lightning upon the peak of a cloud.
"By what means do you possess such a complexion? By what means are you successful here?
And how do those enjoyments arise for you, whatever is dear to the mind?"
“I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?
Thus questioned by Moggallāna, that deity was uplifted in mind.
When questioned, she answered: "Of what karma is this the fruit?
"When I was among humans as a human being, I gave a seat to those who approached me;
I paid homage, I performed the añjali-gesture, and I gave gifts according to my means."
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this; because of that, I prosper here;
and whatever wealth arises for me that is dear to the mind.
I declare to you, O monk of great power, that when I was a human being, I performed meritorious deeds.”
"Thus I am one whose majesty blazes forth, and my complexion illumines all directions.
In that context, "made of beryl" (*veḷuriyamaya*) means made of beryl-gems (*veḷuriyamaṇi*). A beryl-gem is a stone that arises not far from Mount Viḷūra and the village of Viḷūra.
It is said that its mine is located in the vicinity of the village of Viḷūra, while [the gem itself] is found near Viḷūra.

He appeared as if made of beryl. Because he possessed a complexion resembling that [color], his name in the world of the devas was likewise established, just as the names of the sons of devas in the world of the devas correspond to the names they received in the human world.
That color, moreover, is either the color of a peacock’s neck, or the color of a crow’s wing, or the color of a smooth bamboo leaf. Here...
However, its color should be understood as that of a peacock’s neck. All else is exactly as described in the first *pīṭhavimāna*.
The commentary on the second *pīṭhavimāna* is finished.
3. Commentary on the third *pīṭhavimāna*.
"The seat for you is made of gold" refers to the third celestial mansion (vimāna) with a golden seat. The origin story (*vatthu*) of this occurred in Rājagaha.

It is said that a certain elder (*thera*) whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), having wandered for alms in Rājagaha and taken his meal, approached a house with its door open as the time for eating drew near, wishing to perform his meal duties.
Now, in that house, the mistress of the home was a woman of faith.
Having observed the elder’s demeanor, she, being full of faith, said, “Come, venerable sir, sit here and perform your meal duties.
She prepared her own fine seat, spread a yellow cloth over it, and gave it away with a spirit of total detachment, making this aspiration:
“May this merit of mine lead to the acquisition of a golden throne in the future.”

Then, after the Elder had sat there, finished his meal, washed his bowl, and was rising to depart, she said, "Venerable sir, this seat has been offered exclusively to you; please use it out of favor toward me.
Out of compassion for her, the Elder accepted the bench and gave it to the Saṅgha. After some time, she...
At one time, having been afflicted by a certain illness, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
all such details are to be understood according to the method already explained in the commentary on the first *Vimāna*. Therefore it was said:
“Your magnificent golden throne, swift as thought, goes wherever you desire.”
Adorned with garlands, wearing fine clothes, you shine like lightning upon a mountain peak.
“By what means do you have such a complexion?
By what means is it fulfilled for you here? And how do those enjoyments arise that are dear to the mind?”
“I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?
That goddess, being asked by Moggallāna, was delighted.
“When asked a question, she answered: ‘Of what karma is this the fruit? [The king replied:
‘This is the fruit of a small deed of mine, by which I am thus possessed of radiant power.
In a former birth, when I was a human being among humans in the world of men—’”
“I saw a stainless monk, serene and unperturbed;
with my own hands, full of faith, I gave him a seat.
Because of that, such is my complexion; because of that, I prosper here.”
“Riches arise for me, whatever is dear to my heart.
“I declare to you, O monk of great power: when I was a human being, I performed meritorious deeds;
because of that, I possess such blazing majesty, and my complexion shines in all directions.”
19. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in a previous birth in the human world" and so forth in the fifth verse: here, the word *jāti* (birth) has several meanings.

It occurs in the sense of a conditioned characteristic (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), as in such passages as "Birth is comprised by two aggregates. It occurs in the Nikāyas in the sense of a class or type, as in "The Nigaṇṭhas are a class of recluses.
And it occurs in the sense of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), as in "the first consciousness that [arises] in the mother's womb..."
[The word *jāti*] occurs in such passages as: “The first consciousness has arisen; having that as its basis, there is his birth (*jāti*)”; it occurs in reference to a family in such passages as:

“In this family he is unassailed and unreviled by talk of birth”; it occurs in reference to descent (*pasuti*) in such passages as: “The Bodhisatta, Ānanda, was born immediately after [the conception]”;
and it occurs in reference to existence (*bhava*) in such passages as: “One birth, two births. Here too, it should be understood in the sense of existence. Therefore—
"In a previous birth" (*purimāya jātiyā*) means in a former existence, in the immediately preceding past, in a former personal identity (*attabhāva*); this is the meaning.
Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative. "In the human world" (*manussaloke*) refers to the existence in the human world; he speaks with reference to Rājagaha.
For here, the "world as space" (*okāsaloka*) is intended, whereas the "world of beings" (*sattaloka*) is already expressed by the word "among humans" (*manussesu*).
20. *Addasanti* means "I saw. *Virajanti* means "dustless" because of being free from the dust of passion and so forth. *Bhikkhunti* means "a bhikkhunī" because she has broken the defilements;
she is "serene" (*vippasanna*) due to the state of her mind being completely purified of the turbidity of defilements, and "untroubled" (*anāvila*) due to having untroubled intentions.
In this context, each preceding word is a statement of the cause for each subsequent one: because she is free from the dust of passion and so forth... [and so on].

A *bhikkhu* is so called because his defilements have been shattered (*bhinna-kilesatā*). Because his defilements have been shattered, he is serene (*vippasanna*) due to the absence of the turbidity of defilements.
He is "untroubled" (*anāvila*) because he is serene. Alternatively, each subsequent term is a statement of the cause for each preceding one:

he is "dustless" (*viraja*) because of his possession of the qualities of a *bhikkhu*. For a *bhikkhu* is one whose defilements are shattered; he is a *bhikkhu* because of his state of serenity; [he is serene] because of the absence of the turbidity of defilements.
"For a bhikkhu whose mind is serene" (*vippasannamānaso hi bhikkhu*): it is "serene" because his intention is unperturbed.

Alternatively, it is called "dustless" (*viraja*) due to the absence of the dust of lust; "serene" (*vippasanna*) due to the absence of the turbidity of hatred; and "unperturbed" (*anāvila*) due to the absence of the confusion of delusion.
One who is thus constituted is a "bhikkhu" in the ultimate sense; hence it is said, "a bhikkhu. "Adāsahan" means "I gave."
"I. "A seat" (*pīṭha*) refers to the auspicious seat (*bhaddapīṭha*) that was present near me at that time.
"With a clear mind" (*pasannā*) means with a mind clarified by faith in the fruit of karma and faith in the Triple Gem. "With her own hands" (*sehi pāṇibhī*);
the meaning is that she did not have anyone else instructed, but having brought the seat herself and arranged it, she gave it to me.
And here, by the phrase “the stainless monk, serene and untroubled,” he shows the excellence of the field;
by “serene,” the excellence of the mind; and by “with his own hands,” the excellence of the means.
Likewise, by “serene,” these two qualities of giving are shown: giving with due care and giving without causing injury; and by “with his own hands,” [the quality of personal effort is shown].
By this, it should be understood that two qualities of giving are shown: "giving with one's own hand" and "uninterrupted giving.
By the spreading out of the yellow cloth, two further qualities of giving are shown: "giving with consideration for the time of sitting" and "giving at the proper time.
The remainder is exactly as explained below.
The commentary on the Third Pīṭha-vimāna is finished.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Pīṭha-vimāna:
"Your throne is made of beryl" refers to the Fourth Pīṭha-vimāna. The story for this one also originated in Rājagaha.

This should be understood in the same manner as described in the second *vimāna*. Because she spread out a blue cloth and gave it to the seat, her *vimāna* was produced as being made of beryl (*veḷuriya*).
The rest is similar to what was stated regarding the first *vimāna*. Therefore it is said:
“Your magnificent seat is made of beryl; swift as thought, it goes wherever you desire.”
Adorned with garlands, wearing fine clothes, you shine like lightning upon a mountain peak.
“By what means do you possess such a complexion?
By what means are you successful here? And how do those riches arise for you that are dear to the mind?”
“I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: when you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?
The goddess, delighted, being questioned by Moggallāna:
“Being questioned, she answered: ‘Of what karma is this the fruit?
‘This is the fruit of a small deed of mine, by which I am thus possessed of blazing power.
In a former birth, when I was a human being among humans in the world of men—’”
“I saw a stainless monk, serene and unperturbed;
with my own hands, full of faith, I gave him a seat.
Because of that, such is my complexion; because of that, I prosper here.”
“Riches arise for me, whatever is pleasing to the mind.
“I declare to you, O monk of great power: when I was a human being, I performed meritorious deeds.
Because of that, my majesty blazes forth in this way, and my complexion shines in every direction.”
For here too, because a seat was given after being spread with a blue cloth, her celestial mansion (vimāna) was produced as being made of beryl.
For that very reason, it was stated at the beginning: "Your seat is made of beryl. The remainder is exactly like the third [mansion];
thus the meaning should be understood according to the method explained therein.
The commentary on the Fourth Pīṭha-vimāna is finished.
5. Commentary on the Kuñjara-vimāna:
"Kuñjaro te varāroho" refers to the Kuñjara-vimāna. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha.
In the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Now one day, a festival was proclaimed in the city of Rājagaha.
The citizens, having cleared the streets and strewn them with sand, scattered flowers—of which parched grain was the fifth—and placed plantain trees and full water-jars at every door;
according to their means, they decorated them with various colors and diverse hues.

They hoisted banners, flags, and the like; all the people, adorned and arrayed according to their respective means, engaged in the festival of the constellations, and the entire city became as beautifully decorated and prepared as a city of the gods.
Then, King Bimbisāra, out of his former conduct and for the sake of protecting the minds of the great multitude, from his royal palace...
Having gone out with a great retinue, with great royal majesty, and with sublime splendor and glory, he circumambulated the city.

At that time, a daughter of a noble family living in Rājagaha, having seen that perfection of wealth, splendor, and royal majesty of the king, was struck with a sense of wonder and amazement, thinking: "This perfection of wealth is like the power of a deity."
“By what kind of kamma is this obtained? she asked those esteemed as wise.
They replied to her, “Lady, meritorious kamma is like a wish-fulfilling gem and like a wishing-tree;

when there is excellence of field and excellence of intention, whatever one prays for and performs, that very thing it brings to fruition. Furthermore, by the gift of a seat, one gains birth in a high-born family.”
“Through the gift of food, one obtains an abundance of strength; through the gift of clothing, one obtains an abundance of beauty;

through the gift of a vehicle, one obtains a distinction of happiness; through the gift of a lamp, one obtains an abundance of eyesight; through the gift of a dwelling, one obtains all forms of abundance.
Having heard this, she thought, “I believe the celestial attainments are even more sublime than these,” and fixed her mind upon that goal.
She became exceedingly zealous in performing meritorious deeds.
Her parents sent her a pair of new garments, a fresh seat, a bunch of lotuses, ghee, honey, sugar, rice, and milk for her use.
Upon seeing these, she thought, "I too wish to give alms."
Thinking, "I have obtained this gift to be given," she was delighted in heart; on the following day, while preparing the alms-offering,
she prepared milk-rice with honey and little water, and having further prepared many other kinds of solid and soft foods as an accompaniment to it,
she arranged a fragrant decoration at the head of the offering and set out seats upon lotuses adorned with the filaments and pollen of blooming lotus petals.
Having prepared it, he spread a new white cloth over it, placed four lotuses and a flower bouquet upon the four legs of the seat,
tied a canopy above the seat, hung down garlands and festoons of flowers,
and covered the ground all around the seat with a carpet made of lotus petals together with their filaments.
Thinking, "I shall honor the one worthy of offerings when he arrives," she placed a basket filled with flowers in a secluded spot.

Then, having thus prepared the requisites for giving, bathed her head, dressed in clean lower garments and a pure upper robe, and waited for the auspicious moment, she gave this command to a maidservant:
"Go, girl, and search for such a person worthy of our offerings."
At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was walking through the street of Rājagaha for alms, as if setting down a thousand bags of gold.
Then that female slave, having paid homage to the Elder, said, "Venerable sir, give me your bowl.
He replied, "Come this way for the sake of favoring a certain laywoman. The Elder [went] with her.
She gave him an alms-bowl. She led the Elder into her house.
Then that woman, having gone out to meet the Elder and shown him a seat, said, "Please sit down, venerable sir;

this seat has been prepared," and when the Elder was seated there, she honored him with lotus petals still bearing their filaments, scattering them all around his seat, and [prostrated] with the five-limbed salutation.
Having paid homage, she served him with rice porridge mixed with honey and sugar, containing very little water. While serving, she made this aspiration:
"By the power of this merit of mine, may I possess celestial splendors adorned with divine elephants, gabled houses, and couches;
and in all my existences, may I never be without the lotus named Padumā. Then, to the Elder...
Having finished his meal, he washed his bowl, filled it with ghee, honey, and sugar, and made a cushion out of a cloth spread upon a couch.
Placing the bowl in the Elder’s hand and having the Elder offer a blessing of thanksgiving, as the Elder was departing, he commanded two men:
"Take this bowl and this couch to the monastery and deliver them to the Elder."
"Come," she said. They did so.
Later, having passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden celestial mansion (vimāna) one hundred yojanas in height, surrounded by a retinue of a thousand nymphs (accharā).
By virtue of her aspiration, it was five yojanas in height and adorned with garlands of lotuses.

An excellent elephant was produced, adorned on all sides by lotus petals, filaments, and stamens; it was pleasing to behold, pleasant to the touch, and resplendent with a network of rays from various jewels and decorated with golden ornaments.
Above it, there appeared a golden couch a yojana in size, endowed with the aforementioned excellence of splendor.
Experiencing that divine prosperity, she [sat] here and there upon that elephant-palace, which was variegated with jewels.
Having ascended his palanquin, he goes to the Nandana Grove by means of the great power of a deity.

Now, on a festival day, when the deities were going to the Nandana Grove for a pleasure excursion according to their respective divine majesty—this and all else is identical with what has been related in the commentary on the first *pīṭhavimāna* and should therefore be understood according to the method stated there. But here, the Elder—
“An elephant of noble gait is yours, adorned with various jewels;
beautiful, powerful, and endowed with speed, it ranges through the sky.
With eyes like lotus petals, you wear the splendor of the lotus and the blue water-lily.”
His body was strewn with lotus pollen, and he wore a garland of golden lotuses.
The elephant, standing there, lovely and enchanting, walked with measured steps along a path covered in lotuses and adorned with lotus leaves.
As he was departing, the sound of golden and bronze instruments,
resonant with delight, was heard like that of a fivefold musical ensemble.
Upon the back of that elephant, women dressed in fine garments and adorned with ornaments [followed].
“You outshine a great assembly of celestial nymphs with your radiance.
Is this the fruit of your giving, or perhaps of your virtue, or of your acts of joining your palms in reverence? Tell me this when asked. Thus he spoke.
31. In this context, "an excellent steed, a kuñjara": it delights and finds pleasure in a *kuñja*, that is, on a mountain slope;
or it roams about there, uttering its cry with a *koñca*-like sound. Alternatively, it is called a *kuñjara* because it wears down (*jarayati*) the earth (*kuṃ*) by its impact.

In the human world, elephants are divided into those that roam the mountains and so forth; however, this [horse] is described thus because, at the time of play, it resembles a *kuñjara*. It is "mounted" (*āruyhati*).
*Āroha* means that which is to be mounted. *Vara-āroha* means the excellent, foremost, or best mount; thus it is said to be "the supreme vehicle. *Nānāratana-kappaṇo*:
those who possess various kinds of jewels are "possessors of various jewels"—namely, hand-ornaments such as bracelets and other decorations for the body.

One whose armor (*kappaṇa*) or equipment is fashioned with these is "one whose armor is made of various jewels" (*nānāratana-kappaṇo*). *Ruciro*: that which gives pleasure or delight is "radiant" (*ruciro*).
"Manuñño" means pleasant. "Thāmavā" means firm; the sense is "possessing strength. "Javasampanno" means endowed with speed;
what is meant is that it possesses swift velocity. "Ākāsamhi samīhati" means it strives properly in the sky, in the atmosphere;
the sense is that it moves and travels without causing agitation to those who have mounted upon it.
