32. *Padumī*: Because her complexion is similar to that of a lotus (*paduma*), she has acquired the name "Lotus" (*paduma*); furthermore, because she possesses the color of a water-jar (*kumbha*), she is called *Padumī*.
*Padmapattakkhī*: This means "one whose eyes resemble lotus petals"; this is an address to that deity. *Padmuppalajutindharo*:

Because her body is adorned with divine garlands of lotuses and water-lilies (*uppalas*), she bears the shimmering, radiant splendor of lotuses and water-lilies (*padmuppalajuti*) flashing here and there.
"He wears" means he wears the splendor of lotuses and water-lilies (*padumuppalajutindharo*).
"His limbs are strewn with lotus pollen" means his body is covered on all sides by lotus petals, filaments, and stamens.
"Wearing a garland of golden lotuses" means he bears a wreath made of gold lotuses. "The path followed by lotuses, adorned with lotus petals" refers to the elephant's footprint after every step.

The construction is as follows: he walks upon a path that is traversed and strewn with great lotuses supporting his feet, and which is especially adorned by their petals of various variegated colors moving here and there.
The word "standing" (*ṭhita*) is an adjective qualifying the path; [it means] being adorned by lotus petals.
The meaning is: "the path is established. *Vaggu* means beautiful; this is an adverbial modifier (*kiriyāvisesana*), and the letter *m* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*).
*Anugghātī* means not shaking; the meaning is that it does not cause even the slightest agitation in those seated upon it.
*Mitaṃ* means measured; the meaning is that they transgress the limit of what has been set down. This is the meaning here: "beautiful and lovely..."
"Having placed down his foot, he goes. "Measured" (*mita*) means limited or proportionate; it is said to be neither too fast nor too slow.
"Elephant" (*vāraṇa*) refers to a tusker. For he is called "elephant" because he wards off enemies and because he wards off the defilements of travel.

34. As he was departing, "golden bells with delightful sounds" means that as that aforementioned elephant was walking, golden bells made of gold—possessing delightful sounds and charming resonance—were hanging down;
for on both sides of that elephant, there were [bells] the size of large jars, inlaid with gems, pearls, and other such materials.
Hundreds of large golden bells, hanging here and there, sway to and fro;
from them, an exceedingly captivating sound issues forth, played by a skilled musician. Therefore he said: "Their sound is heard, like that of the fivefold musical ensemble.
The meaning of this is: just as, for example, [the sound] of a stretched [string], a loose [string], and a string both stretched and loose...
Just as when a five-fold musical ensemble is played by skilled musicians—
who demonstrate the distinction between soft and loud tones according to the occasion— the sound of the instruments, being melodious and enchanting, is heard;
even so is the sound of those golden bronze [vessels] and refined-bell-metal bells heard.
35. *Nāgassa* means of an elephant-king (*hatthināga*). *Mahantaṃ* means great both by way of the greatness of its excellence and by way of the greatness of its number.

*Accharāsaṅghaṃ* means a multitude of celestial maidens. *Vaṇṇena* means by way of form. 36. *Dānassa* means of merit consisting of giving. *Sīlassa* means of the virtue of restraint, such as bodily restraint and so forth. The word *vā* has the sense of including what has not been mentioned; by it, it includes the unmentioned virtue of conduct, such as respectful salutation and the like.
Thus, having been questioned by the Elder, that deity answered the question. To show this matter:
“The deity, being delighted when questioned by Moggallāna, answered the question asked, [explaining] the fruit of which kamma this is.
This verse was spoken by the compilers of the Dhamma; its meaning has already been explained above.
Having seen one endowed with virtues, meditative, delighting in *jhāna*, and mindful,
I gave him a seat strewn with flowers and covered with cloth.
Around half of that seat, I placed a garland of lotuses.
With palms full of lotus petals, I scattered them over him with my own hands out of faith:
"Such is the fruit for me of that skillful deed—
this honor and respect, for I am one who honors the devas."
“Whoever, with confidence, should give a seat to those who are rightly liberated, peaceful, and living the holy life— may that person rejoice just as I do.
Therefore, one who desires their own welfare and longs for greatness [should act accordingly].”
"A seat should be given to the bearer of the final body"—this is the verse spoken by the deity. 38.
Therein, "endowed with virtues" means possessed of all the qualities of a disciple, or fulfilled by them.

By this, he shows the attainment of the pinnacle of the disciple's knowledge of the perfections (*pāramiñāṇa*). "Meditating" refers to meditation upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and meditation upon characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*).

One whose nature is to meditate by means of both kinds of *jhāna*, or who stands having burned away the entire side of defilements that are to be burned by it—precisely for that reason, one who delights in *jhāna* is "one who delights in *jhāna*" (*jhānarata*). "Sata" means equal or peaceful;
the meaning is "a true person" (*sappurisa*). "Strewn with flowers" (*pupphābhikiṇṇa*) means covered with flowers; the meaning is "completely strewn with lotus petals."
“Dussasaññatam” means spread over with cloth.
“Upaḍḍhaṃ padumamālāham” means half a lotus garland; that is, half a lotus flower.
“Āsanassa samantato” means on the ground all around the seat where the Elder was sitting. “Abbhokirissanti” means I scattered over, I strewn over. How? [As follows:]
“With petals” means that they sprinkle [him] with the individual petals of that half-lotus, according to the manner of raining down a shower of flowers; this is the sense.

With the words “Such is my fruit,” the Elder has shown together his own divine prosperity—comprising longevity, vitality, happiness, beauty, and so forth—both what was explicitly mentioned by him, such as “the noble elephant with its excellent stride,” and what was not explicitly mentioned; furthermore, he shows even that which was not mentioned by the Elder.
In order to demonstrate the excellence of his own majesty, he said, “Honoring, veneration,” and so forth. By this, he shows:
“Venerable sir, it is not only the fruit of my merit as previously described that exists here for me, but furthermore, there is also this divine sovereignty.
In this context, “honoring” (sakkāra) means the act of showing respect; the sense is that he is to be honored by the devas. Likewise...
"Respects" means that which is worthy of being respected. "By the gods" means by the deities. "Honored" means worshipped.

"Of those who are rightly liberated" means of those who are well-liberated, having abandoned all defilements. "Of the peaceful" means of the virtuous ones whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are tranquil.
"Of the practitioners of the holy life" means of those who have practiced both the holy life of the Path and the holy life of the Teaching.
"Being confident, one should give a seat": having become confident in mind through faith in the fruits of action and faith in the Triple Gem, if one were to give even a mere seat;
"so that I rejoice, Nandā, as I do"—just as I now rejoice and exult because of that gift of a seat, so too would another rejoice and exult.
42. *Tasmā* means for that reason. The word *hi* is a mere particle. *Attakāmena* means by one who desires his own welfare.
For he who performs an action that brings about his own benefit, and not what brings harm, is one who desires his own welfare (*attakāma*).

*Mahattaṃ* means the greatness of the result (*vipāka*). *Sarīrantimadhārinaṃ* means those who bear their final body; the meaning is "those whose taints are exhausted" (*khīṇāsava*). This, then, is the [meaning] here.

The meaning is this: because I myself rejoice in such celestial prosperity through the gift of a seat to the Arahants, therefore, anyone else who desires their own advancement should also give a seat to those standing in their final existence;
there is no merit equal to this—thus he shows. "For them, it is exactly as described."
The commentary on the Kuñjaravimāna is finished.
6. Commentary on the First Boat-Vimāna:
"A boat with a golden canopy" refers to a boat-vimāna. How did it originate? While the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī...
Sixteen monks, having spent the rains retreat dwelling at a certain village monastery,
set out on the road during the summer season toward Sāvatthī with the intention of seeing the Blessed One and hearing the Dhamma.
On the way, there was a waterless wilderness, and being scorched by the heat, exhausted, and parched, they found no water to drink.
They were traveling not far from a certain village. There, a certain woman, having taken a water vessel, was walking toward a well for the sake of water.
Then those bhikkhus, seeing her and thinking, "If we go where this woman is going, we will be able to obtain drinking water," being overcome by thirst, set out in that direction.
Having seen a well, they stood not far from it. That woman, having taken water from there and wishing to turn back, saw those bhikkhus;
perceiving that "these venerable ones are in need of water and are thirsty," she established a heart of deep respect and invited them with water.
They took out the water-strainer from their bowl-bags, strained the water, and [drank] as much as they required.
Having drunk the water and cooled their hands and feet, they departed after expressing words of appreciation for the woman’s gift of water.
She, keeping that merit in her heart and recollecting it from time to time, passed away at a later date and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
By the power of that merit, a great celestial mansion appeared for her, adorned with a wish-fulfilling tree (kapparukkha). It...
Surrounding the celestial palace was a river whose banks were like white sandbanks strewn with grit, adorned as if with nets of pearls and silver;

it carried waters as pure as a mass of jewels. On both its banks, at the gates of the pleasure gardens and the celestial palace, there appeared a great lotus pond, adorned with clusters of five-colored lotuses, together with a golden boat. There, she—
Experiencing divine prosperity, she wandered about playing and sporting on a boat.
Then one day, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was wandering on a tour of the devas, he saw that goddess playing on the boat and, asking her about the meritorious deed she had performed, said:
"O woman, you stand having boarded a boat with a golden canopy; ... [the verse continues]"
“You plunge into the lotus pond and pluck a lotus with your hand.
By what means is your complexion so radiant? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those enjoyments arise for you that are dear to the mind?”
“I ask you, O goddess of great majesty:
what merit did you perform while you were a human being?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing power?”
"And your radiance illuminates all directions," he said.
Then, in order to show the manner in which the deity answered when questioned by the Elder, the compilers of the collection [recorded]:
"That deity, being delighted, was questioned by Moggallāna."
“When asked a question, she answered: ‘Of what karma is this the fruit?’—this verse was spoken.
‘In my previous birth, when I was among humans in the human world;’”
Seeing the monks thirsty and exhausted, I rose and gave them water to drink:
“Whoever rises and gives water to drink to those who are weary and thirsty,
for him there shall be rivers of cool water, abundant with lotuses and many white lilies.”
“Rivers always flow around it— rivers with cool waters and beds of sand—
and mangoes, sal trees, tilakas, rose-apples, uddālakas, and trumpet-flowers are in full bloom.
That most excellent celestial mansion shines intensely, endowed with the beauty of its various grounds.”
This is the ripening of that very action here: those who have performed merit obtain such as this.
"Because of that, I possess such beauty; because of that, I am successful here;
and whatever wealth arises for me, it is all dear to my heart."
“I declare to you, O monk of great power, that while I was a human being, I performed meritorious deeds; because of that,
my majesty blazes forth in this way, and my radiance illuminates all directions.”—
This is the manner of the deity’s reply.

43. In this context, "gold-canopied" (*suvaṇṇacchadana*) refers to that which has its interior concealed by both sides being covered with variegated wall-paintings made of red gold, and which is further covered above by golden ornaments resplendent with various gems.
"Ship" (*nāvā*) means a vessel; for it moves, travels from this shore to the further shore.
A boat is called a *nāvā* because it carries beings across. *Nārī* is an address for that daughter of the gods.

A man (*nara*) is so called because he leads (*narati*, *neti*). For just as a being who has become the primary nature (*pakati*) is called a "man" (*purisa*) because he lies in front (*puri seti*) in the sense of being superior to other natures, so too he is called a "man" (*nara*) in the sense of leading. For even a person who has become a son or a brother...
She stands in the place of a father to her mother’s elder sisters, let alone to her husband. She belongs to a man (*nara*), hence she is called a *nārī*;
this conventional designation, which applies primarily to human women, is extended by way of metaphorical usage (*ruḷhivasena*) to others as well.

"You plunge into the lotus pond" (*ogāhasi pokkharaṇim*): although there are many kinds of jewel-like water-born flowers, such as red and blue lotuses, [the term] refers to those designated as *pokkhara*.

Because celestial lotuses (*dibbapaduma*) were present there in abundance, you entered that divine lake—which had received the name "Pokkharanī" (Lotus Pond)—for the pleasure of sporting in the water.

"You pluck a lotus with your hand": out of a desire to make a playful lotus, you break with your hand a celestial *kamala*, which has a silver stalk, is composed of petals made of ruby (*padumarāga*), and possesses a pericarp and filaments made of gold.

47. "Thirsty" (*tasita*) means parched with thirst. "Exhausted" (*kilanta*) means one whose body is worn out by that thirst and by the fatigue of traveling the road. "Having risen up" (*uṭṭhāya*) means having exerted the energy of effort; the meaning is, without falling into indolence. 48.

By the words beginning with "Or whoever," the Elder demonstrates the method of inference for what has not been seen based on what has been seen—namely, that just as I have, so too others obtain such a fruit through the merit of giving water at a watering place. This explains the matter asked about by the Elder.
He answers in a general sense. Therein, the word "his" refers to those who have performed the aforementioned meritorious deeds.
49. "Anupariyanti" means they surround it in a fitting manner.
By surrounding his dwelling place, he too is said to be surrounded. "Tilaka" is a species of tree with flowers resembling the *bandhujīvaka* flower.
*Uddālaka* trees are wind-destroyers; they are also called "royal trees. 50. *Taṃbhūmibhāgehi*:
by means of such portions of land; the meaning is: by those regions of earth possessing the aforementioned lotus ponds, rivers, and groves.
*Upetarūpaṃ*: endowed with a state that is praiseworthy, namely, those lotus ponds and so forth.
"By way of [that], it is said to be 'a delightful settlement. The construction is: 'They obtain a most excellent mansion that shines intensely, that is, that radiates exceedingly.
"The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the first ship-mansion is finished.
7. Commentary on the Second Ship Mansion (*Nāvāvimāna*).
"A ship with a golden canopy"—this is the second ship mansion. How did it originate?

While the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a certain elder whose taints were destroyed, as the time for entering the rains retreat drew near, [decided] to spend the rains retreat in a village monastery.
Desiring to go to that village from Sāvatthī, he set out on the highway after his meal;
exhausted by the fatigue of the road and parched with thirst, he arrived at a certain village along the way.
Not seeing any place endowed with shade and water outside the village, and being overcome by exhaustion, he put on his robe, entered the village, and went straight to the house of the headman.
He stood at the gate. There, a certain woman, seeing the elder, asked, "Venerable sir, from where have you come?
Having perceived his fatigue from the journey and his thirst, she said, "Come, venerable sir," and led him into her house.
She prepared a seat, saying, "Sit here," and offered it to him. While he was seated there, she provided water for washing the feet and oil for anointing the feet.
Having given it, she took a palm-leaf fan and fanned him. When the fever had subsided, she prepared and gave him a sweet, cool, and fragrant drink.
The Elder, having drunk it, his fatigue allayed, offered words of thanksgiving and departed.
Later, when she passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; all of this is similar to the account in the immediately preceding *Vimānavatthu*.
This should be understood. There is nothing new even in the verses. Therefore it was said:
“O woman, having boarded a boat with a golden canopy, you stand there;
you plunge into the lotus pond and pluck a lotus flower with your hand.”
“By what means is your complexion so radiant? By what means do you prosper here?
And from where do those riches arise that are dear to your heart?
I ask you, O lady of great majesty: while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?”
“By what means have you become so radiant in majesty, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?
The deity, being delighted and questioned by Moggallāna,
answered the question asked, [explaining] the fruit of that deed.
“In a former birth, while among humans in the human world, I saw a bhikkhu who was thirsty and exhausted. Rising up, I gave him water to drink.
Indeed, whoever gives water to one who is exhausted and thirsty after rising to drink it—”
There are rivers for him with cool water, abundant with flowers and many white lotuses.
Rivers with cool water and beds of sand flow around it at all times;
there are mango trees, *sāla* trees, *tilaka* trees, rose-apple trees, *uddālaka* trees, and *pāṭalī* trees in full bloom.
“Endowed with the splendors of that very realm, this most excellent celestial mansion shines forth intensely.
This is the ripening of that karma here; those who have performed meritorious deeds obtain such a result as this.
By that [karma] my complexion is thus, and by that I am gratified here.”
“Riches arise for me, whatever is pleasing to my mind.
“I declare to you, O monk of great power: when I was a human being, I performed meritorious deeds.
Because of that, I am thus blazing with majesty, and my complexion shines forth in all directions.”
In the commentaries (*atthavaṇṇanā*) as well, there is nothing new here in that "only one elder" [is mentioned].
The commentary on the second ship-vimāna is finished.
8. Commentary on the third ship-vimāna.
The third ship-palace is the *Suvaṇṇacchadana-nāvā*. What is its origin?
While the Blessed One was wandering on a tour of the countryside together with a great saṅgha of bhikkhus, he arrived at a brahmin village named Thūṇa in the Kosala country.
The brahmin householders of Thūṇa heard: "It is said that the ascetic Gotama has come to us..."
“has arrived at the village field. Then the brahmin householders of Thūṇā—lacking faith, holding wrong views, and being stingy by nature—thought:
“If the ascetic Gotama enters this village and stays for two or three days, he will establish all these people in his own teaching;
consequently, the dharma of the brahmins will lose its standing.”
There, seeking to prevent the Blessed One from staying, they removed the boats placed at the river fords, and they blocked the bridges and causeways;
likewise, they did the same with the pavilions at the waterfalls and other such places.
With the exception of one well, they filled all the other wells with grass and other debris and covered them over. Thus it is said in the Udāna: "Then the brahmin householders of Thūṇa..."
They filled the well with grass and chaff up to its brim, thinking, "Lest those shaveling ascetics drink the water.
The Blessed One, perceiving their misconduct and feeling compassion for them, went through the air together with the community of monks, crossing over the river.
Proceeding by stages, he reached the brahmin village of Thūṇa, and descending from the road, he stopped at a certain spot.
He sat down on the seat prepared at the foot of a tree. At that time, many women carrying water were passing by not far from the Blessed One.

In that village, a pact had been made: "If the ascetic Gotama comes here, we must not go out to meet him or perform such honors; nor should alms be given to him or his disciples when they come to our homes."
There, a certain brahmin’s female slave, while carrying water in a jar, saw the Blessed One seated surrounded by the community of monks;

perceiving that the monks were weary from the fatigue of the road and thirsty, her heart was filled with faith and she desired to give them water, thinking: "Even though the village-dwellers [say] of the ascetic Gotama..."
They stood there having made an agreement, saying, "Nothing at all should be given, nor should even the customary respectful greeting be performed.

Even so, if I, having obtained such a field of merit and one worthy of offerings, were not to establish my own footing by giving even as much as a drink of water, when would I ever be released from this miserable life?
Granted, my grandfather [may have been right], yet so too are all these village dwellers.
"Let them kill me or bind me; I shall give a gift of drinking water at such a field of merit," she resolved.

Although restrained by other water-carriers, being indifferent to her own life, she lowered the water-jar from her head, held it with both hands, set it aside in a secluded spot, and, filled with joy and gladness, approached the Blessed One.

Having prostrated with the fivefold contact, she invited him to drink water. The Blessed One, observing her clarity of mind and wishing to favor her, strained the water, washed his hands and feet, and drank;
yet the water in the jar did not reach exhaustion. Seeing this, her heart became even more confident, and she gave it to a certain bhikkhu.
In this way, she gave to one person after another until she had given to everyone, yet the water did not diminish at all.
Joyful and elated, she went toward her home with the jar as full as before.

When her husband, the brahmin, heard that she had given away the drinking water, he thought, "She has broken the village custom, and I have been brought into disrepute. Blazing with anger and seething with rage, he—
Having thrown her onto the ground, he struck her with his hands and feet. By that assault, she met her end and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
a celestial mansion appeared for her, exactly as described for the first ship-mansion.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Come now, Ānanda, fetch some water from the well."
“Bring it,” [the Blessed One said]. The Elder replied, “Venerable Sir, the well has now been fouled by the Thūṇeyyakas; it is not possible to bring drinking water.
The Blessed One commanded him a second and a third time. On the third occasion, the Elder took the Blessed One’s bowl and went toward the well.
As the Elder was walking, the water in the well became full, and having stepped out [of the well], he—
It flows out on all sides; having washed away all the grass and chaff, it recedes of its own accord.
As that flowing water increases further and further, filling other reservoirs and surrounding the village, the area of the village is overwhelmed.
Having seen that miracle, the brahmins were struck with a sense of wonder and amazement, and [approached] the Blessed One.
They asked for forgiveness, and at that very moment the flood of water disappeared.
Having provided a dwelling place for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and invited them for the following day, they prepared a great almsgiving on the second day.
They served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by the Buddha, with excellent hard and soft foods, and then [honored] all...
When the Blessed One had finished his meal and withdrawn his hand from the bowl, the brahmin householders of Thūṇeyya sat down in attendance upon him.
At that time, a certain deity, reflecting upon her own prosperity and investigating its cause, realized it was due to that "gift of water.
Filled with joy and gladness, she thought: "Come now, I shall pay homage to the Blessed One this very moment."
Thinking, “I shall make manifest in the world of men how even small services rendered to those who have entered the right path yield magnificent fruits,” she became filled with zeal;
surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs and accompanied by her palace complete with gardens and other delights,
she arrived with great divine splendor and vast celestial power while the great multitude of people looked on.
Descending from her celestial palace, she approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood with palms joined in reverence.
Then the Blessed One, desiring to make the fruit of karma manifest before that assembly, said:
“O woman, you stand having boarded a ship with a golden canopy.”
"You plunge into the lotus pond and pluck a lotus with your hand.
Your gabled mansions as dwellings are well-proportioned and measured out in divisions;
they shine brilliantly, resplendent in all four directions."
“By what means is your complexion such as this? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those enjoyments arise for you, whatever is dear to the mind?
I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: when you were a human being, what merit did you perform?”
“By what means have you become so radiant in power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?”—
thus he asked with these four verses.
That deity, being highly pleased, was questioned by the Fully Awakened One himself.
“When asked a question, she explained: ‘Of what karma is this the fruit?’—thus said the compilers of the collection.
‘I, having been a human among humans, in a previous birth in the world of men;’”
Seeing the monks thirsty and exhausted, I rose and gave them water to drink:
“Whoever rises and gives water to drink to those who are weary and thirsty,
for him there shall be rivers of cool water, abundant with lotuses and many white lilies.”
“Rivers always flow around it—rivers with cool waters and beds of sand.
Mangoes, *sāla* trees, *tilaka*, rose-apples, *uddālaka*, and *pāṭali* trees are all in full bloom.
That most excellent celestial mansion shines brilliantly, endowed with various sections of land.”
This is the ripening of that karma here: those who have performed such merit obtain this.
"My gabled mansions are my dwellings, divided and measured out in parts;
they shine brilliantly, resplendent in all four directions."
“Because of that my complexion is such as this; because of that I prosper here;
and whatever wealth is dear to the mind, that my enjoyments fulfill.
“I declare to you, O Buddha of great power: when I was a human being, I performed meritorious deeds.”
“Thus was my power so blazing that my complexion shone forth in all directions;
this is the fruit of that deed of mine: for my sake, the Buddha drank the water.
— These are the verses of response.

63. In this regard, although that deity was not actually standing on the boat when the Blessed One questioned her, nor was she plunging into the lotus pond, nor cutting the lotus—at that time—nevertheless, because she was impelled by the power of her karma and was constantly intent on dwelling in the water, she would act in such a way;
thus, it was stated in this manner by way of showing the interruption of that activity. And this meaning applies not only here.
Now, it should be understood in the same way for those below as well.
72. *Kūṭāgārā* means houses provided with golden pinnacle-roofed gables; *nivesā* means dwellings, that is to say, residences.
Therefore he said, "divided and measured out by parts. For they consist of four courtyards and are like reflections of one another.
The forms are as if individually distinguished; by virtue of their equal proportions, they are as if measured out part by part.
*Daddallamānā* means shining exceedingly brightly. *Ābhanti* means they illuminate with the nets of rays from jewel-gems and gold.
(74) *Mama* refers to what precedes and follows it; the construction here is: "of my karma" and "for my sake."
"He drank the water" refers to this gift of water that was mentioned;

this is the fruit of that meritorious deed, namely this divine success, because for my sake the Buddha, the Blessed One—the supreme recipient of offerings in the world with its devas—drank the water given by me.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
To the deity whose mind was thus serene, the Blessed One, delivering a Dhamma teaching that exalts the supreme goal, proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of that teaching, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and the Dhamma instruction was likewise fruitful for the assembled company.
The commentary on the third Vimāna of the Ship is finished.
9. The Exposition of the Lamp Mansion (*Dīpavimānavanṇanā*).
"With surpassing beauty" refers to the Lamp Mansion. How did it originate?
While the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, on an Uposatha day, a great number of lay followers, having observed the Uposatha, gave gifts according to their means before the meal.

Having given [the offerings] and eaten at the proper time, dressed in clean lower garments and upper robes, with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, they go to the monastery after the meal.
Having paid homage to the venerable monks, they listen to the Dhamma in the evening.
For those who wish to stay right there in the monastery, the sun sets while they are still listening to the Dhamma.

It became dark. Then, a certain woman there thought, "Now it is fitting to provide the light of a lamp," and having had a lamp brought from her own house and lit it, she placed it before the Dharma seat and listened to the Dharma.
Delighted by that gift of a lamp, filled with joy and gladness, she paid homage and [departed] from her own...
She went home. Later, having passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in the Jotirasa-vimāna.
Her bodily splendor was exceedingly radiant; surpassing other deities, it remained illuminating the ten directions.
Then one day, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was wandering on a tour of the heavens—all as related by the method already explained below—
It should be understood as follows: "O goddess, with your exquisite beauty,
you stand there illuminating all directions like a medicinal herb among the stars."
“By what means is your complexion such as this? By what means do you prosper here?
And from whence arise those riches that are dear to the mind?
By what means, O deity of stainless radiance, do you outshine all others?”
“By what means do all your limbs illuminate every direction?
I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: while still a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means do you possess such blazing majesty, and why does your beauty shine forth in every direction?”
She questioned him with four verses.
That deity, being asked by Moggallāna, was delighted;
having been questioned, she answered the question concerning the fruit of that karma.
“In a former birth, when I was among humans in the human world,
in that darkness within the depths of the ocean, I gave a lamp at the time when a lamp was needed.
Whoever gives a lamp at the time when a lamp is needed in the darkness within the depths of the ocean— ”
A celestial mansion of radiant essence arises, abundant with garlands and many white lotuses.
"Because of that, my complexion is such as this; because of that, I am honored here;
and whatever riches are dear to my heart arise for me."
“Because of that, O deity of stainless radiance, I outshine you;
therefore, with all my limbs, I illuminate all directions.
I tell you, O monk of great power, when I was a human being, I performed a twin act of merit.”
“Thus I am one whose majesty blazes forth, and my complexion illuminates all directions,” she replied.
(75) Therein, regarding the phrase “with a surpassing complexion,” the word *abhikkanta* means: “The night has passed, venerable sir.”

In such passages as "the first watch has passed," it occurs in the sense of passing away (*khaya*). In such passages as "this one is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons," it means beautiful (*sundara*).
In such passages as "Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante! it means expressing approval (*abbhanumodana*).
In such passages as "With your excellent complexion, you illuminate all directions," it means handsome (*abhirūpa*). Here, too, [it is used in this sense].
He should be seen as truly beautiful. Therefore, "abhikkanta" means exceedingly lovely, extremely pleasing;
the meaning is "beautiful. "By complexion" means by the color of the skin. "Illuminating all directions" means making all ten directions radiant, making them one single light.
To the question "Like what?", he said: "Like a medicinal herb-star. By this [light], the accumulated radiance is sustained; it is the "osadhi" (herb) of lights.
Or, considering her as one who provides support, she is known by the name "Osadhī" (the Herb);
just as a star stands illuminating the surroundings on all sides, even so do you stand illuminating all directions. 77.
"With all limbs" means with all parts of the body; the intended meaning is that she shines with every major and minor limb.
In this context, the word is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). “All directions shine forth” means that all ten directions are illuminated.
Some read it as “obhāsare”; for them, “all directions” should be understood as being in the plural.
81. “At the time of lighting a lamp” means at the time of making a lamp; the meaning is: in the darkness suitable for the kindling of a lamp. Therefore he said:
“*Yo andhakāramhi timīsikāyan*”: the meaning is “in thick, great darkness. “He gives light” means that by lighting a lamp or even by not letting it go out, he gives the gift of a lamp;
he relinquishes the requisites for a lamp, dedicating them to those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
“He is reborn in a celestial mansion of radiant essence” means that by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), he is reborn in a celestial mansion of radiant essence.
"He approaches. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Then, when the deity had explained the matter as she was asked, the Elder took that very account as the occasion for his discourse;
having understood her state of mind through her talk on giving and so forth, he proclaimed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, together with her retinue...
That deity was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*). The Elder returned from there and reported the matter to the Blessed One.
On that occasion, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled multitude.
That teaching became beneficial to the great masses, and the people became especially diligent in the offering of lamps.
The commentary on the Dīpa-vimāna is finished.
10. The commentary on the Tiladakkhiṇa-vimāna:
"With most excellent beauty... This is the Tiladakkhiṇa-vimāna. What is its origin? The Blessed One was at Sāvatthī.
He was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
At that time, in Rājagaha, a certain pregnant woman, having washed some sesame seeds, was drying them in the sun, desiring to make oil. Her life span had been exhausted;
she was destined to pass away on that very day. Furthermore, a deed of hers conducive to rebirth in hell had found its opportunity and stood ready. Then—
At dawn, as the Blessed One surveyed the world with his divine eye, he saw her and thought:
"This woman, having died today, will be reborn in hell; what if I were to cause her to attain heaven by accepting this offering of sesame seeds?
Thereupon, he went from Sāvatthī to Rājagaha at that very moment, and having dressed in the morning, he—
Taking his bowl and robe, while wandering for alms in Rājagaha, he eventually arrived at the door of her house.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, that woman was filled with joy and gladness;
she rose up suddenly, joined her palms in reverence, and finding nothing else suitable to give, washed her hands and feet, made a heap of sesame seeds, and grasped it with both hands.
Having poured a handful of sesame seeds from her cupped hands into the Blessed One’s bowl, she paid homage to the Blessed One.

Out of compassion for her, the Blessed One said, “May you be happy,” and departed. At the break of dawn that very night, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden celestial palace twelve yojanas in size, appearing like one who has just awakened from sleep.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while wandering on a tour of the celestial realms, approached that [deity] who was surrounded by a thousand nymphs and shining with great divine splendor,
and said: “O deity, you who stand there with such exquisite beauty,
illuminating all directions like the star Osadhi.”
“By what means do you have such a complexion? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those enjoyments arise for you that are dear to the mind?
I ask you, O goddess of great majesty.”
"What merit did you perform while being a human being?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?"— thus he asked.
“Delighted, that deity, when questioned by Moggallāna,
answered the question asked, which was the fruit of such karma:
‘In my previous birth, I was a human being among humans in the world of men.’”
“I saw the stainless Buddha, serene and untroubled;
having approached him, I gave a gift—a handful of sesame seeds—though unwillingly.
With my own hands, full of faith, I offered this to the Buddha, the one worthy of offerings.”
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this; because of that, I prosper here;
and whatever riches are dear to my heart arise for me.
“I declare to you, O monk of great power, that when I was a human being, I performed meritorious deeds.”
"Thus I possess such blazing majesty, and my complexion shines in all directions"—thus she replied. 90.
Regarding that, the word *āsajja* occurs here in the sense of "striking," as in such passages as "having struck the Tathāgata."
In such passages as “gives a gift having encountered [someone],” it refers to a meeting; here too, it should be understood as occurring only at a meeting.
Therefore, “āsajja” means having come together, having arrived by way of a gathering. Thus he said, “unwillingly.

For she spoke with reference to the sesame seed gift which was offered suddenly when the Blessed One had arrived, without the prior intention to give that had been established earlier through the preparation of the items to be given.
“I gave a gift by force; unwillingly was the sesame-offering. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Tiladakkhiṇa-vimāna* is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Paṭhamapatibbata-vimāna*.
The *Patibbatā-vimāna*: "The curlews, peacocks, and celestial swans. What is its origin?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There, a certain woman was devoted to her husband;
she conducted herself in accordance with his wishes, was patient, and accepted things gracefully. Even when provoked to anger, she did not resist; she spoke gently and was truthful in speech.
With faith and confidence, she gave gifts according to her means.
Stricken by a certain illness, she passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wandering on his tour of the devas as before, saw that goddess enjoying great prosperity and approached her.

Surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, her person adorned with ornaments weighing sixty cartloads, she bowed her head at the feet of the Elder and stood to one side. The Elder, inquiring about the meritorious deeds she had performed, said:
“Cranes, peacocks, and celestial swans, And cuckoos with melodious voices fly together;”
"This delightful celestial mansion is strewn with flowers, variegated and frequented by men and women.
You dwell there, O goddess of great majesty, manifesting manifold supernatural powers in various forms;
and these nymphs all around you dance, sing, and bring you joy."
“You have attained divine power, O lady of great majesty;
while still a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing splendor?”
"And your complexion shines in all directions," he said.
"That deity, being asked by Moggallāna, was delighted;
having been questioned, she answered the question concerning the fruit of that karma."
“Among humans, having become a human being, I was devoted and not unkind to my husband;
like a mother protecting her son, even when angry, I did not speak harshly.
Established in truth, having abandoned the fault of lying, I delighted in giving and maintained my own character.”
With a mind full of faith, I gave abundant gifts of food and drink with due respect.
"Because of that, such is my complexion; because of that, I prosper here;
and whatever riches arise that are dear to my heart, they come to me."
“I declare to you, O monk of great power, that when I was a human being I performed meritorious deeds;
because of that, my majesty blazes forth in this way, and my radiance shines in all directions.
Thus did that deity reply.
93. Therein, *koñca* refers to the *koñca* birds, which are also called *sārasa*. *Mayūra* means peacocks. *Diviya* means possessing divine power.
Indeed, this term should be connected with all four words as in the phrase: "divine *koñca*s, divine peacocks," and so forth.
*Haṃsa* refers to swans such as the golden swan and others. *Vaggussara* means those with sweet voices. *Kokila* refers to both black cuckoos and...
And white cuckoos. "Flying about" means that they fly and wander all around, sporting and playing for the sake of the deity's delight.
For deities who serve as a retinue, sporting and playing for the sake of generating pleasure in the deity by assuming the forms of cranes and so forth, are described by such terms as "cranes.
"Strewn with flowers" means [strewn] with various kinds of jewel-like blossoms, both woven and unwoven.

*Okiṇṇaṃ*: "Delightful" (*ramma*) means beautiful; the sense is that it is pleasing to the mind. "Variegated" (*anekacitta*) means variegated by many things such as pleasure groves, wish-fulfilling trees, lotus ponds, and so forth, as well as by various types of walls and other features within the celestial mansions.
"Frequented by men and women" (*naranārisevita*) means attended by the sons of gods and daughters of gods who serve as their retinue.

94. “*Iddhī vikubbanti anekarūpā*”: the construction is that you remain performing various transformations through the manifestation of manifold forms—transformations accomplished by the power of karma, exercising the supernormal powers of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*).
97. “*Añaññamanā*”: she whose mind (*mano*) has fallen toward another is *aññamanā*;
one who is not so is *anaññamanā*. The meaning is: “She does not give rise to an evil thought toward any man other than my husband.”
“Like a mother protecting her son”: just as a mother [protects] her son, so too did I protect my husband;
or rather, out of a desire for the welfare of all beings and a wish to remove what is harmful, I felt compassion for them. “Even when angry, I did not speak harshly”:
even though I was angry on account of some discomfort caused by another, I did not utter a harsh word; on the contrary—
The intended meaning is that they speak only pleasant words. 98.

"Established in truth" means firmly grounded in truth. Since one is said to be established in truth by virtue of abstaining from false speech, and not merely by the utterance of truthful words at any time, he says: "Having abandoned the fault of lying," that is, having abandoned false speech.
"Delighting in giving" means being devoted to giving; the sense is that they were thoroughly engaged in it.
"Having their own persons gathered" means they were by their very nature inclined to gather others to themselves through the bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), as if gathering themselves.
With hearts clear through faith in the fruit of kamma, they gave food and drink with due care and respect, and they also gave other gifts such as clothing, vast and sublime.
The construction [of the commentary] is as follows. The remainder is exactly according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the *Patibbatā-vimāna* is finished.
12. Commentary on the Second *Patibbatā-vimāna*.
The *Veḷuriyathambha* (Jewel-Pillar) is the second Mansion of the Faithful Wife. How did it originate?
It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain female lay follower was a devoted wife; with faith and confidence, she maintained the five precepts in perfect purity and gave gifts according to her means.
Having passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The rest is exactly as described below.
“Having ascended a celestial mansion made of lustrous, radiant beryl, adorned with many colors,
you dwell there, O goddess of great power, manifesting various supernatural feats.
And these nymphs all around you dance, sing, and bring you joy.”
“O lady of great majesty, you have attained divine power;
while still a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing splendor?”
"And your radiance shines in all directions," he asked.
The deity, being pleased and questioned by Moggallāna, answered the question when asked: "This is the fruit of that karma."
“Among humans, having become human myself, I was a female lay disciple of the One with Vision;
I abstained from taking life and avoided what is not given in the world.
I did not drink intoxicants nor did I speak falsehoods; I was content with my own husband.”
With a mind full of faith, I gave abundant gifts of food and drink with due respect.
"Because of that, my complexion is such as this; because of that, it shines here for me;
and whatever wealth arises that is dear to my heart, it comes to me."
“I declare to you, O monk of great power,
that when I was a human being, I performed meritorious deeds; because of that,
I am thus possessed of such blazing majesty.”
"And my radiance shines in all directions"—thus he replied. 101.
Therein, "veḷuriyathambha" means a pillar made of beryl gems. "Rucira" means delightful. "Pabhassara" means exceedingly brilliant. "Uccāvacā" means high and low; the meaning is "various. 104–5.
"Upāsikā" refers to one who stands in the characteristics of a female lay follower by virtue of having gone for refuge. For it is said:

“Mahānāma, when a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, to this extent, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is a lay follower.
The phrase “of the One with Vision” refers to the Buddha, the Blessed One, who possesses vision by means of the five kinds of vision.

Having thus shown the purity of intention (āsayasuddhi) by describing the state of a lay female follower (upāsikā), the text says “abstaining from the taking of life,” and so forth, in order to show the purity of practice (payogasuddhi). In that regard:
"I was satisfied with my own husband"—thus she spoke of abstaining from sexual misconduct. The remainder is exactly as stated below.
The commentary on the second *Paṭibbatā-vimāna* is finished.
13. Commentary on the first *Suṇisā-vimāna*.
"By his excellent beauty" refers to the *Sūṇisā-vimāna*. What is its origin?
In a certain house in Sāvatthī, a daughter-in-law, upon seeing an elder whose taints were destroyed (khīṇāsava) who had entered the house for alms, was filled with joy and gladness.
Thinking, "This supreme field of merit has appeared before me," she took a portion of the cake she had received and—
She respectfully offered it to the Elder; the Elder accepted it, gave a blessing, and departed.
Later, having passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. All the rest is exactly as described below. Therefore it is said:
“O goddess, you who stand there with such exquisite beauty;”
Illuminating all directions like a star among the herbs:
“By what means is your complexion such as this? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those enjoyments arise for you that are dear to the mind?”
“I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing power, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?
“Thus questioned by Moggallāna, that deity was delighted.”
“Being questioned, she answered: ‘Of what karma is this the fruit?
‘When I was among humans, being a human myself, I was a daughter-in-law in my father-in-law’s house.
There I saw a stainless monk, serene and unperturbed.’”
With my own hands, full of faith, I gave him a cake;
having given a portion after dividing it into shares, I now rejoice in the Nandana Grove.
"Because of that, such is my complexion; because of that, I prosper here."
“Riches arise for me, whatever is dear to my heart.
“I declare to you, O monk of great power: when I was a human being, I performed meritorious deeds;
because of that, I am thus ablaze with majesty, and my complexion shines in every direction.”

112. In this context, "daughter-in-law" (*suṇisā*) means the wife of one's son. For a woman, the father of her husband is called "father-in-law" (*sasura*), and she is his "daughter-in-law. With reference to that, [the verse says]: "I was a daughter-in-law in my father-in-law’s house. 113.

"Half a share" (*bhāgaḍḍhabhāgaṃ*) means half of the portion received by oneself. "I rejoice in the Nandana grove" (*modāmi nandane vane*): the Elder spoke thus because he had seen [this state] in the Nandana grove.
The rest is exactly as previously explained. The commentary on the *Suṇisā-vimāna* is finished.

14. Commentary on the Second Daughter-in-Law’s Mansion (*Dutiyasuṇisāvimānavannanā*) “With surpassing beauty, you stand there, O deity”—this is the Second Daughter-in-Law’s Mansion. Herein, there is nothing new; the only distinction lies in the occasion for the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*), which concerns the gift of sweetmeats (*kummāsa*). Therefore it was said:
“With surpassing beauty, you stand there, O deity;”
Illumining all directions like a star among the herbs, [he asked:
“By what means is your complexion such as this? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those enjoyments arise for you, whatever is dear to the mind?”
“I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?
Thus questioned by Moggallāna, that goddess was delighted.
When asked the question, she explained: "Of what karma is this the fruit?
"When I was among humans as a human being, I was a daughter-in-law in my father-in-law's house.
There I saw a monk free from passion, serene and undisturbed."
With my own hands, full of faith, I gave him a portion;
having given that lump of boiled rice, I rejoice in the Nandana Grove.
"Because of that, such is my complexion; because of that, I am successful here."
“Riches arise for me, whatever is dear to my heart.
“I declare to you, O monk of great power: when I was a human being, I performed meritorious deeds.
Because of that, my majesty blazes forth in this way, and my radiance illuminates every direction.”

121. In this context, "a portion" (*bhāga*) refers to a portion of boiled barley meal (*kummāsa*). Therefore, it says, "having given a lump of barley meal. And by "barley meal," barley-based meal is meant. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the second *Sunisā-vimāna* is finished.
15. Commentary on the *Uttarā-vimāna*.

"By his surpassing beauty" refers to the *Uttarā-vimāna*. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place. At that time, there was a poor man named Puṇṇa who lived dependent upon the Rājagaha merchant;
he had a wife named Uttarā and a daughter also named Uttarā—these two were the only people in the household.
Then one day in Rājagaha, they made a proclamation: "The great multitude shall celebrate a festival for seven days.
Hearing this, the merchant said to Puṇṇa, who had arrived early in the morning, "Dear son, our dependents wish to enjoy the festival;
will you join them in the festivities, or will you work for wages? "Master, as for what is called a 'festival'..."
"It will be a festival for others, but in my house there are not even grains of rice for the sacrificial offering tomorrow; what use is a festival to me?
If I can get some oxen, I shall go to plow. "In that case, take the oxen," [the king said].
He took strong oxen and a fine plow, and said, "My dear lady, the city-dwellers are celebrating a festival, but because of my poverty, I am going to work for wages."
"Having cooked double the amount of grain for the offering today, you should bring me my meal," he said to his wife, and then went to the field.
Meanwhile, the Elder Sāriputta, having emerged from seven days of meditative absorption in cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), looked about, thinking, "Whom should I favor today?
and saw Puṇṇa had entered within the net of his knowledge.
Reflecting, "Is this man faithful? Will he be able to provide for me?

and perceiving his faith, his capacity to offer support, and the great prosperity he would thereby obtain, [the Teacher] took his bowl and robes and went to the place where he was plowing. Standing by the edge of a trench, he looked toward a grove of trees.
As soon as Puṇṇa saw the elder, he set aside his plow and paid homage to him with the fivefold prostration.
Thinking, "He will need a tooth-stick," he made the tooth-stick allowable and gave it to him. Then the elder took out his bowl and water-strainer and gave them to him.
Thinking, "He will need drinking water," Puṇṇa took them, strained the water, and gave it to him.
The Elder thought: "This man lives in the last house of the village.
If I go to his door, his wife will not be able to see me. I shall remain right here until his wife sets out on the road taking her meal.
Having waited there for a short while, he [waited] for the moment when she had set out on the road.
Having learned this, he set out toward the interior of the city. Seeing the Elder on the road, she thought:
"Sometimes when there is something to give, I do not see the noble sir; sometimes while I am seeing the noble sir, there is nothing to give.
But today I have seen the noble sir, and here is something to give. Will he perhaps show me favor?"

Having set down the food vessel and paid homage to the Elder with the fivefold prostration, she said, "Venerable sir, without considering whether this food is coarse or refined, please accept it as a favor to your servant. Then the Elder held out his bowl;
as she supported the vessel with one hand and gave him the rice from it with the other, when half the food had been given—
When it was given, she covered the bowl with her hand, saying, "Enough. She said, "Venerable sir, there is only one portion; it cannot be divided into two.
Without providing for your servant in this world, please provide for him in the next world. We wish to give everything without reserve.
Having thus placed it all into his bowl, she said, "May you be a partaker of the visible Dhamma."
He made this aspiration. The Elder said, "So be it," and while standing there, he offered words of thanksgiving;
then, sitting down in a place convenient for water, he performed his meal duties. She too returned, sought out rice, and cooked the meal.
Puṇṇa, having plowed a plot of land measuring half a karīsa, was unable to endure the hunger; so he released his oxen.
Having entered the shade of a single tree, he sat down watching the road.
Then his wife, while going along carrying the meal, saw him and thought: "This man, oppressed by hunger, sits watching me;
if he rebukes me for being too late and strikes me with his goad-stick, the work I have done will become useless."
Thinking, "I shall tell him first," she said this: "Master, today for one day please set your mind at ease;
do not let the work I have done be in vain. As I was bringing your meal early in the morning, I saw the Dhammasenāpati on the road;
I gave your meal to him, and having returned home, I am now cooking another meal."
“Come, Master, let your heart be confident. He asked, “What are you saying, lady?
and having heard that matter again, he said with a mind full of faith, “Lady, it is truly well done by you for giving my meal to the noble sir;
I too have given him tooth-sticks and water for rinsing the mouth this very morning. Having thus rejoiced in those words, his heart being confident, he—
Because he had obtained his meal late in the day, his body was weary; placing his head on her lap, he fell asleep.
Then, at dawn, the entire field where he had plowed—covered in dust—became pure red gold and stood there shining like a heap of *kaṇikāra* flowers.
Having woken up and looked, he said to his wife, "My dear, this is the field I plowed."
"Everything appears to me as gold; could it be that my eyes are spinning because I have received my meal so late in the day?
"Master, it appears exactly the same way to me too.
He rose up, went there, took a clod of earth, struck it with the tip of his plough, and perceiving its golden nature, exclaimed, "Oh, how wonderful for the Master, the General of the Dhamma!"
"The fruit of the gift given has been seen this very day; however, it is not possible to consume such wealth while keeping it hidden.
Having filled his wife's brought food-bowl with gold, he went to the royal palace.
Being granted entrance by the king, he entered, paid homage to the king, and when the king asked, "What is it, dear one? he replied, "Your Majesty, today the entire area I plowed..."
"It stands there as if it were a single heap of gold; it is right to have that gold brought back," he said.
"Who are you? "I am named Puṇṇa. "But what did you do today? "At dawn, tooth-sticks and water for rinsing the mouth were given to me by the General of the Dhamma;
and even the food I had brought for my wife was given to him instead."
Hearing this, the king said, "It seems, sir, that the ripening of the gift given to the General of the Dhamma has been shown this very day," and he asked, "Dear son, what shall we do?
[The son replied,] "Send many thousands of wagons and have gold brought back.
The king sent the wagons. As the royal men were taking it, saying, "This belongs to the king," each time they took some, more was taken.
It became mere clay. When they went and informed the king, he asked them, "Sirs, what did you say when you took it?
They replied, "It was yours. He said, "In that case, sirs, go again; take it, saying, 'It belongs to Puṇṇa.
They did so, and whatever they took turned out to be gold. All of that—
Having brought it, they made a heap in the royal courtyard; the heap was eighty cubits high. The king, having caused the citizens to assemble, asked:
"Is there anyone in this city who possesses so much gold? "There is none, Your Majesty," they replied. "What, then, should be given to him?
"The title of Chief Merchant (Seṭṭhi), Your Majesty. The king, thinking, "Let him be known as Bahudhana-seṭṭhi," with great...
He gave him the merchant’s parasol along with his wealth.
Then he said to him, “Sire, for all this time we have lived in another’s house; give us a place to live. [The King replied,] “In that case, look!
This thicket appears there; have it cleared away and build a house. Thus he spoke to the former merchant.
He pointed out the site for the house. Within just a few days, he had the house built there;

then, performing the auspicious ceremony for entering the new home and the auspicious ceremony for the parasol simultaneously, he gave alms for seven days to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Then the Teacher, expressing his appreciation for the gift, delivered a gradual discourse. At the conclusion of the Dhamma talk—
The merchant Puṇṇa, his wife, and his daughter Uttara—all three of them—had become stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*).
Later on, the merchant of Rājagaha requested the hand of Puṇṇa’s daughter for his own son.
When Puṇṇa replied, "I will not give her," the other said, "Do not do this; consider that you have enjoyed such prosperity only by depending upon us for all this time."
"Having obtained [this wealth], give your daughter to my son," he said. He replied, "You all hold wrong views;
my daughter cannot live without the Three Jewels, so I will not give her to him.
Then many sons of noble families, including merchants and householders, said to him, "Do not break off your friendship with him; give him your daughter."
They made their request. Having accepted their words, he gave his daughter on the full moon day of Āsāḷha.
From the time she went to her husband’s family, she was unable to approach a monk or a nun, nor could she give alms or listen to the Dhamma;
thus, when two and a half months had passed, while her attendants were standing by her side...
She asked, "How much of the rainy season remains now? "Half a month, Noble Lady," they replied.
She sent a message to her parents: "Why did you cast me into such a prison?
It would have been better for you to have branded me with a mark and sent me as a slave to others, rather than giving me to a family of such wrong views. From the moment I arrived..."
“Ever since she began, I have not been able to perform even a single meritorious deed such as visiting the monks.

Then her father, expressing his displeasure by thinking, “Alas, my daughter is truly suffering,” sent fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas, saying, “In this city there is a courtesan named Sirimā who receives a thousand [kahāpaṇas] daily; with these coins, go to her—”
She sent a message saying, "Bring her here, hand her over to my husband, and let her perform meritorious deeds herself as she wishes.
Uttarā did accordingly. When her husband saw Sirimā and asked, "What is this?", she replied, "Husband, for these half-months let my friend attend upon you;
however, for these half-months I wish to give alms and listen to the Dhamma."
“I wish to hear it,” she said. Seeing that beautiful woman, he felt a surge of affection and accepted, saying, “Very well.
Uttarā, for her part, invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and obtained the Teacher’s promise, saying, “Venerable Sir, for this half-month, please do not go elsewhere;
alms should be received right here. “From now on, until—”
Thinking, "At the Great Pavāraṇā, I shall have the opportunity to attend upon the Teacher and hear the Dhamma," she wandered about the kitchen with a joyful mind, assigning all the tasks:
"Cook the rice-gruel thus; cook the meal thus; bake the cakes thus.
Then her husband, thinking, "Tomorrow will be the Great Pavāraṇā," turned toward the kitchen.
Standing at the window, she looked out, wondering, "What indeed is that foolish woman doing as she wanders about?

Seeing her wandering there, covered in sweat, smeared with ashes, and stained with charcoal and soot—having arranged herself in such a manner—she thought, "Alas, this foolish woman does not enjoy such glorious prosperity in a place like this;
rather, she wanders with a heart full of joy, thinking, 'I shall attend upon shaven-headed recluses.'"
Having laughed and said, "He wanders about," he departed.
When he had gone, Sirimā, who was standing near him, thought, "What indeed did he look at that made him laugh?
Looking out through that very window, she saw Uttara and thought, "It was because of looking at this woman that he laughed; surely it must be because of her."

She thought, "I have an intimacy with him. It is said that although she had lived for half a month in that house as an outsider, even while enjoying that prosperity, she did not realize her status as an outsider and maintained the perception, "I am the mistress of the house.
Having harbored resentment toward Uttarā, she thought, "I shall cause her suffering," and descended from the palace.
Having entered the kitchen, she took some boiling ghee from the place where the cakes were being baked with a ladle and set out facing north.
Seeing her approaching, Uttarā thought: "My companion has done me a great service;
the world-system is too narrow and the Brahma-world is too low, for my companion’s virtue alone is truly great, and I too shall [follow] her."
"Since I have obtained the opportunity to give this gift and hear the Dhamma by relying on her, if I harbor any anger toward her, may this ghee burn me;
if not, may it not burn me. Thus he suffused her with loving-kindness (*mettā*).
Although she poured the boiling ghee over his head, it became like cool water. Then he said to her, "This is cool..."
Thinking, "She will come," the slave-girls saw Uttarā approaching, carrying a ladle full [of ghee] again;
they rebuked her, saying, "Hey, you ill-behaved woman! You are not fit to pour boiled ghee over our mistress!
and rising up from here and there, they struck her with their hands and feet, threw her to the ground, and though Uttarā tried to ward them off, they continued to beat her.
She was unable to stop her. Then, standing above and pushing back all the other maidservants, she admonished Sirimā, saying, "Why have you committed such a grave deed?
Having bathed her with hot water, she anointed her with oil refined a hundred times.
At that moment, realizing her own status as an outcast woman, she thought: "I have committed a grave deed."
“Because of nothing more than her husband’s smile, she poured boiling ghee over her;
yet even when she was being harassed by the female slaves, she did not command them, saying, ‘Seize her! Instead, she warded off all the slaves and did for me exactly what ought to be done.
If I do not ask her forgiveness, my head shall split into seven pieces!”—and so he fell at her feet.

Having lain down, he said, “Noble lady, forgive me for my fault. She replied, “I am a daughter who possesses the ‘bitterness’ [of pride]; I shall forgive you once my father has been made to forgive me. He said, “Very well, noble lady;
I shall also make your father, the merchant Puṇṇa, forgive you. She said, “Puṇṇa is my father in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa);
but when my father in the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa) has been made to forgive me, then I shall forgive you. “But who is that? [he asked].
“Are they the ones who turned the wheel of the Dhamma? “The Perfectly Enlightened One.
“I have no acquaintance with him; what shall I do? “The Teacher will come here tomorrow morning taking the community of monks with him.
Take whatever honors you have received and come right here to ask his forgiveness. She replied, “Very well, noble lady,” and rising from her seat, she [prepared] for herself...
Having gone home, she commanded five hundred female attendants to prepare various kinds of hard foods,
soft foods, and soups; then, on the following day, taking that honorarium with her, she came to Uttarā’s house and stood there,
unable to place it into the bowls of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha— all of this.
Having taken it, he made arrangements for the north.
At the conclusion of the Teacher’s meal, Sirimā also lay down at the Teacher’s feet together with her retinue.
Then the Teacher asked her, “What is your offense? She replied, “Venerable Sir, yesterday I did such-and-such; then to me—”
“While my companion was harassing me, she restrained the female slaves and actually rendered me a service.
Having recognized her virtue, I asked her for forgiveness; then she said to me, ‘Once you have asked for forgiveness from them, I shall forgive you.
“Is that so, Uttara? “Yes, venerable sir; my companion poured boiling ghee on my head. “Then...”
"What did she think? [He replied: "She thought: 'The world-system (cakkavāḷa) is too narrow; the Brahma-world is too low. The virtue of my companion alone is great;
for it is by relying on her that I was able to give gifts and hear the Dhamma.
If I have any anger toward her, let this burn me; if not, let it not burn me. Having thought thus, she—
“I pervaded them with loving-kindness, Bhante. The Teacher said, “Excellent, excellent, Uttara! It is right to conquer anger in this way.
For one who is angry should be conquered by non-anger; one who reviles, by not reviling; one who insults, by not insulting;
one who is stubborn and stingy, by giving away what belongs to oneself; and one who speaks falsehood, by speaking the truth. Thus he spoke, demonstrating this meaning.
“Conquer anger with non-anger; conquer the wicked with goodness;
conquer the miser with generosity; conquer the liar with truth.
Having spoken this verse, at the conclusion of the verse he preached a discourse on the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, Uttarā—
She was established in the fruit of once-returning, while her husband, father-in-law, and mother-in-law realized the fruit of stream-entry;
Sirimā, too, together with her retinue of five hundred, became stream-enterers. Later, after Uttara passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wandering on a tour of the heavens in the manner previously described, [encountered] Uttara.
Having seen the daughter of the gods, he said:
“O goddess, with your most excellent beauty, you stand there,
illuminating all directions like the star-herb at night.”
“By what means do you have such a complexion? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those enjoyments arise for you, whatever is dear to the mind?
I ask you, O goddess of great majesty.”
"What merit did you perform when you were a human being?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?"— thus he questioned her.
“Delighted, that deity, when questioned by Moggallāna,
answered the question asked, [explaining] the fruit of which karma this is:
‘While living in my home, envy, stinginess, and also spite did not exist in me.’”
Free from anger, obedient to her husband, always heedful on the Uposatha days—
on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight, as well as during the fortnight of miracles—
she was perfectly endowed with the eight factors [of the Uposatha].
“I observed the Uposatha, always restrained in my virtues;
being self-controlled and generous, I now dwell in this celestial mansion.
Abstaining from taking life and restrained from false speech,”
Far from theft, misconduct, and the drinking of intoxicants—
delighting in the five training rules and skilled in the Noble Truths,
these are the female lay disciples of the illustrious Gotama, the Visionary One.
“By my own virtue and by my fame, I am renowned;
I enjoy my own merit, and I am happy and free from illness.
Because of that, such is my complexion, and because of that, I prosper here.”
“Riches arise for me, whatever is dear to my mind.
‘I declare to you, O monk of great power, what I did when I was a human being;
because of that, I am thus blazing with majesty, and my complexion shines in all directions.’”
The deity also gave him leave.
"Venerable sir, you should pay homage with your head at the Blessed One's feet in my name, saying:
'Venerable sir, the female lay follower named Uttarā pays homage with her head at the Blessed One's feet. And it is not surprising, venerable sir, that [the Blessed One would grant me leave].
"The Blessed One might have explained [this] in terms of one of the other fruits of recluseship, yet the Blessed One explained it in terms of the fruit of a once-returner.
128. Regarding that, "there was neither envy, nor stinginess, nor yet spite in me while living as a householder":
this refers to the characteristic of envying the success of other women living in the midst of the household, which has as its object their own prosperity and so forth.

Envy (*issā*), as well as stinginess (*macchariya*)—which has the characteristic of hiding one's own prosperity due to an unwillingness to give anything even for a temporary loan to those who ask—and the rivalry (*paḷāsa*) that arises with the characteristic of seeking parity with others by way of family, status, and so forth:
these three kinds of evil states did not exist, nor did they arise, in me while staying at home, even though the necessary conditions were present. "Free from anger" (*akodhanā*): [and so on].
She is of a nature that does not give way to anger because she is endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion.
"Obedient to her husband" means she is by nature one who conducts herself under his authority through such acts as rising before him and retiring after him; the meaning is that she behaves agreeably.
"Always heedful regarding the Uposatha" means that I am constantly heedful and dwell in non-negligence in the observance of the Uposatha precepts.

129. Showing heedfulness specifically on the Uposatha days, he says "on the fourteenth" and so forth, in order to demonstrate on which days it should be observed, what kind of observance it is, and how it should be observed.
Therein, "the fourteenth and the fifteenth" is connected with "of the fortnight" (*pakkhassa*);
this is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). And "that which is the eighth of the fortnight" [is likewise connected].
"Ettha ca" (and here) is an elliptical expression (*vacana-seso*). "And the fortnight of miracles" (*pāṭihāriya-pakkhaṃ*) means the fortnight for warding off (*paṭiharaṇaka-pakkhaṃ*);

that is, the fortnight during which the Uposatha precept must be maintained by entering and departing respectively on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days—in sequence, from the beginning and from the end.

This refers to the thirteenth, the first of the month (*pāṭipada*), the seventh, and the ninth. "Well-endowed with the eight factors" (*aṭṭhaṅga-susamāgataṃ*) [refers to] abstaining from taking life and so forth.
Well-endowed and possessed of these eight factors. 130.
*Upavasissanti* (they will observe) and *upavasiṃ* (I observed): this is a future verb used in the sense of the past. Some, however, read it simply as *upavasiṃ*.
*Sadā* means on all Uposatha days, including those with obstacles. *Sīlesu* means in the Uposatha precepts.
Regarding "to be accomplished" (*sādhetabbesu*): this locative case is used in the sense of that which is to be produced. "Restrained" (*saṃvutā*) means restrained by body, speech, and mind;
or alternatively, "always" (*sadā*) means at all times. "In the precepts" (*sīlesu*) refers to the constant precepts. "Restrained" (*saṃvutā*) here means restrained by body and speech.
Now, in order to show those constant precepts, it is said: "Abstaining from the destruction of life," and so forth. Therein, "life" (*pāṇo*)...

Conventionally, it is a "being"; ultimately, it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). The taking of life—called the killing, the slaying, or the destruction of a living being—is, in terms of its meaning, the volition of a killer that arises through either the door of body or the door of speech, which instigates an action that cuts off the life-faculty in one who perceives a living being as a living being.
From that, there is abstention from the taking of life. "Abstention" (*virati*) means being on this side of it; the sense is "turning away."
"False speech" (*musāvāda*): "False" (*musā*) refers to a verbal or bodily exertion intended to deceive and resulting in the destruction of another's welfare.
False speech is the volition that originates a bodily or verbal exertion intended to deceive another with the purpose of deception.
Alternatively, "false" (*musā*) is an unreal or untrue matter, and "speech" (*vāda*) is the act of one who wishes to make that known as real and true.
Likewise, it is the volition that originates the intimation (*viññatti*). "From lying" means restrained from, abstained from; this is the meaning. The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction.
Regarding "theft": theft is called the state of stealing; the meaning is the taking of another's property by means of robbery.
In terms of its essential nature, theft is the volition of stealing that originates the preparatory effort of taking what belongs to another while perceiving it as belonging to another. From that—
"Restrained from theft" (*theyyā saññatā*) is connected with "far from" (*ārakā*).

Regarding "transgression" (*aticāra*): *aticāra* is the act of going beyond (*aticca cāro*). Its meaning is: transgression of conduct (*micchācāra*), which is the act of going toward an improper place out of sensual desire, having overstepped the boundaries of the world (*lokamariyāda*).
An "improper place" (*agamanīyaṭṭhāna*) refers to [women] protected by men—those protected by a mother, those protected by a father, and so forth.

There are ten [types of women]: one protected by her mother and father, one protected by her brother, one protected by her sister, one protected by her relatives, one protected by her clan, one protected by the Dhamma, one who has a protector, and one for whom there is legal penalty.

There are another ten: one purchased with wealth, one who lives by her own will, one who lives on her earnings, one who wears a cloth (as a sign of betrothal), one who is [merely] water-jar-bound, one whose head-covering has been removed, a female slave as a wife, a female servant as a wife, one captured under a banner, and a momentary wife. Thus, there are twenty.
Women. Among women, however, there are twelve types: the two protected by guardians and punished by law, and the ten such as those purchased for money and so forth;
these are the ones intended here as places not to be approached by another man. As for its characteristic:

misconduct (aticāra) is the volition that transgresses a place not to be approached, proceeding through the door of the body with the intention of unrighteous conduct (asaddhamma). Therefore, it is called "misconduct."
"Intoxicant drinks" (*majjapāna*): "Intoxicant" (*majja*) refers to *surā* and *meraya* in the sense of being intoxicating; "drink" (*pāna*) means that which is drunk by means of it;
thus, "intoxicant drink" (*majjapāna*) is the drinking of intoxicants. By means of which unwholesome volition one drinks *surā*—which is reckoned as intoxicant and has five varieties, namely:
*piṭṭhasurā*, *pūvasurā*, *odaniyasurā*, *kiṇṇapakkhittā*, and *sambhārasaṃyuttā*—or *puṣpāsava*...
