Fermented fruit liquor, honey liquor, molasses liquor, and that which is prepared from various ingredients—this fivefold *meraya* (intoxicant), or even if one drinks it starting from the seed down to the tip of a blade of *kusa* grass, the volition (*cetanā*) involved is the drinking of intoxicants.
Therefore, they are abstinent and far removed from the drinking of intoxicants.
132. Thus, having been shown by way of analysis according to the factors to be abandoned, beginning with "abstaining from the destruction of life," this is the perpetual virtue (*niccasīla*).
Showing them as grouped together by way of their being things to be undertaken again, he said, “delighting in the five training precepts.

Therein, *sikkhāpada* means a footing for training; the meaning is a division of training. Alternatively, all wholesome states such as the jhānas and so forth are called *sikkhā* because they are to be trained in;
however, among those trainings, any one of the five factors of virtue (*sīlaṅga*) is [included].
In the sense of a foundation, it is a "footing" (*pada*); because it is the footing for the trainings, it is a "training precept" (*sikkhāpada*). There are five factors of virtue (*sīla-aṅga*).
Those who delight in—that is, take pleasure in—that fivefold training precept are "delighting in the five training precepts.

"Skilled in the Noble Truths" means they are proficient and expert in the four Noble Truths—namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—by way of the clear realizations of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing; that is, they have penetrated the Four Truths.

The meaning is as follows: “Of Gotama” refers to the Blessed One by way of his clan (*gotta*). “Renowned” (*yasassino*) means possessed of fame or possessed of a retinue. (133) “I am she” (*sāham*) means that I possess the aforementioned qualities.

“By my own virtue” (*sakena sīlena*) means by way of the cause consisting of my own natural virtue (*sabhāva-sīla*), such as freedom from longing (*anussukitā*), and my virtue of undertaking observances (*samādāna-sīla*), such as the Uposatha precepts.
For that [virtue] brings about welfare and happiness for beings through their ownership of their own karma (*kammassakatā*).
And specifically, it is called "one's own" (saka). Therefore it was said:
"For that is one's own; taking that along, one goes;
and that follows one, like a shadow that never departs."

And she was "famous for her fame" (yasasā ca yasassinī), meaning she was possessed of renown and reputation because of the report of her qualities as they truly were—such as being "an upāsikā named Uttarā, endowed with virtue and conduct, free from envy, not stingy, and without anger"—and such as being "one who has attained the fruit and understood the teaching.
This fame spread in all directions like oil upon the surface of water; or rather, she was so called because of that quality of virtue attained here [in this life].
“Possessing glory with a retinue of glory” means she is glorious and endowed with a retinue.

“I experience my own merit” means I personally experience the merit I have accumulated. For when the fruit of merit is experienced, that merit itself is said to be experienced by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit.
Alternatively, even the fruit of good conduct is called “merit” because it is distinct from the state of an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*).
As it is said: “Bhikkhus, it is through the undertaking of wholesome states that this merit increases in this way.

“And I am happy and free from illness” means that I am happy by means of both divine bliss and the bliss of the fruit [of my actions], and I am free from illness—meaning healthy—due to the absence of bodily and mental suffering.
Regarding the phrase “and for me,” the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction; by it, [the meaning is] “you should pay homage with my words as well, not with yours.”
The phrase “by her very nature” includes the act of homage. By the words “It is not wonderful,” etc., she shows that her status as a noble female disciple (ariyasāvikā) was already well known.
“To the Blessed One,” etc., are the words of the compiler (saṅgītikāra). The rest is exactly according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the *Uttarāvimāna* is finished.
16. Explanation of the *Sirīmā-vimāna*:
"Horses yoked and supremely adorned—this is the *Sirīmā-vimāna*. How did it originate?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. At that time, [the story] previously mentioned in the immediately preceding section occurred.
The courtesan Sirimā, having attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti), abandoned her defiled occupations and established eight *salāka*-meals for the Saṅgha.
From the very beginning, eight monks would come to her house regularly.
She would say, "Take ghee! Take milk! and so forth, filling their bowls; what one had received...
It was sufficient for three or four people; daily alms-food was provided with a cost of sixteen kahāpaṇas.
Then one day, a certain bhikkhu ate a meal of eight dishes at her house and went to a monastery three yojanas away.
When he sat for his evening visit to the Elder, they asked him, "Friend, where did you get your alms-food?"
“Did you take it and come here? “I ate the eight-grain meal of Sirimā. “She gives it having made it agreeable, friend.
“It is impossible to praise her meal; she gives it having made it exceedingly refined.
What one person receives from her is sufficient for three or four others. Yet, even compared to the gift she bestows, the mere sight of her is superior.”
He spoke of that woman’s virtues, saying, "She is such-and-such and such-and-such.
Then, a certain bhikkhu, having heard this account of her virtues, developed an affection for her through mere hearing even though he had not seen her.
Thinking, "It is fitting for me to go there and see her," he announced his seniority and assigned that bhikkhu as his attendant.

Having asked, and having heard, "Friend, tomorrow you will be the senior monk of the Saṅgha at that house and receive the eight-course meal," he took his bowl and robes at that very moment and departed. At dawn, as the sun was rising, he entered the hall for voting sticks and stood there;
being the senior monk of the Saṅgha, he received the eight-course meal at that house. As for that other monk—
Having eaten yesterday, she departed; at the very moment of her departure, a disease arose in her body.
Therefore, she removed her ornaments and lay down. Then, seeing the monks who had come to receive their meal of eightfold rice, her female slaves informed her.
Unable to go herself to take the bowls in her own hands or to seat them, she commanded her slaves: "Ladies..."
“Taking the bowls, noble ladies, please have her sit down, give her rice gruel to drink, give her some solid food, and at the time for the meal, fill her bowl and give it to her.

They replied, “Very well, noble lady,” and having ushered the bhikkhus inside, given her rice gruel to drink, given her solid food, and filled her bowl with the meal at the proper time, they informed her. She said, “Take me along, noble ladies; I shall pay my respects.”
Having spoken thus, she was escorted by those women and led into the presence of the monks; with her body trembling, she paid homage to the monks.
The monk, looking at her, thought: "Such is the beauty of her form even while she is ill;
but what kind of perfection of form must she possess when she is healthy, adorned with all her ornaments? Then, [the merit] accumulated over many tens of millions of years...
An affliction arose within him. Being ignorant, he was unable to eat his meal;
taking his bowl, he went to the monastery, covered the bowl, set it aside in a corner, spread out the edge of his robe, and lay down.
Then, even though one of his companions tried to entreat him, he could not get him to eat, and thus he missed his meal.
On that very day, in the evening, Sirimā passed away. The king sent a message to the Teacher:
"Venerable Sir, Sirimā, the younger sister of Jīvaka, has passed away. When the Teacher heard this, he sent a reply to the king:
"There is no need for the cremation of Sirimā’s body; let her be placed in the raw charnel ground so that crows and other scavengers do not devour her."
"Having laid him down in that manner, guard him. The king did accordingly.
After three days had passed in succession, on the fourth day the body swelled up; worms oozed out from the nine openings, and his entire body became like a cracked bowl of cooked rice.
The king caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, [announcing]: "Excepting the children who were guarding the house..."
“For those who do not come for the sake of seeing Sirimā, there shall be a fine of eight kahāpaṇas. He also sent a message to the Teacher:
“May the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, please come for the sake of seeing Sirimā. The Teacher announced to the bhikkhus:
“We shall go for the sake of seeing Sirimā.”
That young bhikkhu also, for four days, did not accept anyone's advice and lay down without even eating.
The food in his bowl became putrid, and even filth arose in the bowl.
Then, when he was approached by his companion bhikkhu who said, "Friend, the Teacher is going to see Sirimā," although his stomach was thus tormented with hunger, he replied, "Sirimā."
At those very words, he rose up suddenly and asked, "The Teacher is going to see Sirima; will you go as well?
"Yes, I shall go," he replied. Discarding his food, washing his bowl, and placing it in its bag, he departed together with the community of monks.
The Teacher stood to one side surrounded by the community of monks, and the community of nuns likewise.
The assembly of kings, the assembly of laymen, and the assembly of laywomen each stood on one side.
The Teacher asked the king, "Who is this, Great King? "Venerable Sir, she is Jīvaka’s younger sister, named Sirimā.
"Is this Sirimā? "Yes, Venerable Sir. "In that case, have a drum beaten throughout the city: 'A thousand [pieces of gold]..."
“Having given five hundred, let them take it. The king did accordingly; not even one person was heard saying “Ha! or “Hu!
The king reported to the Teacher, “They will not take it, Bhante. “In that case, Great King, have the price lowered,” he said.
The king, having caused a drum to be beaten with the proclamation, “Let them take it for five hundred,” found no one at all who would take it.
Having caused the drum to be beaten with the proclamation, "Let them take the glory by giving two hundred and fifty, two hundred, one hundred, fifty,
twenty-five, twenty, ten, five, one, half, a quarter, a māsaka,
or even a kākaṇika kahāpaṇas," he then had the drum beaten again, saying, "Let them take it for free."
Nevertheless, there was no one who would say, "I will give," or "I am giving. The king said, "Venerable sir, even if one were to take her for free, there is no one [who would do so].
The Teacher said, "Behold, monks, how dear this woman is to the multitude!
Previously, they obtained her in this very city by paying a thousand pieces of gold on a single day; now, even if one were to take her for free, there is no one [who would do so]. Such is she."
He showed [this] as follows: "Name-and-form has reached its destruction and decay;

it is made variegated by external ornaments, yet it is a mass of nine openings of various colors, erected upon three hundred bones, perpetually afflicted, and a selfhood that is unstable, being conceived in many ways by the foolish multitude."
“Behold this figure fashioned by the mind, a heap of diseased limbs piled together;
it is afflicted, full of many thoughts, and for it there is no lasting stability.

Thus he spoke this verse. At the conclusion of the teaching, the monk who had been attached to Sirimā became free from desire and lust; having developed insight, he attained Arahantship, and eighty-four thousand living beings realized the Dhamma.
At that time, the celestial maiden Sirimā, having surveyed the abundance of her own wealth and looking back toward the place from which she had come,
saw the Blessed One standing surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in her previous existence,
as well as a great multitude of people gathered together; then, surrounded by five hundred celestial maidens and with her body visible upon five hundred chariots, she approached.
Having arrived and descended from her chariot, she, together with her retinue, paid homage to the Blessed One and stood with palms joined in reverence.
At that time, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa was standing not far from the Blessed One. He said this to the Blessed One:
"It occurs to me, Blessed One, to ask a question. "Let it occur to you, Vaṅgīsa," the Blessed One replied.
The Venerable Vaṅgīsa said to that glorious daughter of the gods:
“Your horses are yoked, supremely adorned, with faces cast downward, moving swiftly and powerfully.
And five hundred chariots, magically conjured, follow you, their horses urged on by the charioteer.”
“You stand there upon your excellent chariot, adorned,
illuminating like a firebrand in the water.
I ask you, O woman of exquisite form, concerning Anomadassi.”
“Why indeed have you come to this non-superior body?”—thus he questioned him. 137.
In that context, “your horses are yoked and supremely adorned” means they are supremely, exceedingly, and especially adorned;
or, adorned with supreme, most excellent, divine horse-ornaments; or, they are supreme, foremost, and noble breeds.

“Adorned with all ornaments” means that those horses were yoked to your chariot; they were either suitable for the chariot when yoked, or they were joined together in mutual likeness—this is the sense of “joined” (*saṃsaṭṭhā*).

And here, in the first alternative, one should see the compound as *parama-alaṅkatā* without performing the euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*), while in the second alternative it is to be regarded as a case-ending-less designation (*avibhattikaniddesa*). “With faces turned downwards” (*adhomukhā*)...
"Facing downwards. Even though they were naturally situated in that way, they are called "downward-facing" by virtue of their descent from the world of the gods (*devaloka*).
"Moving through the air" means traveling through the sky. "Powerful" means strong. "Swift" means possessing speed; the meaning is that they are both powerful and swift.
"Manifested" means produced and brought into existence by your own meritorious deeds (*puñña-kamma*). "Created by yourself" means exactly so.
Or, having in mind [the goddess] Sirimā, the daughter of the gods, because of her state of delighting in creation (*nimmāna-rati*), it is said that she was "created" (*abhinimmitā*).
The expression "five hundred chariots" (*pañca-ratha-satā*) is stated by lengthening the letter *tha* for the sake of metrical ease and by means of a change of gender;

alternatively, the elision of the case-ending (*vibhatti-lopa*) should be understood, meaning "five hundred chariots. "The horses, urged on by the charioteers, follow him"—thus [it is said] by the charioteers.
“O Bhaddā, these horses yoked to the chariots follow him as if urged on; O deity, they follow him.
Some read “sārathiacoditā,” meaning that they follow even without being urged by charioteers.

Alternatively, “sārathicoditā hayā” may be treated as a single compound word with the vowel lengthened for metrical convenience; the construction is then: “five hundred chariots [each] with horses urged on by charioteers.”
138. “Sā tiṭṭhasi” means you stand there. “Rathavare” means on the best of chariots. “Alaṅkatā” means with your body adorned by divine ornaments weighing sixty cart-loads.
“Obhāsayaṃ jalamiva joti pāvakā” means you stand shining like a light, blazing like a flame, and glowing like fire;
what is meant is that you stand illuminating and blazing all around.
“*Joti*” is a common name for the moon, the sun, the lunar mansions, and the forms of the stars. “*Varatanu*” means one who possesses a supreme form, beautiful in every limb.
For that very reason, “*anomadassane*” means of wondrous appearance; the sense is that he is lovely to behold and inspiring.
Why indeed did she approach the unsurpassed one from among the hosts of deities? [That is,] from which host of deities did she come to the Unsurpassed One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha?
"I approached you for the sake of attending upon you;
thus have I come. Being questioned in this way by the Elder, that deity revealed herself:
"The deities, having repeatedly created whatever is called the unsurpassed attainment of the peak of sensual desires, take their delight therein."
"Therefore, a nymph of celestial form has come here from that body [of beings] to pay homage to the Supreme One.
Thus he spoke this verse.

(139) Therein, "that which is called the unsurpassed for those who have reached the pinnacle of sensual pleasures" refers to the Paranimmittavasavatti devas, who have attained the highest state among the enjoyments of sense-desires.
From that body of the gods which they call "unsurpassed" by virtue of their glory, enjoyments, and so forth.
The gods who delight in what they have created themselves are called the *Nimmānarati* gods;
having created for themselves whatever objects of desire they wish, they delight, sport, frolic, and take pleasure therein. Therefore, from that group of *Nimmānarati* gods.
“Kāmavaṇṇinī” means one who possesses a desirable form, that is, one who assumes whatever form she desires.
“Idhāgatā” means come here, to this human world, or having arrived at this human world.

When the deity had thus described herself as a Nimmānarati deity, the Elder, wishing again to have her describe her previous existence, the meritorious deed she performed there, and her destiny, said:
“What good conduct did you practice in the past, by what means do you wish to dwell in happiness with immeasurable splendor?
Your supernatural powers are unsurpassed among the birds, and your beauty shines throughout the ten directions.
You are surrounded by devas and are held in high honor.”
“From where have you passed away, O deity, to go to a happy destination?
Whose instruction do you follow and carry out?
Tell me this, if you are a disciple of the Buddha. Thus he spoke these two verses.
140. Therein, *ācarī* is spoken with a long vowel; the meaning is "one who has accumulated. *Idha* is a mere particle, or it means "here" in this state of existence as a deva.
*Kenacchasī* means "by what meritorious deed do you dwell, being well-situated? Some read *kenāsi tvaṃ*.
*Amitayasā* means "with an immeasurable retinue," that is, one whose followers are not few. *Sukhedhitā* means "well-nurtured by happiness."
"Augmented" means that celestial happiness has been fully nourished; this is the meaning. "Iddhi" means divine power (*dibbānubhāva*). "Anadhivarā":
she has no other superior or more distinguished [power] than this, thus she is "anadhivarā," meaning "supremely excellent. "Vihaṅgamā" means one who travels through the air.
"The ten directions" refers to all ten directions. "Virocati" means she illuminates them.
141. You were surrounded, honored, and encompassed on all sides by eighty [attendants], and you were highly esteemed.

From where did you pass away to reach this happy destination? Having passed away from which of the five destinations, did you approach this happy destination—the celestial realm—by way of rebirth-linking?
Or whose word-doer and follower of instruction are you? By receiving the counsel and instructions within the teaching and the word of which Teacher have you come to this?

"You are one who carries out the word" is the construction. Or rather, the meaning here should be understood thus: "Whose word do you carry out—that of a Teacher, by establishing yourself in the instruction of an instructor?
Having thus questioned her tenet by way of a non-statement (*anuddesika*), he asks again by way of a statement (*uddesika*): "If you are a disciple of the Buddha, explain it to me. In that regard:

“Disciples of the Buddha” (*buddhasāvikā*): because the Blessed Buddha has awakened by means of his self-arisen knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*) to all knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*), perceiving them directly as if they were an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of his hand, those who are born at the end of the hearing of the Dhamma from the Buddha are “disciples of the Buddha.
Speaking thus to explain the matter asked by the Elder, the deity uttered these verses:
“In a most excellently constructed city, situated within a forest, I was an attendant to a glorious and eminent king.
I was highly trained in dance and song; in Rājagaha, they knew me as Sirimātī.
Then the Buddha, the leader and bull among seers, taught me the impermanence, suffering, and arising of all conditioned things.”
The unconditioned cessation of suffering is eternal; this path is straight, direct, and auspicious.

Having heard the teaching of the Tathāgata, the best of men, regarding the unconditioned state of the Deathless, I became perfectly restrained in my virtues and remained established in the Dhamma taught by the Buddha, the supreme among men.
“Having known the stainless state, the unconditioned, taught by the Tathāgata with his own authority, right there I attained the concentration of tranquility;
that itself became for me the supreme certainty.
Having obtained the excellent, distinguished nectar of immortality, I was distinguished by the one-sided realization.”
“Without doubt, I am honored by many people, experiencing no small amount of pleasure and delight.
Thus, I am an immortal goddess in the realm of the gods, a disciple of the Tathāgata, the Best of Men;
seeing the Dhamma, established in the first fruit, a stream-enterer, and there is no longer any state of misery for me.”
“I approached to pay homage to the unsurpassed One, and to the pleasing monks who delight in wholesome deeds;
with reverence for the glorious King of Dharma, I came to worship that auspicious assembly of recluses.
Seeing the Sage, the Tathāgata, the supreme man and charioteer of those to be tamed, my heart was filled with joy and I was deeply satisfied.”
“I pay homage to the Leader, the cutter of craving, who delights in the wholesome and is compassionate for our supreme welfare.

(142) Therein, “between the mountains” means in the midst, between the five mountains known as Isigili, Vepulla, Vebhāra, Paṇḍava, and Gijjhakūṭa; because of this, that city is called “Giribbaja” (the Mountain Enclosure). “In the excellent city” means...
"In the supreme city" refers to Rājagaha. "Well-laid out" means it was properly established by the wise Mahāgovinda according to the methods of the science of site-selection (*vatthuvijjā*).
"Attendants" refers to those who serve him with musical performances. "Of the excellent king" refers to the great King Bimbisāra.
Regarding "of the glorious one," they say that "glory" (*siri*) is a designation for wisdom and merit; or alternatively, it is produced by merit.
The attainment of excellence, such as the beauty of the body, depends upon merit performed, or it arises from those who have performed merit;
thus it is called "glory" (*sirī*). One who possesses this is "glorious" (*sirīmā*); [the phrase] "of that glorious one" refers to him.
"Well-trained in the supreme" means trained exceedingly and correctly. "Was" (*ahuṃ*) means "I was. "They knew" (*avediṃsu*) means they understood.

143. *Nisabha*: A bull (*usabha*) is the leader of a hundred cattle; a steer (*vasabha*) is the leader of a thousand cattle—or alternatively, a bull (*usabha*) is the leader of a hundred bulls, while a steer (*vasabha*) is the leader of a thousand bulls.

One who is the best of all cattle, capable of enduring all hardships, white, handsome, a bearer of great burdens, and unshakable even by the sounds of a hundred thunderclaps, is a *nisabha*. By means of his own *nisabha*-strength, he [draws] the chariot.
Just as one endowed with four feet, having pressed down upon the earth, stands firm in an unshakable position,
imperturbable by any danger; even so the Blessed One, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata,
having pressed down upon the earth of the eight assemblies with the four feet of self-confidence, is imperturbable by any adversary or enemy in the world with its devas.
He stands by means of an immovable state; therefore, he is like a bull, thus "Nisabha.

Among those called "Isis" in the sense of seeking the aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue and so forth—namely, among the Isis who are both trainees and those beyond training—he is the bull (chief), or the bull among the Isis, or he is both an Isi and a bull, thus "Isinisabha.
He guides beings who are to be guided, thus he is a "Vināyaka"; he is one devoid of [other] leaders.
Or "Vināyaka" means the Self-Existent One (*sayambhū*).
He taught that the origin, suffering, and impermanence [are such]; he spoke of the nature of decay in both the truth of the origin and the truth of suffering.
By this, [he meant]: "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation."

He shows the mode of occurrence of his own knowledge of realization (*abhisamaya-ñāṇa*). "The origin, suffering, and impermanence" refers to the truth of the origin, the truth of suffering, and impermanence.
Therein, by mentioning the truth of the origin and the truth of suffering, he shows the ground for insight (*vipassanā*);
by mentioning impermanence, he shows its mode of occurrence. For, in the aspect of impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*),...
When the aspect of suffering is discerned, the aspect of non-self is also discerned, because the latter is dependent upon the former.
Therefore it was said: "What is impermanent, that is suffering; what is suffering, that is non-self. The unconditioned (asaṅkhata) is the cessation of suffering, which is eternal.

It is called "unconditioned" because it is not conditioned by any cause; it is "eternal" because it remains as such at all times, owing to its nature as the cessation of the entire suffering of saṃsāra.
The construction is: "And he taught me the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. He taught this path as *akuṭila* (straight), *añjasa* (direct), and *siva* (peaceful).

It is *akuṭila* because, by avoiding the two extremes, it abandons deceit and the like, as well as physical crookedness and so forth, which cause crookedness; for that very reason, it is *añjasa* (direct).
It is *siva* (peaceful) because, by utterly cutting off sensual lust and the like, which cause a state of insecurity, it is the peace of Nibbāna.

The construction is as follows: "And he taught me that Noble Truth known as the practice leading to the cessation of suffering— which is called 'the path' because it is sought after by those seeking Nibbāna, or because it goes while slaying the defilements—
and which is directly evident both to you and to me."
144. “Having heard the deathless state, the unconditioned, the teaching of the Tathāgata, the supreme among men”—herein this is the summarized meaning:

because it was taught for the sake of the deathless, unconditioned Nibbāna, it belongs to the Tathāgata in the sense of having come thus (tathā-āgata), etc.; and to the one who is supreme among men (anadhivara) because of his preeminence in the world including the devas;
that is, to the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha). Or else, [it refers] to the deathless Nibbāna itself.
"Having heard the teaching, the True Dharma—the deathless state which is unconditioned because it is the means for practice and because it cannot be contrived by anyone"—thus [it is said].
"In regard to virtues" means in regard to those virtues that are to be accomplished;
"I was exceedingly well-restrained" means I was perfectly restrained. "I was" (ahum) means I existed. "Established in the Dhamma" means established in the Dhamma of practice.
145. "Having known" means having understood by way of the clear realization through direct experience (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*).
"Right there" means at that very moment, or within that very same personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"He attained the concentration of calm" means he reached and acquired the supramundane concentration (*lokuttara-samādhi*), which is the ultimate calm because it thoroughly calms and pacifies adverse states by way of their total eradication.
Even though at the very moment when there is the clear realization of the actualization of cessation, there is likewise at that same moment the clear realization of the development of the Path,
yet— in order to show that the penetration of the object serves as the cause for the prior establishment of the penetration of development—
it is said: "Having known the stainless state, the unconditioned, taught by the Tathāgata with his own authority."
In that very context, it is said, "I attained concentration through serenity," just as it is said: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.
Alternatively, "having known" (*ñatvāna*) should be understood as stated by way of simultaneity, just as:
"Having destroyed all darkness, the sun has risen in the sky. "That very same" refers to the attainment of supramundane concentration which was obtained.
That very same [state]. "Supreme certainty" (*paramaniyāmatā*) means the supreme, most excellent certainty regarding the Path. 146.
"Distinguishing mark" (*visesanam*) means that which distinguishes one from ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), establishing a state of distinction.

"One-sided" (*ekaṃsikā*) means possessing a one-sided conviction in the Three Jewels, free from doubt, such as: "The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha has practiced rightly."
“Distinguished in realization” means having attained distinction by way of the penetration of the truths. Some also read “distinguishing” (*visesinī*);

the meaning is that she possesses distinction because of the cause of realization. “Free from doubt” means being devoid of doubt, owing to the abandonment of the sixteen-based and eight-based forms of uncertainty. Some read “asaṃsiyā. She is “honored by many people.”

The meaning is: "qualities desirable by those in higher happy realms" (*sugatīhi*). "Delight in play" (*khiḍḍāratim*) means delight that consists of play; or alternatively, both play and delight, as well as the pleasure of dwelling in play and the happiness of delight.
147. "In the state of seeing the Deathless" (*amatadasamhi*):
*amatadasā* refers to me who am one who sees Nibbāna. "Seer of the Dhamma" (*dhammaddasā*): [one who sees] the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
"Diṭṭhavatī" means one who has seen. "Sotāpannā" means one who has attained the stream of the Noble Path from the beginning.
"Na ca pana matthi duggatī" means "and yet there is no miserable rebirth for me," because I am by nature not subject to falling into states of ruin.
"Pāsādike" means inspiring confidence. "Kusalarate" means delighting in wholesome, blameless states and in Nibbāna. "Bhikkhave" means O monks.

The construction is: "They approached to pay homage to the monks. The connection is: "They approached to attend upon the assembly of recluses (*samaṇa-samāgama*), which is auspicious (*siva*), and the Dhamma—the auspicious, secure meeting and gathering of recluses who have stilled evil, namely the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha.

In the phrase "of the glorious King of Dhamma" (*dhammarājino*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative; thus it means "in the glorious King of Dhamma. Alternatively, it may be read as "Sirimati dhammarājinī."
This is the meaning. And some read it in this way as well. 149.
*Muditamanamhi* means "I am one whose mind is gladdened. *Pīṇitā* means "satisfied," or "thrilled" by means of the flavor of joy. *Naravaradammasārathiṃ* means:

he is a "supreme man" (*naravara*) because he is the foremost of persons; and he is a "charioteer of those to be tamed" (*dammasārathi*) because he leads those to be tamed (*dammānaṃ*), that is, those who are to be disciplined (*veneyyānaṃ*), toward *nibbāna*.
"He who is a charioteer of those to be tamed by means of restraint" means he is a supreme charioteer of men who are to be tamed; him.
"Compassionate for the supreme welfare" means compassionate for the highest, most excellent welfare of all beings.
Thus the glorious goddess Sirimā, by way of announcing her own attainment, proclaimed her faith in the Triple Gem.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and having circumambulated them, they departed for the world of the devas.
The Blessed One, taking that very incident as the occasion for a teaching, preached the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the discourse, the discontented bhikkhu attained arahantship, and that Dhamma teaching became fruitful for the assembled multitude as well.
The commentary on the *Sirīmā-vimāna* is finished.
17. The commentary on the *Kesakārī-vimāna*:
This celestial mansion, beautiful and radiant, is the *Kesakārī-vimāna*. How did it come into being? The Blessed One was at Bārāṇasī.
He was staying at Isipatana in the Deer Park. Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus, having dressed in the morning and taken their bowls and robes, entered Bārāṇasī for alms.
They were passing near the door of a certain brahmin’s house. In that house, the brahmin’s daughter, named Kesakārī, was standing near the door.
A louse living on her head saw those monks as they were departing and said to her mother, "Mother, these renunciants are endowed with the prime of youth;
they are handsome, beautiful to behold, inspiring, and delicate.
I imagine they have not been overcome by any loss of fortune; why then do they go forth at this very stage of life? Her mother replied to her:
“There is, mother, a son of the Sakyans who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan; a Buddha has appeared in the world.

He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing, proclaiming a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. Having heard this Dhamma of his, people go forth.”
At that time, a certain lay follower who had attained the fruit and understood the teaching,
while walking along that street, heard this conversation and approached those women. Then the brahmin woman said to him, "Lay follower, at present many sons of good family,
having abandoned great wealth and a large circle of kinsmen, [have gone forth] in the Sakyan tradition..."
“They go forth; what benefit do they perceive that leads them to go forth?

Having heard this, the lay follower said, “Perceiving the danger in sensual pleasures and the advantage in renunciation,” and he explained that matter in detail according to the power of his own knowledge, proclaiming the virtues of the Three Jewels and the five precepts.
He proclaimed the benefits and advantages pertaining both to the present life and to future lives.
Then the brahmin’s daughter asked him, “Is it possible for us also, by being established in the refuges and the precepts, to attain the benefits and advantages you have described?
He replied, “These teachings were spoken by the Blessed One as common to all; why should they not be possible?”
He gave her the refuges and the precepts. Having taken the refuges and undertaken the precepts, she asked again, "Is there anything further to be done beyond this?

Perceiving her intelligence and knowing that she would be endowed with the necessary spiritual capacity (*upanissaya*), he explained the meditation subject of the thirty-two parts of the body, analyzing the nature of the physical form.
Having produced dispassion toward the body and having inspired her with a discourse on the Dhamma connected to impermanence and other such themes, he taught her the path of insight and departed.
She, attending to everything according to the method he had explained, concentrated her mind on the contemplation of repulsiveness;
and having established insight, through the perfection of her supporting conditions, she before long attained the fruit of stream-entry.
She was established there. Then, at a later time, having passed away, she was reborn as a handmaid to Sakka, the king of the gods, and she had a retinue of one hundred thousand nymphs.
When Sakka, the king of the gods, saw her, he was struck with a sense of wonder and amazement, and with a heart full of joy, he said:
“This celestial mansion is radiant and brilliant, With pillars of beryl, eternally well-constructed.”
This place of mine, produced by the ripening of my own karma, is completely covered on all sides with golden trees.
Born there, these former miserly ones—numbering hundreds of thousands through their own deeds—have come to you, O illustrious one;
you stand illuminating [the place], a deity from a former life.
“Just as the moon shines forth, having surpassed the host of stars like the king of constellations,
even so do you, O Apsarā, shine brilliantly with glory over this assembly.
From where have you come, O Anomadassī, to be reborn here in this abode of mine?”
“Even as the gods of the Thirty-Three, together with Indra and Brahmā, we all are not satiated by the sight of you.
With these four verses, she asked about the deed performed by that deity.
In this context, “this celestial mansion” refers to her own celestial mansion, the one in which that deity was reborn.

"Everlasting" (*satataṃ*) means at all times; "beautiful and radiant" (*ruciraṃ pabhassaraṃ*) is how it should be construed. Alternatively, "everlasting" (*satataṃ*) means being perfectly right; the sense is that it is exceedingly vast.
"Covered on all sides" (*samantamotthataṃ*) means spread out and shielded from every direction. "Place" (*ṭhānaṃ*) refers specifically to the celestial mansion (*vimāna*);
for it is called a "place" because those who have performed meritorious deeds abide therein. "Arising from the ripening of kamma" (*kammavipākasambhavaṃ*).
"Born by way of the ripening of karma" means born through the state of the ripening of karma, or born together with the ripening of karma.
Regarding the word "mine," it should be construed with both phrases as: "This is my place;

mine is that which arises from the ripening of karma. 151. The summary meaning of the verse beginning with "Tatrūpapannā" (Born there) is as follows: "Born there" means born in that aforementioned celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
"Reborn"—how much more so since they have already arisen—these former deities, these earlier nymphs, are in number one hundred thousand.
"Thou art" (*tuvaṃsi*) means that you have arrived and been reborn through your own karma. "Glorious" (*yasassinī*) means endowed with a retinue;
by that very same karma, through the power of your deeds, you stand shining and radiant.
152. Now, illustrating that very illumination by means of a simile, he spoke the verse beginning with “sasī. Its meaning is as follows:

Just as the moon—known by the name “sasī” due to its association with the mark of a hare, and known as the “king of constellations” because its qualities surpass those of the stars—shines forth, outshining and overwhelming the entire host of stars; even so, you...
"You shine exceedingly, radiant and resplendent with your own glory amidst this host—that is, this multitude—of celestial nymphs.
In this context, "imā" and "imaṃ" are merely particles. Some, however, read: "Just as the king of stars [the moon] shines among the host of stars, so do you."
153. Now, asking about that deity’s previous existence and the merit performed therein, he spoke the verse beginning with "From where have you come?

Therein, "From where have you come" means: from which state of existence, and by reason of what meritorious deed, have you come to this abode of mine, O blessed one, O Anomadassinī, beautiful in every limb, and been reborn here by way of taking birth?

“Approached. Explaining by way of a simile the very meaning already stated in the words “to Anomadassi,” he said: “Just as the gods of the Thirty-three, together with their Indra, all are not satiated by the sight of Brahmā, so we are not satiated by the sight of him.
In this context, just as the Tāvatiṃsa gods, together with Indra (sahindakā), are not satiated by the sight of Brahmā Sahampati or Sanaṅkumāra when they have approached them—so too [is it for us].
“They are not tormented; likewise, by the sight of you, we all gods are not tormented”—this is the meaning.
Thus questioned by Sakka, the lord of the devas, that deity, explaining the matter, said:
“O Sakka, as for what you ask me: ‘From where have you passed away to come here?’”
“In the city of Kāsi, named Bārāṇasī, I was formerly a hairdresser.
With a mind full of serene confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, having reached a state of certainty free from doubt;
with my training unbroken, having attained the fruit, I am destined for the state of perfect enlightenment and am free from all ailment.”
He spoke two verses (154–5).
Therein, *yam etam* means "this which," i.e., "this question. *Anupucchase* means you ask in a manner that is favorable. *Mamam* means "me. *Puratthi* means "there is a city.
*Kāsinaṃ* means "of the kingdom of Kāsi. *Kesakārī* refers to [the woman] in her previous existence.
She speaks her own name. By saying "In the Buddha and the Dhamma," and so forth, she makes manifest her own merit.
Then Sakka, rejoicing in both that attainment of merit and her divine fortune, said: "We welcome you; may you rejoice."
And you shine with glory through righteousness;
with a mind full of serene confidence in the Buddha and the Dhamma,
and having placed your trust entirely and without doubt in the Saṅgha.
"In the unimpaired training rules, in the fruit that has been attained,
in the Dhamma of full enlightenment which is certain and free from affliction"—
thus he spoke. Regarding this, "we rejoice in that web" means we rejoice in— that is, we express appreciation for— both those kinds of excellence.
"Welcome to you" means that your arrival here is welcome; it is indeed an increase of joy and gladness for us.
The rest is according to the method already stated.
Sakka, the king of the gods, related that occurrence to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera, and the Thera—
He reported this to the Blessed One. Taking that matter as the occasion for instruction (*aṭṭhuppatti*), the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the assembled company.
That teaching became beneficial for the world including the devas.
The commentary on the *Kesakārī-vimāna* is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the meaning of the first chapter, the Pīṭhavagga, adorned with seventeen stories, within the Vimānavatthu of the Paramatthadīpanī, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.
2. Cittalatāvagga 1.
Dāsivimānavaṇṇanā:
In the second chapter, there is also the *Dāsivimāna*, beginning with the words "Just like Sakka, the lord of the gods. What is its origin? [It was spoken] by the Blessed One at Jetavana.
While the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a certain lay follower living there went to the monastery in the evening together with several other lay followers.

After hearing the Dhamma and the assembly having risen, he approached the Blessed One and said, "From this day forward, venerable sir, I shall provide four regular meals for the Saṅgha. Then the Blessed One spoke to him in a manner appropriate to that.
Having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, he dismissed him. [The householder] said, "Venerable sir, four regular meals have been provided by me for the Saṅgha.
From tomorrow onwards, may the masters come to my home.
Having informed the meal-designator thus, he went to his own home, explained the matter to his female slave, and said, "There, you must always be diligent..."
"It must be so," she said. She consented, saying, "Very well. By her very nature, she was endowed with faith, desirous of merit, and virtuous;
therefore, rising early every day, she prepared excellent food and drink, thoroughly swept and plastered the place where the monks would sit, arranged the seats, and waited for the monks to arrive.
Having seated her there, paid homage, and worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he served her with great care.
Then one day, when the monks had finished their meal, she approached them, paid homage, and said:
"Venerable sirs, how is one liberated from this suffering of birth and so forth? The monks [taught her] the refuges and the five precepts.
Having given [the gift] and revealed the true nature of the body, they directed her toward the contemplation of repulsiveness;

others delivered a discourse on the Dhamma connected with impermanence. For sixteen years she guarded her virtue, and from time to time applying wise attention, one day, having obtained a favorable opportunity to hear the Dhamma and because her knowledge had reached maturity, she increased her insight.
She realized the fruit of stream-entry. At a later time, having passed away, she was reborn as a beloved attendant of Sakka, the king of the gods.

Being entertained by sixty thousand musical instruments and surrounded by a retinue of a hundred thousand nymphs, she wandered through gardens and other places, joyfully and exultantly enjoying great divine splendor together with her attendants.
Having seen him in the manner described above, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said:
“Like Sakka, the lord of the gods, in the delightful Cittalatā Grove,
you wander about on all sides, surrounded by a host of women.”
Illumining all directions like a star among the herbs, [he asked:
“By what means is your complexion such as this? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those riches arise for you that are dear to the mind?”
“I ask you, O goddess of great majesty:
while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing power?”
"And your complexion shines in all directions," he asked.
That deity, being pleased, when questioned by Moggallāna,
answered the question, [explaining] the fruit of which karma this was.
“Among humans, having been born as a human, I was once a slave in a family dependent on others for food.
Yet I became a female lay follower of the illustrious Gotama, the one with vision;
I applied myself with diligence to the teaching of that Neutral One.”
“Let this body break apart; there is no stability in it here.
The path of the five training rules is auspicious and blissful.
Thornless and unobstructed, it is straight and proclaimed by the virtuous.”
Behold the fruit of renunciation, as it has been attained by this woman:
"I am the attendant of the King, Sakka, the wielder of power;
sixty thousand musical instruments awaken me."
“Ālamba, Gaggaro, Bhīma, Sādhuvādī, and Saṃsaya;
Pokkhara and Suphassa, and the women Vīṇā and Mokkhā.
Nandā and Sunandā, Soṇadinnā, and Sucimhitā.”
Alambusā, Missakesī, Puṇḍarīkā, and Dāruṇī;
Eṇīphassā, Suphassā, Subhaddā, and Muduvādinī—
these and other excellent ones are the awakeners of the Apsarases.
“Then those deities, approaching me at the proper time, addressed me:
‘Come, let us dance; come, let us sing; come, let us delight you.
This is not for those who have performed no merit; this is only for those who have performed merit.”
The sorrowless, delightful, and charming Great Forest of the Thirty-three gods.
“Happiness exists neither here nor in the world beyond for those who have not performed meritorious deeds;
but happiness exists both here and in the world beyond for those who have performed meritorious deeds.”
“For those who desire companionship with them, much wholesome merit must be performed;
for those who have made merit rejoice in heaven, endowed with enjoyments. Thus the deity replied.
In this context, in the phrase “even like Sakka, the lord of gods,” the word *api* expresses esteem (*sambhāvanā*), and the word *iva* has its vowel *i* elided.
It was stated by way of a simile; therefore, the meaning is "just as Sakka, the lord of the gods.
The phrase "equal to Sakka" was stated to show the excellence of that deity’s retinue. Some say that *api* is merely a particle.

*Cittalatāvana* refers to the grove produced by the power of the merit of a celestial maiden named Cittā, or else it refers to those [trees] endowed with various distinctions such as variegated flowers and fruits.
In that celestial park, which had acquired the name "Cittalatāvana" (The Grove of Mind-creepers) because it was for the most part filled with *santānaka* creepers and the like—161.
*Parapessiyā* means one who is sent to various tasks in the families of others; the meaning is one who performs services for others.

162. *Tassā me nikkamo āsi, sāsane tassa tādinoti*: even though I was but a maidservant, toward him who is "Such-like" (*tādī*) in his teaching, I possessed exertion (*nikkama*). With these five [qualities]...
Having become a female lay follower of the Buddha, the Blessed One who possesses the eye, for sixteen years I have guarded my virtue and attended to the meditation subject;

through the power of that mental attention, as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment arise within me, by virtue of my attainment of the characteristic of equanimity (*tādi-lakkhaṇa*) toward desirable and other objects,
[I have attained] that which is included in the teaching of the Teacher who is himself equanimous (*tādin*), [and which belongs] to the side of purification rather than defilement.
"Exertion" (*nikkama*) is the name given to right effort (*sammāvāyāma*) because it issues forth; thus it "was," "became," or "arose.
To show the mode of activity during the preliminary stage of that exertion, it was said:
"Let this body break up; there is no stability here. Its meaning is: even if this body of mine should break up...

"Let it perish; having no concern whatsoever for that, there is neither stiffening nor slackening of my energy here in this application of the meditation subject"—thus she encourages her energy and rouses her insight.
Now, having thus roused her insight, she shows the quality obtained:
“The path of the five training rules is auspicious and blissful;
it is thornless, unobstructed, straight, and proclaimed by the virtuous.
Behold the fruit of renunciation, as this woman has attained. Thus he spoke.

Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: because it has been obtained as the supporting condition for the five training precepts (sikkhāpada) and the sections of training undertaken by way of constant virtue, and because those five training precepts have been fulfilled, it is connected with them;
and because it brings about a state of complete security and possesses a beautiful purpose within the mental continuum in which it arises.

It is *suvatthika* (well-secure) and *sotthika* (safe); it is *siva* (peaceful) because it is unafflicted by the factors of defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*) and because it is the cause for attaining security;
it is *akaṇṭaka* (thornless) due to the absence of the thorns of lust and the like; it is *agahana* (unobstructed) because it utterly cuts through the thickets of defilements, views, and misconduct;

it is *uju* (straight) because it is the cause for the departure from all crookedness, curvature, and deviousness; and it is [so called] because it has been proclaimed by true persons such as the Buddhas.

"The Noble Path proclaimed by the virtuous"—he addresses Sakka, saying: "Behold this fruit of that exertion, of that aforementioned energy, by means of which method even a woman, though possessing only a two-finger-breadth of intelligence, has attained it.
(165) "I am a messenger of the King, one who acts under the command of Sakka"—this is because he conducts himself with self-mastery; in both [cases]...
Alternatively, he is called *vasavattī* because he exercises his own power and sovereignty over the worlds of the gods (*devaloka*).
This is an address to Sakka, the king of the gods, who possesses such sovereignty; it is a form of speech suitable for conversation, or one by which he may be addressed at the time of play:
"Behold the fruit of exertion and energy"—this is the construction. There are five types of musical instruments, distinguished as *ātatavitata* and so forth, [accompanied] by twelve...

When played together by the hands, there are sixty; however, referring to those approximately one thousand that were present for the purpose of attendance, he said: "Sixty thousand musical instruments awaken me.
In this context, "awakening" (paṭibodha) means the arousing of joy and gladness.
166–8. Regarding the passage beginning with "Ālambā," some say it is a partial mention of the names of the sons of gods who play musical instruments;
however, this is actually a mention of the names of the instruments themselves. "Vīṇāmokkhā" and so forth are names of divine maidens.

"Sucimhitā" means "well-placed" (*suddhamihitā*), or it may simply be a proper name. "Muduvādinī" means she speaks with gentleness, thus she is "gentle-spoken"; she is one whose nature is to speak very softly.
Or it is merely a name. *Seyyāseti* means "better than a bed. *Accharānaṃ* means "among the celestial nymphs (*accharā*), they are more praiseworthy in song.

*Pabodhikā* means "those who cause awakening. 169. *Kālena* means "at the appropriate and opportune time. *Abhibhāsanti* means they speak while being face-to-face, or speaking with delight. To show how they speak, it is said: "Come, let us dance and sing; come, let us delight you. 170.
*Idaṃ* means "this place obtained by me. *Asokaṃ* refers to forms and so forth that are desirable, lovely, dear, and agreeable.
It is "free from sorrow" because it is possible [for such sorrow to be absent there]. Precisely because it increases joy at all times, it is "delightful" (*nandana*).
It is the "Great Forest of the Thirty-three" (*tāvatiṃsa*), the great and venerable park of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.

Having thus stated, by way of specific designation, that such celestial prosperity arises solely through meritorious karma, he then spoke the verse beginning with "Happiness for those who have not done merit" in order to show it by way of general designation.
172. Furthermore, preaching the Dhamma out of a desire for others to share in the divine state she herself has attained, she spoke the concluding verse beginning with “tesaṃ sahabyakāmānaṃ.
“Tesaṃ” means “of those,” namely the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. “Sahabyakāmānaṃ” means “by those desiring companionship”; this genitive case is used here in the sense of the agent (kattuatthe).

“Sahavo” means that which proceeds together; thus, one who desires such a state is called a “sahabya” (companion). Those who desire such companionship are “sahabyakāmā. It is these [gods] that are referred to.
The state of being that is "companionship" (*sahabya*), just as the state of a hero is "heroism" (*vīriya*).
Thus, when the deity had revealed her own meritorious deeds, the Elder taught the Dhamma to her and her retinue;
then, having returned from the world of the gods, he reported that occurrence to the Blessed One. The Blessed One [took] that matter as the occasion for the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
Having done so, he taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. That teaching was beneficial to the world including its devas.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Dāsivimāna*.
2. Commentary on the *Lakhumāvimāna*.

"By his surpassing beauty" refers to the *Lakhumā-vimāna*. What is its origin? While the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī, there was one gate of the city of Bārāṇasī named Kevaṭṭadvāra; the village situated not far from it was also known simply as "Kevaṭṭadvāra.
There, a certain woman named Lakhumā—faithful, confident, and endowed with wisdom—[lived] by that gate.
Seeing monks entering, she would greet them, lead them to her own home, and give them alms with a ladle;

through that very familiarity, as her faith increased, she had a rest-house built and there provided seats for the monks who entered, and set out drinking water and water for washing. Whatever rice, boiled grain, vegetables, and so forth she had herself—
Whatever was found in the house, she gave it to the bhikkhus. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus, she established herself in the refuges and the precepts;
becoming concentrated, she mastered the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna).

As she exerted herself in insight, due to her possession of the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), she before long became established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Later on, she passed away.
Having done so, she was reborn in a great celestial mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, and she had a retinue of a thousand nymphs.

There, experiencing divine splendor, she wandered about in delight. While wandering on his tour of the devas, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned her with the verses beginning, “With such surpassing beauty,” and so forth;
all of this is exactly as previously described. Thus it was said:
“O deity, with such exquisite beauty as you stand here,
illuminating all directions like a star among the herbs—
by what cause is your complexion so radiant? By what means is it perfected in you here?”
“And those riches arise for you, whatever is dear to the mind.
‘I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: when you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?’”
“Delighted, that deity, being questioned by Moggallāna,
answered the question asked, [explaining] the fruit of which karma this is:
‘Having gone out through the gateway of a fisherman, there was my dwelling.’”
There, as the disciples of the Great Sage were wandering about,
I gave them boiled rice, gruel, vegetables, and sour salt-water,
with a mind full of serene confidence toward those who had become upright.
"On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as during the fortnight of miracles, I shall observe the Uposatha fully endowed with its eight factors,
always restrained in my virtues."
“Through self-restraint and sharing, I dwell in a celestial mansion.
We abstained from taking life, were restrained from false speech,
and stayed far away from theft, sexual misconduct, and the drinking of intoxicants.”
“Delighting in the five precepts, skilled in the Noble Truths, [I am] a female lay follower of Gotama, the illustrious One with Vision.
Because of that, my complexion is such as this... my complexion shines forth in all directions.”
"And with my word, venerable sir, you should pay homage at the Blessed One’s feet with your head, saying:
‘Venerable sir, the female lay follower named Lakhumā pays homage at the Blessed One’s feet with her head.

It is not surprising, venerable sir, that the Blessed One would have declared me [to be established] in one of the fruits of recluseship; rather, it was the fruit of a once-returner that the Blessed One declared for me."
177. "Having gone out through the fishermen’s gate" means at the place of exit from the fishermen’s gate.

178. *Ḍāka* refers to vegetable side-dishes such as *taṇḍuleyyaka* (potherb) and the like. *Loṇasovīraka* is a certain beverage prepared with many ingredients such as grain broth and so forth; some also call it "rice-scum, sour gruel, and salt water.

At the conclusion of the question-and-answer session, she attained the fruit of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmiphala*) through the Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma. The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Uttarāvidhāna*.
The commentary on the *Lakhumā-vimāna* is concluded.
3. The commentary on the *Ācāmadāyikā-vimāna*:
"As you were wandering for alms... This is the *Ācāmadāyikā-vimāna*. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha.
In the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Now at that time, a certain family in Rājagaha was afflicted by a plague of snake-bite.
There, all the people had died except for one woman.
She abandoned her house and all the wealth and grain within it, and, terrified by the fear of death, she fled through a hole in the wall, left without a protector.

Having gone to another’s house, she lived on its back veranda. In that house, people, feeling compassion, gave her whatever remained of the rice gruel, cooked rice, and sour gruel in the cooking pots and other vessels. Having eaten that, she sustained her life.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa had entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) for seven days, and from there—
Having emerged from meditation, he thought, "Whom shall I assist today by accepting food? Whom can I deliver from poverty and suffering?
While reflecting thus, he saw that woman whose death was imminent and who had committed karma leading to rebirth in hell.
He perceived that once he had gone there, she would offer him the rice-gruel she had obtained; by that very act, she would be reborn in the Nimmānarati heaven.
"Since she will be reborn in hell, let me first release her from that rebirth in hell and then bring about for her the attainment of heaven.
Having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robes, he set out toward her residence.
Then Sakka, the lord of the devas, appearing in the guise of a stranger, offered him divine food of many flavors, accompanied by various soups and condiments.
Knowing this, the Elder rebuked him, saying, "Kosiya, you are skilled in performing deeds; why do you act thus?
Do not plunder the prosperity of those who are miserable and destitute! Having thus refused, he stood before that woman.
Seeing the Elder, she thought, "This is a powerful Elder; to him there is suitable food, whether hard or soft, to be given."

"Or rather, there is nothing here; this [food] contained in a defiled vessel is strewn with grass, husks, and dust, it is unsalted, cold, and of little flavor—merely a bit of rice-scum and sour gruel.
I cannot bring myself to give such as this," he thought, and said, "Please pass on.
The Elder stepped back only the distance of a single footstep and stood there. The householders then [offered] alms...

They brought it forward, but the Elder did not accept it. That woman of ill-repute, realizing, "He has come here solely out of compassion for me, desiring to receive only what belongs to me," became clear-minded and full of reverence;
she poured that rice-scum into the Elder’s bowl. To increase her faith, the Elder made a show of eating; the people [prepared] a seat.
They set it out. The Elder sat down there, ate that rice-gruel, drank [the broth], and when his hands were withdrawn from the bowl, he gave a blessing of thanksgiving.
He then said to that woman of wretched birth, "In your third future existence, you will be my mother," and departed.
Having conceived great faith in the Elder because of him, she passed away during the first watch of that night and was reborn among the Nimmānarati devas.
She was reborn into the company of the devas. Then Sakka, the king of the devas, having learned of her death, reflected, "Where has she been reborn?
Not seeing her among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, he approached the Venerable Mahākassapa during the middle watch of the night and, inquiring after the place of her rebirth, said:
“As you were walking for alms, standing there in silence, a poor and wretched woman, who had never seen another’s house,
gave you rice-scum with her own hands out of faith. “She who gave you that ācāma, with a mind full of confidence and with her own hands— ”
"Having abandoned her human body, to what destination has she gone?"—with these two verses he spoke. 185.
Therein, "for alms" (*piṇḍāya*) means for the sake of alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*). "Standing silent" (*tuṇhībhūtassa ṭhito*) is a description of the manner in which he was wandering for alms.
"Waiting for" means "waiting for [him]. "Poor" (*daliddā*) means those who are destitute. "Miserable" (*kapaṇā*) means wretched.
By the word "poor," he shows her loss of wealth; by the word "miserable," he shows her loss of kinsmen.
"Dependent on another's house" means relying on another's home, living in dependence upon the back wall and roof of others' houses.
186. "To what direction has she gone?"—to which direction has she gone by way of being reborn in the six heavenly worlds of the sense-sphere gods?

Thus Sakka, seeing that the Elder had bestowed such great favor upon her so that she was now partaking of sublime divine success yet could not be seen, asked this while remaining in doubt, as he did not see her in the two lower deva-worlds.
Then the elder said to him:
“While I was walking for alms, standing there in silence,
a poor and wretched woman, who had never seen another’s house, [offered me food].”
“She who gave me rice-scum with her own hands, full of faith—
having cast off this human body and passed away from here, she is now liberated.
There are gods of great psychic power named Nimmānarati.”

"In that regard, that woman was happy, rejoicing as she gave the *ācāma* (sour gruel)," he said, giving his reply according to the very order of the questions and describing the place where she had been reborn.
"There, she was 'completely freed' (*vippamuttā*): she was freed from, or departed from, that human wretchedness and that life of extreme misery."

189. "Modatā cāmadāyikā" means she was a giver of mere gruel; yet even she rejoices in divine prosperity in the fifth heaven of sensual bliss. This shows you, look, the fruit of the excellence of the field [of merit].
Then Sakka, having heard of the great fruit and great benefit of that gift, praised her, saying:
"Oh, the gift of this poor woman, well-established under Kassapa!"
Through this gift brought from afar, may the offering indeed be successful!
May that woman who rules as the chief queen of a wheel-turning monarch—
perfect in every limb and pleasing to her husband— [attain this success].
It does not equal even a sixteenth part of this gift of unboiled sour gruel.
“A hundred mares with gold ornaments, a hundred chariots drawn by mules,
and a hundred thousand maidens adorned with jeweled earrings— ”
They are not worth even a sixteenth part of this gift of fresh water.
“Hundred elephants from the Himavat mountains, with tusks like chariot-poles,
powerful, with golden girths, well-proportioned limbs, and clad in golden trappings;”
“Compared to this gift of *acāma*, it does not equal even a sixteenth part.
‘Even if one were to exercise sovereignty over all four continents,
that does not weigh even a sixteenth part against this gift of *acāma’— so he said.”
190. In this context, *ahoti* is a particle used in the sense of wonder.

*Varākiyā* means by a wretched woman. *Parābhūtena* means brought from elsewhere; the meaning is: obtained through the practice of begging from the houses of others. *Dānena* means by that which is to be given, even a mere gift of gruel-water.
*Ijjhittha vata dakkhiṇā* means: "Ah, the sacrificial gift—the act of giving—has indeed succeeded! Ah, it has become of great fruit!"
The meaning is: "They became possessed of great radiance and great expansion.
Now, in order to show that "even the woman-treasure and the others do not approach even a hundredth part or a thousandth part of that gift," it was said:
"She who would exercise the sovereignty of a queen," and so forth. Therein, "beautiful in all her limbs" means "neither too tall..."
"Not too tall, not too thin, not too stout, not too dark, and not too fair—having transcended human appearance yet not having reached divine appearance.
By all these limbs and reasons thus stated, or by all her major and minor limbs, she is beautiful, radiant, and lovely.
And "pleasing to the sight of her husband" means she is exceptionally beautiful and charming to the eyes of her spouse. Of this gift of ambrosia...

Regarding the phrase "it is not worth a sixteenth part": even the status of the woman-treasure (*itthiratana*) of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*) does not equal, does not enjoy, and does not attain even a sixteenth part—meaning a portion taken by dividing the fruit of this gift of rinsing-water (*ācāma-dāna*) given by her into sixteen parts, and then dividing that single part again into sixteen parts.
[As for the verse: "Fifteen *dharana* of gold..."
Some say they are "nikkhas," others say they are "satadharaṇas. 193.
*Hemavatā* means born in the Himavat mountains, or of Himalayan origin; for they are large and endowed with strength and speed.
*Īsādantā* means having tusks like the pole of a chariot; the meaning is that their tusks are slightly curved downward. By this, [the text] indicates their state of having broad, prominent tusks.
He restrains [them]. "Urūḷhava" means one who is increased by strength, speed, and prowess; the sense is that he is capable of bearing the great task of battle.
"Suvaṇṇakaccha" refers to one whose girth-band is adorned with a collar made of gold. For by the term "girth" (kaccha), all the equipment suitable for an elephant is meant.
"Hemakappanavāsasā" means endowed with hand-ornaments such as the elephant's saddle-cloth (kappana) and bracelets (kaṅkana), which are inlaid with gold.
194. "Lord of the four continents" refers to the sovereignty over the four great continents, such as Jambudīpa, each surrounded by two thousand minor islands.
By this, he describes the entire glory of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), resplendent with the seven treasures.
As for what remains here, it is exactly according to the method explained below.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera reported everything that had been said by Sakka, the King of the Devas, to the Blessed One.
Taking that as the occasion for instruction, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled company.
That teaching was of great benefit to the multitude.
The commentary on the Ācāmadāyikā-vimāna is finished.
4. The commentary on the Caṇḍālī-vimāna:
"O Caṇḍālī, worship my feet"—this is the Caṇḍālī-vimāna. How did it originate? While the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha...

At the hour of dawn, having entered the Great Compassion Absorption as practiced by the Buddhas and then arising, he surveyed the world and saw an old Caṇḍāla woman living in a Caṇḍāla dwelling in that very city, whose life-span was exhausted and whose karma leading to hell had manifested.
With his mind impelled by great compassion, [he resolved]: "May she attain a state leading to heaven..."
Thinking, "Having caused her to perform [meritorious] deeds,
I shall prevent her rebirth in hell and establish her in heaven," he entered Rājagaha for alms together with a great community of monks. At that time,
as the Caṇḍālī woman was coming out of the city leaning on a staff, she saw the Blessed One approaching and stood facing him.
She stood there. The Blessed One also stood before her as if to prevent her departure.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, knowing the Teacher’s mind and perceiving that her life-span was exhausted, directed her toward the worship of the Blessed One, saying:
“O Caṇḍālī, worship the feet of the illustrious Gotama!”
Out of compassion for her, the Seventh Sage stood [there] and spoke these two verses:
“Place your mind in full confidence in the Arhat, the Neutral One (Tādin);
quickly pay homage with palms joined, for your life is at its end.”
195. Therein, he addresses her by the name "Caṇḍālī," which has come down through birth. "Vanda" means pay homage.
"Pādāni" refers to the feet that are the refuge for the world including its devas. "Tameva anukampāya" means for the sake of favoring her; the intention is:
for the purpose of preventing her from rebirth in the states of misery (apāya) and causing her to be reborn in heaven. "Aṭṭhāsi" [means] he stood [over] the city as well.
He stood there without entering [the village]. "The seventh among sages" (*isisattama*) means the most excellent and supreme among worldly learners, those beyond learning, and paccekabuddhas;
or alternatively, he is the seventh among the Buddhas, such as Vipassī and the others, thus "the seventh sage.
196. "Inspire your mind with confidence" means: inspire your heart with the thought, "The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One. In the Arhat...

"Tādinī" (one who is such) refers to one who is an *arahant* because of being far from the defilements (*kilesa*), because those very enemies have been slain, because the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have been destroyed, because of having reached worthiness (*araha*) regarding conditions, and because of the absence of secrecy (*raha*) in performing evil deeds;

and it refers to "one who is such" (*tādin*) due to having attained a state of suchness (*tādibhāva*) toward desirable objects and so forth. "Quickly, with palms joined, pay homage" means: quickly indeed, having placed your hands together in the gesture of reverence (*añjali*), pay homage. Why?
"Short is your life"—because its nature is to break up this very moment, it is short and exceedingly brief.

Thus, by means of these two verses, the Elder, extolling the virtues of the Blessed One and standing upon his own spiritual power, inspired her with a sense of urgency by revealing that her lifespan was exhausted, and directed her toward paying homage to the Teacher. Having heard this, she was filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

With a mind full of faith toward the Teacher, she prostrated herself with the fivefold salutation, joined her palms in reverence, and stood there with a one-pointed mind filled with joy directed toward the Buddha.

The Blessed One, thinking, "This much is sufficient for her rebirth in heaven," entered the city together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then, a certain exhausted cow with a young calf followed after them from there.
As she was thus rushing forward, he struck her with his horn and took her life. To show all of this, the compilers of the collection said:
“Urged on by him whose mind was cultivated, the bearer of his final body, the Caṇḍālī woman paid homage at the feet of the illustrious Gotama.”
“Then the cow killed him, though he stood with palms joined, paying homage to the Fully Awakened One, the light-bringer in the darkness. Thus they spoke these two verses.

(198) Therein, regarding the phrase “standing with palms joined, paying homage to the Fully Awakened One,” even though the Blessed One had already departed, [his mind remained] directed toward the Buddha as its object.
Having become concentrated through rapture, she stood paying homage with palms joined as if face to face.
"In darkness" means in a world shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and the entire darkness of the defilements. "Light-maker" means one who creates the radiance of knowledge.
Having passed away from there, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, and a retinue of one hundred thousand celestial nymphs attended upon her.
And on that very day, she came together with her celestial mansion, descended from the mansion, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and paid homage to him. To illustrate this matter:
“To the one whose taints are exhausted, free from passion, unshakable, sitting alone in seclusion in the forest;”
"Having attained divine power, I have approached you; I pay homage to you, O Hero of great majesty," said the deity. The Elder questioned her:
"O one of golden hue, radiant and of great fame, having ascended a celestial mansion of manifold splendor..."
“Surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, who are you, O auspicious goddess, that pays homage to me?
In this context: *jalitā* means shining and illuminating with the radiance of her own body and the luster of her garments, ornaments, and so forth.
*Mahāyasā* means having a great retinue. *Vimānamoruyhā* means having descended from her celestial mansion (*vimāna*). *Anekacittā* means endowed with manifold mental states.
“Subhā” means one possessing beautiful qualities. “Mamam” means me.
Thus questioned again by the Elder, she said:
“I am a Caṇḍālī, O Blessed One, sent by you, the Hero.”
I paid homage at the feet of the Arahat Gotama, the illustrious one.
Having paid homage at his feet and passed away from the womb of a caṇḍāla,
I have been reborn in the Nandana grove in a celestial mansion auspicious on all sides.
“Standing before a hundred thousand nymphs,
I am their most excellent and best, in beauty, fame, and life-span.
Having performed many deeds of merit, I am clearly comprehending and mindful.”
“We have come, venerable sir, to pay homage to the Sage, the compassionate one in the world.
Thus she spoke these four verses (201–4).
Therein, “sent forth” means urged toward paying homage by [the words] beginning with, “Caṇḍālī, pay homage at his feet. Even though...
That merit consisting of homage is small by way of the moment of its occurrence;
however, because of the greatness of the field and the greatness of the fruit, it is exceedingly great—thus he said, "having performed much that is wholesome.
Likewise, with reference to the clarity of wisdom and mindfulness at the moment of the occurrence of joy directed toward the Buddha, he said, "clearly comprehending and mindful. Furthermore—
“Having said this, the Caṇḍālī, grateful and mindful of what had been done for her,
bowed at the feet of the Arahant and vanished right there.”—
This verse was placed by the compilers of the collection.

205. And herein, she is called “Caṇḍālī” because she had previously been a Caṇḍālī; this is stated as a conventional usage based on a designation well-known in the human world, even though it is customary in the world of the gods to use such terms. The rest is exactly as already explained.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reported this occurrence to the Blessed One. Taking that matter as the occasion for a discourse, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the assembled company, and that teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The commentary on the Caṇḍālī-vimāna is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Bhadditthi-vimāna:
"Blue, yellow, and black"—this is the Bhadditthi-vimāna. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
At that time, in the city of Kimilā, there was a householder’s son named Rohaka.
He was faithful and confident, endowed with virtue and good conduct.
In that very city, there was a young woman from a family of equal wealth and status who was likewise faithful and confident; she was naturally so virtuous that she was known by the name Bhaddā.
Then Rohaka’s parents, having sought out that maiden, brought her at an appropriate time and performed the marriage ceremony.
Both of them lived together in harmony. Because of her own perfection in conduct, she became well-known and famous in that city as "Bhadditthī" (the Fortunate Woman).
At that time, two chief disciples, each with a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus, were wandering through the countryside.
While traveling, they arrived at the city of Kimila. Rohaka, learning that they had reached that place, was filled with joy;
he approached the elders, paid homage to them, and invited them for the following day.
On the second day, having satisfied them and their retinue with excellent hard and soft foods, he and his wife and children listened to the Dhamma teaching bestowed by them.
Establishing himself in their instruction, he took the refuges and undertook the five precepts.
His wife, moreover, observed the Uposatha on the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, and the day of the miracle;
she was especially endowed with virtue and conduct and was protected by the deities. And through that very protection of the deities, the false accusation that had fallen upon him—
Due to her perfectly pure conduct and virtue, she became exceedingly renowned throughout the world.
