While she herself was staying in the city of Kimila, her husband—who was residing in Takkasilā for the sake of trade—developed a desire for a festival celebration on a holiday when incited by his companions; then, [the house deity] spoke to her...
By means of her divine power, she was led there and united with her husband; through that very union, she became pregnant.
She was then escorted back to the city of Kimilā by the deity. When her state of pregnancy eventually became apparent, her mother-in-law and others suspected her of being unchaste.
Then, by the power of that same deity, [she was carried] across the great flood of the Ganges to the city of Kimilā.
Having turned back the great flood of the Ganges— which was surging toward her like a mass of waves stirred by the force of the wind—
with an oath preceded by a solemn declaration of truth that indicated her own state of devotion and appeared as if it were spreading over her,
she was reunited with her husband; yet even then, she remained suspicious of him, just as she had been previously suspected by her mother-in-law and others in Takkasilā.
They placed the signet ring and the token given by him there; having dispelled that suspicion, she became highly esteemed by her husband, his kinsmen, and the public.
Therefore it was said: "By virtue of her perfectly pure conduct and behavior, she became exceedingly renowned in the world."
At a later time, having passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Then, when the Blessed One had gone from Sāvatthī to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and was seated upon the yellow sandalwood stone at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree, the assembly of devas approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side; and Bhadditthī also approached.

Having paid homage, he stood to one side. Then the Blessed One, in the midst of the assembly of devas and brahmās gathered from the ten thousand world-systems, asked that deity about the meritorious deed she had performed:
“Blue, yellow, black, madder-red, and crimson;”
Surrounded by the pollen of various flowers,
you bear upon your head a garland of mandārava blossoms.
O wise one, such trees as these do not exist among other bodies.
“By what means were you reborn in the glorious Tāvatiṃsa realm?
O devatā, being questioned, tell me: of what karma is this the fruit?”—thus he spoke. 206–7.
Regarding the passage: “Blue, yellow, black, madder-red, and then crimson”—here the word *ca* (and) functions as a conjunction of the meanings already stated.
This should be applied individually with "blue," "yellow," and so forth. The word *atha* is a particle used in the sense of "other than" (*aññatthe*).

By it, it includes the unmentioned colors such as white (*odāta*) and others. The word *iti* should be understood as being indicated by elision (*luttaniddiṭṭha*). Alternatively, the word *ca* is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) for the unmentioned meanings.
The word *atha* is a particle in the sense of the word *iti*. Regarding the phrase "of high and low colors" (*uccāvacānaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ*), here *uccāvacānaṃ* is [the stem] of the case ending.
*Alopa* should be understood [as *alopena*]; the meaning is "of various colors," that is, of high and low colors.
Or, "of colors" (*vaṇṇānaṃ*) means "of those possessing color. "Encircled by filaments" (*kiñjakkhaparivāritā*) means "surrounded by filaments";
for this is a nominative case used in the sense of the genitive. This is what is meant: blue and yellow, black and madder-red, crimson and then others such as white.
O Devatā, you wear upon your head—meaning you have adorned yourself with—the garland, that is, the string of flowers made from those blossoms;

these flowers are of various heights and colors, surrounded by filaments (kiñjakkha) and stamens (kesara) of corresponding types, or they possess diverse shapes and so forth, and they are produced from Mandārava trees, thus they are "Mandārava" flowers. You bear this garland fashioned from them upon your own head.
In order to show that those flowers, because of their distinctive color, are not shared by other [trees], it is said:

“These trees do not exist in other bodies, O wise one. Therein, the construction is: “These”—meaning trees possessing flowers endowed with the aforementioned colors, shapes, and so forth—“do not exist.
“In bodies” means among the classes of deities. “O wise one” (sumedhasa) means one of beautiful wisdom.
In this context, "blue" means having a blue luster due to gems such as sapphire (*indanīla*) and great sapphire (*mahānīla*).

"Yellow" means having a yellow luster due to gems such as *puppharāga*, *kakketana*, and *pulaka*, as well as yellow gold (*siṅgīsuvaṇṇa*). "Black" means having a black luster due to gems such as *asmaka* and *upala*.
"Madder-red" (*mañjiṭṭha*) means having a madder-red luster due to gems such as *jotirasa*, *gomuttaka*, and *gomedaka*. "Red" (*lohita*)...

They have a reddish luster by way of gems such as ruby (*padumarāga*), ruby-red (*lohitanka*), and coral (*pavāḷa*). However, some explain by connecting the words "blue" and so forth with the word "trees," as in "blue trees" and so on.
For even trees, being covered with flowers of blue and other colors, receive the designation "blue" and so forth through their association with those colors;
thus, according to them, [the phrase] "blue... pe... red... pe... [applies here, and] these [colors] are not found in other bodies.
The construction should be made thus: “O wise one, there are trees, since you wear a garland of *mandārava* flowers, which are surrounded by filaments and possess various colors.
Therein, the first method demonstrates the uniqueness of the trees by praising the flowers endowed with specific colors as they were seen, thereby showing their uncommon nature.
The second method demonstrates the exclusive nature of the flowers by showing the non-commonality of the trees.
In the first method, color and other qualities are taken in their own form (*sarūpena*); in the second method, they are taken by way of their support (*nissayamukhena*).

This is the distinction between them. 208. "By what" means by what meritorious deed; the construction is: "to the Tāvatiṃsa [heaven]. "Being asked, explain" means: you, being asked, explain—that is, speak.
Thus questioned by the Blessed One, that deity replied with these verses:
“They know me as Bhadditthikā, a lay follower from Kimilā;
Endowed with faith and virtue, I am always delighted in sharing.”
“Clothing and food, lodgings and lamps,
I gave to those who were upright, with a mind full of serene confidence.
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,”
And on the fortnight of miracles, perfectly endowed with the eight factors:
“I shall observe the Uposatha, always restrained by moral precepts;
being self-controlled and generous, I shall dwell in a celestial mansion.”
“Abstaining from taking life, restrained from false speech,
far removed from theft, sexual misconduct, and the drinking of intoxicants;
delighting in the five precepts and skilled in the Noble Truths.”
“As a female lay follower dwelling in heedfulness under the One with Vision,
having completed my residence and performed wholesome deeds, I have passed away from there and now roam at will in Nandana,
self-luminous. I also fed a pair of ascetics, monks who were supremely compassionate for our welfare, along with the Great Sage.”
“Having completed my dwelling and performed wholesome deeds, passing away from there, I now roam at will in Nandana, self-luminous.
I constantly observed the Uposatha, which possesses eight factors, is immeasurable, and brings happiness;
having completed my dwelling and performed wholesome deeds, passing away from there, I now roam at will in Nandana, self-luminous.”
209–214. Regarding the passage beginning with "There they knew me as Bhadditthikā" and "the lay follower of Kimilā":

because of her perfection in conduct and because she had turned back the great flood that was rising through her *saccakiriyā* (act of truth), the inhabitants of the city of Kimilā came to know me as "the lay follower Bhadditthikā," having reached the firm conviction that this woman was auspicious (*bhaddā*) and beautiful (*sundarā*), and thus possessed of unbroken virtue (*akhaṇḍasīla*). [The rest of the passage begins: "Endowed with faith and virtue," and so forth.
Because it follows the method explained below, its meaning is self-evident.
Furthermore, by the word "faith" (*saddhā*), the treasure of faith is indicated;

by the verse, "I gave with a serene mind to those who were upright—gifts of sharing, clothing, food, lodgings, and lamps," the treasure of generosity (*cāga*) is indicated; and by "endowed with virtue" (*sīlena sampannā*), [the treasure of virtue is indicated].

By the words, “Delighting in the fourteenth and fifteenth [days]... devoted to the five training rules,” the wealth of virtue (*sīladhana*), the wealth of moral shame (*hiridhana*), and the wealth of moral dread (*ottappadhana*) are shown;

by the words, “Skilled in the Noble Truths,” the wealth of learning (*sutadhana*) and the wealth of wisdom (*paññādhana*) are shown—thus she demonstrated her own attainment of the sevenfold noble wealth (*ariyadhana*).

By the words, “I am a female lay follower of the One with Vision... I roam about in the Nandana Grove,” she demonstrated his [the Buddha’s] benefits pertaining both to this present life and to future lives.
He clarifies the benefit. In this context, "those who have made their dwelling" (*katāvāsā*) means those who have established a dwelling for good conduct.

For wholesome action is called "the dwelling of happy abiding" because it is the cause of a happy dwelling both in this life and in the future. Therefore, he said, "those who have performed what is skillful.

Having first described his own merit consisting of giving toward a specific field of merit not previously mentioned, he now describes its quality of being directed toward a worthy recipient (*āyatanagatatā*).
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “bhikkhū ca” was spoken. Therein, “bhikkhū” means those who are monks by virtue of having completely shattered the defilements.
“Paramahitānukampako” means one who assists others with the highest benefit, such as that pertaining to the present life and so forth.
“Abhojayiṃ” means I fed them with excellent food. “Tapassiyugaṃ” means a pair [of ascetics] who, having scorched the stains of all defilements with supreme austerity...
Because he stands having utterly severed [the defilements], he has become an ascetic (*tapassin*); thus he is called a "Great Sage" (*mahāmuni*).
Alternatively, he is a "Great Sage" because he is a great seer (*mahesi*), or because he is a sage (*muni*) who discerns and delimits his own vast domain through his own vast knowledge.
All of this is said with reference to the two chief disciples.
216. It is stated as *aparimitaṃ sukhāvahaṃ* without eliding the nasal (*anunāsika*).

Because of the statement, “To such an extent, monks, it is not easy to reach through description the happiness of the heavenly realms,” it brings about immeasurable happiness that transcends the path of words even for the Blessed One;
or, by its own power, it brings about immeasurable happiness, being the carrier of happiness. *Satataṃ* means at all times.

The construction is as follows: by not neglecting each respective day for observing the Uposatha, or by making each respective day for observing the Uposatha unbroken and complete, it brings happiness constantly or at all times. The remainder is exactly as explained below.
Then the Blessed One [addressed] the assembly of devas and brahmas dwelling in the ten-thousandfold world system, headed by the divine son Mātādevaputta.
Having taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka for three months, he returned to the human world and taught the Bhadditthi-vimāna to the monks.
That teaching was beneficial to the assembled assembly.
Thus ends the commentary on the Bhadditthi-vimāna.
6. Commentary on the *Soṇadinnā-vimāna*:
"With surpassing beauty" refers to the *Soṇadinnā-vimāna*. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, there was a female lay follower named Soṇadinnā in Nāḷandā, who was faithful and confident in the monks.
Attending upon him with due care through the four conditions and possessing perfectly purified perpetual virtue, she observed the Uposatha endowed with its eight factors.

Having obtained the favorable condition for hearing the Dhamma, she cultivated the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths through her possession of the necessary supporting causes and became a stream-enterer. Then, she was afflicted by a certain disease.
Having passed away, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw her and said:
“O goddess, you who stand there with such exquisite beauty, illuminating all directions like a star among the herbs.”
“By what means is your complexion so radiant? By what means do you prosper here?
And how do those enjoyments arise for you that are dear to the mind?
I ask you, O goddess of great majesty: when you were a human being, what merit did you perform?”
“By what means have you become so radiant in power, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?”—
with these three verses he questioned her.
That deity, being delighted, was thus questioned by Moggallāna.
“Being questioned, she answered: ‘Of what karma is this the fruit?
‘They knew me as Soṇadinnā... [as described] ...of the illustrious Gotama.
‘Because of that, my complexion is such as this... and my complexion shines in all directions.’”
The deity explained [the matter]. All of that is exactly according to the method stated below.
The commentary on the Soṇadinnā-vimāna is finished.
7. Commentary on the Uposatha-vimāna.
“With surpassing beauty” refers to the Uposatha Vimāna. Here, in the origin story, the specific distinction is that there was a certain female lay follower (upāsikā) named Uposatha at Sāketa;
the rest is similar to the immediately preceding vimāna.
Therefore it is said: “With surpassing beauty... your radiance illuminates all directions.”
“Delighted, that deity... [said: ‘This is the fruit of such karma.
‘They knew me as Uposatha, this lay follower from Sāketa...
[a follower] of Gotama, the illustrious One with Vision.’”
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this...
[and so on] ...and my complexion shines in all directions.
Thus the deity answered. Then, pointing out one of her own faults—
“Having repeatedly heard of Nandana, desire arose within me;
having directed my mind toward it, I have been reborn in Nandana.
I did not follow the word of the Teacher, the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.”
“Having set my heart on what is lowly, I am now filled with remorse”—with these two verses she spoke.
(233) Therein, “They knew me as ‘Uposathā’” means that people recognized her by the name “Uposathā. “In Sāketa” means in the city of Sāketa.
(241) “Frequently” means often. “Hearing of Nandana” refers to the grove named Nandana in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
"Of such and such a kind"—having heard there of various kinds of divine prosperity.

*Chando* means either the wholesome desire (*kusalacchanda*) that serves as the cause for the meritorious deed producing that state, or the craving-desire (*taṇhāchanda*) consisting of the aspiration for rebirth there.
*Udapajjatha* means it arose. *Tattha* means in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; for he refers to that celestial world even by way of the Nandana Grove.
“I have been reborn” means I have arisen, I have been produced.
“I did not do the Teacher’s bidding” means I did not act upon the words spoken by the Teacher, beginning with, “Monks, I do not praise even the slightest state of existence”;
the meaning is that I did not abandon desire and lust for states of existence. Ādicca is of the Gotama clan.
The Blessed One is also called "of the Gotama clan" because of their shared lineage, as stated in the verse: "Of the Buddha, the kinsman of the Ādiccas.

Alternatively, he is the "kinsman of the Ādiccas" (Ādiccabandhu) because he is the kinsman of the Ādicca [clan]. Or, because he was born into that noble birth in dependence upon him, or because the Ādicca is his kinsman by virtue of being his legitimate son, he is the Blessed One, the "kinsman of the Ādiccas. For it has been said:
“He who makes light in the darkness and gloom, Vairocana, the radiant one with his orb and fierce splendor—O Rāhu, do not swallow him as he moves through the sky!
O Rāhu, release my progeny, the Sun! “Hīne” means base or lowly.
He speaks this with reference to his own delight in existence (*bhava*). “Sāmhī” means “I am that.”
When the deity had thus expressed her remorse regarding her delight in existence,
the Elder comforted her by explaining that it is easier to transcend the suffering of the round of rebirth by remaining in a human state in the future—
thereby demonstrating the limited duration of life in existence— and by pointing out that the state of one whose taints are entirely exhausted is of great benefit.
“How long will you remain here in this celestial mansion on the auspicious uposatha day?
O deity, being asked, tell me if you know [the duration] of your life.
Thus he spoke this verse. Again, she—
“Having stayed here for sixty thousand years and thirty million years,
O Great Sage, when I pass away from this state,
I shall go to the company of human beings,” he said.
Again the Elder said:
“Do not fear on the Uposatha day; you have been declared by the Perfectly Enlightened One to be a stream-enterer, distinguished, with the miserable states abandoned.”
With this verse he inspired him. 243–4.
In that context, *kīva ciraṃ* means "for how long a duration"? *Idha* means "in this world of the gods" or "here in this celestial mansion.
*Āyu no* means "the lifespan"; *no* is merely a particle. It refers either to the length or brevity of the lifespan, or alternatively, it means "if you know the lifespan."
The meaning [is as follows]. "O Great Sage" (Mahāmuni) is an address to the Elder.
245. "Do not fear on the Uposatha day": O Bhaddā, do not be afraid on the Uposatha day. Why? Because you have been declared [as such] by the Fully Enlightened One (Sambuddha). How so?
"You have attained distinction"—that is, you have reached and realized the distinction known as the path and its fruit; therefore...
"All your miserable rebirths have been abandoned"—he distinguished [the Buddha] by adding this further distinction as well. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Uposatha-vimāna is finished.
8–9. Commentary on the Niddā and Suniddā-vimānas.
The eighth and ninth Vimānas have Rājagaha as their nidāna. In the *Aṭṭhuppatti*, they should be stated respectively as:
“The laywoman named Niddā... [and so on] ...of the illustrious Gotama. Because of that, my complexion is such as this... [and so on] ...the laywoman named Suniddā.
The remainder is exactly according to the method already stated. There is nothing new even in the verses; for indeed, in some manuscripts, the Pāli is presented by way of abbreviation (*peyyāla*).
"She was established [in this way]. Therefore it was said:
"With a most excellent complexion... your complexion illuminates all directions."
“Delighted, that deity... [this is the fruit of such karma].
“They knew me as Nandā, a lay follower in Rājagaha...
[of the illustrious Gotama].”
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this… [and so on] …and my complexion illuminates all directions.
“With a most excellent complexion… [and so on] …it illuminates all directions.
“That deity was uplifted in mind… [and so on].”
“In Rājagaha, they knew me as Suniddā, a female lay follower...
[of] the illustrious Gotama.
Because of that, my complexion is such as this...”
"And my radiance shines in all directions.
The commentary on the *Niddā-suniddā-vimāna* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Paṭhamabhikkhādāyikā-vimāna*.
"By her exquisite beauty" refers to the *Vimānavatthu* on the Almsgiver Woman (*bhikkhādāyikā*). What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, in Uttaramadhurā, a certain woman had reached the end of her lifespan and was destined to be reborn in a state of woe (*apāya*).
At the hour of dawn, the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*), surveyed the world...

Beholding that woman, he saw that she was destined for rebirth in the woeful states; his mind stirred by great compassion and desiring to establish her in a happy destination, he went alone and unaccompanied to a sweet-smelling place.
Having gone there, at the time of the morning meal, he dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered the city for alms. At that time, that woman was preparing food in her house.
Having prepared [the food] and set it aside in a secluded spot, she took her water-jar and went to a watering place.
After bathing and filling her jar with water, she was walking along the road toward her own home when she saw the Blessed One.
She asked, "Venerable Sir, have you received any alms? When the Blessed One replied, "I shall receive some," she realized that he had received nothing and [set out with her] jar.
Setting aside her usual duties, she approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and said, "Venerable sir, I shall give you almsfood;
please accept it. The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Knowing that he had consented, she went ahead, prepared a seat in a place that was sprinkled and swept, and stood waiting for the Blessed One’s arrival.
The Blessed One entered the house and sat down on the prepared seat. Then she fed the Blessed One.
When the Blessed One had finished his meal, he set aside his bowl and hands, and after giving her a blessing, he departed.
Having heard the blessing, she experienced no small measure of joy and gladness, and until the Buddha had passed from her sight, she kept the Buddha as her mental object.

Not abandoning her joy, she stood there paying homage. After the passing of only a few days, she died and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, where she had a retinue of a thousand celestial nymphs (accharās). The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw her and said:
"With a most excellent complexion... like a medicinal herb among the stars."
“By what means do you have such a complexion… [as in the verse] …and your complexion illuminates all directions?”— thus he questioned him with verses.
“The deity, being delighted… [as in the verse] …this is the fruit of that deed.”
“In a former birth, while among humans in the world of men,
I saw the stainless Buddha, serene and untroubled.”
I gave him almsfood with my own hands out of faith.
“Because of that, such is my complexion...
[and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.”
The deity explained [the matter]. Since the rest is all according to the method already stated below, its meaning is self-evident.
The commentary on the First Almsgiver’s Mansion is finished.
11. Commentary on the Second Almsgiver’s Mansion.
"By your exquisite beauty" refers to the *Vimānavatthu* story of the second alms-giver. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha.
There, a certain woman, faithful and confident, saw a certain elder whose taints were destroyed wandering for alms;
she invited him into her own house and gave him food. At a later time, she passed away.
She was reborn in the Abode of the Thirty-three. The rest is exactly as in the immediately preceding vimāna:
“With surpassing beauty... [she] illuminates all directions.
“That deity, joyful... [is the result] of that karma whose fruit is this.”
“I was born among humans as a human being...
[and so on] ...and my beauty shines forth in all directions.
The commentary to the second Vimāna of the Almsgiver of Food is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the meaning of the second chapter, the Cittalatā-vagga, adorned with eleven stories, within the Vimānavatthu of the Paramatthadīpanī,
the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.
3. The Chapter on the Pāricchattaka Tree.
1. Commentary on the *Uḷāravimāna*:
In the Pāricchattaka Chapter, the *Uḷāravimāna* begins with the words, "Exalted is your fame and your beauty. How did it originate? The Blessed One...
The Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
At that time, in a family that supported the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in Rājagaha, there was a young girl who was inclined toward giving and delighted in sharing.
Whatever hard or soft food arose in that house before the meal, she would set aside half of her own portion for it.
She gives; she enjoys half herself, but she does not eat without having given.
Even when she does not see those worthy of offerings, she sets aside [the portion] and gives it at the time she sees them; she gives even to beggars.
Then her mother, delighted and joyful, thinking, "My daughter has a disposition for giving and delights in sharing," gives her a double portion. And while giving, in one portion...
When she had shared [the food] with him, he gave more again, and she likewise shared it out from that as well.
As time passed in this manner, when she reached marriageable age, her parents gave her to a youth in a certain family in that very city.
However, that family was of wrong view, lacking faith and confidence. Then the Venerable One...
While Mahāmoggallāna was walking for alms from house to house in Rājagaha, he stood at the door of that girl’s father-in-law’s house.

Seeing him, the girl, with a heart full of faith, said, “Enter, venerable sir,” and having ushered him in and paid her respects, she realized she had not seen the cake placed there by her mother-in-law.
Thinking, “I will tell her and have her offer a blessing,” she did so with confidence.
Having taken it, she gave it to the Elder; the Elder, having offered words of thanksgiving, departed.
The girl told her mother-in-law, "The cake you set aside you gave to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Upon hearing this, she cried out in indignation, "What kind of insolence is this?
He has given my property to a recluse without even asking my permission! and she began to beat her breast.
Overcome by anger and failing to consider what was appropriate or inappropriate, she took a piece of a pestle standing before her and struck him on the shoulder.
Because of her delicate nature and because her life-span was exhausted, she was overcome by intense pain from that very blow;
after only a few days, she passed away and was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Even though she possessed other deeds of good conduct, [she was reborn there solely due to this act].
The gift given by the elder appeared with exceptional splendor. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having gone there in the manner described above, said:
“Exalted is your fame and renown; all the quarters are illuminated.”
Women dance and sing, and adorned sons of the gods rejoice and attend upon you in worship, O deity;
these golden celestial mansions are yours, O Sudassanā.
“You are the mistress of those [beings], successful in all your desires;
you are of noble birth and great, rejoicing in the host of gods.
O deity, being questioned, tell us: of what karma is this the fruit?”
He asked with three verses.
286. Therein, *yasas* means retinue. *Vaṇṇa* means complexion, the radiance of the body’s appearance.
Because it is stated specifically as "exalted" (*uḷāra*), both that deity’s excellence of retinue and excellence of complexion are expressed. Among those, "exalted..."
Having briefly stated the perfection of complexion with the words "Your complexion," [the text] says "all directions shine" to show that perfection of complexion in detail by way of its object;

then, having stated the perfection of retinue with the words "Your glory is sublime," [the text] says "women dance" and so forth to show that perfection of retinue in detail by way of its basis. Therein, "all directions shine" means in all directions.

It shines; it illuminates all directions; the meaning is "it causes to shine. Regarding the word *obhāsate*, some explain its meaning as *obhāsante* through a grammatical transposition (*vacanavipallāsa*);
by them, the case ending of the word *vaṇṇena* must be transformed.
Furthermore, *vaṇṇena* is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is "by means of color as a cause. And regarding the phrase *sabbā disā*:
When the commonality of direction is intended by way of genus (*jāti*), there is no purpose even for a change in the grammatical number.
In the word *nāriyo* (women), the word *alaṅkatā* (adorned) should also be brought forward and connected. In the word *devaputtā* (sons of gods), the particle *ca* is indicated as elided;
by that, a conjunction should be understood as "women and sons of gods."
287. "Modenti" means they gladden. "Pūjāya" means for the purpose of worship or on account of worship; the construction is: "they dance and sing. "Tavimāni" means "these [songs] of yours. 288.
"Sabbakāmasamiddhini" means perfected with all five strands of sensual pleasure, or perfected with all things desired and wished for by you.
"Abhijātā" means well-born. "Mahantāsī" means you are great, possessed of great power, in the body of a deva.
"You rejoice": you rejoice with supreme joy caused by divine excellence in this host of devas.
Thus questioned by the Elder, that deity explained the matter:
"When I was among humans, having been born as a human in the world of men in a previous birth..."
I was a daughter-in-law in a family lacking virtue, among those who were faithless and miserly. But now,
endowed with faith and moral conduct, always delighting in sharing,
I gave you a cake as you were wandering for alms.
“Then I told my mother-in-law: ‘A recluse has come here;
with my own hands, full of faith, I gave him a cake.
But her mother-in-law reviled me: ‘You are ill-mannered, daughter-in-law!’”
"She did not wish to ask me, 'I am giving this to the ascetic.
Thereupon my mother-in-law became enraged and struck me with a pestle;
she crushed my head and killed me, so that I was unable to live for long."
“When my body broke up and I passed away from there,
I was released and reborn into the company of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Because of that, such is my complexion…” [and so on].
"And my complexion shines in all directions.

(289) Therein, "among those lacking faith" means among those who lack faith in the Three Jewels and faith in the results of kamma; among those who are miserly due to stubborn avarice—such as mothers-in-law and others—I was endowed with faith and virtue. This is the construction. (290–1) "Apūva" means a cake baked in a pan.
"Tena" is merely a particle. The intention is that she informed her mother-in-law of the fact that [the food] had been taken, and for the purpose of expressing gratitude.
292. *Itissā* means "to her. Here, *assā* is merely a particle. Regarding *samaṇassa dadāmaham*: "I am giving a cake to the ascetic. The construction is:
"Because he did not wish to question me, therefore you, daughter-in-law, are ill-mannered," thus the mother-in-law reproached her.

293. *Pahāsī* means she struck. In the phrase *kūṭaṅgacchi avadhi maṃ*, the word *kūṭa* refers to the shoulder-blade (*aṃsakūṭa*), with the first part of the compound elided. She struck me on the shoulder-blade.
“Kūṭaṅga” means that which has a peak (kūṭa) as its limb (aṅga); one who cuts that is a “kūṭaṅgacchi. Thus, having been overcome by anger, she killed me;
she cut off the peak of my shoulder. The meaning is that because of that very act, she caused my death.
Therefore he said: “I was not able to live for long.”
294. "Vippamuttā" means completely liberated from that suffering. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the *Uḷāravimāna* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Ucchudāyikāvimāna*.

"Having illuminated the earth together with its devas"—this is the *Ucchudāyikā-vimāna*. What is its origin? "The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha," and so forth—all is identical to what was stated in the immediately preceding *vimāna*.
However, this is the distinction: here, sugarcane was given [to her], and she was struck by her mother-in-law with a bench;
at that very moment she died and was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, on that very same night.

Having come to attend upon the Elder, illuminating the entirety of Vulture Peak like the moon and like the sun, she paid homage to the Elder and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence. Then the Elder said to her:
“Having illuminated the earth together with its devas, you outshine the moon and the sun;”
“In glory, beauty, fame, and splendor, you are like Brahmā among the thirty-three gods and their lord.
I ask you, O wearer of the lotus garland, adorned with a head-ornament, whose skin is like refined gold—
you who are so well-adorned and wear exquisite garments— who are you, O radiant goddess, that pays me homage?”
“What deed did you perform for yourself in the past, when you were a human being in a former birth?
Was it a gift well-bestowed, or was it the restraint of moral conduct? By what means have you been reborn in this fortunate realm, O illustrious one?
O deity, being questioned, tell us: of what karma is this the fruit?”
He asked with these verses.

296–7. Therein, "having illuminated the earth together with the devas" means that because it was shining forth with floods of radiance issuing from the slopes of Sineru, mixed with the rays of the moon and sun, it was the terrestrial region reached by the devas along with the sky; thus, it is "together with the devas."
The meaning is: having illuminated this earth, having made it a single radiance and a single light.

The construction is: "having caused the earth to shine like the moon and sun. "Atirocasi" means you shine surpassing [all others]. To the question, "By what means, like what, and in what manner do you thus outshine them?
he says "By glory," and so forth. Therein, "by glory" (siriyā) means by a particular excellence of splendor such as supreme fortune and the like.
“By majesty” means by her own power. “Wearing a fillet” means possessing a flower-fillet made of jewels.
Thus questioned by the Elder, the deity replied with these verses:
“Just now, venerable sir, you came to this very village for alms, having approached our house.”
Then, with a mind full of faith and incomparable joy, she gave a piece of sugarcane to him.
Later, her mother-in-law questioned her: "Where did you put the sugarcane, daughter-in-law?
You did not throw it away, nor was it eaten by me; I gave it myself to a peaceful bhikkhu."
“This sovereignty is yours as well as mine,” so my mother-in-law reviled me;
taking a stool, she struck me, and having passed away from there, I am now a deity.
That very wholesome deed was performed by me, and I myself experience the happiness resulting from that deed.
“I am enjoying myself together with the devas, and I rejoice in the five strands of sensual pleasure.
That very same wholesome deed was performed by me; I myself experience the fruit of that pleasant karma.
Protected by the Lord of Devas and guarded by the Thirty-Three Gods, I am provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure.”
“Such is the fruit of merit, not small; my offering of sugarcane has great ripening.
Together with the devas I enjoy myself; I rejoice in the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Such is the fruit of merit, not small; my offering of sugarcane has great radiance.”
"Guarded by the lords of gods and protected by the Thirty-Three, you were like the thousand-eyed Indra in the Nandana grove.
'And having approached you, O Venerable One, who are compassionate and wise, I paid homage and asked after your welfare;
then, with a serene mind and incomparable joy, she gave you a piece of sugarcane.'"
299. Therein, he says "now" (*idāni*) because it refers to the day immediately preceding; the meaning is "recently" (*adhuna*). "In this very village" (*imameva gāmaṃ*) means in this very village;
he speaks with reference to Rājagaha. For it has been said: "A village, a market town, and even a city are all called 'village'.
And this accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. "He approached" (*upāgamī*) means he arrived. "Incomparable" (*atulāya*) means peerless or immeasurable.
300. *Avākirīti* means he removed, discarded, or destroyed. *Santassā* refers to one who is of good character, whose defilements are stilled, or who has not yet fallen into distress.
301. *Tuyhaṃ nūti*: the particle *nu* is used here to indicate displeasure; it should be brought over and connected with the word "mine" (*mamā*) as well, thus reading "mama nū" (surely mine).
He says this referring to sovereignty, that is, lordship over the household. *Tato cutā* means from there, from the human world.

"Passed away" (*cutā*). Since one who has departed from their place of residence is also called "passed away," the term "deceased" (*kālakatā*) was used to specify that particular kind of passing away.
Furthermore, to show that even though she had passed away, she was not reborn just anywhere, but rather had attained the state of a deity, he said, "I am a deity."
302. "That very wholesome deed was done by me": the meaning is that only that wholesome deed consisting of the mere gift of a piece of sugarcane was performed by me;
I know of no other. "And happiness as the result of the deed": and happiness as the fruit of the deed.

For here, the word "deed" (*kamma*) is used for the fruit of the deed (*kammaphala*) by means of the elision of the latter member of the compound, or through a metaphorical designation of the cause [for the effect]. "Of wholesome deeds, monks... [and so forth].
It is as in such passages as: "By reason of the undertaking of wholesome states (dhammā), this merit increases in this way; I experience my own merit.

Alternatively, *kamma* is used in the accusative case in the sense of the instrument, meaning "by means of action" (*kammena*). Or, it is that which exists in action (*kamme*), just as in the word *kamma*.
Or else, it is called *kamma* because it is to be desired (*kāmetabbatāya*); for it is connected with sensual desire (*kāma*) due to its state of being pleasant and delightful.
“Kāmetabbaṃ” means desirable. “Attanā” means by oneself; the sense is that one enjoys it through one’s own self-mastery and sovereignty, by oneself.
In the phrase “paricārayāmahaṃ attānaṃ,” the word “attanā” mentioned in the preceding verse should be construed as “attānaṃ” by changing its grammatical case.
"Guarded by the Lord of Devas" means guarded by Sakka, the Lord of Devas; or alternatively, guarded like the Lord of Devas due to having a great retinue.

"Well-endowed" means thoroughly endowed or possessed [of these qualities]. "Great fruition" means having abundant results. "Great radiance" means possessing great splendor; the meaning is that they possess great power.

306. "They honor him" means they revere him. "The compassionate one" refers to the merciful one. "The wise one" means the one possessed of wisdom; the sense is that he has reached the pinnacle of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramī*).
"Having approached" means having drawn near. "I paid homage" means I prostrated with the five-pointed salutation (*pañcapatiṭṭhita*).
"And I asked after his welfare and health" means I inquired after them; the intention is: "With incomparable joy, I am mindful of this welfare [of yours]."
The remainder is exactly as described below.
The commentary on the Ucchudāyikā-vimāna is finished.
3. Commentary on the Pallaṅka-vimāna.
"Pallaṅkaseṭṭhe maṇisoṇṇacitte" refers to the Pallaṅka-vimāna. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.

At that time, a certain lay follower in Sāvatthī had given his daughter in marriage to a young man of a family of equal standing in terms of lineage and so forth, residing right there. She was free from anger and endowed with virtue and good conduct.
She was devoted to her husband, had undertaken the five precepts, and observed the Uposatha precepts with diligence on the Uposatha days.
Later, having passed away, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera went there in the same manner as described above and—
“Upon this most excellent couch, variegated with jewels and gold, a sublime bed strewn with flowers—
there you sit, O goddess of great power, manifesting various supernatural feats.
And these nymphs all around you dance, sing, and bring you delight.”
“You have attained divine power, O lady of great majesty; while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?”—thus he questioned her with verses.
She answered him with these verses:
“In the world of humans, having been born as a human, I was a daughter-in-law in a wealthy family.
Free from anger, I lived in obedience to my husband, and I was diligent in observing the Uposatha days.”
“Having been born as a human, young and blameless, with a confident heart I delighted my husband;
by day and by night acting agreeably, I was virtuous in the past.
Abstaining from taking life and from theft, with body purified, I lived the pure life of celibacy.”
I did not drink intoxicants, nor did I speak falsehood; I was one who fulfilled the training rules.
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight, as well as during the fortnight of miracles, I was one whose mind was full of faith.
“Endowed with the eight factors, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, I observed the Uposatha with a joyful mind.

Having undertaken this noble Uposatha, endowed with the most excellent eight factors, which is wholesome and brings about happiness, I was a virtuous wife who lived in obedience to my husband; formerly, I was a female disciple of the Sugata.”
“Having performed such wholesome deeds in the world of the living, she has become a partaker of distinction.
With the breakup of the body, in the life hereafter, having attained divine splendor, she has come to a happy destination.
Surrounded by a host of nymphs, she dwells in a most delightful and excellent celestial mansion.”
“The self-luminous hosts of gods delight me, who have come to this long-lived celestial mansion.
(307) Therein, “on the best couch” means on the most excellent couch, the supreme seat. To demonstrate its excellence, it is said:
“inlaid with gems and gold,” meaning with gems and gold made radiant by networks of rays from various jewels.

And regarding the words *vicitte* (“in the variegated”) and *tatthā* (“therein”), when *sayane* (“on the bed”) is stated, it refers to the most excellent couch (*pallaṅka-seṭṭha*) which serves as the place for lying down.

308. *Tet* means “from all around you. However, with reference to the word *pamodayantī* (“delighting”), the case ending of *taṃ* must be modified. Alternatively, *pamodayantī* means “they cause delight”; the sense is that they produce delight for you. 310.
*Daharā apāpikā* means “even though young, she is not wicked. Or there is the reading *daharāsu pāpikā*, which has the same meaning.
“*Daharassāpāpikā*” is also read; it means she is blameless toward her young husband, and auspicious due to her diligent attendance and lack of transgression.
Therefore it is said, “with a confident mind,” and so forth. *Abhirādhayiṃ* means I pleased [him]. *Ratto* means at night.
311. *Acorikā* means free from thievery; the meaning is that she abstains from taking what is not given.
There is also a reading, *viratā ca coriyā*, which means she has desisted from theft. She is "one whose body is completely purified" (*saṃsuddhakāyā*) because her bodily actions are thoroughly pure;
for that very reason, she is a "pure practitioner of the holy life" (*sucibrahmacārinī*), since no unchaste conduct occurs with anyone other than her husband. For it has been said:
We do not transgress against our wives,
nor do our wives transgress against us;
apart from them, we lead the holy life.
"Therefore indeed, even our young ones die.

Alternatively, "pure in holy life" (*sucibrahmacārinī*) means she is pure in the holy life of the pure, the stainless, the supreme—the Uposatha precepts—or in the preliminary holy life corresponding to the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*). 313.
"Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma" (*anudhammacārinī*) means she is habitually one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. And immediately following this...

It is called "noble" (ariya) because it is faultless; or alternatively, it is noble because it possesses the eight excellent limbs as its supreme members. It is "endowed with the eight excellent limbs" (ariyaṭṭhaṅgavarehi upetaṃ).

It is "wholesome" (kusala) in the sense of being free from disease and in the sense of being blameless. It has "happiness as its outcome" (sukhudrayaṃ) because it has happiness as its result and happiness as its benefit. The construction [of the sentence] is: "they approach [it]."
314. *Visesabhāginī*: one who partakes of distinction—that is, one who shares in the distinguished state of celestial attainment (*sampattibhava*).
*Sugatimhi āgatā*: arrived at or approached a happy destination (*sugati*); or, arrived in a happy destination, that is, in the celestial attainment of a happy destination.
There is also the reading *sugatiṃ hi āgatā*. In this case, *hi* is merely a particle, or it has the sense of a reason; because she has arrived at a happy destination, therefore...
The construction is: "a partaker of distinction.

(315) "In a supreme palace among palaces" means in the highest palace within the celestial mansions (*vimāna*), or in the foremost palace designated as a *vimāna*, or in a great, excellent palace that is measureless and free from pride (*vigatamāna*).
She dwells there surrounded by a host of apsarases, possessing her own radiance.
“I rejoice,” or rather, the word “I am” (*amhi*) should be brought in and connected. Regarding “long-lived”:

because those who have been reborn there have a longer lifespan than the lower deities and do not suffer from a short life, the construction is: “the hosts of gods delight me—who am long-lived and have arrived at, or entered, the aforementioned divine mansion.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Pallaṅka-vimāna* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Latā-vimāna*:
"A creeper, ready and excellent, [is] a deity"—thus it is the *Latā-vimāna*. How did its origin come about? The Blessed One was at Sāvatthī.
He was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove. At that time, there was a certain lay follower living in Sāvatthī whose daughter, named Latā—wise, competent, and intelligent—had gone to her husband’s family.

She was pleasing in her conduct toward her husband, her mother-in-law, and her father-in-law; she spoke kindly, was skilled in managing the household staff, capable of sustaining the burden of the family estate, and free from anger.
She was endowed with virtue and good conduct, delighted in giving and sharing, maintained the five precepts without breach, and was diligent in observing the Uposatha days.
Later, having passed away, she was reborn as a daughter of the Great King Vessavaṇa, named Latā.
She also had four sisters: Sajjā, Pavarā, Accimatī, and Sutā. These...
Sakka, the king of the devas, brought all five of them and established them in the position of attendants in the form of dancing girls.
Among them, however, Latā was the most beloved because of her skill in dancing, singing, and other arts.
While they were gathered together and seated comfortably, a dispute arose concerning their proficiency in music.
They all went into the presence of the Great King Vessavaṇa and asked, "Dear father, which of us is skilled in dancing and the other arts?
He replied, "Go, daughters; perform a musical concert at the confluence of deities on the banks of Lake Anotatta.
There, your excellence will become manifest. They did accordingly. There—
As the creeper danced, the sons of the gods were unable to remain in their natural composure;

filled with laughter and struck by a sense of wonder and amazement, they raised a great clamor that seemed to shake the Himālaya mountains, continuously shouting "Bravo!", uttering cries of exultation, and waving their garments.
But when the other [creepers] danced, they remained silent like cuckoos in the cold season.
They sat down. Thus, through that assembly there, the excellence of the creeper became manifest.

Then, upon hearing of this, it occurred to another daughter of the gods: "What deed must have been performed by this creeper so that she stands surpassing us in both beauty and glory? Suppose now I were to find out what deed was done by the creeper..."
“...should ask. She asked him, and the other answered her on that matter.
Then Vessavaṇa the Great King related all of this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, who had approached him while traveling among the gods.
The Elder, reporting that matter to the Blessed One starting from the very root cause of the inquiry, said:
“Latā, the excellent and noble deity Accimatī,
the daughter of King Vessavaṇa, and Rājīmatī, who shone with the virtues of the Dhamma—
these five women came there to bathe in the auspicious river Sītodakā, which was filled with lotuses.”
Having bathed there, enjoyed themselves, danced, and sung, the goddess Suta spoke to the creeper:
“I ask you, O wearer of a garland of blue lotuses, you who have a braid and a complexion like gold;
you with eyes as dark-brown as a *timira* flower, beautiful as the sky—by what cause has your long life and fame been brought about?”
“By what means, Bhaddā, are you dearer to your husband than one who is more distinguished and more beautiful in form?
You are skillful in dancing, singing, and instrumental music; being questioned by men and women, tell us.”—This is the question asked by Suta.
“Among humans, having been born as a human, I was a daughter-in-law in a family of great wealth.
Free from anger, I lived in obedience to my husband, and I was diligent in observing the Uposatha.
As a young woman among humans, free from evil, with a confident heart, I delighted my husband.”
"Together with my husband, my father-in-law, and my attendants, I brought him great delight; therein my glory was established.
By virtue of that wholesome deed, I attained distinction in four respects:
long life, beauty, happiness, and strength, as well as no small measure of playful delight."
“Does this creeper speak what she has heard? She has proclaimed to us that which we asked.
It is said that our husbands are the most distinguished among women, their refuge, their excellence, and their deity.
We all practice the duty toward our husbands, wherein women remain devoted to their husbands.”
"Having practiced the Dhamma toward our husbands, we all shall obtain whatever this creeper speaks of.
"Just as a lion, whose domain is the mountain ridges, having taken up residence on Mount Mahindhara,
overpowers and slays other four-footed creatures, devouring small animals as a meat-eater;"
“Just so, a noble female disciple here, relying on her husband and devoted to her spouse,
having destroyed anger and overcome stinginess, that practitioner of Dhamma rejoices in heaven.”—
Thus he spoke regarding the answer of the creeper.
316. In this context, *latā*, *sajjā*, *pavarā*, *accimatī*, and *sutā* are their names. The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
“Of the excellent king” (*rājavarassa*) means of the best and most eminent of the four Great Kings, the King of the Devas; the intention is that she is an attendant of Sakka.
“Of the king” (*rañño*) refers to the Great King. Therefore he said, “the daughter of Vessavaṇa”; this should be applied to each [name] individually.
Or it is a permutation of words; the meaning is "daughters. She shines and radiates, thus she is a *rājī*;
one who is considered or known as a *rājī* is *Rājimatī*. This is an epithet for all of them. Some say this is merely the name of a single deity;
according to their view, "excellent" (*pavarā*) is an epithet for all of them. "By means of the qualities of the Dhamma" means by those things pertaining to the Dhamma, not departing from the Dhamma.
"By qualities" means by qualities as they truly are (*yathābhūta*). "They shine" means they radiate.
317. "Five women here" refers to five daughters of the gods with the names previously mentioned, who are here in this region of the Himālaya.
He speaks of the "auspicious river with cool waters and lotuses" with reference to the mouth of the river that flows out from Lake Anotatta.
"Having danced and sung" refers to the dancing and singing performed by them at the assembly of the gods by the command of their father, Vessavaṇa.
"Sutā spoke to Latā": *sutā* means the daughter of the gods; she spoke to *latā*, her own sister.
They also read it as "sutā latam bravuṃ," meaning the daughters of the Great King Vessavaṇa spoke to *latā*.
318. *Timiratambakkhī*: one whose eyes are endowed with copper-colored streaks resembling the filaments of the *nicula* flower. *Nabheva sobhanā*:

shining like the sky; the meaning is that she is radiant due to the extreme purity of her limbs and members, like the sky in the autumn season when it is freed from the defilements of clouds, mist, and the like.
Alternatively, *nabheva* means "in the sky itself," used here in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The word *eva* means "shining everywhere," [referring] both to the celestial palaces situated in the sky and to the places connected to the earth such as the Himavanta and Yugandhara mountains.
"By what made? means by what kind of merit was it produced? "Glory" (*yasa*) refers to the excellence of one's retinue and one's reputation;
and by the mention of "reputation," the virtues that are the cause of that reputation are also included.
319. "Piyatarā patino" means dearer than her husband; she is the beloved of her husband.
By this, he shows her good fortune (*subhagatā*). "Visiṭṭhakalyāṇitarāsi rūpato": in terms of beauty, she is distinguished, supreme, more beautiful, and lovelier.
*Assu* is a mere particle. Some read it as "visiṭṭhakalyāṇitarāsīti rūpato. "Padakkhiṇā" means by various ways.
Or rather, the offerings are especially wholesome. Regarding the phrase "in dancing, singing, and instrumental music," here the case ending has been dropped after *naccana*;

the meaning is "in dance, in song, and in instrumental music. "Questioned by men and women" means questioned by the sons of the gods and the daughters of the gods for the purpose of seeing their forms and for the purpose of seeing their skills, [asking]: "Where is the creeper? What does the creeper do?"
321. Because she is always unassociated with the body [of others], she delights like a *devo* (a god); thus, *devaro* means "the second excellent one" or the husband’s younger brother.
*Sadevaraṃ* means "together with the *devara*. *Sassuraṃ* means "together with the mother-in-law (*sassu*) and father-in-law (*sasuro*), i.e., the parents-in-law.
*Sadāsakaṃ* means "together with male slaves (*dāsa*) and female slaves (*dāsī*). The connection is: "pleasing her husband. In that [context]...
"Was performed" (*kato*) means that fame was produced for that family or at that time—specifically at the time of becoming a daughter-in-law—by the generation of the merit that brought it about;
this is the intended meaning. Regarding the word "by me" (*mama*), it should be understood as "by me" (*mayā*) by referring back to the word "was performed.
(322) "By four grounds" (*catubbhi ṭhānehi*) means by four causes, or in four places serving as the basis [for praise]. "He attained distinction" (*visesam ajjhagā*).
She attained a pre-eminence over others. The phrase "in four respects" is a statement showing, in their specific form, her longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength.
Indeed, these very qualities—longevity and the rest—are called "distinctions" (*visesa*) because they constitute her distinct nature compared to others;
and they are called "grounds" (*ṭhāna*) because they serve as the causes for her being perceived in that way through the process of esteem. She attained distinction.
Of what kind? The construction is: "life-span, beauty, happiness, and strength.

(323) "Have you heard that which this creeper speaks?"—by this she asks the other three sisters: "Has this creeper, our eldest sister, spoken something that you have heard, or has it not been heard by you? She asks them, "Is it *no*?"—that which [she spoke] to us...
"Saṃsayitaṃ" (doubtful). "No" is a mere particle; or again, "no" means "of us," used for emphasis, as in such expressions as "na no samaṃ atthi" (there is nothing equal to us).
Therefore, the meaning is: "He has indeed proclaimed it; he has indeed explained it without error. "Pati" refers to our husbands, who are distinguished among women;
and their destination is the most excellent deities. Etymologically, because they protect (*pālanato*), they are called *pati*; that is, our husbands.
The meaning is: for women, they are the distinguished destination and their refuge;
as the supreme and most excellent deities among these womankind, when properly propitiated, they bring welfare and happiness both now and in the future.
(324) "Let us all practice the Dhamma toward our husbands" means that we, all together, [should practice] rising before our own husbands and so forth.

"We shall practice the duty that ought to be practiced. Regarding the word "wherein" (*yattha*): it refers to whichever sign (*nimitta*), or rather, to whichever duty toward husbands that ought to be practiced;
when such duties are being practiced, women are called "faithful wives" (*patibbatā*). Regarding the phrase "we shall obtain":

she says this because this creeper (*latā*)—meaning this woman—obtains whatever prosperity she does now; [the meaning is] "by practicing the duty toward husbands, we shall obtain that same prosperity."
325. "One whose range is the mountain ridges" means one who roams through mountain forest thickets.
"Having dwelt upon Mount Mahindhara" means having dwelt—that is, having resided—upon the immovable mountain named Mahindhara (the Earth-Sustainer);
the sense is that he was living there. For, in consideration of the word "having dwelt," this accusative case ending is used in the sense of the locative. "Pasayha" means...
"Having overcome": even small animals that are inferior in strength, or even large animals such as elephants and the like in terms of size, he kills them all. 326.
Regarding the verse "In the same way," this is the application of the meaning together with the correlation of the simile:
just as a lion, dwelling in dependence upon a mountain that serves as his own dwelling place and range for food, accomplishes whatever purpose he desires.
In the same way, that faithful, devoted noble female disciple, living in dependence upon her husband, master,
and lord for her sustenance and clothing, follows him in all matters through conduct characterized by compliance with her husband;
she has destroyed and abandoned anger arising toward her attendants and the like, as well as [anger] arising toward the objects of her possession.

Having overcome, having conquered, and not giving rise to stinginess, because she practices correctly the duty of a devoted wife and the duty of a lay follower, that practitioner of the Dhamma rejoices in the heavenly world of the devas; she attains great joy.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Latāvimāna* is finished.
5. The commentary on the *Guttilavimāna*:
"Seventy strings, most sweet"—this is the *Guttilavimāna*. What is its origin? While the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha...
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wandering on a tour of the celestial realms in the manner previously described,
went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There, seeing thirty-six divine maidens— each stationed in succession within thirty-six palaces,
each surrounded by a retinue of a thousand nymphs and enjoying great celestial splendor— he observed the kamma they had performed in the past.
He questioned [the deities] in succession with three verses beginning with, “With most excellent beauty.

They, in turn, answered his questions immediately thereafter with verses beginning, “The woman who gave the supreme cloth. Then the Elder returned from that world of humans to the human realm and reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Having heard it, the Blessed One said, “Moggallāna, those deities are not only...

Having said, "When questioned by her, they answered thus; moreover, when previously questioned by me as well, they answered in exactly the same way," he related his own past life as the teacher Guttila when requested by the Elder.
In the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of musicians (gandhabba).

There was a teacher named Guttila, who, through the purity of his craft in the art of music, was like Timbaru and Nārada, renowned and famous in all directions. He supported his blind and aged parents.
Having heard of the perfection of his craft, a musician from Ujjeni named Musila approached him, paid homage, and standing to one side, asked: "Why..."
When he was asked, "Have you come? he replied, "I have come to learn a craft from you.
Master Guttila, having observed him and being skilled in the science of marks (*lakṣaṇa*), thought, "This man will be of uneven disposition, harsh, cruel, and ungrateful;
he should not be taken under my care," and thus did not grant him permission to learn the craft. He [then] went to his parents...
Having waited upon him, he made a request of him. Being pressured by his parents, the teacher Guttila thought, "The word of a teacher must not be transgressed," and so he began his training.
Out of freedom from stinginess and compassion, he did not keep anything back as a "teacher’s fist" but taught him the craft in its entirety.
By virtue of his intelligence, his previous practice, and his lack of indolence, he soon became a master of his craft.
He then thought: "This city of Bārāṇasī is the foremost city in Jambudīpa; what if I were to display my skill here before the assembly together with the king?
In this way, I shall become renowned and famous throughout Jambudīpa, even more so than my teacher. He [approached] the teacher...
He announced, "I wish to display my craft before the king; please let me see the king.

Out of compassion, thinking, "May this man, who has learned his craft in my presence, find a firm footing," the Great Being led him into the presence of the king and said, "Great King, behold the proficiency of this pupil of mine on the lute. The king replied, "Excellent!"
Having agreed and heard his playing of the lute, the king was delighted;
wishing to prevent him from leaving, he said, "Stay right here with me, and I will give you half of what has been allotted to your teacher. Musila replied, "I do not fall short of my teacher;
give me exactly the same amount. The king said, "Do not speak thus; a teacher is indeed a great person; [give him] only half."
When he said, "I will give it to you," [the other] replied, "Come, let us both see the craft of myself and my teacher.

Having spoken thus, he departed from the royal palace and went about here and there, proclaiming: "On the seventh day from now, there shall be a display of our crafts in the royal courtyard; let those who wish to see it come and behold it."
Having heard this, the Great Being thought, "This man is young and strong, whereas I am old and weak;
if I should suffer defeat, death would be better for me than life. Therefore, I shall enter the forest, hang myself, and die.
Terrified by the fear of death, he went into the forest, but then turned back. Desiring to die once more, he went again, and yet again...
He turned back out of fear of death. As he was thus making his way back and forth, that place became free of grass.
Then the king of the gods approached the Great Being, standing in the sky in a visible form, and said: "Teacher, what are you doing? The Great Being—
“I recited the *Sattatanti*, so very sweet and delightful;

The meaning of this is as follows: "O King of Devas, [I praise] that which is 'well-sweet' (*sumadhura*)—meaning it is exceedingly sweet because it does not fail to produce the twenty-two varieties of musical tones (*sutibheda*) as appropriate, having made its object the 'seven-stringed' (*sattatanti*) due to the presence of seven strings and the manifestation of the sevenfold sounds beginning with *chañja*;

And because it was exceedingly delightful for those listening to the mutual blending of the lute and the voice, I taught, caused him to learn, and trained that musical art—

On the stage, he struck out, intending to display his own excellence by means of his boldness, saying:

Your pupil shall not defeat you, O teacher; you, teacher, shall defeat the pupil,” he said.
It is said that in a previous existence, the Great Being had been the teacher of Sakka, the king of the gods. Therefore he said, “I am one who honors his teacher.”

On the seventh day, the king sat in the royal court together with his retinue.
The teacher Guttila and Musila, having prepared themselves to display their skills, approached, paid homage to the king, and each took his respective seat.

The assembly remained impartial toward the playing of both. Sakka said to Guttila, "Sever one string.

Seeing this, Musila appeared utterly defeated and stood with his head bowed, while the assembly, delighted and thrilled, raised their garments and gave Guttila a great round of applause. The king [dismissed] Musila from the assembly hall...

It is said that those women, while existing in human form during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, performed various meritorious deeds.
Therein, one woman gave a cloth; one, a *sumana* garland; one, perfume; one, excellent fruits; one, sugarcane juice;
one, offered a five-finger-mark of perfume at a shrine of the Blessed One; one, observed the Uposatha;

One served her mother-in-law and father-in-law without anger; one, having become a maidservant, was untiring in her conduct;

One gave him a shoulder-strap, one a fly-whisk, one a palm-leaf fan, one a peacock-feather fan, one an umbrella,

(333) Regarding the phrase "giver of the most excellent garment": it refers to the most excellent or best among garments, or having selected the finest from among many garments.
She is the giver of that cloth which is taken as the most excellent, sublime, supreme, reaching the pinnacle, the best of cloths.
The same method applies to the phrases “giver of the finest flowers” and so forth. “Giver of what is lovely” means she is the giver of an object whose nature is dear and whose kind is dear.

“Agreeable” (manāpa) means that which increases the mind’s delight. “Divine” (dibba) means divine because it exists in heaven (divi). “Having approached” (upecca) means having gone near and having intended, [thinking] “such...”.
The meaning is: "having resolved, 'May I obtain [it]'". *Ṭhānaṃ* means a place such as a celestial mansion (*vimāna*), or sovereignty.
There is also the reading *manāpā*, which means "becoming pleasing to others.
(334) "Behold the ripening of merit": she speaks thus, extolling the prosperity she herself has obtained, saying, "Behold such a fruit as this for the gift of the most excellent object."
341. Regarding "giver of the best flowers": she is a giver of the best flowers by way of making offerings to the Triple Gem; likewise, she should be understood as a "giver of the best perfumes.

In this context, the "best flowers" should be known as jasmine flowers (*sumana*) and so forth; the "best perfumes" as sandalwood fragrance and so forth; the "best fruits" as jackfruit (*panasa*) and so forth;
and the "best tastes" as cow's milk, clarified butter (*sappi*), and so forth.

"Welcome indeed to me!"—my coming here is truly auspicious; oh, how beautiful! Today has dawned well.

(618) "Having heard the Dhamma" means: having heard the wholesome Dhamma performed by you, which serves as a direct manifestation of the fruit of kamma.
Having heard this: "I shall do it" means "I will perform it. "By even conduct" means by practicing the good behavior of bodily conduct.
"By restraint" means by the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*). "By self-control" means by the control of the faculties, with the mind as the sixth.
Now, in order to show that this wholesome state is a supporting condition for one's own turning away from the world (*vivaṭṭa*), he says: "Therefore, I shall go there..."
"Wherever one goes, one does not grieve"— thus it is said.
Although this teaching, comprising thirty-six vimānas, was delivered by way of the *Vatthuttamadāyikā-vimāna* and others—
just as it occurred for the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna— it is nevertheless called the "Guttila-vimāna" because it was manifested by the teacher Guttila.
They are included in the *Saṅgaha*; however, because those celestial mansions (*vimāna*) are dependent upon women, they are included specifically within the *Itthivimāna*.

Those women, during the time of Kassapa the Ten-Powered One, through the force of successive volitions arising from their practice of the Dharma as previously described, transmigrated only in the world of the devas for one interval between Buddhas (*buddhantara*), beginning from their second existence, until our own Blessed One.

It should be understood that they were reborn at that very moment in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; when questioned by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, they gave their account in accordance with the nature of their past deeds, just as they had done when questioned by the teacher Guttila.
The commentary on the Guttila-vimāna is concluded.
6. Description of the Daddalla Palace "Shining with beauty" refers to the Daddalla Palace. How did it come into being? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, there was a certain supporter of the Venerable Elder Revata in the village of Nālaka.
The householder had two daughters: one named Bhaddā and the other named Subhaddā.
Of them, Bhaddā, who was faithful, confident, and endowed with wisdom, went to her husband’s family; however, she was barren.
She said to her husband, "I have a younger sister named Subhaddā; bring her here, and if she should have a son, he shall be my son as well."
“May it be so, and may this family lineage not perish. He agreed, saying, “Very well,” and did accordingly.
Then Bhaddā exhorted Subhaddā: “Subhaddā, be devoted to giving and sharing, and be diligent in righteous conduct;
in this way, both your welfare in this present life and that in the future will come entirely into your hands. She—[did as she was told].
Abiding by that advice and practicing according to the method described, one day she invited the Venerable Revata Thera along with seven others as her eighth guest.
Desiring to increase Subhaddā’s store of merit, the Elder took seven monks under the designation of the Saṅgha and went to her house.
With a heart full of faith, she [attended] the Venerable Revata Thera and those monks.
With her own hands, she satisfied him with excellent hard food and soft food; having offered words of thanksgiving, the Elder departed.
Later, after passing away, she was reborn into the company of the Nimmānarati devas.
But Bhaddā, having given gifts to various individuals, was reborn as a handmaid to Sakka, the lord of the devas.
Then Subhaddā, reflecting upon her own prosperity and pondering, "By what merit have I been reborn here?",
perceived that she had attained this success through the alms given to the Saṅgha while abiding by Bhaddā’s advice.
Looking further to see where Bhaddā had been reborn, she saw that she had been reborn as a handmaid to Sakka.
Seeing her, Bhaddā entered her celestial mansion out of compassion.
Then she said to her: "Radiant in beauty and illustrious in fame, you outshine all the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa realm in splendor."
“I do not recall ever seeing you before; this is my first sight of you.
From what body have you come, and why do you address me by name?”—with these two verses she questioned her. She, in turn—
“In my former human existence, O Bhaddā, I was Subhaddā;
I was your wife, and your younger sister.
Having passed away from there, with the breaking up of the body, I am now fully liberated.”
“I have been reborn into the company of the Nimmānarati devas”—thus he answered with two verses.
(619–20) Therein, “by beauty” means by the perfection of beauty and so forth. “I do not recall seeing you” means that prior to this I did not recall seeing you;
the sense is that you had never been seen by me before. Therefore he said, “This is my first sight of you.”
“From what body have you come, that you address me by name? means: from which class of devas have you come to address me by the name “Bhadde”?
621. Regarding the words “I am Bhaddā”: here “Bhaddā” is the form of address. “Subhaddāsī” means:
I was named Subhaddā, your younger sister; there, in our previous human existence, we were co-wives, sharing the same husband.
They were the wife of that one alone; the meaning is that they were the wife of your husband alone. Again Bhaddā said:
“Many beings go to the devas who have performed much merit, Subhaddā, those whose own lineage you will praise.”
“By what virtue, or by whom instructed, and by what kind of giving and excellent observance of vows have you become renowned?
Having attained such fame, you have reached this vast distinction.”
“O deity, being questioned, tell me: what is the fruit of this deed?
Thus she asked with three verses. Then Subhaddā said:
“The eight alms-offerings which I gave as a gift in the past...”
“With my own hands, I gave to the Saṅgha worthy of offerings.
By that deed, such is my complexion...
[and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.”
He explained:
"623. Therein, 'many who have performed good deeds go to those gods' means that many beings—those of great merit—go by way of rebirth to those Nimmānarati gods; among those Nimmānarati gods..."
"You will proclaim your own birth; you spoke"—this is the construction. 624.

"By what quality" means by what cause. "Of such a kind as" (*kīdiseneva*): the word *eva* has the sense of inclusion, meaning "and of such a kind as"; or this is simply the reading. "By good conduct" (*subbatenā*) means by beautiful conduct, that is, by well-purified virtue (*sīla*).
626. "Eight alms-meals": he speaks with reference to the alms-food given to eight monks. "Adadanti" means she gave.
When Subhaddā had spoken thus, Bhaddā replied again:
“I myself, with my own hands, full of faith, satisfied many more bhikkhus— those who are self-restrained and lead the holy life— with food and drink.”
“Having given much more than you, I have been reborn in an inferior body;
how is it that you, having given less, have attained such vast distinction?
O deity, being asked, tell me: what is the fruit of this karma?”
He asked. In that context, *tayā* is an instrumental case used in the sense of the ablative. Again Subhaddā said:

I invited him for a meal, with Revata as the eighth."
“Thus, with my purpose in mind and out of compassion for Revata,
I said to him, ‘Give it to the Saṅgha,’ and I acted upon his word.
That gift, having gone to the Saṅgha, is established in the immeasurable.”
"What you have given to these persons is not of great fruit for you"—thus he spoke of the deed done by himself. 631.
In this context, "one who is to be honored" (*manobhāvanīya*) means one who increases the mind, being worthy of esteem due to his sublime qualities. "Seen in person" (*sanditṭha*)...
This was stated by way of an invitation to the Bodhi tree. Therefore he said: “I invited him with a meal, Revata being the eighth among us.
This means that I invited that venerable Revata, who is worthy of esteem, together with myself as the eighth, for a meal.
632–3. “He had my welfare in mind”: that venerable Revata, by making the fruit of the gift great, [acted] for my sake.
“Intent on the goal, seeking welfare, he said to me, ‘Give to the Saṅgha. This means:
“Subhaddā, if you wish to give to eight bhikkhus, since an offering made to the Saṅgha is more fruitful than an offering made to individuals, therefore give to the Saṅgha;
give a gift dedicated to the Saṅgha. *Taṃ* refers to that gift.
When Subhaddā had spoken thus, Bhaddā, accepting that matter and desiring to practice accordingly in the future, said:
“Only now do I know that what is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit;
therefore, having gone to the human state, may I be generous and free from stinginess.”
"I shall give gifts to the Saṅgha, being heedful again and again"—thus she spoke this verse.
But Subhaddā departed for her own celestial realm. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, beheld the goddess Subhaddā shining forth, having surpassed all the Tāvatiṃsa gods with the radiance of her own body.
And having heard that conversation and discourse of theirs, and while Subhaddā had just vanished, not knowing who she was—[he asked]:
“Who is this goddess, O Bhaddā, who is consulting with you?
She outshines all the Tāvatiṃsa gods in beauty.”
Bhaddā asked him. He replied to her:
"O Lord of Devas, when we were humans in a former human existence, you were my co-wife and also my younger sister."
“Having given gifts to the Saṅgha, one who has performed merit shines forth.
Thus she spoke. Then Sakka, demonstrating the great fruitfulness of that offering made to the Saṅgha, preached the Dhamma. Therefore it was said:
“In the past, sister Bhagini, you shone forth through the Dhamma, O Bhaddā.”
“He who established a gift within the Sangha, which is immeasurable—
when I was questioned by me on Mount Vulture Peak regarding the ripening of sharing, where what is given bears great fruit.”
“Tell me of that place where what is given bears great fruit for human beings who are sacrificing, for living beings seeking merit, while they perform worldly meritorious deeds—
O Buddha, you who know the fruits of one’s own actions, explain this to me.”
The ripening of sharing, wherein what is given bears great fruit:
"The four who have entered the path and the four who are established in the fruit—
this is the Saṅgha, upright, endowed with wisdom, virtue, and concentration."
“For people who are making offerings, for living beings seeking merit, for those performing worldly meritorious deeds—what is given to the Saṅgha yields great fruit.
For this Saṅgha is vast and sublime; it is immeasurable, like the ocean.”
For these are the best disciples, heroes among men; illuminators, they proclaim the Dhamma.
"Well given, well offered, well sacrificed is that gift which people give directed toward the Saṅgha.
That offering, established in the Saṅgha, is of great fruit and praised by those who know the world."
“Those who, having become wise, wander the world recollecting such a sacrifice as this—having eradicated the stain of stinginess along with its root—blameless, they go to the heavenly state.
(637) Therein, *dhammena* means by way of cause or by way of method. *Tayā* is the instrumental case used in the sense of the ablative. Now, that...
To show the reason for saying "by means of the Dhamma," it was stated: "that which he established in the Sangha, immeasurable.
"Immeasurable" (appameyye) means that which cannot be measured by way of the power of his virtues and the excellence of the fruits of the services rendered to him.
638–9. Showing that this meaning was both heard in the presence of the Blessed One and received in his presence, he said, "When asked," and so forth.
