Therein, *yajamānānaṃ* means "of those giving. The expression *puññapekkhāna pāṇinaṃ* is a grammatical designation formed by eliding the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*), meaning "of beings desiring the fruit of merit.
*Opadhikaṃ*: "upadhi" refers to the aggregates (*khandhā*).

"Opadhika" means having the nature of producing *upadhi* (clinging/substratum), or being employed for the sake of *upadhi*; it is that which generates an individual existence (*attabhāva*) and bestows the resultant fruit of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence (*pavatti*).
"Jānaṃ kammaphalaṃ sakaṃ": knowing one's own respective fruits of karma;

that is, knowing each being's own respective merit and the fruit of merit as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of one's hand. Alternatively, "sakaṃ" is stated by changing the letter *ya* to *ka*; thus, the meaning is "one's own" (*sayaṃ attano*).
641. *Paṭipannā* means those who are practicing; the meaning is "those standing on the path.
*Ujubhūto* means one who has attained straightness through straight practice and has become worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). *Paññāsīlasamāhito* means concentrated by means of wisdom and virtue;
that is, endowed with right view and virtue, possessed of noble view and noble virtue. By this, his status as the ultimate Saṅgha is indeed established.
He clarifies this. For the Saṅgha is so called because it is bound together by the commonality of view and virtue. Alternatively, *samādhi* means that which is concentrated;

one who possesses wisdom, virtue, and concentration is "endowed with wisdom, virtue, and concentration" (*paññāsīlasamāhito*). By this, he clarifies the Saṅgha’s status as the foremost object of offerings due to its perfection in the three aggregates of Dhamma, beginning with virtue.
643. "Vipulo mahaggato" means he has attained greatness through his qualities; thus he is "mahaggato.
For that very reason, because he is the cause for the vastness of the fruit of deeds performed toward him, he is "vipulo.

"Udhīva sāgaro" means just as the ocean is named "udadhi" because water is held (*dhīyati*) therein, and is immeasurable in terms of its water—such that one could not say, "There are this many *āḷhaka* measures of water"—so too is he.
The meaning is "by way of qualities. Regarding the phrase *ete hi*: the particle *hi* is used here for emphasis; the meaning is "these alone are the best. For it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, whatever assemblies or groups there may be, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared to be the foremost among them.
*Naravīrasāvakā* means the disciples of that man who is endowed with heroism among men. *Pabhaṅkarā* means those who create the light of knowledge for the world.
"Proclaiming the Dhamma" means they recite the Dhamma. How so? For the Lamp of the Dhamma has been placed by the Master of the Dhamma within the Noble Saṅgha.

644. "Those who give gifts dedicated to the Saṅgha" refers to those beings who give gifts dedicated to the Noble Saṅgha, even to the conventional Saṅgha, including individuals at the stage of *gotrabhū*; such a gift, though given through the principle of sharing, is well-given.
Whether offered as an *āhuna* or a *pāhuna*, it is well-offered; whether sacrificed as a great sacrifice, it is indeed well-sacrificed.
Why? Because that alms-gift, when directed toward and established in the Saṅgha, is of great fruit and praised by those who know the world—the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, the World-Knowers—saying:
"But in no way at all, Ānanda, do I [praise] an alms-gift directed toward the Saṅgha..."

The meaning is that its great fruitfulness has been described, praised, and extolled by such passages as: “I say that an offering made to an individual is of even greater fruit; for those desiring merit, the Saṅgha is indeed the foremost field of sacrifice, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
645. "Recalling such a sacrifice" means recalling the gift they themselves gave for the sake of such a Saṅgha.
"Born of wisdom" means having given rise to joy. "Having removed the stain of stinginess along with its root": stinginess itself is called the "stain of stinginess" because it makes the mind impure;
alternatively, it refers to stinginess together with other stains such as envy, greed, and hatred, which is thus "the stain of stinginess."

The construction is as follows: having eradicated—that is, having removed, suppressed, and not censured—that [state] together with its roots, such as ignorance (*avijjā*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and perversion (*vipallāsa*), they go to the blameless state of heaven. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Furthermore, Sakka, the Lord of the Devas, [described] this entire process to the Venerable [Ānanda] with the words beginning, "Shining forth in beauty... and so on.
He informed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reported it to the Blessed One.
Taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the assembled company. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The commentary on the *Daddallavimāna* is concluded.
7. Explanation of the Pesavatī Mansion (*Pesavatīvimānavaṇṇanā*).
"Covered with nets of crystal, silver, and gold" refers to the Pesavatī mansion. How did it come into being?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove. At that time, in the village of Nālaka in Magadha, there was a certain family of great wealth belonging to householders.

There was a daughter-in-law of a noble family named Pesavatī. It is said that when a golden stupa one *yojana* in height was being constructed for the Blessed One Kassapa, she was a young girl who went with her mother to the site of the shrine. She asked her mother, "Mother, what are these people doing?
"They are making golden bricks to build the shrine," she replied. Upon hearing this, the young girl’s mind was filled with serene faith.
He said to his mother, "Mother, I have this small golden ornament on my neck;

I give it for the sake of the shrine. His mother said, "Very well, give it," and having removed it from his neck, she placed it in the hands of the goldsmith, saying, "This has been renounced by this girl; add this as well and make it into a brick."
The goldsmith did exactly so. Later, after passing away, that girl—by virtue of that very meritorious deed—was reborn in the world of the devas.
Continuing to wander from one happy destination to another, she was reborn in the village of Nālaka during the time of our Blessed One, and in due course reached the age of twelve.
One day, having taken the capital money sent by her mother, she went to a certain shop to obtain oil.
In that shop, a certain son of a householder was digging up a great deal of gold, silver, pearls, gems, and jewels that had been buried and stored there by his father;
through the power of his karma, these appeared to him in the form of gravel, stones, and pebbles.
Having seen this, he set aside a portion of it and placed it in a heap to test whether gold, silver, and other riches would appear through the power of those possessed of merit.
Then, seeing that, the girl said, "Why are these jewels placed like this in the shop?
Should they not indeed be properly arranged? When the shopkeeper heard this, he thought, "This girl possesses great merit."

Thinking, "By means of her, all this gold and other wealth will become ours for our own use, and I shall take possession of it," he went to his mother’s presence and insisted, "Give this girl to me for my son.
Having paid much wealth and performed the marriage rites, he brought her to his own home. Then, regarding her virtuous conduct—
Having understood this, he opened the storehouse and asked, "What do you see here?

When she replied, "I see gold, silver, and jewels heaped up in a mass," he said, "These things were disappearing through the power of our own karma, but by the excellence of your merit they have become even more abundant once again.
Therefore, from now on, you alone shall manage everything in this house; by you..."
Having said, "We shall consume only what has been given," from that time forth they called her "Pesavatī.
At that same time, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati, knowing that the constituent forces of his own life were exhausted, thought:
"I will enter final nibbāna after giving the funds for my mother, the brahmin lady Rūpasārī’s maintenance."
Having approached the Blessed One and requested permission for his final passing away (parinibbāna), and having displayed a great miracle by the Teacher’s command,
he praised the Blessed One with thousands of hymns of praise. Then, turning back toward him until he was out of sight,
and having bowed once more, he departed from the monastery surrounded by the community of monks (bhikkhusaṅgha).
Having given his exhortation and comforted the Venerable Ānanda, he dismissed the fourfold assembly.
Proceeding by stages, he reached the village of Nālakā; there, having established his mother in the fruit of stream-entry, he attained final nibbāna at dawn in his birth-chamber.
For seven days, both gods and humans spent their time performing the funeral honors for his body after he had passed away.
They constructed a funeral pyre one hundred cubits high with aloeswood, sandalwood, and other fragrant woods.
When Pesavatī heard of the Elder’s parinibbāna, she thought, “I shall go and pay homage. She had caskets filled with golden flowers and various perfumes prepared;
wishing to depart, she asked her father-in-law for permission, but he said to her, “You are carrying a heavy burden.”

There was a great crush of people there. Although she was told, "Send flowers and perfumes and stay right here," she conceived faith and, disregarding those words, thought, "Even if there should be a danger to my life there, I shall go and pay homage.
Accompanied by her retinue, she went there, worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and stood with palms joined in reverence. And in that...
At that time, as the royal retinues arrived to honor the Elder, an elephant became intoxicated and approached that place.
Seeing this, while the people fled in terror of death, the great multitude stepped upon Pesavatī, who had fallen amidst the crush of the crowd, and killed her.
Having performed acts of worship and honor, her mind was perfected through faith directed toward the Elder.
Having passed away at that time, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with a retinue of a thousand celestial nymphs (accharā).
Immediately upon seeing her own divine splendor, she wondered, "By what kind of merit have I obtained this?
As she investigated the cause, she saw the honor and offerings made in honor of the Elder; her mind became deeply devoted to the Triple Gem.
Surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, her person adorned with ornaments weighing sixty cartloads, she came with great divine majesty, illuminating the ten directions like the moon and the sun.
Arriving together with her celestial mansion, she descended from it, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood with palms joined in reverence. At that time...
The Venerable Vaṅgīsa, sitting near the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
“It occurs to me, Blessed One, to ask about the deed performed by this deity. “Let it occur to you, Vaṅgīsa,” the Blessed One replied.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, desiring to ask about the deed performed by that deity, first spoke while praising her celestial mansion:
“I beheld a most delightful celestial mansion, covered with nets of crystal, silver, and gold, with a floor of various and wonderful colors.
It was a well-constructed heavenly abode, adorned with archways, strewn with precious gems, and beautiful.
It shone through the ten directions like the sun in the sky, dispelling the darkness like the thousand-rayed autumnal sun.”
“Thus does this celestial mansion of yours shine, like a flame of smoke rising from water at the peak of the night sky.
It steals the eye with its shimmering luster, a lovely thing placed in the firmament;
with the sounding of lutes, drums, and cymbals, it is as radiant as the city of Indra.”
“There are red, white, and blue lotuses, water-lilies, and fragrant bandhuka flowers;
there are sal trees in full bloom and ashoka trees, and this place is frequented by the sweet scents of various trees and shrubs.
It is entwined with saḷala, labuja, and bhujaka vines, and hung with kusa grass and well-flowered creepers.”
A beautiful, glorious lotus pond, resembling a net of jewels, has appeared for you.
Whatever species of water-born flowers grow there, and whatever species of trees exist upon the land—
whether human, non-human, or divine— all have been produced within your dwelling.
“What is the fruit of that self-restraint and discipline? By what result of karma have you been reborn here?
And how was this celestial mansion attained by you? Speak of that immediately, O lady of beautiful thighs.
(646) In this context, *phalikarajatahemajālachannaṃ* means covered with nets of crystal gems, silver, and gold.
I saw that it was covered on all sides—above and below—with walls made of crystal gems and lattices made of silver and gold;
and I beheld its floor as having various wonderful surfaces, by way of floors and grounds of diverse colors and variegated arrangements.
"Suramma" means very delightful. It is called a *byamha* because those desiring to dwell there reside within it.
The abode. "Adorned with archways" means endowed with archways made of the seven precious gems, variegated with various floral designs and the like.
Alternatively, "archway" (*toraṇa*) is a name for a gate-tower or palace;

and by that, the celestial mansion (*vimāna*) is endowed with many stories and diverse forms. "Strewn with golden chains" means its courtyard is covered with golden sands. For they are similar to sand...
*Suvaṇṇakhaṇḍā* means "shining" (*rucā*); it is called *rucaka* because it is indeed shining. *Subha* means "it shines" (*sobhati*), or alternatively, "it appears beautifully" (*suṭṭhu bhāti*).
*Vimāna* means "excellently appearing," the sense being that it is great in its dimensions. 647. *Bhāti* means "it shines," "it glows.
*Nabheva suriyo* means "like the sun in the sky," like the Āditya in the atmosphere. *Sarade* means "in the autumn season."
“Dispeller of darkness” means the destroyer of gloom. It shines and glows just as the thousand-rayed sun shines during the autumn season;
in this way your celestial mansion (vimāna) shines and glows—the letter *m* serves to join the words.
“Like a flame of smoke” means like a blazing fire; for since smoke is seen rising from that fire, it is called “a flame of smoke.”
It is called "dhūmaketu. *Niseti* means *nisati*, which signifies "by night. *Nabhagge* means in a portion of the sky;
what is meant is a region of space. Alternatively, the reading is *nagagge*, meaning on a mountain peak. The construction is: "This is your celestial mansion (*vimāna*). (Verse 648:
*Musatīva nayanaṃ*—it is as if it steals away the eye, because by its extreme brilliance it obstructs the function of seeing.
It is as if it steals the eyes of those looking on who are unable to look away. Therefore he said, "sateratāvā," meaning "like a flash of lightning.

"Resounding with the sounds of vīṇās, murajas, saṃmattas, and tāḷas" means it was filled with a single, uniform resonance by the sounds of large lutes and the like, of kettledrums such as the bherī, and of hand-claps and bronze cymbals.
"Iddha" [means] by the sons of the gods, the daughters of the gods, and divine prosperity.
"Blazing" (samiddhaṃ). "Like Indapura" means like the city of Sudassana. 649.
"Lotuses and water-lilies, blue lotuses and white water-lilies"—this is stated as a single compound (*ekattavasena*) for *paduma*, *kumuda*, *uppala*, and *kuvalaya*.
The word "there are" (*atthi*) should be supplied and connected [to each term]. In that context, by the inclusion of *paduma*...
It should be understood that by the mention of the *puṇḍarīka*, the white lotus is included; by the mention of the *kumuda*, all varieties of white and red water-lilies are included;
by the mention of the *uppala*, the red lotus or the entire genus of blue lotuses is included; and by the mention of the *kuvalaya*, only the blue lotus is intended.
In the phrase "and there are *yodhika*, *bandhuka*, and *anojaka*," the word *ca* is a mere particle; it refers to the *yodhika*, *bandhujīvaka*, and *anojaka* trees.
And the meaning is "they exist. Some, having cited the reading "anojakāpi santi" (there are also *anojaka* trees), explain the meaning as "it is stated that there are also *anojaka* trees.

Regarding "the *asoka* trees are blossoming and in flower along with the *sāla* trees," it should be construed as: "the *sāla* trees are blossoming and in flower, and the *asoka* [trees are likewise].
"This place is frequented by the beautiful fragrances of various excellent trees" means by the lovely scents of diverse, superior trees.
The meaning is: "This celestial mansion (vimāna) of yours has been served and cultivated.
Regarding the phrase *saḷalalabujabhujakasaṃyuttā*: it means joined with *saḷala* trees, *labuja* trees, and *bhujaka* trees standing on the bank.
The *bhujaka* is a certain fragrant tree found in the world of the gods and on Mount Gandhamādana, but not elsewhere.
They say it does not exist. The phrase *kusaka-suphullita-latā-valambinīhi* is to be construed as:
"connected with *kusaka* grasses such as palm and coconut, with hanging creepers such as *santānaka*, and with well-flowered vines.
*Maṇijāla-sadisa* means "having water resembling a net of jewels. There is also a reading in the Pāḷi of *maṇijala-sadisa*, which means "having water resembling jewels. *Yasassinī* means...
This is an address to the deity. "They stand near you" means that the delightful lotus pond, possessing the qualities already described, stands in the vicinity of your celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
"Water-born" refers to the lotuses and other such flowers mentioned above. "Those women" means those who are there. "Land-born" refers to jasmine (*yodhikā*) and other such plants.
"And whatever others exist" refers to other species of trees as well, both those that bear flowers and those that bear fruit.
They are indeed right here near your celestial mansion (vimāna).

652. "Of what self-restraint and what subduing is this the result? means: of what kind of self-restraint among bodily restraint and so forth, and of what kind of subduing among the subduing of the sense faculties and so forth, is this the result?
"By what [deed] did you attain it? refers to that which produces a different rebirth, distinct from that which produces the pleasure of enjoyment.
Having said, "By what fruit of karma have you been reborn here?", he spoke again, "And how did you obtain this celestial mansion?

In that context, "by the fruit of karma" (*kammaphalena*) implies the remainder of the phrase "by the fruit of karma having begun to ripen"; furthermore, this instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*).
"He spoke immediately after that" (*tadanupadaṃ avacāsi*) means he spoke immediately following the words of the karma mentioned by me.
Having composed appropriate verses, you should speak them. Regarding "Aḷārapamhe," the intended meaning is "gopakhume," which refers to thick and closely joined eyelashes.
Then the deity said:
"Just as this celestial mansion was attained by me, frequented by flocks of cranes, peacocks, and cakoras;"
It was frequented by divine swan-kings, and resounded with the cries of birds, ducks, and cuckoos.
"It is filled with various *santānaka* flowering trees of many kinds, and possesses *pāṭali*, *jambu*, and *asoka* trees;
just as I have obtained this celestial mansion, so shall I describe it to you—listen, O Venerable One."
“Venerable sir, to the east of the excellent city of Magadha there is a village named Nālakagāma.
There, in former times, I was a daughter-in-law, and they knew me there as Pesavatī.
I [served] him who was skilled in the purpose and the Dhamma, honored by gods and humans, and great.”
With a joyful mind, I scattered flowers over the immeasurable Upatissa who had attained Nibbāna.
Having honored that sublime Seer, who had reached the supreme goal and was bearing his final body,
I left behind my human frame and came here to this place among the Thirty-three gods, where I shall not dwell again.
653. "Frequented by flocks of cranes, peacocks, and cakoras" means that it was roamed about here and there by groups of *sārasa* cranes, *sikhāṇḍika* peacocks, and *kumbhakāra* wild cocks.

"Traversed by divine swans and king-goose" means that it was frequented here and there by water-birds known as "swimmers" (*pilava*) because they move by swimming on the water, and by king-goose. "Resounding with the cries of *dija*, *kāraṇḍava*, and cuckoos."
It resounded with the cries of *kāraṇḍava* ducks, *kādamba* geese, cuckoos, and other birds.
(654) "Variegated with various *santānaka* flower-trees": there are various kinds of flowering trees possessing manifold branches and twigs;

these various flowering trees, which are *santānaka* flower-trees, are "variegated with various *santānaka* flower-trees. It is "variegated" because it possesses diverse forms and a variegated arrangement due to those [trees].
For where it should have been said “various” (*vividha*), it is stated as “of various kinds” (*vividhā*). “*Santānakā*” refers to the creepers of sensual desire;
and since various flowering trees are present there, it is “variegated by those,” meaning “variegated by various *santānaka* creepers and flowering trees.
Some read: “Variegated by various *santānaka* creepers and flowering trees, possessing *pāṭali*, *jambu*, and *asoka* trees. According to them, the phrase “there are flowering trees” [is understood].
Having brought [the words] together, they should be connected. Or, "puppharukkha" is a caseless (avibhattika) designation; it means "flower-trees. 655.
"To the east of the excellent city of Magadha" means to the eastern direction of the excellent Magadha, that most supreme kingdom of Magadha by virtue of being the place of full enlightenment.
There, in former times, I was a daughter-in-law; formerly, I was in that village of Nālaka.
In a certain household, I was the daughter-in-law.
(656) *Sāti* means "myself. One who is skilled in both meaning (*attha*) and the Dhamma is "skilled in meaning and Dhamma" (*atthadhammakusala*), referring to the Blessed One.

One by whom the one skilled in meaning and Dhamma is honored is "one who honors the one skilled in meaning and Dhamma" (*apacitatthadhammakusala*), namely the General of the Dhamma (*Dhammasenāpati*). He is honored...
Or, it is *kusala* because it is conducive to decrease (*apacaya*), to Nibbāna, and to the remaining meanings and phenomena (*attha-dhamma*) therein;

or it is *kusala* because it is conducive to the decrease of venerable meanings, phenomena, cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*magga*). It is "great" (*mahanta*) because it is endowed with great and sublime aggregates of virtue (*sīla-kkhandha*) and so forth.
"With flowers" means with flowers made of jewels and with other [ordinary] flowers.
657. "One who has gone to the supreme goal" means one who has attained *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*). "The body" (*samussaya*) refers to the physical frame.

"Gone to the realm of the Thirty-three" (*tidasagatā*) means having gone to the celestial abode of the Thirty-three, having been reborn in the *Tāvatiṃsa* divine host. "Here" (*idha*) means in this world of the gods.
"I dwell in this place" (*āvasāmi ṭhānaṃ*) means I inhabit this celestial mansion (*vimāna*). The rest is exactly as previously explained.

Thus, taking the discourse delivered by the Venerable Vaṅgīsa and the deity as the introductory narrative (*aṭṭhuppatti*), the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled multitude. That teaching was of great benefit to the people.
The commentary on the *Pesavatī-vimāna* is concluded.
8. The commentary on the *Mallikā-vimāna*.
The *Mallikā-vimāna*: "Yellow-robed, yellow-bannered. What is its origin?

Beginning from the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, up until the taming of the wanderer Subhadda—once the Buddha’s work was completed—at Kusinārā, in the Upavattana Sāla grove of the Malla kings, between the twin Sāla trees on the full moon of the month of Visākha at the hour of dawn, [he passed away] into the Nibbāna-element without residue.
When the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, had attained final Nibbāna, while the worship of his relics was being performed by gods and humans,
there then lived in Kusinārā an upāsikā named Mallikā, the wife of the wrestler Bandhula and daughter of the Malla king;
she was faithful and confident, and her own great garland of jasmine ornaments was like those of the great upāsikā Visākhā.
Having washed [the body] with scented water, rubbed it with a *dukūla* cloth, and taken other various perfumes, garlands, and so forth, she honored the Blessed One’s body.
This is the summary here; for the detailed account, however, it has already been related in the commentary on the *Dhammapada* in the story of Mallikā.
Having passed away at a later time, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas; by the power of that offering, her [splendor] became uncommon compared to others.
His divine prosperity was magnificent. His garments, ornaments, and celestial palace were radiant with the seven precious gems, especially glowing with the luster of refined gold;
they were exceedingly brilliant, making all directions appear as if drenched by streams of molten gold, turning them a deep golden hue.
Then the Venerable Nārada, while wandering on his journey through the heavens, saw this and approached him. Upon seeing him, she paid him homage.
He stood with his hands joined in reverential salutation.
He said to her: "Clad in yellow robes, with a yellow banner, adorned with yellow ornaments, and encircled by lovely yellow inner garments, you shine indeed."
“Wearing bracelets and armlets, adorned with golden earrings,
draped in a net of gold, and garlanded with various jewels.
Made of gold, ruby, pearl, and beryl;”
Variegated with emeralds, rubies, and sapphires, and with gems as blue as the eyes of a pigeon;
here, the melodious cries of various peacocks, the king of swans,
and the sweet-voiced cuckoos are heard, sounding like a five-fold musical ensemble being played.
“Your chariot is beautiful and lovely, adorned with various jewels;
it shines, perfectly fashioned from minerals of diverse colors.
Standing upon that chariot, which has the hue of refined gold, you illuminate this region.”
“O deity, being questioned, tell me: what is the fruit of which deed is this?”—thus he asked.
658. Therein, “clad in yellow garments” means wearing robes that shine with a golden-yellow luster due to their being as bright as pure gold.

“With a yellow banner” means having banners of golden-yellow radiance because of the large golden flags raised at the gate and on the chariot of the celestial mansion. “Adorned with yellow ornaments” means...

She was adorned with ornaments that shone with a yellow luster. Although her ornaments were variegated with various jewels blazing with networks of diverse rays, because they were produced by such specific excellence of her own virtuous conduct, they were especially characterized by a yellow radiance, as if illuminated by a network of rays from perfectly pure gold.
"With yellow inner garments" means with upper robes (*uttariya*) of yellow color.
In such passages as, “That bhikkhu may accept a robe from him, with an inner and an outer garment at most,” the word *antara* refers to the lower garment (*nivāsana*).
However, here it should be understood as referring to the upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*), as in the expression “inner and outer robes” (*antarasāṭaka*).
*Antara-uttariya*, *uttarāsaṅga*, and *upasaṃbyāna* are synonyms. “With beautiful ones” means with those that are lovely, soft, and smooth.
"You shine even when unadorned": although you are not adorned with these ornaments, you shine by the excellence of your own physical form alone.
However, those ornaments shine having reached your body; therefore, the intended meaning is that even though you are unadorned, you are like one who is adorned.
659. "Who are you, wearing shell-bracelets and armlets?": who are you, belonging to which class of devas, wearing golden bracelets?
"Or wearing golden armlets. *Kambuparihāraka* refers to a specific type of hand ornament, while *kāyūra* refers to a specific type of arm ornament.
Alternatively, *kambu* means gold; thus, "wearing golden armlets" (*kambukāyūradhare*) means wearing golden ornaments for the upper arms.
"Adorned with golden hair-ornaments" (*kañcanāveḷabhūsita*) means adorned with hair-ornaments made of gold. "Covered with a net of gold" (*hemajālakasañchanna*).
Her body was covered by a golden lattice-work inlaid with jewels. "Wearing garlands of various gems" means:
she is wearing various strings of gems upon her head like a garland of constellations on a night during the dark fortnight; thus he asks, "Who are you, O wearer of garlands of various gems?
(Verse 660). Regarding the passage beginning with "made of gold": those gem-garlands by which that deity is said to be "wearing garlands of various gems," of them—
...the vision. In that context, "made of gold" means garlands made of *siṅgī* gold. "Made of ruby" (*lohitaṅga*) means made of red gems such as the *paduma-rāga*.

"Masāragalla" means made of *masāragalla* gems. "Together with rubies" means together with those made of *lohitaṅga* gems, as well as those made of *kabara* gems and those made of the red gems known as *lohitaṅga*;
this is the meaning. "Variegated with pigeon-eye gems" means with gems resembling the eyes of a pigeon.
The intention is that these garlands of jewels upon your head are composed of the very finest gems as previously described.
661. "Koci koci" means "this or that," referring to various individuals. "Ettha" means "among these," specifically among these flower-garlands and wreaths.
"Mayūrasussara" means a beautiful sound like that of a peacock. "Haṃsassarañña" means one with a voice like a swan; another has a voice similar to a swan. "Karavīkasussara" means...

Their voice is as beautiful as that of the *karavīka* bird. Just as the cry of those flower garlands is like the call of a peacock, a swan, or a *karavīka*, so too is their voice heard—sweet in form and lovely. Like what? Like the sounding of a fivefold musical ensemble (*pañcaṅgika-tūriya*).
Just as when a fivefold musical ensemble is played by a skilled musician, so too is their voice heard; "lovely in form" is the meaning.
For this is the accusative case in the sense of location (*bhumm-attha*).
"By means of various-colored parts" means by means of the constituent parts (*dhātu*) of various forms, such as the axle, wheels, spokes, and so forth.
"It shines, being well-proportioned" means that it shines because of the mutual proportionality of its parts and the perfection of their distinct divisions.

Having offered it, it shines forth. Alternatively, "well-proportioned" means that even though it is produced solely by kamma, it shines as if it were fashioned and arranged by a highly skilled master craftsman.
663. "With the color of a golden image" means in that chariot which resembles a golden statue due to its exceedingly radiant yellow luster.

"Kañcanabimbavaṇṇe" is an address to that deity; the meaning is: "like a golden image washed with scented water, rubbed with a paste of vermilion, and polished with a cotton pad. "Bhāsasi maṃ padesaṃ" means:
"you illuminate and make shine this entire region of the earth."
Thus questioned by the elder, that deity also answered with these verses:
“A golden net, variegated with gems and gold, inlaid with pearls and covered with a lattice of refined gold—
this I offered with a devout heart when Gotama, the immeasurable one, had attained final Nibbāna.”
“Having performed that wholesome deed praised by the Buddha, we are now free from sorrow, happy, joyful, and free from illness.
(664) In this context, *sovaṇṇajālaṃ* means a golden net made to the size of the body. *Maṇisoṇṇacittitaṃ* means inlaid with jewels and gold.
It was variegated with various kinds of gems and gold by way of ornaments such as head-pieces, neck-pieces, and so forth, placed upon the head and other parts.
It was "studded with pearls" (muttācita), meaning it was covered with strings of pearls fastened here and there.
It was "covered with a golden net" (hemajālena channa), meaning it was shrouded by a radiant net made of gold; for it was indeed variegated with both various kinds of gems and gold.

Though strewn with strings of pearls, it stands like a golden mirror, becoming a single expanse of light as it is almost entirely covered by a shimmering net of golden radiance—extremely brilliant due to contact with the rays of the sun—that belongs to the most perfectly pure, glowing gold.
"Parinibbute" means having attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without residue. "Gotama" refers to the Blessed One.
He identifies [the Buddha] by his clan name. "Immeasurable" means one who cannot be measured due to the power of his qualities.
"With a confident mind" means with a mind made serene by faith directed toward the Buddha, which has the fruit of karma as its object. "I offered" means I placed them upon his body by way of worship;
I fastened them [as ornaments].
665. *Tāhaṃ* means "I call that. *Kusalaṃ* means wholesome (*kusala*) in the sense of being free from what is blameworthy (*kuccha-salana*).
*Buddhavaṇṇitaṃ* means praised by the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*), as in the passage beginning, "Monks, as far as there are beings, whether footless or two-footed...

*Apeta-sokā* means those from whom sorrow has departed; because of the absence of the causes of sorrow, such as the loss of wealth, they are free from grief. By this, he expresses the absence of mental suffering.
“Happy” (*sukhitā*) means having experienced happiness and having attained happiness. By this, he speaks of the absence of physical suffering.

Through the absence of mental suffering, she has attained joy; through the absence of physical suffering, she is healthy. Therefore, he said, “joyful and free from illness. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
And this meaning was established at the time of the recitation (*saṅgīti*) precisely according to the sequence spoken by himself and the deity.
The Venerable Nārada informed the compilers of the Dhamma, and they included it in the collection exactly as it was.
The commentary on the Mallikā-vimāna is finished.
9. The commentary on the Visālakkhi-vimāna.
"Who are you, O large-eyed one?"—thus begins the *Visālakkhivimāna*. What is its origin?

After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, King Ajātasattu took the relics of the Blessed One which he himself had obtained and performed both a stupa ceremony and a great festival in Rājagaha.
At that time, there was a certain female garland-maker’s daughter named Sunandā, a lay follower and noble disciple residing in Rājagaha.
The stream-enterer sent abundant garlands and perfumes from her father’s house and performed daily worship at the cetiya;
moreover, on Uposatha days, she would go there herself and make offerings.
Later, when she was afflicted by a certain illness and passed away, she was reborn as a handmaid to Sakka, the king of the gods. Then, one day—
She entered the Cittalatā Grove together with Sakka, the lord of the devas.
There, the radiance of other deities was struck by the light of the flowers and other objects, and thus appeared variegated in color;
however, Sunandā’s radiance, not being overwhelmed by them, remained in its natural state. Seeing this, Sakka, the king of the devas, [reflected upon] the well-performed deeds she had done.
Desiring to know her, he questioned her with these verses:
“Who are you, O large-eyed one, in this delightful Cittalatā grove?
Surrounded by a host of women, whom do you circumambulate on all sides?”
“When the gods of the Thirty-three enter this grove,
they all come here adorned with their equipment, chariots, and various ornaments.
And for you, having arrived here and wandering in the park— ”
“The mind is not seen in the body; by what cause is your form such as this?
O deity, being asked, tell us: of what karma is this the fruit?

(666) In that regard, “Who indeed were you? means: in your previous existence, who were you by name, and of what kind were you, such that by the well-performed conduct practiced therein, this excellence of power has come to be yours—this is the intended meaning. “O large-eyed one” (*visālakkhī*) means: O you with expansive eyes.
667. *Yadā* means at which time. *Imaṃ vananti*: they enter this grove called the "Creeper-Grove of the Mind. *Citrā hontīti*:

in this Creeper-Grove of the Mind, through contact with various radiant splendors, their own bodies, garments, ornaments, and so forth, attain a state of excellence that surpasses even their natural luster, and thus become of variegated appearance.
*Idhāgatā* means having come here, having arrived; or, [it refers to] those for whose sake they have come here.
668. *Idha pattāya*: having arrived at, having approached this place. *Kena rūpaṃ tavedisaṃ*: by what means do they know your form?
By what cause does your form—your body—stand thus, of such a kind, overwhelming the radiance of the forest of mind-vines?
This is the intended meaning.
Thus questioned by Sakka, that deity replied with these verses:
“O Lord of Devas, Purindada, listen to the kamma by which my form,
my destination, my psychic power, and my majesty came to be.”
“In delightful Rājagaha, I was a female lay follower named Sunandā;
endowed with faith and virtue, I was always delighted in sharing.
Clothing, food, lodgings, and lamps—”
I gave to those who had become upright, with a mind full of serene confidence.
On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as during the fortnight of miracles, I offered the fast-food complete with its eight factors.
“I observed the Uposatha, always restrained in my virtues;
being self-controlled and sharing with others, I dwell in a celestial mansion.
Abstaining from taking life and restrained from false speech,”
Far from theft, misconduct, and the drinking of intoxicants—
delighting in the five precepts and skilled in the Noble Truths,
these are the female lay disciples of the illustrious Gotama, the Visionary One.
“From my family’s household, a female slave was always bringing garlands for me;
I offered them all at the stupa of the Blessed One.
And on the Uposatha day, having gone there, [I offered] garlands, perfumes, and ointments.”
With my own hands, full of faith, I offered a garland upon the stupa.
"Because of that deed, O Lord of Devas, this is my form, my destiny,
my psychic power, and my majesty— because I offered that garland."
“And as for that virtue which I possessed, it has not yet ripened;
yet my hope, O Lord of Devas, is that I may become a once-returner.
(669) Therein, “destination” means this destination of the gods, or rebirth. “Success” means this success of a deity, the fulfillment of one’s intention.
“Power” (*ānubhāva*) means majesty. “Purindada” is an address to Sakka; for he is called “Purindada” because he gave gifts in the past (*pure*).

(676) “From the family of kinsmen” refers to his father’s house. “She always brings garlands” means that at all times, day after day, a maidservant brings flowers from the family of kinsmen for me. “They offer them all” means...
I did not use for myself any of the garlands, perfumes, and other offerings brought from my father’s house for my own adornment;
instead, I offered them all as worship at the stupa of the Blessed One and performed that act of devotion.

(677–8) “And on the Uposatha day, having gone” means that on the Uposatha day, I myself went to the site of the stupa. “The garland which I offered” refers to the offering of garlands and perfumes made at that time to the stupa of the Blessed One; the construction of the sentence is: “by that deed.”

679. "That has not yet ripened" means that because of the power of the merit consisting of worship, that observance of virtue—namely, the fact that I was virtuous and that protected virtue which was thus guarded—has not yet found an opportunity to ripen; it has not begun to ripen.
The meaning is that its fruition occurs in another very next existence. And furthermore, O Lord of Devas, I am a once-returner (sakadāgāminī).
“O Lord of Devas, my aspiration—‘How indeed might I become a once-returner?’—is directed solely toward the domain of the Noble Dhamma, not toward a specific state of existence.
Yet that [aspiration], like seeking clarified butter from curds, is incapable of producing its result.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Sakka, Lord of the Devas, then related this matter to the Venerable Vaṅgīsa Thera exactly according to the sequence spoken by himself and that goddess.

At the time of the communal recitation (saṅgīti), the Venerable Vaṅgīsa related it to the Great Elders who were the compilers of the Dhamma, and they included it in the recitation exactly as it was told.
The commentary on the *Visālakkhivimāna* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Pāricchattakavimāna*:
Regarding the *pāricchattaka* coral tree, there is the *Pāricchattakavimāna*. What is its origin? The Blessed One was at Sāvatthī.

The Blessed One was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove. At that time, a certain lay follower living in Sāvatthī approached the Blessed One, invited him for the following day’s meal, and prepared a large pavilion at the gate of his own house.
He enclosed it with a screen-wall, tied a canopy above, hoisted flags and banners, and adorned it with cloths of various colors and garlands of perfumed flowers.
Having hung [the canopy] and prepared seats in a place sprinkled and swept, he announced that it was time for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One,
having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered the pavilion— which was adorned and prepared like a celestial mansion—
and sat down on the prepared seat, illuminating it like the thousand-rayed sun shining upon the depths of the ocean.
The lay follower honored the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.

At that time, a certain woman gathering firewood, having seen an ashoka tree in full bloom in the Andhavana forest, was returning after picking up many ashoka flowers along with their sprouts and buds; she [approached] the Blessed One.
Seeing him seated there, with a mind full of faith, they spread a carpet of flowers all around his seat.
Having performed this worship of the Blessed One, having paid homage, and having circumambulated him three times, they departed while continuing to pay their respects.
At a later time, she passed away and was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, surrounded by a retinue of a thousand celestial nymphs.
For the most part, she was dancing, singing, weaving garlands of *pāricchattaka* flowers, rejoicing, playing, and experiencing happiness in the Nandana Grove.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wandering on a tour of the devas in the manner previously described, went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
having seen her and understood the deed she had performed, he questioned her with these verses:
“Under the delightful and enchanting Pāricchattaka coral tree,
weaving celestial garlands, you sing and rejoice.
As you dance there, from every one of your limbs— ”
Divine sounds resound, lovely and delightful to hear.
As you dance, from every limb of yours,
divine fragrances waft forth— pure scents, enchanting.
As they were being loosened from their bodies,
the sound of the ornaments upon their braided hair was heard like that of a fivefold musical ensemble.
The flower-crests, shaken by the wind and trembling in the breeze—
Their sound was heard like that of a fivefold musical ensemble:
“Even the garland upon your head, fragrant and delightful,
its scent wafts in all directions like that of a mañjūsaka tree.”
“You smell that pure fragrance and see a form unlike that of humans;
O deity, being questioned, tell me: of what karma is this the fruit?
(680) Therein, “having taken a *koviḷāra* flower from the *pāricchattaka*” means having taken a divine garland from a *koviḷāra* flower named *pāricchattaka*.
The construction is: "they were binding it. For that which worldly people call "Pārijāta" is called "Pāricchattaka" in the Māgadha language.
And as for the "Koviḷāra," it is of the *koviḷāra* species; and they say that while there is a *koviḷāra* both in the human world and in the heavenly world, this is of its species (*jāti*). 681.
However, at the time of that deity's dancing, by virtue of the weight of her limbs, from her body and from her ornaments...
An exceedingly sweet sound issues forth, and its fragrance remains pervading all directions at all times. Therefore, he said: “As you were dancing,” and so forth.
In that context, *savanīyā* means worthy of being heard, or beneficial for hearing; the sense is that it is pleasant to the ear. (Verse 683) *Vivattamānā kāyena*:
by your body—that is, by your physical form—as it was turning; this is used in the sense of a characteristic mark of a particular state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*).
This is a word expressing the instrument (*karaṇavacana*). "Those ornaments on the braids" (*veṇīsu piḷandhanā*): these are the ornaments upon her hair-braids;
here, one should understand either an elision of the case-ending (*vibhattilopa*) or a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
684. "Ear-ornaments" (*vaṭaṃsaka*): the meaning is jeweled ear-rings (*kaṇṇika*). "Shaken by the wind" (*vātadhuta*): by a gentle breeze.
“Fumigating. “Shaken by the wind” means shaken and moved on all sides, especially by the wind.
Alternatively, “the ear-ornaments shaken by the wind” means that whether not stirred by the wind or indeed stirred by the wind, those ear-ornaments which were shaken—their sound is heard;
such is the construction of the meaning.
685. "The fragrance wafts through all directions"—the fragrance of that divine garland upon your head wafts through all directions.

How so? "Like the mañjūsaka tree"—just as the mañjūsaka tree, when in full bloom, pervades many *yojanas* with its own scent and wafts through all directions, so too does the garland adorning your head.
"Gandha" means fragrance. It is said that this tree stands in the midst of the Uposatha assembly hall for the Paccekabuddhas on Mount Gandhamādana.
Whatever fragrant flowers exist in the world of the gods and the world of humans, they all blossom upon its branch-tips.
Because of this, it is exceedingly fragrant. Thus, it is called "Gandha" because of the fragrant garland worn by that deity.
Therefore it was said: “Just as the Mañjūsaka tree.

(686) Although all objects there are indeed pleasant forms because that heaven possesses the six bases of contact, yet because that deity obtains especially excellent odors and visible forms, [it is said]: “You smell that pure fragrance...”
"Do you see a non-human form? it was asked.
Then the deity replied with two verses:
"Radiant, possessing rays of light, endowed with color and fragrance;"
“I offered a garland of *asoka* flowers to the Buddha.
Having performed that wholesome deed praised by the Buddha,
I am now free from sorrow, happy, joyful, and free from illness.”

687. In this context, with reference to the Asoka flower’s excellence—which, resembling a mass of well-polished coral, was then present like a shimmering net of rays through its collection of filaments and anthers—the Buddha said, "Radiant and luminous.
The remainder is exactly as previously explained.

Then, after the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna had taught the Dhamma to that deity and her retinue once she had related her own deeds of good conduct, he returned from there to the human world and reported the matter to the Blessed One.
Taking that as the occasion, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the great assembly that had gathered; that teaching was of great benefit to the multitude.
The commentary on the *Pāricchattaka-vimāna* is finished.
Thus ends the third chapter, the *Pāricchattaka-vagga*, adorned with ten stories, within the *Vimānavatthu* of the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.
The commentary on the meanings is finished.
4. The Mañjiṭṭhaka Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Mañjiṭṭhaka Vimāna.
In the Mañjiṭṭhaka Chapter, "in the Mañjiṭṭhaka mansion" refers to the Mañjiṭṭhaka Mansion. How did its origin come about?

The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove. There, a certain lay follower invited the Blessed One and, having prepared a pavilion in the same manner as described in the immediately preceding mansion, he worshipped the Teacher seated there and gave a gift. By that—

At that time, a certain female slave of a household, having seen a *sāla* tree in full bloom in the Andhavana grove, gathered its flowers there, strung them with fibers, and fashioned them into ear-ornaments (*vaṭaṃsaka*).
Then, taking many loose flowers and choice blossoms, she entered the city. In that pavilion stood the morning sun, illuminating the interior of Mount Yugandhara.
Seeing the Blessed One seated there, emitting rays of six-colored Buddha-light as if they were fireflies, her heart was filled with serene faith.

As if worshipping him with those flowers, she placed flower-earrings all around his seat, scattered the remaining flowers, paid him respectful homage, circumambulated him three times, and departed. Later, when her time had come—
Having done so, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
there, for her, a palace made of ruby appeared, and before it, a great grove of sal trees manifested with its ground strewn with golden sand.
Whenever she emerged from the palace and entered the sal grove, the branches of the sal trees would bend down and shower flowers over her.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having approached him in the manner described above, questioned him regarding his past deeds with these verses:
“In the Mañjiṭṭhaka mansion, strewn with golden sand,
you delight in the fivefold music that sounds so beautifully.”
“Descending from that celestial mansion made of jewels which you have fashioned,
you enter the sal grove that is in full bloom at all times.
O deity, at the foot of whichever sal tree you stand, [there you remain].”
That supreme tree, bowing down, releases its flowers:
“The sāla grove, stirred by the wind, shaken and frequented by birds,
its fragrance wafts in all directions like the mañjūsaka tree.”
“You smell that pure fragrance and see a form unlike that of humans;
O deity, being questioned, tell us: of what karma is this the fruit?
(689) In that context, “in the Mañjiṭṭhaka mansion” means in a mansion made of red crystal. For its color is like that of the *sinduvāra* and *kaṇavīra* flower buds.
“Mañjiṭṭhaka” is what is said. “Spread with golden sand” means on ground-surface strewn all around with scattered golden sand.
“You delight in the well-played” means you take pleasure in the fivefold musical ensemble that is played excellently.

“Signs made of jewels” means the celestial mansions made of jewels, fashioned by your own skillful artisan of good conduct. “You plunge into” means you enter. “Belonging to all seasons” means pleasant at all times, suitable for all seasons, or blooming at all times.
692. "Vāteritam" means shaken or moved by the wind, just as flowers are scattered [by it].
"Ādhutam" means being gently shaken, slowly and steadily, by a mild breeze. "Dijasevitam" means frequented by flocks of birds such as peacocks, cuckoos, and others.
Thus questioned by the Elder, that deity answered with these verses:
“In my human existence among men, I was a slave in a noble family.
Having seen the Buddha seated, I scattered *sāla* flowers over him.
I also fashioned a well-crafted ear-ornament made of *sāla* flowers.”
With my own hands, full of faith, I offered it to the Buddha.
Having performed that wholesome deed praised by the Buddha,
I am now free from sorrow, happy, joyful, and healthy.

694–5. Therein, *ayirakule* means in a noble family; the meaning is "in the husband’s home. *Ahuṃ* means "I was. *Okiriṃ* means "I scattered [flowers]. *Upanāmesiṃ* means "I offered" by way of worship. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having taught the Dhamma to that deity together with her retinue, returned to the human world and reported the matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, taking that as the occasion for instruction, [spoke] to the great assembly that had gathered.
He taught the Dhamma. That teaching was beneficial to the world with its devas.
The commentary on the Mañjiṭṭhaka-vimāna is finished.
2. Commentary on the Pabhassara-vimāna.
The *Pabhassaravimāna* (The Radiant Mansion) depicts a splendor of exquisite, radiant color. How did it come to be? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha.
At that time, there was a certain lay follower (*upāsaka*) in Rājagaha who was deeply devoted to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
He had a daughter who was faithful and confident; she, too, possessed great reverence and deep respect for the Elder. Then, one day—
While wandering for alms in Rājagaha, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached that family. Upon seeing the Elder, she was filled with joy;
she prepared a seat, and when the Elder had sat down there, she honored him with a garland of *sumana* flowers and poured sweet sugar-cane molasses into his bowl.
The Elder sat down, desiring to give a blessing of thanksgiving. However, because of the many duties of household life, she—
Having announced that she had no opportunity [to hear the Dhamma], she paid homage to the Elder, saying, "I shall listen to the Dhamma on another day," and took her leave.
On that very day, she passed away and was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached her and questioned her with these verses:
“O radiant one, with a complexion like the finest gold, clothed in garments of deep red, possessed of great psychic power and limbs as beautiful as sandalwood—
O auspicious goddess, who are you that pays homage to me?”
“Your couch is costly, variegated with various jewels, and beautiful;
seated upon it, you shine like the king of the gods in the Nandana grove.
What good conduct did you practice in the past, O lady? Of what deed is this the fruit?”
"You experience [this] in the world of the gods; O deity, being questioned, tell us:
what is the fruit of which kamma? (697).
Therein, "radiant with the luster of excellent beauty": it shines, it glows, thus it is *nibhā*; beauty itself is the radiance, hence "beauty-radiance" (*vaṇṇanibhā*).
“Of radiant and excellent complexion” (*pabhassaravaravaṇṇanibhā*) means that she possesses a radiant and excellent appearance due to the absence of any blemishes on her skin.
It is stated as “of radiant and excellent complexion” by way of addressing her. “Clad in well-dyed garments” (*surattavatthavasaṇe*) means dressed in well-dyed clothes.
“With limbs beautiful with sandalwood” (*candanaruciragatte*) means having limbs beautiful as if anointed with sandalwood—that is, with *gosīta* sandalwood.
The meaning is that his bodily limbs were very red and pleasing, as if thickly smeared [with ointment], or rather, his limbs were beautiful due to an application of sandalwood paste.
Thus questioned by the Elder, the deity answered with these verses:
“Bhante, while you were wandering for alms, I gave you a garland and molasses.”
“This is the result of that karma which I am experiencing in the world of the gods.
Yet, O Venerable One, I feel remorse; I have erred and am now suffering.
For I did not listen to the Dhamma so well-taught by the King of Dhamma.”
“I say this to you, O venerable ones, whoever has compassion for me:
exhort me to those teachings so well-expounded by the King of Dhamma.
Those who have faith in the Buddha, in the Dhamma, and in the Jewel of the Saṅgha—”
“They outshine me in life-span, fame, and glory;
in brilliance and beauty they are superior, other gods who possess greater psychic power than I.
(700) In this context, *māla* refers to the *sumana* flower. *Phāṇita* refers to the inspissated juice made from taking sugarcane juice.
701. *Anutāpa* means remorse (*vippaṭisāra*). He states its cause: "I have offended you, venerable sir, and I am suffering.
Now he shows that [remorse] in its true nature: "I did not hear the Dhamma. That I, at that time, did not listen to the Dhamma which you desired to teach.
Of what kind? "The well-taught Dhamma by the King of Dhamma," meaning by the Perfectly Enlightened One, because it is excellent in the beginning and so forth.
"And well-expounded" means by virtue of its being exclusively conducive to liberation (*ekantaniyyānika*). 702. "That" (*taṃ*) means:
because it was well-taught by the King of Dharma (*dhammarāja*), and because [the state] free from taints (*āsava*) is not a cause for remorse for those like me.
"That" (*taṃ*) means you; "to you" (*tuyhaṃ*) is the meaning. "Of whom" (*yassa*) means of whoever. "Worthy of compassion" (*anukampiya*) means one who should be pitied. "Anyone" (*koci*)...

"Whoever": anyone at all. "In the teachings" (*dhammesu*): in the teachings such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. Alternatively, the reading is "in the Dhamma" (*dhamme hi*), meaning in the Dhamma of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
*Hi* is merely a particle, or it is a grammatical inversion. *Taṃ*: that person who is to be pitied. "Well-taught" (*sudesitaṃ*): well-expounded. 703–4. "They outshine me":
those sons of the gods (*devaputta*) who have faith in the Triple Gem outshine me by surpassing me.
"By heat" means by brilliance, by power. "Others" refers to those others. "Than me" is the instrumental case used in the sense of comparison.

This shows that those gods who are even more excellent in beauty and more possessed of great psychic power (*mahiddhika*) are indeed those who have full confidence in the Three Jewels. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Radiant Mansion (*Pabhassara-vimāna*) is concluded.
3. Description of the Nāga Mansion (*Nāgavimānavanṇanā*).
"Adorned and covered with jewels and gold" refers to the Nāga mansion. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
At that time, there was a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) living in Bārāṇasī who was faithful, confident, and endowed with virtue and good conduct.
Having had a pair of robes woven for the Blessed One, having had them well-washed, she approached him, placed them at the Blessed One’s feet, and said:
"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept this pair of robes out of compassion, so that it may be for my benefit and happiness for a long time. The Blessed One accepted it from her.
Seeing her excellence of supporting conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*), he taught the Dhamma; at the conclusion of that teaching, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him to the right, she went home.
Not long after, having passed away, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas as the beloved and cherished consort of Sakka, the king of the gods, known by the name Yasuttarā.
Through the power of her merit, there arose a preeminent elephant covered with a net of gold;
upon its back appeared a pavilion made of jewels, and in its center, a well-arranged couch of precious gems.
From its two tusks emerged two delightful lotus ponds, radiant with lotuses and water-lilies. There, celestial maidens stood upon the lotus hearts, holding five-fold musical instruments.
They danced and sang.
Having stayed at Bārāṇasī for as long as he pleased, the Teacher set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī.
Gradually reaching Sāvatthī, the Blessed One indeed stayed there at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
In the monastery. Then that deity, having observed the divine splendor she was experiencing and investigating its cause, realized it was "due to her gift of a pair of garments to the Teacher.

With joy arisen and great faith and reverence for the Blessed One, desiring to pay homage, she arrived through the air at the end of the night, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, and alighted from it.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One and raising his hands in reverential salutation, he stood to one side. With the Blessed One’s permission, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa questioned him with these verses:
“Adorned with gems and gold, covered with golden nets, vast and great;”
Having mounted a well-prepared, excellent elephant, he came here through the air across the sky.
Upon the two tusks of the elephant were fashioned lotus ponds with clear water and full-blown lotuses;
amidst those lotuses, groups of musical instruments resounded, and these enchanting women danced.
“You have attained divine power, O lady of great majesty; while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means do you possess such blazing majesty, and why does your beauty illuminate all directions?
(705) In that context, “adorned” means decorated with all types of ornaments. “Studded with jewels and gold” refers to those celestial gems.
“Covered with jewels and gold” means overspread with a golden net. “Great” means vast.
“Well-equipped” means properly harnessed for the purpose of travel. “In the air” means upon the back of an elephant that has become airborne;
“in the sky” means in the atmosphere. There is also a reading: “adorned with jeweled gold. This is the summary of the meaning here.
"O deity, you, adorned with all ornaments, having mounted upon the back of a great, exceedingly vast,
and supreme elephant that is covered with various ornaments of gems and gold— studded specifically with divine, highly radiant gems and gold,
and arrayed with golden nets and hand-ornaments such as the *kumbhālaṅkāra* and others— [should proceed]."
"Sitting [there], they have come here into our presence by way of the sky. 706.
"Fashioned upon the two tusks of the nāga": just as with the royal nāga Erāvaṇa, two lotus ponds were beautifully constructed upon the two tusks of this [nāga] by a master artisan (*sucaritasippin*).
"Multitudes of musical instruments" refers to collections of fivefold musical ensembles (*pañcaṅgikatūriya*).
“They become divided” means they go to division by way of twelve different types of abodes (*laya*).
Some also read “*pavajjare*,” which means they are spoken of in various ways.
Thus, when questioned by the Elder, the deity answered with these verses:
“Having approached Bārāṇasī, I gave a pair of garments to the Buddha;
having bowed at his feet, I sat upon the ground, and filled with joy, I joined my palms in reverence.
And the Buddha, whose skin was like refined gold, taught me the arising, suffering, and impermanence.”
“When I understood, he taught the unconditioned, the eternal cessation of suffering, and the path thereto:
‘Having lived a short life and passed away from there, I was reborn among the glorious hosts of the Thirty-three.
I am one of Sakka’s consorts, renowned in all directions by the name Yasottarā.’”

708–9. Therein, *chamā* means on the ground; this is the nominative case used in the sense of the locative. *Vittā* means satisfied. *Yato* means from which—from the Teacher’s proclamation of the Dhamma as supreme. *Vijānissanti* means they will penetrate and realize the Four Noble Truths. 710.
*Appāyukī* means being short-lived due to karma that has reached exhaustion, as if with a latent intention (*abhisandhi*) born [at the time of death] thinking:
"Having performed such sublime merit, you should not remain thus in this human existence so full of suffering. Thus, they are short-lived because their karma has been spent.
"A certain Pajāpatī" means one among the sixteen thousand chief queens. "Renowned in all directions" means she was well-known and famous in every direction throughout the two worlds of the devas.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Nāgavimāna* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Aloma-vimāna*:
"With surpassing beauty" refers to the *Aloma-vimāna*. How did it originate?
While the Blessed One was dwelling at Isipatana in the Deer Park near Bārāṇasī, he dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Bārāṇasī for alms.
He entered. There, a certain woman of wretched appearance named Alomā, seeing the Blessed One, felt a heart full of faith;
seeing nothing else to give, she thought, "Even such a gift as this, when given to the Blessed One, will be of great fruit for me," and she offered some unsalted, dry, broken-colored kummāsa.
The Blessed One accepted it. Taking that gift as her object of focus, she—
She announced her joy, and later, having passed away, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna asked her:
"With such exquisite beauty... [and so on] ...your radiance illuminates all directions.
She then explained it to him; in order to demonstrate that, [the Buddha said]:
“That deity, being delighted... [as before] ...this is the fruit of such karma,” it was said:
“And I, in Bārāṇasī, gave dry sour gruel to the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, with my own hands, full of serene faith.”
“Behold the fruit of that dry, saltless ball of millet;
seeing one so hairless and happy, who would not perform meritorious deeds?
By that [merit], such is my complexion... indeed, my complexion shines forth in all directions.”
716. "There, having seen one hairless and happy": this means having seen one made happy by divine bliss simply by giving even a hairless measure of dry *kummāsa* (gruel).
"Who would not perform merit?": who indeed, desiring their own welfare and happiness, would not perform merit?
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Aloma-vimāna* is finished.
5. The commentary on the *Kañjikadāyikā-vimāna*:
"With most excellent beauty... This is the *Kañjikadāyikā-vimāna*. What is its origin? The Blessed One was at Andhakavinda.
He was dwelling there. At that time, a wind ailment arose in the Blessed One’s belly. The Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Go, Ānanda, wander for alms and bring me some rice-gruel for the sake of medicine.
“Very well, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having accepted his instruction, [he went] with the gift provided by the Great King.
Taking his bowl, he stood at the door of the residence of his personal physician.
Seeing him, the physician’s wife went out to meet him, paid homage, took the bowl, and asked the Elder, "Venerable sir, what kind of medicine do you require?
It is said that she was endowed with great intelligence and thought, "Since the Elder has come here when there is a need for medicine..."
She observed, "He does not come for alms. When it was said, "With sour gruel," she thought, "This medicine is not for my noble sir;
for such is his bowl belonging to the Blessed One. Come now, I shall prepare sour gruel suitable for the Lord of the World.
Filled with joy and inspired by great reverence, she prepared rice-gruel with jujube juice, filled the bowl, and [offered it].
In order to attend upon him, she prepared other food as well and sent it.

As soon as the Blessed One had consumed that, his affliction was completely pacified. Later, having passed away, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods and rejoices, enjoying great divine prosperity.
Then, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was wandering on a tour of the celestial realms, he [encountered her].
Seeing her wandering about surrounded by a retinue of a thousand celestial nymphs, he questioned her regarding the karma she had performed with these verses:
“With a most excellent complexion... [and so forth] ...your beauty illuminates all directions.
She, too, gave an explanation.
“Delighted, that deity... [said: ...of what deed is this the fruit?
“In Andhakavinda, I gave to the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, a meal of boiled grain soaked in sour gruel and perfumed with oil.”
“I gave [alms] mixed with long pepper, garlic, and *lāmañjaka* to one who had become upright,
with a mind full of serene confidence.
‘One might exercise the great sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch;’”
A woman who is beautiful in all her limbs and pleasing to her husband does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of giving a single portion of sour gruel.
"A hundred gold coins, a hundred horses, and a hundred chariots drawn by mules— "
A hundred thousand maidens adorned with jeweled earrings do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a single gift of sour gruel.
A hundred Himalayan elephants, with tusks like plow-poles and in full rut—
“Even Mātaṅga elephants with golden girths, clad in garments of refined gold,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of giving a single portion of sour gruel.
‘Even if one were to exercise sovereignty over all four continents;’”
“It is not worth even a sixteenth part of a single gift of sour gruel.

(723–4) In this regard: “I gave sour gruel seasoned with oil and fried with kola-berries”—meaning that after cooking a broth made from jujube-meat balls (*badara-modaka*) mixed with four parts water, which was reduced to one-fourth by the boiling process, and adding to it the three pungent spices (*tikaṭuka*), ajamoda, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), cumin (*jīraka*), garlic (*lasuṇa*), and so forth; [the merit of that]—

It shows that, having prepared it with pungent spices, having made it well-perfumed, and having had the scent of *lāmajjaka* added, she, with a devout mind, poured it into the Blessed One’s bowl and, dedicating it to the Teacher, gave it, saying, "I place it in the hand of the Elder. Therefore he said:
"Mixed with long pepper and garlic, and with *lāmajjaka*..."
“To him who had become upright, I gave with a serene mind.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Thus, when that deity, together with her retinue, had revealed the kamma of her own well-performed deeds accumulated by herself, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—
Having taught her the Dhamma and returned to the human world, he reported that occurrence to the Blessed One.
Taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly. That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Kañjikadāyikā-vimāna*.
6. Description of the Mansion of the Monastery (*Vihāravimānavannanā*).
"With most excellent beauty" refers to the mansion of the monastery. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, on a certain festival day, the great female lay devotee Visākhā went out into the park for the purpose of wandering about.

Encouraged by her female companions and her attendants, having bathed and anointed herself, eaten a fine meal, and donned the great *mahālatā* ornaments, she departed from her home with great majesty and a vast retinue, surrounded by about five hundred companions.
As she was proceeding toward the pleasure grove, she thought: "What is the use of this vain play for me, like that of a mere young girl?"
"Come now, I shall go to the monastery, pay homage to the Blessed One and the noble ladies who are worthy of veneration, and listen to the Dhamma.

Having gone to the monastery, she stood to one side, removed her great garland of *mālā* flowers, gave it into the hands of her maidservant, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One taught the Dhamma to her.
Having heard the Dhamma, she paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to her right, and paid homage to the venerable monks.
Then, departing from the monastery and having walked a short distance, she said to her slave girl, "Come now, my girl, let us put on our ornaments.
She tied that bundle up, placed it in the monastery, and after wandering here and there, at the time of departure—
Because she had forgotten it while on her way, she wished to turn back, thinking, "I have forgotten it; wait, noble lady, I shall fetch it.
Visākhā said, "If, my dear, you forgot it after placing it in the monastery, I shall relinquish it for the sake of that very monastery.
Having gone to the monastery, she approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and, making known her intention, said, "The monastery..."
“Venerable sir, I shall have it built; may the Blessed One consent out of compassion for me,” she said. The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

She then disposed of that jewelry, worth nine hundred and one million, and with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna acting as the overseer of the construction, she had the walls, pillars, beams, rafters, ridge-poles, door-frames, and windows well-proportioned.
It was a charming house with stairs and other architectural members, delightful with well-crafted woodwork,
beautiful with well-applied plastering, pleasing with various artistic works such as well-arranged floral and creeper designs,
its floor surface resembling a polished gem-studded pavement like a celestial mansion; on the lower level were five hundred chambers, and on the upper level...
"Five hundred cells" means that she completed the monastery in nine months, having had constructed a great palace suitable for the dwelling of the Buddha, the Blessed One, and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus—
a palace adorned with a thousand cells— and a thousand surrounding palaces,
as well as huts, pavilions, walkways, and so forth, by way of being an adjunct to those. When it was finished...
And while she was having a monastery built at Vihāra for nine crores of gold, she ascended a palace together with about five hundred female companions;
seeing its splendor, she became joyful and said to her companions:
"Rejoice in the merit I have acquired by having such a palace built; I give you the gift of this merit."
“I give it. “Oh, how excellent! Oh, how excellent! they all rejoiced with hearts full of faith.
Among them, a certain female lay follower (upāsikā) paid particular attention to that gift of merit. Not long after she passed away, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
By the power of her merit, [her celestial abode] was adorned with many gabled houses, walls, gardens, lotus ponds, and so forth.
A great celestial mansion appeared, sixteen *yojanas* in length, breadth, and depth, pervading a hundred *yojanas* with its own radiance and capable of traveling through the sky.
As she traveled, she was accompanied by a retinue of a thousand nymphs and moved together with that mansion.
However, the great female lay disciple Visākhā, due to her vast generosity and the perfection of her faith, was reborn among the Nimmānarati devas.
She attained the status of chief queen to Sunimmita, the king of the gods.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha, while wandering on a tour of the celestial realms, saw that friend of Visākhā reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and said:
“O goddess, you who stand there with such exquisite beauty;”
Illumining all directions like a star among the herbs,
as you dance, from every one of your limbs there issue forth divine sounds, lovely and delightful to hear.
“As she dances, from every limb divine fragrances waft forth— pure scents, most delightful.
As she turns her body, the ornaments upon her braided hair [scatter their luster].”
Their sound was heard like that of a fivefold musical ensemble:
"The flower-ornaments shaken by the wind, trembling in the breeze—
their sound was heard like that of a fivefold musical ensemble."
“Even this garland upon your head, fragrant and delightful,
its scent wafts in all directions like that of a *mañjūsaka* tree.
You smell that pure fragrance and behold this superhuman form.”
“O deity, being questioned, tell me: what is the fruit of which deed is this?”—with these verses she asked. She, in turn, explained it to him thus:
“In Sāvatthī, O Venerable One, I had a friend who built a great monastery for the Saṅgha.”
With faith in that, I rejoiced, seeing both my home and this beloved [friend].
By that very pure rejoicing of mine, I have obtained this wondrous celestial mansion, beautiful to behold;
extending sixteen yojanas on all sides, it travels through the air by means of my psychic power.
“My gabled mansions and dwellings are divided and measured out in parts;
they shine brilliantly, extending for a hundred yojanas in every direction.
And here are lotus ponds for me, frequented by large fish.”
With clear water, perfectly serene, strewn with golden sands,
covered with various lotuses and overspread with white lilies,
they waft fragrant scents, delightful when stirred by gentle breezes.
“Jambu, rose-apple, and palmyra trees, and groves of coconut palms;
various trees, not planted by hand, have grown within the inner courtyard.
Resounding with the music of various instruments and filled with the voices of throngs of celestial nymphs.”
“Even the man who should see me in a dream would be filled with joy.
‘Such a wondrous and marvelous mansion, radiant in every way, has arisen through my own deeds;
enough, therefore, with performing meritorious acts.’”
736. "In that regard, venerable sir, my friend in Sāvatthī, O Bhante Anuruddha, has built a great monastery for the Saṅgha.

"Venerable sir, near Sāvatthī, on its eastern side, my witness—my companion, the great female lay follower Visākhā—having renounced nine crores of gold, dedicated [the land] to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from the four quarters and established the Pubbārāma."
She had a great monastery built. When that monastery was finished and being offered to the Saṅgha, she expressed her appreciation, saying, "I rejoice.
At the dedication of merit made by her, I rejoiced, thinking, "Oh, what a magnificent gift has been given in this place!
Through that object, my rejoicing was born of faith in the Triple Gem and in the fruit of kamma. By way of that object, my rejoicing was [the cause].
In order to demonstrate his noble state, he said: "Having seen both the house and that which is dear to me.

The construction is as follows: having seen that house—which contained a thousand chambers, was exceedingly delightful, and resembled a celestial mansion—and having seen such a great renunciation of wealth made for the sake of the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, which was so dear to him, he offered his appreciation.
"By that very pure rejoicing of mine" means by that pure and exclusive rejoicing as previously described,
which was devoid of any actual relinquishing of material gifts. "I have obtained this wondrous palace to behold" means that I have obtained this celestial mansion (vimāna),
which is wonderful because such a thing had never occurred before, and which is most beautiful to behold due to its all-encompassing excellence and extreme loveliness.

It was attained. Having thus shown the beauty of that celestial mansion (*vimāna*), he now says "sixteen yojanas all around," etc., in order to demonstrate its greatness of dimension, greatness of power, and greatness of the objects of enjoyment.
In that context, "by my psychic power" (*iddhiyā mama*) means by my merit-based psychic power (*puññiddhiyā*).
739. "Pokkharañño" means lotus ponds. "Frequented by broad-scaled fish" means attended by divine fish.
740. "Covered with various lotuses" means strewn with various kinds of red lotuses and red water-lilies, such as those with a hundred petals, a thousand petals, and so forth.
