"Spread over with white lotuses" means covered on all sides with various kinds of white water-lilies.
The construction is: "Various fragrant trees were planted, emitting sweet scents.
(742) "He too" means that dreamer as well. "Vitta" means satisfied.
(743) "Radiant on all sides" means shining everywhere. "In the act" (*kamme hi*) means as the sign of the action; *hi* is a mere particle.
Or, because of the multiplicity resulting from the successive arising of volitions (*cetanā*), it is said "by kamma. *Alaṃ* means "it is fitting. *Kātavē* means "to do.
Now, desiring to have Visākhā explain the place where she was reborn, the Elder spoke this verse:
"By that very same pure rejoicing of yours..."
Having obtained this wondrous sight of a celestial mansion,
tell me the destiny of that woman who gave the gift: where has she been reborn?

744. In this context, the phrase "that very woman who gave that gift" refers to the Mahā-upāsikā Visākhā, with whom he speaks regarding the gift for the rejoicing (*anumodanā*) in which you obtained such prosperity.
Desiring to have that deity speak of her prosperity, he said: "Tell me her destination; where has she been reborn?"
"Her destination": her rebirth-destination as a deva produced by that [merit].
Now, showing the matter asked about by the Elder, she said:
"O Venerable Sir, she who was my friend built a great monastery for the Saṅgha."
Having understood the Dhamma, she gave a gift and was reborn among the Nimmānarati devas.
"Pajāpatī was the daughter of Sunimmita;
inconceivable is the ripening of her kamma."
"As for what you asked, 'Where was she reborn?', I have explained that to you exactly as it is, and not otherwise.
(745) In this context, "those who have understood the Dhamma" means those who have understood the Dhamma of the Teaching; the meaning is those who have penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
"Of Sunimmita" means of the divine king Sunimmita. "The ripening of his karma is inconceivable" is a designation formed by the elision of a case ending;

the meaning is that for my friend—who has been reborn among those who delight in Nibbāna—the ripening of her karma, the celestial excellence resulting from meritorious deeds, is inconceivable and immeasurable. "Not otherwise" means unerringly, according to its true nature.
But how did she learn of her excellence? Just as Subhaddā did for Bhaddā, Visākhā the goddess-daughter also came into her presence.
Now, the goddess-daughter, encouraging others as well to practice giving, taught the Dhamma with these verses:
“Therefore, exhort others as well; give gifts to the Saṅgha with your wealth.
Listen to the Dhamma with a serene mind, for this human birth, so very difficult to obtain, has been gained.
That path which the Lord of the Path taught—the one with the Brahma-voice and skin like refined gold—”
Give gifts to the Saṅgha with wealth, wherein offerings become of great fruit.
“Those eight persons praised by the virtuous, who constitute these four pairs—they are the disciples of the Sugata worthy of offerings; what is given to them yields great fruit.”
“Four who have entered the path and four who are established in the fruit—
this is the Saṅgha, upright, endowed with wisdom, virtue, and concentration.
For people who are making offerings, for living beings seeking merit...”
The merit consisting of the fruits of the acquisitions performed for the Saṅgha yields great fruit when given to the Saṅgha.
For this Saṅgha is vast and sublime; it is immeasurable like the ocean, the sea.
These disciples, the best among the heroes of men, are radiators of light who proclaim the Dhamma.
“Whatever is well given, well offered, and well sacrificed by those who give a gift dedicated to the Saṅgha—
that offering established in the Saṅgha is of great fruit and praised by those who know the world.
Remembering such a sacrifice, those who are born of wisdom wander through the world.”
“Having removed the stain of stinginess along with its root, the blameless ones go to the heavenly state.
(747) In this context, *tenahaññepi* means “for by that [reason], others too. *Tena* signifies “by that reason,” while *hi* is merely a particle.
Having said, “Exhort [others],” the passage beginning with “Give gifts to the Saṅgha” was spoken in order to demonstrate the manner of exhortation.
Referring to the human state when it is free from the eight inopportune moments (*aṭṭha akkhaṇā*), he said: "The attainment of human birth, so very difficult to obtain, has been gained.

In this context, the eight inopportune moments are: the three lower realms (*apāya*), the formless realm (*arūpa*), non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), being born in a border region (*paccantadesa*), deficiency of the sense faculties (*indriyavekalla*), being fixed in wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhikatā*), and the non-appearance of a Buddha (*buddhassa apātubhāvo*).

748. "That which is the path": a gift given to a particular field of merit is, by its very nature, a path leading to a happy destination (*sugati*), because it invariably results in rebirth there. It is designated as "the lord of the path" (*maggādhipa*) because it is far superior to the path to the states of woe (*apāya*) and to the path of the dead (*jagghamagga*). For even a gift is called "the path leading to the world of the gods," just like faith and energy. As it has been said: [The verse follows: ...just as faith is the path leading to the world of the gods, so too is giving the path leading to the world of the gods. As it is said: *“Saddhā hi kho, bhikkhave, devayāniyo maggo, sīlaṃ maññe devānaṃ patho; Dānaṃ hi kho, bhikkhave, devayāniyo maggo, cāgo maññe devānaṃ patho.”* "Faith indeed, monks, is the path leading to the world of the gods; virtue, I consider, is the path of the gods. Giving indeed, monks, is the path leading to the world of the gods; relinquishment, I consider, is the path of the gods. Thus, because it leads to a happy destination, it is the path; and because it is preeminent over other paths, it is the lord of the path. Therefore, one should practice giving with great effort. This is the meaning. Herein, the "field of merit" (*puññakkhetta*) is that which is called a "field" because it is a source of fruit, just as a field of paddy is so called because it yields grain. It is a "field of merit" because it is a source of merit. It is of three kinds: the field of recipients, the field of service, and the field of objects. Among these, the field of recipients is the most excellent. This is because it is the basis for the arising of the volition of merit, and because it possesses the qualities of being a field, such as being a recipient of offerings and being a vessel for the ripening of karmic fruit. The field of service is the field of those who provide assistance, such as parents, teachers, and those who have provided shelter. The field of objects consists of things such as water, food, and clothing. Among these, the field of recipients is the most excellent because it is the primary cause for the arising of the volition of merit. Furthermore, it is distinguished by the excellence of the recipient's qualities, such as their moral conduct, learning, and renunciation. Among the various types of recipients, the field of the Noble Ones (*ariyapuggala*) is the most excellent. Within that, the field of the Buddhas is the most excellent of all. This is because they possess the highest degree of purity and power, and because they are the supreme field for the planting of seeds of merit. Thus, one should understand the gradations of the fields of merit according to their relative superiority. This concludes the section on the field of merit. Now, regarding the "gift" (*dāna*): it is the act of relinquishing one's own possessions for the sake of another. It is of two kinds: material and spiritual. Material gifts consist of robes, alms-food, dwellings, and medicinal requisites. Spiritual gifts consist of teaching the Dhamma and providing protection from fear. Among these, the gift of the Dhamma is the most excellent. This is because it leads to the attainment of the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, and because it is the cause for the purification of the mind. One should give gifts with a mind free from stinginess, honoring the recipient and reflecting upon the fruit of giving. This is the essence of the practice of generosity. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "path" (*magga*): it is the way leading to liberation. It is the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This path is to be cultivated through the development of the perfections (*pāramitā*). By practicing these perfections, one traverses the path and reaches the city of Nibbāna. Therefore, one should strive to cultivate the path with diligence. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "lord of the path" (*maggādhipa*): it refers to the Buddha, the Teacher, who is the master of the path. He is the lord of the path because he discovered the path through his own effort and taught it to others. He is the refuge for all beings wandering in the cycle of existence. Therefore, one should take refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "fruit of giving" (*dānaphala*): it is the result of the act of giving. It is of two kinds: worldly and supramundane. Worldly fruits consist of wealth, beauty, health, and long life. Supramundane fruits consist of the attainment of the stages of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and Arahantship. Among these, the fruit of the gift of the Dhamma is the most excellent. This is because it leads to the destruction of all suffering. Therefore, one should give gifts with the aspiration for the attainment of the fruit of the Dhamma. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "field of merit" (*puññakkhetta*): it is the basis for the accumulation of merit. It is like a field because it yields the harvest of happiness. One should plant the seeds of merit in the field of the Noble Ones, for they are the most fertile soil. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "practice of generosity" (*dānacariyā*): it is the habitual performance of giving. It is the foundation for all virtues. One should practice generosity daily, even if it be only a small amount, for the mind of a generous person becomes pure and bright. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "perfection of giving" (*dānapāramitā*): it is the fulfillment of the practice of generosity to the highest degree. It is characterized by the absence of attachment and the desire for the welfare of others. One should fulfill this perfection by giving without regard for one's own body or life. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "benefits of giving" (*dānānisamsa*): they are manifold and immeasurable. They include rebirth in the celestial realms, the attainment of sovereignty, and the eventual realization of Nibbāna. One should reflect upon these benefits and practice giving with joy. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "obstacles to giving" (*dānavibandha*): they are primarily stinginess and attachment to possessions. One should overcome these obstacles through reflection on the impermanence of wealth and the suffering inherent in greed. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "method of giving" (*dānavidhi*): it involves giving with respect, at the proper time, and with a pure heart. One should give what is appropriate, in a manner that does not cause harm to oneself or others. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "conclusion": having explained the field of merit, the nature of the gift, the path, the lord of the path, the fruits of giving, the benefits, the obstacles, and the method, one should conclude by dedicating the merit to the welfare of all beings and aspiring for the attainment of Buddhahood. This is the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "summary": the field of merit is the most important factor in the production of merit. The gift is the means by which merit is produced. The path is the vehicle for reaching the goal. The lord of the path is the guide. The fruits are the rewards. The benefits are the secondary advantages. The obstacles are the hindrances. The method is the proper procedure. This is the summary of the meaning. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "exhortation": one should always remember the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. One should practice the ten wholesome courses of action. One should develop the four bases of psychic power. One should cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment. One should maintain the eightfold noble path. This is the exhortation. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "final verses": *“Dānaṃ sīlañca bhāvanā, Saṅgaho ca catubbidho; Ete dhammā visuddhikarā, Nibbānassa ca sādhakā.”* "Generosity, virtue, meditation, And the fourfold social integration— These qualities bring about purification And are the achievers of Nibbāna. This is the final verse. Thus ends this section. Now, regarding the "closing remarks": this treatise has been composed for the purpose of clarifying the principles of giving and the cultivation of merit. May it be of benefit
“Faith, moral shame, and wholesome generosity—these qualities are followed by the virtuous.
For they call this the divine path; by means of it, one goes to the world of the devas.
Alternatively, there is the reading “Lord of the Path,” meaning that the Teacher is the sovereign over the world including its devas by means of the Noble Path.

The meaning should be understood as follows: by saying, "Give gifts to the Saṅgha," and so forth, she speaks again, urging [people] toward the distribution of gifts to those worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya).
Now, showing that Saṅgha of Noble Ones (ariyasaṅgha) worthy of offerings in its true nature, she recites the verse beginning, "Those eight persons who are praised by the virtuous.
In this context, *ye* is an indefinite demonstrative; *puggalā* means beings (*sattā*); and *aṭṭha* refers to their number.
The analysis by enumeration: For they consist of eight—namely, the four who are practicing and the four established in the fruits.
They are "praised by the good" (satampasatthā), meaning they are praised by true persons—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples—as well as by other gods and humans. Why?
Because of their possession of innate qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth. Indeed, for them, [virtue] is like the fragrance of the *campaka* and *bakula* flowers.

The qualities of innate color, fragrance, and so forth, as well as innate virtue, concentration, and so forth—because of these, like flowers endowed with color, fragrance, and the like, they become dear, pleasing, and praiseworthy to both gods and humans. Therefore it was said:
"Those eight persons who are praised by the good. Briefly stated, however, they consist of those established on the path of stream-entry and those established in its fruit.
One pair consists of the path and the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, up to the path and fruit of arhatship, there is one pair—thus there are four pairs.
Therefore he said: "These four are the pairs; they are the ones worthy of offerings. The word "they" (*te*) is used to specify those who were previously mentioned without specification.
For all of them, having placed faith in both karma and the fruit of karma, [are worthy of] that which is called the gift of the object to be given.
They are "worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyya*) because they are capable of producing great fruit for a gift by virtue of their possession of distinguished qualities.

They are "disciples of the Sugata" (*sugata-sāvaka*) because, at the conclusion of hearing the Dhamma from the Perfectly Enlightened One, they hear that Dhamma through being born into the noble lineage.
"Gifts given to them yield great fruit" means that even small gifts given to these disciples of the Sugata [yield great results].
Gifts given to a recipient become of great fruit through the purification of the offering (*dakṣiṇā-viśuddhi*). Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, as far as there are communities or groups, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the foremost," and so forth.
The passage beginning with "And the four who have entered the path" has its meaning already explained below.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha, having returned to the human world, reported to the Blessed One the matter that had been spoken by himself and the deity.
Taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the assembled company.
That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The commentary on the *Vihāra-vimāna* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Caturitthi-vimāna*:
"With most excellent beauty," thus begins the *Caturitthi-vimāna*. What is its origin? It was spoken by the Blessed One at Sāvatthī.
While dwelling there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wandering on a tour of the celestial realms in the manner described below,
arrived at the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There, seeing four goddesses stationed in four successive palaces,
each enjoying divine splendor with a retinue of a thousand nymphs, he asked them about the kamma they had performed in the past:
755. “With a most excellent complexion… [etc] …and your complexion illuminates all directions”—with these verses he questioned him in succession.
And she answered those questions in succession immediately after his questioning. To show that:
758. “That deity, with a joyful mind… [etc] …the fruit of which deed this is.”—Thus it was said.
This verse was spoken.
It is said that at the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, they were born into a noble family in a city named Paṇṇakaṭa in a kingdom called Esika.
Having reached maturity, they went to their husbands' families in that same city and lived there in harmony. Of those women, one—
Seeing a certain alms-collecting bhikkhu, one woman with a devout heart gave him a cluster of blue lotuses;
another gave a handful of blue water lilies; another gave a handful of red lotuses; and another gave jasmine buds.
At a later time, having passed away, they were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as a thousand celestial nymphs.
They became his retinue. Having experienced divine prosperity there for as long as their lifespan lasted, they passed away from that state;
then, due to the remaining ripening of that same karma, wandering on from birth to birth in that very same place, they were reborn right there at the arising of this Buddha.
When questioned by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the manner described, one among them related her own past karma to the Elder: [The rest of the text follows with the specific karmic account.]
“I gave a handful of blue lotuses to a bhikkhu wandering for alms at the high pillar in the delightful city of Paṇṇakata. Because of that, such is my complexion...
[and so on] ...and my complexion shines in all directions.”
She said: "Another [said]:
'I gave a handful of blue lotuses to a bhikkhu wandering for alms at the high gateway of the excellent city of Paṇṇakata.'"
767. “Because of that, my complexion is such as this… [and so on] …and my complexion shines forth in all directions,” she said.
Another said:
“I gave [the lotus] with white roots and green leaves, grown in the water of a lake.”
While I was walking for alms as a bhikkhu on the high ground of pillars in that delightful, excellent city of Paṇṇakata, [I attained this state].
"Because of that, my complexion is such as this... and my complexion shines forth in all directions."—774.
She said: "Another— 'I,
being well-disposed, gave jasmine blossoms, white as the color of ivory,
to a bhikkhu wandering for alms at the high point of the pillars.'"
"In this delightful Paṇṇaka, the best of cities.
"Therefore my complexion is such as this... [and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions," he said.
759. Therein, "a hand of blue lotuses" (*indīvara*) refers to a handful of *uddālaka* flowers, a cluster of *vātaghātaka* blossoms.
"Of the pillars" (*esikānaṃ*) means of those things that have the nature of pillars.

"In the excellent city on high" (*uṇṇatasmiṃ nagaravare*) means in the preeminent city situated on an elevated piece of ground, which is raised up by its palaces, gabled chambers, and so forth, as if they were licking the belly of the clouds. "In Paṇṇakata" means in the city of that name.
766. "The hand’s luster like a blue lotus" means a cluster of water-lilies (*kuvalaya*).
773. "With white roots" means having white bases; this is said because of the whiteness of the roots of the lotus stalks (*bhisamūla*), referring to a cluster of lotuses (*paduma*).
Therefore he says, "with green leaves," and so forth. Therein, "green leaves" means blue leaves, [referring to] those whose unopened buds have not yet been shed.
For the outer petals of a lotus are indeed green in color. "Born in a lake of water" means born in the water of a lake;

the sense is "lake-born" (*saroruha*). 780. *Sumanā* is its name. *Sumanassa* means of one with a beautiful mind. *Sumanamakuḷāni* means buds of the *jātisumanā* flower. *Dantavaṇṇāni* means having a color like that of freshly polished ivory.
When they had thus related the deeds they themselves had committed, the Elder delivered a discourse on gradual instruction to them and proclaimed the Truths.
At the conclusion of the Truths, all of them, together with their retinue, became stream-enterers.
The Elder returned to the human world and reported this occurrence to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion for a teaching, [spoke] to the assembled company.
He taught the Dhamma. That teaching of the Dhamma became beneficial to the great multitude.
The commentary on the Four Female Vimānas is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Mango Vimāna.
“Your celestial mango grove is delightful—this mango mansion! How did it come to be? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, a certain female lay follower in Sāvatthī, having heard of the great fruit and great benefit of giving a dwelling place, conceived a desire [to do so].
She paid homage to the Blessed One and said: “Venerable Sir, I wish to have one dwelling place constructed.”
“I wish for such a place; please point one out to me. The Blessed One gave the instruction to the monks, and the monks showed her a location.
She had a delightful dwelling constructed there and planted mango trees all around it.
That dwelling was surrounded on all sides by rows of mango trees, endowed with shade and water, and its bright ground was strewn with sand resembling a net of pearls.
It became exceedingly beautiful. She adorned that monastery like a celestial mansion with cloths of various colors, garlands of flowers, perfumed wreaths, and so forth;
she lit oil lamps and wrapped the mango trees in new, unwashed cloths, and then dedicated it to the Saṅgha.
In the course of time, having passed away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, where a great celestial mansion appeared for her, surrounded by a grove of mango trees.
There, attended by a host of nymphs, she enjoyed divine splendor.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached her and questioned her with these verses:
“Your divine mango grove is delightful, and here stands a great palace,
resounding with various musical instruments and filled with the voices of throngs of celestial nymphs.
And here a great golden lamp burns constantly.”
Surrounded on all sides by trees bearing bitter fruit.
(785) “By what means do you have such a complexion... [as before] ...and your complexion shines forth in every direction?
(787) That deity, being delighted... [as before] ...this is the fruit of that karma. (787)
“In my former birth, when I was a human being among humans in the world of men,
I had a monastery built for the Saṅgha, surrounded by mango trees.
When the monastery was completed and the great festival was being held, I made this vow:”
Having covered them with cloths and fashioned garments from the fruit at the improper time,
I lit a lamp there, fed the supreme assembly, and,
with a heart full of faith, offered it to the Saṅgha with my own hands.
“Because of that, my mango grove is delightful, and here is a great palace,
resounding with various musical instruments and filled with the voices of throngs of celestial nymphs.
And here a great golden lamp burns constantly.”
“Surrounded on all sides by trees bearing bitter fruit, it is because of that that my complexion is such...
[as before] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.
Thus did that deity explain.
783. Therein, "mahallaka" means great in length, breadth, and height; the sense is that it is most magnificent.
"Accharāgaṇaghosita" means it was made resounding by a host of nymphs through both musical performances and pleasant conversation for the sake of their delight.
784. "The lamp burns here" means that the canopy of rays brilliantly shining like the sun's beams and the jewel-lamp burn here, in this palace.
"With garments as their fruit" means those for whom garments are the fruit; the sense is: with divine robes being emitted from them.

789. *Kārente niṭṭhite mahē*: while the festival (*maha*) was being held for the consecration of the vihāra that had been completed; and while the offering (*pūjā*) was being performed for the vihāra that had been finished and dedicated. *Katvā dussamaye phaleti*: having produced fruit upon those mango trees at the very time of their flowering, he caused them to bear fruit.

790. *Gaṇuttaman* means the supreme among groups, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples. *Niyyādēsin* means he offered it up; "he gave it" is the meaning. The rest is exactly as previously stated. The commentary on the Mango Mansion (*Ambavimāna*) is concluded.
9. Description of the Yellow Mansion (*Pītavimāna*).
It is called the "Yellow Mansion" because it has yellow cloth and yellow banners. How did it come into being?
After the Blessed One had attained final *parinibbāna*, King Ajātasattu took the relics of the Blessed One that he had obtained for himself and erected both a stupa and a great festival.
A certain female lay devotee living in Rājagaha, having attended to her physical needs early in the morning, thought, "I shall worship the Teacher’s stupa.
Taking four kosātakī flowers she had obtained, her mind uplifted by the force of her faith, she set out toward the stupa without even considering the dangers on the road.
Then a cow with a young calf rushed toward her with great speed.
Having fallen upon him and struck him with her horn, she brought him to his death.

At that very moment, being reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, she appeared together with her chariot in the midst of two and a half koṭis of celestial dancers who were accompanying Sakka, the king of the gods, as he went on a pleasure excursion;
there, she outshone them all with the radiance of her own body. Seeing her, [Sakka asked:]
Sakka, the king of the gods, his mind struck with wonder and filled with a sense of the marvelous and the extraordinary,
asked her this question with these verses: “Clad in yellow garments, bearing yellow banners,
and adorned with yellow ornaments— by what kind of gross deed has she attained such immense divine power?”
With her limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood and wearing a garland of yellow lotuses— [seated] upon a yellow palace and a yellow couch, on a yellow seat and with yellow vessels;
under a yellow parasol and in a yellow chariot, with a yellow horse and a yellow fan.
“What deed did you perform, O blessed one, in your former human existence?
O deity, being questioned, tell me: what is the fruit of which deed is this?
She answered him with these verses:
“Venerable sir, there is a creeper called *kosātakī*, bitter and undesirable;
of it I brought four flowers to the stupa.
With a mind full of serene confidence, directed toward the body of the Teacher.”
"I would not have looked for his path, nor would I have been mindful of going there.
Therefore, the cow killed me before my mind had reached the stupa;
if I had directed my intention toward that, surely I would have fared even better than this."
“By that kamma, O Lord of Devas, Maghava, the elephant among gods, having abandoned his human body, has come to your companionship.
(795–6) Therein, “with limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood” means with a body smeared with golden-colored sandalwood. “In the yellow palace” refers to the bedchamber.
It was provided with a palace made entirely of gold and couches encrusted with gold.
Thus, in all instances, it should be understood that by the word "yellow" (*pīta*), "gold" alone is intended both below and above. 798.
*Latatthī* means "there is a creeper. *Bhante* is an address to Sakka, the king of the gods, out of respect. *Anabhicchitā* means "not desired."
799. *Sarīraṃ* means the element that constitutes the body. This term for a whole is used here for a part, as in the expressions "the cloth is burnt" or "the ocean is seen.
*Assā* means of the cow. *Maggaṃ* means the path of arrival. *Na avekkhissanti* means they did not look. Why?
Because their minds were not set on going after her; that is, their minds were fixed upon that cow and not elsewhere.
The meaning is that they were, in fact, solely intent upon the stupa of the Blessed One. Regarding the reading "tadaṅgamanasā satī":
she whose mind was directed toward a part (*aṅga*) of that Blessed One—that is, toward his relic (*dhātu*)—was *tadaṅgamanasā*.
This shows that being such as that, she did not look for the path to it at that time.
800. "The stupa has not reached the mind" means the stupa, the shrine, has not attained the intention;

for that which exists in the mind (*manasi*) is called mental (*mānasa*), and intention is synonymous with desire. This was said because the desire that had arisen—"Having approached the stupa, I shall worship it with flowers"—was not yet fulfilled.
However, the mental state of wishing to worship the stupa, the shrine, with flowers was already established.
"By which she was reborn in the world of the gods. "And if I were to accumulate that":
if I were to accumulate—that is, having approached the stupa, by means of the merit of offering flowers, I would properly accumulate and pile up [merit] according to my intention—this is the meaning.
"Surely there would be more than this": surely there would be something further, superior, and higher even than this prosperity already obtained.
The meaning is: "One should think, 'May prosperity be mine.

(801) "Maghavā, elephant among gods" is an address. In that context, "elephant among gods" means one who is like an elephant among the gods due to his excellence in all matters such as strength and prowess. "Sahabya" means companionship. [The verse continues:
"Having heard this, Maghavā, the lord of the thirty-three, the elephant among gods..."

“Winning the confidence of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, he spoke thus to Mātali.”—This is the statement of the compilers of the Dhamma. Then Sakka taught the Dhamma with these verses to the host of devas headed by Mātali:
“Behold, Mātali, this marvel: the mind and the fruit of kamma!”
Even a small gift, when given, becomes a merit of great fruit.
"When the mind is clear and confident, there is no such thing as a 'small' offering,
whether it be toward a Tathāgata, a Perfectly Awakened One, or his disciple."
“Come, Mātali, let us too honor them more and more;
the relics of the Tathāgata are a blissful accumulation of merit.
Whether he is present or has attained Nibbāna, the mind is the same and the fruit is the same.”
“By means of the causes of mental aspiration, beings go to a happy destination.
Indeed, for the benefit of many do the Tathāgatas arise;
having performed service there, donors go to heaven.”
802. *Tattha pasādento* means making [the mind] serene; the meaning is: generating faith in the Triple Gem. 803.
*Cittam* refers to the variegated and inconceivable mind. *Kammaphalam*:

even if the object to be given (*deyyadhamma*) is not sublime, one should see the fruit of a noble meritorious deed through the excellence of the field and the excellence of the mind—this is the construction. Even that which is done in small measure...
Regarding the phrase "that which is to be given, merit becomes of great fruit": here, "done" (*kata*) refers to that which is applied to a field (*āyatana*) by way of performance and by way of honor.
"That which is to be given" (*deyya*) is the object to be given. "Merit" (*puñña*) is the meritorious deed proceeding in such a manner. 804.
Now, demonstrating clearly where even a small amount of merit performed becomes of great fruit, he spoke the verse beginning with "When the mind is serene. This is indeed easy to understand.

805–6. *Amhepi* means "we too. *Mahemase* means "we honor" or "we worship. *Cetopaṇidhihetu hi* means "for the sake of the mental aspiration," that is, for the purpose of correctly establishing one's own mind; the meaning is "by means of one's own right aspiration.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Neither mother nor father could do it, nor any other relatives;
The mind rightly directed would make him better than they."
Having spoken thus, Sakka, the lord of the devas, quelled his enthusiasm for the pleasure-garden excursion and turned back from that very spot;
he then performed an offering for seven days at the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya, which was a place he himself had frequently worshipped.
Later, when the Venerable Elder Nārada went on a journey among the devas, he learned of this occurrence.
The Buddha himself recited the verses; the Elder reported them to the compilers of the Dhamma, and they included them in the collection accordingly.
The commentary on the Yellow Mansion is finished.
10. Commentary on the Sugar-cane Mansion.

"Having illuminated the earth together with its devas"—this refers to the Sugarcane Mansion (*ucchuvimāna*). This is identical to the previous Sugarcane Mansion both in terms of the textual narrative (*pāḷi*) and the origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
The only difference is that in the former case, the mother-in-law killed the daughter-in-law by striking her with a bench, whereas here she did so with a clod of earth;
this is the sole distinction. However, because the subject matter (*vatthu*) differs, both are included as separate cases.
It should be understood that they have ascended.
"Having illuminated the earth together with its devas, you shine forth like the moon and the sun;
in splendor, beauty, glory, and majesty, you are like Brahmā among the thirty-three devas and their lord."
“I ask you, O wearer of a garland of lotuses, with braided hair and skin like gold, adorned and wearing the finest garments:
who are you, O auspicious goddess, that pays me homage?
What deed did you perform for yourself in a former life when you were a human being?”
“Generosity well-practiced, as well as restraint through virtue—by what [deeds] were you reborn in a fortunate realm, O illustrious one?
O deity, being questioned, tell us: of what karma is this the fruit?
Thus asked the Venerable Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Thereupon, the deity replied with these verses:
“Just now, venerable sir, you came to our house in this very village for alms;
then, with a clear mind and incomparable joy, I gave you a piece of sugarcane.
Later, my mother-in-law questioned me: ‘Where, daughter-in-law, did you put that sugarcane?’”
"I did not discard it, nor did I eat it; I gave it myself to a peaceful bhikkhu.
'This wealth belongs to you, and yet to me!'—thus my mother-in-law reviled me;
taking up a clod of earth, she struck me. Having passed away from there, I have become a deity."
“Indeed, that very wholesome deed was performed by me; I myself experience the happiness resulting from that deed.
Together with the devas, I enjoy myself, delighting in the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Indeed, that very wholesome deed was performed by me; I myself experience the happiness resulting from that deed.”
Guarded by the lords of gods and protected by the Thirty-three, I am provided with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"Such is the abundant fruit of my merit; my gift of sugarcane has a great result.
Together with the gods, I enjoy myself; I rejoice in the five strands of sensual pleasure."
“Such is the abundant fruit of merit: my gift of sugarcane has great radiance.
Protected by the Lord of Devas and guarded by the Thirty-Three, I am like the Thousand-Eyed One in the Nandana Grove.
And having approached you, O Venerable One, compassionate and wise, I paid homage and inquired after your well-being.”
"Then, with a mind full of serene confidence and incomparable joy, I gave you a piece of sugarcane.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Sugarcane Mansion is finished.
11. The Description of the Vandanā Vimāna.
"With surpassing beauty" refers to the Vandanā Vimāna. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
At that time, a number of bhikkhus were staying in a certain village residence.

Having spent the rains residence, completed their retreat, and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, they put away their lodgings, took up their bowls and robes, and set out toward Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One.
As they were passing through the middle of a certain village, a certain woman saw those bhikkhus;
with a mind full of serene confidence and having conceived deep reverence and esteem, she [prostrated] with the fivefold salutation.
Having paid homage with her head and raising her hands in *añjali*, she stood gazing at him with eyes as serene as those of faith, opening them wide until he was out of sight.
Later, having passed away, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Then, while she was enjoying celestial splendor there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned her with these verses:
819. “With a most excellent complexion... [as above] ...and your radiance illuminates all directions.
822. “That deity, with a joyful mind... [as above] ...this is the fruit of which deed?
“When I was among humans, being a human myself, I saw recluses endowed with virtue;”
“Having bowed at his feet, I gladdened my mind; filled with joy, I performed the añjali-gesture.
With these verses he explained: “Because of that, my complexion is such as this... [and] my complexion shines forth in all directions. Thus he spoke.
823. Therein, "ascetic" (samaṇa) means one who has stilled evil. "Virtuous" (sīlavanta) means endowed with the quality of virtue.

"I gladdened my mind" means that, regarding their virtues, I gladdened my heart, thinking: "Truly, these noble ones are excellent; they walk according to the Dhamma, they walk in equanimity, they live the holy life.
"And being joyful, I made the añjali-gesture" means that, being satisfied and filled with gladness, I paid homage to those lovely bhikkhus.
Opening his eyes, which were blossomed with serene confidence, he saw that even a mere glance from these beings was of great benefit, let alone their paying him homage.
Therefore he said, "By this [merit] my complexion has become such as this," and so forth. The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Vandanavimāna* is concluded.
12. The Description of the Rajjumālā Vimāna.
"With most excellent beauty" refers to the Rajjumālā Vimāna. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, there was a certain brahmin in the village of Gayā, and his daughter lived in that very same village.
She was given in marriage to a young Brahmin and went to her husband’s family; she remained there exercising authority over the household.
Having seen the daughter of a slave-girl in that house, she could not endure her.
From the moment she saw her, she became seething with anger, reviling and abusing her, and even gave her a blow. But when she reached maturity and was capable of performing tasks...
When she was born, they would strike her with their fists as high as her knees, just as they had done in her previous births when she was bound by enmity.
It is said that this woman had been the mistress of the other during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa; the other was her slave.
She frequently struck her with clods of earth, sticks, and so forth, and with her fists and so on. Becoming weary of this, she performed meritorious deeds such as giving to the best of her ability.
Having made this resolve, she established the aspiration: "In the future, having become her mistress, I shall exercise authority over her.

Then that slave girl, passing away from there and wandering through successive births, was reborn in this era of a Buddha's appearance in a brahmin family in the village of Gayā according to the aforementioned method;
she went to her husband’s home, and the other woman became her slave. Thus, due to their mutual enmity, she tormented her.
Thus harassing her for no reason at all, she seized her by the hair and beat her severely with her hands and feet.
She went to the barber’s shop and had her head shaved, then departed. Her mistress said, "What, you wicked slave? Do you think you are released merely by shaving your head?
Binding a rope around her head, she seized her there, bent her over, and struck her until she died. For her—
And she would not allow that rope to be removed. From that time on, the slave girl was known by the name "Rajjumālā" (The Rope-Wreath).
Then one day, at the hour of dawn, the Teacher emerged from the attainment of Great Compassion and surveyed the world;
he perceived Rajjumālā’s supporting condition for the fruit of Stream-entry, as well as the establishment of that Brahmin woman in the Refuges and the Precepts.
Having seen this, he entered the forest and sat down at the foot of a certain tree, emitting the six-colored rays of a Buddha.
Meanwhile, Rajjumālā, being thus tormented by her every day, became despondent with life, thinking, "What is the use of this miserable existence?
and, longing for death, she left her home as if going to a water-crossing carrying a water-pot.
Having set out and entered the forest in due course, she tied a rope to the branch of a certain tree not far from the tree where the Blessed One was sitting,
and having fashioned a noose, she— desiring to hang herself—
looked here and there and saw the Blessed One sitting there, inspiring confidence, pleasing, and having attained supreme self-mastery and tranquility.
He was emitting the six-colored rays of a Buddha. Seeing him, her heart drawn by reverence for the Buddha, she thought:
"Does the Blessed One teach the Dhamma even to those like me, so that by hearing it I might be freed from this miserable life?
Then the Blessed One, observing the movement of her mind, said: "Rajjumālā. Upon hearing this, as if with the Deathless...
Drenched and continuously suffused with joy, she approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood to one side.
The Blessed One gave her a gradual discourse, culminating in a teaching on the Four Noble Truths; she was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
The Teacher thought, "This much benefit from the garland of cords is sufficient; now she shall be invulnerable to anyone."
Having thought, "She has been born," he emerged from the forest and sat down at the foot of a certain tree not far from the village.

As for Rajjumālā, because she was incapable of throwing herself down and was endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, she thought, "Let the brahmin woman kill me, or harass me, or do whatever she will," and taking water in her jar, she went home. Her husband—
Standing at the door of the house, he saw her and asked, "You went to the water-crossing today; why have you returned so late?
Your complexion is exceedingly serene, and you appear different from your usual self—what is this?
She explained the matter to him.
Having heard her words, the brahmin was satisfied; he went home and told his daughter-in-law, "Nothing at all must be done by you," hanging a rope-noose above [the door].

With a joyful heart, he went even more quickly to the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and after being received with respectful greetings, he invited the Teacher, brought him to his own house, and [served him] with excellent hard food.
Having served him with various kinds of food, he approached the Blessed One when he had finished eating and had removed his hand from the bowl, and sat down to one side;

his daughters-in-law also approached, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The brahmin householders living in Gayā village, having heard of this event, approached the Blessed One; some paid homage and sat down to one side.
Some, having exchanged greetings, sat down to one side.

The Teacher, having related in detail the deeds performed by that brahmin woman and the string-garland maker in their previous births, taught the Dhamma appropriate for the assembled multitude. Having heard it, the brahmin woman and the great multitude there—
Having assembled, he established himself in the refuges and the precepts. The Teacher rose from his seat and returned to Sāvatthī.
The brahmin placed the garland of cords in the place of his daughter.
His daughter-in-law gazed upon the garland of cords with affectionate eyes and cherished it with a pleasing love for as long as she lived. Later, the garland of cords passed away.
She was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, and she had a retinue of a thousand celestial nymphs (accharā).

Her body was adorned with divine ornaments weighing as much as sixty cartloads; surrounded by her thousand nymphs, she wandered through the Nandana Grove and other such places, experiencing great divine splendor with a joyful mind.
Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna went on his journey among the gods.
Having approached and seen her shining with great divine majesty and great celestial power, he asked about the deed she had performed with these verses:
“O goddess, you who stand there with such surpassing beauty;”
Clasping your hands and feet, you dance, O well-sounding one. As you dance, from every limb of yours,
divine sounds issue forth— worthy to be heard and delightful.
“As you dance, from every limb of yours divine fragrances waft forth— pure scents, most delightful.
As you whirl about with your body, the ornaments upon your braided hair [scatter].”
Their sound was heard like that of a fivefold musical ensemble:
"The flower-ornaments shaken by the wind, trembling in the breeze—
their sound was heard like that of a fivefold musical ensemble."
“Even this garland upon your head, fragrant and delightful,
its scent wafts in all directions like that of a mañjūsaka tree.
You smell that pure fragrance and behold this superhuman form.”
"O deity, being questioned, tell us: of what karma is this the fruit?
(826) In that context, "grasping at hands and feet" means seizing the hands and feet in various ways;
it refers to performing various gestures with the branches [of the body], such as the handful of flowers (*puṣpamuṣṭi*) and the flower-offering gesture (*añjali*).
The meaning is: "having grasped the feet in various ways by way of seeing the specific positions of the hands, as well as the palms and soles.
By the word *ca*, the gesturing of branches (*sākhābhinaya*) is included. "You dance" (*naccasi*) means you act as an actor (*naṭasi*).
"You who" (*yā tvam*) means you who perform the dance in the manner already described. "When there is well-spoken [verse]" (*suppavāditeti*) means when there is beautiful recitation.
The meaning is: while the lute, the shoulder-lute, the drum, the cymbals, and so forth were being played in accordance with the dance, and while the fivefold musical ensemble was being performed.
The rest is exactly according to the method explained below in the *Vimānavatthu*.
Thus, having been questioned by the Elder, that deity explained her own previous birth and so forth with these verses:
“In the past, I was a slave-girl to a brahmin at Gayā.
Having little merit and lacking fortune, I was known as ‘Rajjumālā.
I was notorious for my insults, my killings, and my violent threats.”
Taking my water-pot, I went out and set off as a water-carrier.
Having set the pot down on a bypath, I approached a forest thicket, thinking:
"I shall die right here; what is the use of my life?"
“Having made a strong snare and having hidden it in a tree,
I then looked out in all directions, thinking, ‘Who indeed dwells in this forest?
There I saw the Fully Awakened One, the Sage who brings benefit to the whole world.”
As he sat at the foot of a tree, meditating, free from fear from any quarter, a sense of urgency arose within me—extraordinary and hair-raising:
"Who is this dwelling in the forest? Is it a human or a deity?"
“Tranquil and inspiring, having come from the forest to the clearing—seeing him, my mind was filled with faith; he is not like anyone else.
With his sense faculties guarded, delighting in meditation, his mind does not wander outward.”
“This person will become a Buddha for the entire world.
Terrifying and formidable, difficult to approach, he dwells in his cave like a lion.
He is as rare to behold as a flower on an udumbara tree.”
“Thus the Tathāgata, having addressed me with gentle words, said to me:
‘I am wearing a garland of ropes; go for refuge to the Tathāgata.
Having heard those words—faultless, meaningful, and pure—”
Gentle, soft, and charming, dispelling all sorrows.
Knowing me to be of ready mind, serene and pure in heart, the Tathāgata,
the benefactor of the whole world, instructed me.
“This is suffering,” he told me; “this is the origin of suffering;
this is the cessation of suffering and the path leading directly to the immersion in the Deathless.
Standing firm in the instruction of that compassionate and skillful one, I have practiced accordingly.
She has attained the deathless peace, Nibbāna, the immutable state.
“With love firmly established, unshakable in the sight [of the Buddha],
rooted in faith born from the root, I am a true daughter of the Buddha.”
“I rejoice, I play, and I delight, free from fear from any quarter;
I wear celestial garlands and drink the honeyed *maddava* wine.
Sixty thousand musical instruments awaken me.”
Āḷambā, Gaggarā, Bhīmā, Sādhuvādī, and Saṃsayā;
Pokkharā, Suphassā, Viṇāmokkhā, and the women;
Nandā, Sunandā, Soṇadinnā, and Sucimhitā.
“Āḷambusā and Missakesī, Puṇḍarīkā and Atidāruṇī;
Eṇīphassā and Suphassā, Subhaddā and Muduvādinī.
These and other excellent ones, who awaken the celestial nymphs;”
Then those deities, approaching me at the proper time, addressed me:
“Come, let us dance and sing; come, let us delight you!
This is not for those who have performed no merit; this is only for those who have performed merit.”
“The sorrowless, joyful, and delightful Great Forest of the Thirty-three gods does not exist for those who have not performed merit,
neither in this world nor in the next. But happiness exists both in this world and in the next for those who have performed merit.”
For those who desire such companionship, much wholesome merit must be performed;
for those who have made merit rejoice in heaven, endowed with all enjoyments.
"Indeed, for the benefit of many do the Tathāgatas arise."
“Worthy of offerings among humans, mines of fields of merit;
having performed service there, donors rejoice in heaven.
(833) Regarding this, “In former times I was a maidservant” means that in a previous birth, I was a maidservant born within the household. Therein:
"To whom? he asked. "To a certain brahmin in Gayā," [the Blessed One] replied; that is, to a certain brahmin in the village named Gayā.
*Haṃti* is a mere particle. "Of little merit" means those of meager fortune and lacking merit. "Unlucky" means those devoid of splendor, ill-fated.
"They call me a 'rope-wreath'"—that is, when my hair was seized and pulled back and forth with such pain that I was made bald.
Furthermore, because I had a rope coiled tightly around my head and fastened there for that very same purpose, people came to know me as "Rajjumālā" (The Rope-Wreath).

834. *Vadhānaṃ* means of beatings. *Tajjanāya* means by means of terrifying with fear. *Uggatā* means due to the arising of intense dejection. *Udahāriyā* means a water-carrier; the intended meaning is "acting like one who fetches water."
835. *Vipatha* means on a pathless way; the meaning is "having strayed from the path. *Kvattha* means "what is the purpose?
Or rather, that very reading [is correct]. 836. *Daḷhaṃ pāsaṃ karitvāna*: having made the snare firm—that is, having made the binding snare strong and unbreakable.
*Āsumbhitvāna pādapē*: having cast it upon a tree, by way of hanging it upon the branches of the tree. Then I looked out in all directions: "Who indeed..."
"Has anyone entered this forest?"—the intention behind this question is: "Is there perhaps someone who has entered this forest, by whose presence there might be an obstacle to my death?

Regarding the passage beginning with "Sambuddham" (to the Fully Awakened One), although at that time she lacked such a firm conviction, it is stated according to the actual nature of things. Its meaning is as follows:
he is the "Sambuddha" because he has himself and perfectly awakened to everything that is to be awakened to; and through his connection with great compassion...
Because he is of absolute benefit to the entire world—comprising all that is divided by the distinctions of inferior and so forth—he is "the Benefactor of the Whole World" (*sabbalokahita*).

Because he understands both worlds, he is a "Sage" (*muni*). He is "seated" (*nisinna*) by way of his sitting posture, in the sense of being immovable from his place due to the defilements and volitional formations.

He is "meditating" (*jhāyanta*) through both meditation upon the object and meditation upon the characteristics. [He is so called] even while at the foot of the Bodhi tree, because of the causes of fear...
Because all fear has been utterly severed and there is no fear from any quarter whatsoever, it should be understood as "fearless from any source" (*akutobhaya*).
(838) What is called "spiritual urgency" (*saṃvega*) is knowledge accompanied by moral dread; that arose upon seeing the Blessed One. Therefore he said: "In her, spiritual urgency arose.

(839) "Inspiring confidence" (*pāsādika*) means bringing forth serene confidence; for she was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, and the halo of fathom-wide radiance.

The meaning is: "Increasing faith" (*pasādasamvaḍḍhana*) because it is praised by people intent on beholding the form-body (*rūpakāya*) due to the excellence of the beauty of his own body in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

"Inspiring confidence" (*pasādanīya*) means worthy of being inspired with confidence by similar persons through the excellence of the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*), which is endowed with immeasurable qualities such as the ten powers (*dasabala*), the four grounds of self-confidence (*catuvesārajja*), the six unique knowledges (*cha-asādhāraṇañāṇa*), and the eighteen unique Buddha-qualities (*aṭṭhārasāveṇikabuddhadhamma*); thus, the meaning is "graceful" (*pāsādika*). "Forest" (*vana*)...
"Having departed from the forest of defilements. "Come to Nibbāna" means having approached and attained Nibbāna itself, which is the state of being free from craving (*nittaṇha*).
"Whoever he may be" (*yādisakīdiso*) means anyone whatsoever;

the sense is "an ordinary person. 840–41. "Guarded in his faculties" (*guttindriyo*): because he has guarded the six sense-faculties, including the mind, by means of the supreme path for their protection. Through his delight in the jhāna of the highest fruit...

Delighting in meditation (*jhāna*). Precisely because of that, his mind does not go outward, having not departed from the objects of form and so forth that exist externally, and because his mind has plunged into Nibbāna which consumes the sense-objects;

thus he is "one whose mind does not go outward. Because those possessed of perversion (*vipallāsa*)—the holders of wrong views—should fear him for the sake of being released from their false grasp, and because he generates fear in them, he is "one who inspires fear and terror.
Because he is not to be approached by those whose application and disposition have failed, [he is...]
And because he cannot be approached by anyone, he is difficult to approach. "Hard to find" means that he is rare to encounter. "Even for the sight" means even to see him.

"Like the Udumbara flower": just as the flower that grows on the Udumbara tree is difficult to see—occurring only at some time or perhaps not occurring at all—so too is such a supreme person; this is the meaning.
842. Thus, the Tathāgata, having addressed me with gentle words and soft speech, saying "O Rajjumāla," and having called out to me, spoke to me as follows:
"Go for refuge to the Tathāgata. The construction is: he said, "Go for refuge to the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), who has come thus," and so forth.
843–4. *Tāham* means "that I. *Giraṃ* means speech. *Nelaṃ* means faultless. *Atthavatiṃ* means endowed with meaning, possessing a purpose, or exclusively beneficial.
It is *suciṃ* (pure) due to purity of speech; *saṇhaṃ* (gentle) due to the absence of harshness; *muduṃ* (soft) because it makes those to be trained pliant;
and *vagguṃ* (charming) by virtue of its worthiness to be heard. *Sabbasokāpanūdanaṃ* means [the dispelling of all sorrow] through such things as the loss of kinsmen.
The connection is: "Having heard the speech that dispels all sorrow that might arise, they became clear-minded.

This refers to the Blessed One’s gradual discourse (*anupubbikathā*), which proceeds by first initiating a talk on giving and so forth, and then exerting effort to reveal the benefits of renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
For this very reason, he said: "And knowing my mind to be ready," and so on.
In this context, "pliant mind" (*kallacitta*) means a workable mind.
Because the defects of the mind such as lack of faith have been removed by the preceding teaching, it has become a fit vessel for the subsequent teaching;

thus, it is a mind capable of being worked upon, meaning a mind suitable for the task of meditation (*bhāvanā*). For this very reason, it is said: "a serene and pure mind. Therein, by the word "serene" (*pasanna*),...

By the phrase "one whose mind is purified," he speaks of the departure from lack of faith; through this, he demonstrates the pliancy and elation of the mind resulting from the departure from sensual desire and the other hindrances.
"He instructed" means he exhorted him; the meaning is that he pointed out the ways of engagement and withdrawal together with the skillful means of the Dhamma teaching that leads to the highest goal.
For this very reason, he said, "This is suffering," and so forth; for this is a demonstration of the manner in which he was instructed.
845. Regarding the phrase "He told me: 'This is suffering,'" this refers to the entire collection of phenomena belonging to the three planes that are subject to craving;
because they are of a nature that causes affliction, they are contemptible, and because they are of a hollow nature and suchness, he declared to me: "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering.

Regarding the phrase "This is the origin of suffering," this refers to craving, which is divided into types such as sensual craving (*āmataṇhā*) and so forth; it is the origin of the aforementioned suffering.
The connection is as follows: "He told me that 'origination' (pabhava), 'arising' (uppatti), 'cause' (hetu), and 'source' (samudaya) are the Noble Truth;
that 'the cessation of suffering' (dukkhanirodha)—meaning the state of peace of suffering, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), cessation—is the Noble Truth;
and that the path plunging into the Deathless (amatogadha)—because it avoids the two extremes and because it is the straight path leading to Nibbāna—is the Noble Truth."
846. *Kusalassa*: of one who is skillful in giving exhortation and in taming those to be trained, or of one who has reached the pinnacle of the practice of heedfulness (*appamāda*).
"I stand firm in exhortation" means that I am established through the penetration of truth and the fulfillment of the three trainings within the aforementioned exhortation and instruction.
Therefore he said: "He has attained the deathless peace, Nibbāna, the immutable state."
This is the statement of the reason for being established in the Teacher’s instruction. That which has attained the state of Nibbāna— which is "deathless" because it is eternal and free from death,
"peace" because all suffering is stilled, and "unchanging" because there is no cause for the falling away of those who have reached it—
that person has, by one means or another, become established in the Teacher’s instruction.
847. "Firmly rooted in affection" means having steadfast devotion to the Three Jewels and possessing unwavering confidence and love for them. Why? Because they are unshakable in their vision;

that is, they are immovable in this right vision—namely, "The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha is practicing the good way"—and cannot be moved by anyone.
But by what is this unshakability produced? He says: "By faith that has taken root."

This shows that she is "unshakable" by means of the faith rooted in the realization of truth— faith born from the root [of that realization] regarding the Perfectly Enlightened One through the formula beginning, "Thus indeed is the Blessed One, the Worthy One," regarding his Dhamma through the formula beginning, "Well-expounded is the Dhamma by the Blessed One," and regarding his Saṅgha through the formula beginning, "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well. For this very reason, she is a "daughter of the Buddha."
"Orasā" means a legitimate daughter, so called because she was born from the breast of the Perfectly Enlightened One due to the effort exerted there.

"I rejoice" means that I, having then come through noble birth and now through rebirth as a deity, rejoice in the delight of the Path and the delight of the Fruit, play with the delight of the strands of sensual pleasure, and find joy in both. [This is said] regarding the fear of self-reproach and so forth.
Because it is free from [defilements], it is fearless from any quarter. “Madhumaddava”:
this refers to a fragrant drink known as *madhu*, which produces softness (*maddava*)—that is, it brings about a state of pliancy in both body and voice during times of dancing and singing.
They also read it as “*madhumādava*”; the meaning is: “I drink the sweet [drink] for the sake of intoxication (*ādava*), that is, for the purpose of sporting (*davatthaṃ*) as much as possible.”

849. "A mine of fields of merit": the Tathāgatas are the source and place of origin for the Noble Saṅgha—the noble ones established in the paths and fruits—which constitute fields of merit for the world including its devas. "As" means in whichever field of merit. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna brought this conversation, which had been carried on by himself and the deity, to the human world.
Having returned, he reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, taught the Dhamma to the assembled company.
That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Rajjumālā-vimāna*.
Thus ends the commentary on the meaning of the fourth chapter, the Mañjiṭṭhaka-vagga, adorned with twelve stories, within the Vimānavatthu of the Paramatthadīpanī,
the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.
The commentary on the *Itthivimāna* is concluded.
2. *Purisavimāna*, Chapter 5:
The Section on the Great Chariot (*Mahārathavagga*).
1. The Commentary on the Mansion of the Devaputta Maṇḍūka.
In the Mahāratha Chapter, the *Maṇḍūkadevaputtavimāna* begins with the verse: "Who is it that worships my feet? What is its origin?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Campā, on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond. At the time of dawn, he performed the practice customary for Buddhas...
Having entered the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) and emerged from it, he surveyed the beings who were his kinsmen among those to be trained (*veneyya*).
He saw that today, while he was teaching the Dharma at the time of evening, a certain frog had died through the assault of another while taking aim at his voice;
having been reborn in the world of the gods with a vast retinue of deities, it appeared even as the great multitude looked on.
"Having seen that he will come, there will be a great realization of the Dhamma for many," [the Blessed One] dressed in the morning,
took his bowl and robe, and together with a large community of monks, entered the city of Campā for alms.
Having provided the monks with easily obtained almsfood and finished his meal, he entered the monastery and performed the duties toward the monks.
Having shown [these things], when they had each gone to their own daytime resting places,
he entered the Fragrant Chamber and spent the day in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). Then, at the time of evening, when the four assemblies had gathered,
he emerged from the fragrant chamber and, performing a miracle appropriate for that moment, entered the Dhamma Assembly Pavilion on the bank of the lotus pond.
Seated upon a magnificent, adorned Buddha-throne on a surface of emerald, like a fearless lion with a shaggy mane letting out a lion’s roar,
he began to teach the Dhamma, emitting a Brahma-voice endowed with eight qualities, through the inconceivable majesty of a Buddha and the incomparable grace of a Buddha.
At that moment, a frog came from a lotus pond and, perceiving the sound as the Dhamma—grasping it as a sign with the thought, "This is the Dhamma"—lay down at the edge of the assembly.
Then, a cowherd arrived at that place and saw the Teacher teaching the Dhamma and the assembly listening to the Dhamma with supreme tranquility; his mind became fixed upon them.
Standing with his staff raised, he stepped on a frog without noticing it and stood there, pressing down upon its head.
With a mind full of faith due to the perception that it was the Dhamma, he passed away at that very moment and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in size;
there, like one waking from sleep, he saw himself surrounded by a host of nymphs.
Having seen this, he reflected, "From where indeed have I been reborn here? Upon seeing his previous birth, he thought, "I too was born here;
I obtained such prosperity as this. What deed did I perform?
As he investigated, he saw nothing other than his having grasped the sign (nimitta) upon hearing the Blessed One’s voice. At that very moment, he arrived together with his celestial mansion.
Descending from his celestial chariot, while the great multitude was looking on, he approached with a vast retinue and great divine majesty.
He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and standing with palms joined in reverence, he remained there paying homage.
Then the Blessed One, though already knowing it, acted to make the fruit of the people's karma and the power of a Buddha manifest before their very eyes:
“Who is it that worships my feet, shining with supernatural power and glory, illuminating all directions with a most excellent complexion?”—thus he asked.
In this context, *ko* means “who,” referring to someone among the gods, nāgas, yakkhas, humans, and so forth; *me* means “my”; and *pādāni* means “the feet.”
"At his feet. "By means of psychic power" (*iddhiyā*) means by means of such divine power (*deviddhi*). "By means of fame" (*yasasā*) means by means of such a retinue and distinction.
"Shining" means radiating light. "Exceedingly lovely" (*abhikkantena*) means exceedingly desirable and beautiful.
"By means of complexion" (*vaṇṇena*) means by means of the color of the skin; the meaning is the luster of the body's complexion.
Then the young god, revealing his own previous birth and other details, explained it with these verses:
“In the past I was a frog, dwelling in the water and feeding on its creatures;
while I was listening to your Dhamma, a cowherd killed me.”
“Behold my success and my glory arising from a moment’s clarity of mind;
behold my power, behold my beauty and my radiance.
And those who, over the long course of time, have heard the Dhamma from Gotama—”
"You have reached that immovable state, having gone where you shall no longer grieve.
(858) Therein, "formerly" (*pure*) means in a previous birth. "In water" (*udake*) is a demonstration of his own place of rebirth at that time.
By the phrase "a frog in the water," the exclusion of frogs on dry land, such as those that are bloated, is effected.
“Gocara” means a place where cattle graze; it is like a grazing ground, that is, a place for seeking food.
“Vārigocara” means one whose grazing ground is water. For some, such as turtles and the like, are water-dwellers yet do not have water as their grazing ground;
therefore, it is stated specifically as “vārigocara. “Of you who are teaching while listening to the Dhamma” refers to one teaching with a Brahma-voice, as sweet as the song of the cuckoo.
As you listen to my Dhamma with the apprehension of signs, thinking, "This is what is called Dhamma," this genitive case should be understood as expressing disregard.
Just as one says, "The cowherd boy killed me," meaning that while protecting the calves,
the cowherd boy came near me, stood leaning on his staff, pressed the staff against my head, and killed me.
859. *Muhuttaṃ cittapasādassā* means: for the sake of the momentary clarity of mind (*cittapasāda*) that has arisen toward your Dhamma;
*iddhiṃ* means success (*samiddhi*), that is to say, divine manifestation (*dibbavibhūti*). *Yasaṃ* means retinue (*parivāra*). *Ānubhāvaṃ* means divine power such as beauty and so forth.
*Vaṇṇaṃ* means the excellence of bodily color (*sarīravaṇṇasampatti*). *Jutiṃ* means [splendor extending] twelve *yojanas*.
The distinction of radiance capable of pervading [all]. 860. *Ye* means those beings.
The word *ca* is used in the sense of exclusion (*byatireke*). *Te* means "of you. *Dīgham addhānaṃ* means for a long time. *Assosuṃ* means they heard.
*Gotama* is an address to the Blessed One by his clan name (*gotta*). *Acalaṭṭhānaṃ* means Nibbāna. This is what is meant here:

The meaning is this: O Gotama, the Blessed One said that those who have performed meritorious deeds and, unlike me, did not hear your Dhamma for only a short time, but were able to hear it for a long duration—those beings, having gone there, would no longer grieve;
that sorrowless state of peace, which is unshakable due to its eternal nature and is not overcome by the calamities of saṃsāra.
"They have already attained it; there is no obstacle for them in attaining it.
Then the Blessed One, observing the excellence of the spiritual potential (*upanissaya*) of the assembled multitude, taught the Dhamma in detail.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that son of the gods was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), as were eighty-four thousand beings.

There was a realization of the Dhamma. The son of the gods, having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him three times, and having extended his joined palms in salutation to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, departed for the world of the gods together with his retinue.
The commentary on the Maṇḍūka-devaputta-vimāna is finished.
2. The Description of the Mansion of Revatī "Arise, O Revatī, you of very evil character!"—this is the *Revatī-vimāna*. How did it originate?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. At that time, in Bārāṇasī, there was a family endowed with faith...
There was a lay follower named Nandiya, a son who was endowed with faith, a donor, a master of giving, and an attendant of the Saṅgha.
Then his parents desired to bring home from their own household a girl named Revatī, the daughter of their maternal uncle.
She, however, lacked faith and was not disposed toward giving; Nandiya did not wish for her. His mother said to Revatī: "My dear, you..."
Having come to this house, smear the sitting area for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with fresh cow dung, prepare the seats, and set out the stands.
When the bhikkhus arrive, pay homage to them, take their bowls, and have them sit down.
After filtering water with a water-strainer, wash their bowls when they have finished eating; in this way, [serve] for me.
“You will become pleasing to your son. She did accordingly.
Then, having informed her son that she had become capable of receiving his instruction, and when he consented by saying “Very well,” they fixed a date and performed the marriage ceremony.
Then Nandiya said to her: “If you shall serve the Saṅgha of monks as well as my mother and father, then in this—”
“You shall be allowed to live in the house; be heedful.
Having assented with “Very well,” she acted as if possessed of faith for a time, and without being unfaithful to her husband, she gave birth to two sons.
Nandiya’s parents passed away, and all the authority in the household belonged to her alone. Nandiya, too, having become a great master of giving, [bestowed gifts] upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
He established an almsgiving and instituted a regular distribution of cooked food at the doors of the houses for the poor, the destitute, and others.

Having had a four-hall building adorned with four chambers constructed at the Mahāvihāra of Isipatana, and having had beds, seats, and other furnishings provided, he gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha;
then, pouring the water of dedication into the hand of the Tathāgata, he formally dedicated it.
Along with the offering of water for the ritual donation, a celestial palace made of the seven precious gems arose in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven—
twelve yojanas in length and breadth, one hundred yojanas in height, and resounded with the voices of thousands of hosts of celestial nymphs. Then,
while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was wandering on his journey through the deva realms, he saw that palace as the inhabitants came to pay him homage.
The sons of the gods asked, "To whom does this palace belong? They replied, "Venerable sir, the owner of this palace is a householder’s son named Nandiya in Bārāṇasī in the human world;
he had a four-hall building constructed at the Saṅgha’s great monastery at Isipatana, and this palace has arisen for him.
The celestial nymph who had been reborn in that palace also paid homage to the Elder.
“Venerable sir, we were reborn here to become attendants to a lay follower named Nandiya in Bārāṇasī;
please tell him this: ‘You were reborn to be his attendant, yet the deities are weary of your long delay.
The splendor of the deva-world is like discarding an earthenware vessel to take up a golden one.’”
“Tell him to come here, saying that it is exceedingly pleasing,” they said.
The Elder, having consented with “Very well,” came suddenly from the world of the gods and asked the Blessed One in the midst of the fourfold assembly:
“Venerable Sir, does a divine fortune arise for those who have performed meritorious deeds while still remaining in the human world? “Is it not so, [Elder]? he replied.
“Moggallāna, you have seen for yourself the divine splendor in which Nandiya was reborn in the world of the gods; why then do you ask me?

“It is so, Bhante; he is reborn thus. Then the Teacher said: “Just as friends and relatives welcome and rejoice over a man who has returned after living abroad for a long time, even so do those who have performed meritorious deeds [welcome] the person who has come from this world to the next.”
Showing that those who have gone forth receive and welcome their own merits with hands outstretched, he said:
“Relatives, friends, and well-wishers rejoice at the return of a man who has been long away and has come back safely from afar.”
“In the same way, when one who has performed merit passes from this world to the next, the merits receive him just as beloved kinsmen welcome a returning relative.
Having heard this verse, Nandiya gave gifts and performed meritorious deeds even more abundantly. While he was traveling for trade—
He said to Revatī, “Bhadde, you should attend diligently to the alms-giving for the Saṅgha and the food-offerings for the destitute that I have established.
She consented, saying, “Very well. Even when he had gone abroad and was staying wherever he might be, he continued to give alms to the monks and the destitute according to his means.
Out of compassion for him, those whose taints were destroyed came even from afar to accept his offerings.
But when he had departed, Revatī continued the practice of giving for only a few days; she then cut off the food for the destitute and gave the monks only broken rice with sour gruel as a side dish.
From the places where the monks had eaten, she took the remaining grains of rice that she herself had left over.
Having scattered pieces of fish and meat along with moving bones, he showed them to people, saying, "Look at the work of the recluses;
they are thus throwing away what was given out of faith!
Then Nandiya Vohārakasiddhi, having come according to his means and heard of that occurrence, [went] from Revatī’s house...

Having brought her out, he entered his house. On the second day, having offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, he properly established a regular meal and a meal for the destitute;
he then provided Revatī, who had been brought by his companions, with food and clothing as the highest necessity. After some time, having passed away, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
She was reborn in her own celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
But Revatī, having cut off all giving, wandered about reviling and abusing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, saying, “Because of these people, my gains and honor have declined.
Then Vessavaṇa commanded two *yakkhas*: “Go, sirs, and proclaim throughout the city of Bārāṇasī: ‘Seven days from now...’”
"On the seventh day, while she is still alive, Revatī shall be cast into hell. Upon hearing this, the great multitude was struck with agitation and became terrified and trembling.
Then Revatī ascended her palace, closed the door, and sat down.
On the seventh day, commanded by King Vessavaṇa, who was incited by her evil karma, there appeared women with flaming tawny hair and beards, and with flat, deformed noses.
Two yakṣas, with protruding fangs, red eyes, and a complexion like that of a rain-cloud—possessing an exceedingly terrifying form—approached her.

Saying, "Arise, Revatī, you of most wicked character! and so forth, they seized her by various limbs and, saying, "Let the great multitude see!", made her wander from street to street throughout the entire city. Then, soaring into the air, they went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Having led her to the mansion of Nandiya and shown her his prosperity, they brought her, while she was still lamenting, to the vicinity of the Ussada Hell.
The messengers of Yama threw her into the Ussada Hell. Therefore he said:
“Arise, Revatī, you of most evil nature, you who have left the gates open and are devoid of the habit of giving!”
