"Let us go to that place where the miserable ones, consigned to hell, are tormented by suffering.
Therein, "Arise! means: arise! This palace is not able to protect you from the fear of hell;
therefore, the meaning is: arise quickly and come back. "O Revata," he addresses him by name. By the words beginning with "of evil character," etc., [the Buddha speaks].

He states the reason for rising: "Because you are of such extremely base and evil character through your reviling and insulting of the Noble Ones, and because the door to hell is wide open for your entry, therefore rise!
Regarding the phrase "of non-giving character," it means one who has no habit of giving anything to anyone, being stingy and miserly; this too is a statement of the reason for rising.

Because those who possess the virtues of generosity and moral conduct, who are free from stinginess, and who are like your husband, dwell in a happy destination (sugati), whereas those who lack such virtues, who do not give, and who are stingy, dwell in hell; therefore, "Arise!

I will not allow you to remain here even for a moment"—this is the intended meaning. "Those gone to misfortune" (duggata) means they have gone to suffering; "those belonging to hell" (nerayika) [means those who are in hell].

The construction is as follows: "We shall lead them there, we shall carry them there, we shall cast them there"—referring to that hell where they are afflicted and possessed by the suffering of hell; where, unable to escape for as long as their evil karma has not been exhausted, they groan and moan.
“Having spoken thus, those two great red-eyed yakkhas, the messengers of Yama,
seized Revata by his arms and brought him into the presence of the host of gods.”—
This is the statement of the compilers of the collection.
In that context, *icceva vatvāna* means "having spoken thus," namely, having spoken [the words] beginning with "Arise"; the meaning is "immediately after those words were spoken.
*Yamassa dūtā* means "messengers of King Yama" who are not to be resisted. For they were dispatched by Vessavaṇa;
indeed, it was they who led him to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Some read *na yamassa dūtā*, placing the negative particle *na* before the word *yamassa*.
To connect [the term] with the word *pada* and explain it as meaning “messengers of Vessavaṇa” is not tenable;
for they do not become messengers of Vessavaṇa simply by virtue of being messengers of Yama. They are called *yakkhas* because they sacrifice there, that is, because they present offerings.
They are called *lohitakkha* (red-eyed) because their eyes are red; for the eyes of *yakkhas* are exceedingly red. They are called *brahanta* because they are great.
“On separate arms” means on one arm for one [person] and on the other arm for the other; thus, they were on separate arms. “Revata” refers to Revatī.
*Revatā* is also simply her name; for it is said, “O Revatī. “They expelled” means they drove away; the sense is that they led her away.
“Of the host of gods” means of the assembly of deities in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Thus, having been led by those *yakkhas* to the Tāvatiṃsa realm and placed not far from the Nandiya palace, Revatī saw that celestial mansion—which was exceedingly radiant, resembling the solar disk—and thought:
“Resplendent with the color of the sun, beautiful and luminous, this auspicious mansion is covered with a golden lattice.
Whose is this celestial abode, crowded with people, shining like the rays of the sun?”
“Hosts of women, anointed with the essence of sandalwood, adorn the celestial mansion on both sides;
it appears with a color like that of the sun. Who rejoices, having reached heaven, in that celestial mansion?”—thus he questioned those *yakkhas*.
They, too, [replied] to her:
“In Benares there was one named Nandiya, a lay follower, free from stinginess, a lord of giving, and generous.
This is his celestial mansion, crowded with people, shining like the rays of the sun.
Groups of women, anointed with the essence of sandalwood, adorn both sides of the mansion.”
"Behold him, with a complexion like the sun; having reached heaven, he rejoices in his celestial mansion"—thus they described him.

(868) In that context, "smeared with the essence of sandalwood" means their bodies are anointed with the finest sandalwood fragrance. "On both sides of the mansion" means they approach and beautify the mansion on both its interior and exterior with music and other such delights.
Then Revatī said:
“I am the wife of Nandiya, a householder and mistress of the entire household;
I shall delight in my husband’s celestial mansion. I give this gift; I do not wish to see hell.”
He said: "In that context, 'agārinī' means the mistress of the house. They also read it as 'bhariyā sagāminī,' which means the wife who goes together [with her husband].
She said, 'I was the sovereign, the mistress of my husband Nandiya, the head of the entire household;
therefore, even now, I shall be the sovereign in this celestial mansion (vimāna),' and thus she said, 'I shall delight in the mansion through the power of giving.'"
It was precisely for the sake of seducing him that they led him there. As for the words, "I do not desire to see hell," he says:
"Even for the sake of seeing that hell which you wish to lead me to, I have no desire; how much less would I enter it?
While he was speaking thus, [they said], "Whether you desire it or not, what does your desire matter to us? and having led him near to hell—
“This is your hell, O you of evil nature; no merit was performed by you in the world of the living.
For one who is stingy, wrathful, and of evil nature does not attain companionship with those who go to heaven.
Thus they spoke this verse. Its meaning is: “This is your hell,” that is, a place where you must experience great suffering for a long time.
Why? Because no merit was performed by you in the world of the living;

since not even the slightest merit was performed by you in the human world, such a being—one who has failed to perform merit—is stingy, characterized by the concealment of one's own prosperity through stinginess, resentful by provoking anger in others, and possessed of evil states such as greed.
The construction is: "One of evil nature does not obtain companionship or fellowship with the gods who have attained heaven.

Having spoken thus, those two *yakkhas* vanished right there. But seeing two hell-wardens similar to them, named Saṃsava, dragging [beings] away to throw them into the excrement hell (*gūthaniraya*), he thought:
"What indeed is this foul-smelling filth, Excrement and urine, that is being displayed?"
“What is this foul-smelling filth? What is it that reeks so?”—thus he questioned him about that hell.
“This is the one called Saṃsāvaka, deep and a hundred fathoms high.”
“Revered Revatī, where you are roasted for thousands of years”—
when this was said, she asked him about the deed that had been the cause of her rebirth there:
“What evil deed have you committed by body, speech, or mind?”
“By what means was this deep, hundred-fold person obtained? he asked.
“You have deceived ascetics, brahmins, and others who were mendicants with false speech; that evil has been committed by you.”
Having told her that deed, they said to her again:
“Because of that, you have obtained a deep saṃsava-pot;
there, O Revatī, you shall burn for thousands of years.”
They said: "In that regard, it is called 'the oozing one' because of the constant oozing and trickling of impurities such as excrement and urine.

It is not only that you receive the lot of being an oozing one here, but rather, to show that after boiling there for many thousands of years, upon emerging, one receives the cutting off of hands and so forth, [they say]:
'They cut off the hands, and then the feet; they cut off the ears, and then the nose.'"
"Then flocks of *kākoḷa* birds, having gathered and assembled, devour her as she writhes."—In this regard, they spoke of the reason for what was obtained there.
Therein, "flocks of *kākoḷa* birds" refers to swarms of crows.
It is said that many hundreds and many thousands of them fall upon her body, which measures three *gāvutas* in size, with their iron beaks, sharpened to the point and as thick as palm trunks.
Having pierced [him] again and again with their beaks, they devour him; yet, by the power of karma, the flesh fills up at every spot from which it has been taken.
Therefore it was said: "Flocks of *kākoḷa* birds, having gathered and come together, devour him as he writhes.
Furthermore, she lamented various things through begging and other means in order to bring him back to the human world. Thus it was stated:
“It would be well indeed if you would lead me back, so that I may perform much wholesome merit through giving,
righteous conduct, self-restraint, and self-mastery—
that by doing which people become happy and do not later feel remorse.”
Again the hell-wardens say:
“Having previously been heedless, you now lament;
you shall experience the ripening of the deeds you yourself have done.”
They said. Again she said:
"Who, having gone from the world of the gods to the world of men, would say this to me when asked:
'Give gifts to those who have laid down the rod; give clothing, bedding, food, and drink;'"
"For one who is stingy, irascible, and of evil character does not attain companionship with those who go to heaven.
Surely, having gone from here and obtained a human birth,
being generous and endowed with virtue, I shall perform much wholesome merit."
“Through generosity, through even conduct, through self-restraint, and through self-mastery;
with a serene mind, I shall plant groves, build bridges over difficult terrain, dig ponds, and provide wells.”
"On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as during the fortnight of miracles,
I shall observe the Uposatha endowed with its eight factors, always restrained by virtue."
"And I shall not be negligent regarding giving;
this has been seen by me with my own eyes."—Thus she lamented, trembling here and there;
they cast her into the terrible hell, feet upwards and head downwards.
This is the statement of the compiler. Furthermore, she said:
"In the past, I was miserly and used to revile ascetics and brahmins;
having deceived my husband with falsehoods, I am now being cooked in a terrifying hell."

He spoke the concluding verse. It should be understood that therein the verse beginning “In the past I was stingy” was spoken by one reborn in hell, while the other was spoken by one not so reborn. The rest is easily understood.
The bhikkhus reported to the Blessed One that Revatī had been seized and carried away by yakkhas.

Having heard this, the Blessed One related this account from the beginning and then taught the Dhamma in detail. At the conclusion of the teaching, [the bhikkhus attained various stages of realization].
Many attained the fruit of stream-entry and other stages. Although this discourse is commonly designated as the "Revatī Vimāna" because it is predominantly concerned with Revatī,
since Revatī was not actually the deity residing in the celestial mansion, and because this account concerns the excellence of the mansion and other attainments belonging to the young deva Nandiya,
it should therefore be included among the *purisavimānas* (male celestial mansions).
It should be understood as "placed upon.
The commentary on the Revatī-vimāna is finished.
3. Commentary on the Chatta-māṇavaka-vimāna.
"The One Who Is Preeminent Among Men in Speech": This is the *Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna*. What is its origin?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove. At that time, in Setavyā, there was a certain brahmin who had obtained a son with great difficulty;
this brahmin youth was named Chatta. Having reached maturity, he was sent by his father to go to Ukkaṭṭhā.

In the presence of the brahmin Pokkharasāti, through his intelligence and diligence, he mastered the mantras and the fields of knowledge in no long time and attained proficiency in the brahminical arts.
He paid homage to his teacher and said, "I have learned the craft from you; what heavy fee shall I give you? The teacher—
“A teacher’s fee (garudakkhiṇā), it is said, should be according to the student’s means; bring a thousand kahāpaṇas,” he said.

The youth Chattamāṇava paid homage to his teacher, went to Setavyā, and after bowing to his parents and being greeted with joy by them, he made polite inquiries and informed his father of the matter, saying, “Give me what is appropriate to be given; having given it today, I shall return.”
His parents said to him, "Dear son, it is late today; you shall go tomorrow," and having taken out some kahāpaṇa coins, they had them tied into a bundle and set it aside.
When the thieves learned of this news, they hid in a certain thicket along the young man’s path, thinking, "We shall kill the young man and take the kahāpaṇa coins."
At dawn, the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*), surveyed the world.
He saw that the young man Chatta was established in the refuges and the precepts; that one who had been killed by thieves was reborn in the deva-world;

and that when he arrived there together with his celestial mansion, the assembly gathered there would attain the realization of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*). Having seen this, [the Blessed One] even earlier than that—
Having gone there, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree on the young man’s path.
The young man, having taken his teacher’s fee, was traveling from Setavyā toward Ukkaṭṭhā; seeing the Blessed One sitting by the way, he approached and stood before him.
When asked by the Blessed One, “Where are you going? he replied, “To Ukkaṭṭhā, Master Gotama.”
“I shall go to give my teacher Pokkharasāti a heavy gift,” he said.
Then the Blessed One said, “But do you know, young man, the three refuges and the five precepts? When he replied, “I do not know;
for what purpose are they, and of what nature are they? [the Blessed One] said, “They are such as this,” and explained the going for refuge and the undertaking of the precepts.
Having thus clarified the benefits of the fruit [of taking refuge], he said, "Māṇavaka, first learn the procedure for going for refuge.

When the youth requested, "Very well, I shall learn it; please tell me, Bhante," the Blessed One, at his request and in accordance with his inclination, presented the procedure for going for refuge by means of verses:
“The Sakyan Sage, the Blessed One, the most excellent among those who speak,
who has accomplished what was to be done, who has gone to the further shore, and who is endowed with power and energy— to that Sugata, go for refuge. To the Dhamma,
which is the fading away of lust, unshakable, sorrowless, unconditioned, and not repulsive;”
"Come for refuge to this Dhamma, which is sweet, skillful, and well-analyzed.
And come for refuge to this Saṅgha— the eight persons who see the Dhamma, in whom they say a gift given bears great fruit among the four pure pairs of men."
He spoke three verses. 886.
Therein, "he" (*yo*) is an indefinite term; it should be understood as being defined by the word "that" (*taṃ*).
"Vadantaṃ" means "of those who speak. "Pavaro" means "the best," the supreme speaker among speakers—that is the meaning. "Among men" (*manujesu*) is an expression used in its highest sense.
Just as it is said, "The Teacher of gods and humans," the Blessed One is indeed the most excellent among all beings—gods, humans, and even Brahmās.
And because the Blessed One arose among humans in his final existence, it is said, "among men. For this very reason, he is called "the Sage of the Sakyans" (Sakyamuni).
He is a Sakyan because he was born into the Sakya clan, and [he is a sage] because he is endowed with physical modesty and other such virtues.

Because he has measured the entirety of what is to be known (*ñeyya*), he is a Sage (*muni*); thus, he is the Sakyan Sage (*Sakyamuni*). He is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*) by virtue of four reasons, beginning with his possession of good fortune.

Because he has performed and accomplished the sixteenfold task—consisting of the various duties such as full comprehension (*pariññā*)—which is to be done by means of the four paths, he is one who has "done what was to be done" (*katakicca*).
Having gone to the further shore of identity-attachment (*sakkāya*), which is Nibbāna, by means of his self-arisen knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*), he is one who has "gone to the far shore" (*pāragata*).

"Attained" means having gone to the further shore. Because he is endowed with incomparable physical strength, with knowledge-power not shared by others, and with the energy of the fourfold right exertion, he is "possessed of power and energy.
Because his gait is beautiful, because he has gone to a beautiful state, because he has gone rightly, and because he has spoken rightly, he is the "Well-Gone One" (*Sugata*).
For the sake of refuge—to that Well-Gone One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—for the purpose of taking refuge.

"Go to, approach the Refuge for protection from the suffering of the lower realms and the suffering of the cycle of existence; from this day forward, by turning away from the unwholesome and increasing in the wholesome, resort to and serve him, thinking:
'This Blessed One is my refuge, my protection, my shelter, my ultimate resort, my destination, my final resort.
This is the meaning: know it thus, or awaken to it."
887. "The noble path" refers to the path that leads to the fading away of lust (*rāgavirāga*).
For by means of it, the Noble Ones cause even lust, though cultivated since beginningless time, to fade away. "Unshaken and sorrowless" refers to the fruit of the Noble Ones (*ariyaphala*).

For because craving—which is reckoned as "shaking" (*ejā*)—and the remaining defilements that are the causes of sorrow have been entirely stilled, it is called "unshaken and sorrowless. "Dhamma" refers to the dhamma of intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*).
This is a dhamma that must be grasped by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), namely the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna;

it is not [to be grasped] by way of conceptual designation (*paññatti*) like the dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). Or, "dhamma" here means the ultimate dhamma (*paramattha-dhamma*), which is to say, Nibbāna.

That which is made by conditions having come together and combined is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*); that which is not conditioned is "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*). That very thing is Nibbāna. In this [Nibbāna], there is nothing...
It is "not repulsive" because nothing whatsoever is repulsive [to it]. It is "sweet" because it is always desirable—at the time of hearing, at the time of investigation, and at the time of practice.
It is "proficient" because it functions with ease due to its being based on omniscient knowledge, because of its excellence of ingenuity, and because of its subtlety.
[It is so called] by way of the aggregates and so forth, according to the meaning that is to be analyzed.

It is "well-analyzed" (*suvibhatta*) because it is thoroughly divided according to categories such as the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth, and according to headings such as the summary (*uddesa*) and so forth. By all three terms, he refers specifically to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*).

For that very reason, just as at the time of its initial appearance, even at the time of its thorough examination, it is said to be "this" (*imam*) for the purpose of showing its direct perceptibility through the presence [of the teaching] both for the one who speaks and for the one who hears, as if it were right before their eyes. "Dhamma" refers to that which is practiced exactly as it is.
"Dhamma" is used here in the sense of "supporting" one from falling into the suffering of the states of misery (*apāya*); this is a term common to all four aspects of Dhamma.

For even the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) supports one from falling into the suffering of the states of misery through correct practice, by means of merely establishing oneself in the refuges and the precepts.
And it should be understood that this very *vimāna* (celestial mansion) is the proof for this meaning.
Having made manifest the aforementioned Dhamma by way of its commonality, he spoke again, saying "this.
(888) *Yattha* means in which noble Saṅgha. *Dinnaṃ* means that which has been relinquished—the gift of food and other such things to be given.

The elision of the nasal vowel (*niggahīta*) in the phrase *dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ* has been made for the sake of metrical ease in the verse. [It is so called] because of the purification resulting from being completely cleansed of the impurity of the defilements.
"In the pure ones" refers to the four pairs of persons mentioned as "the stream-enterer, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry," and so forth.
"Eight" means eight individuals, by taking them separately rather than forming pairs consisting of those established in the path and those established in the fruit.

And here, for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse, the designation is given in the abbreviated form "puggala-dhammadasā. "Dhammadasā" [means] those who see the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
And [he is] one who sees the Dhamma of Nibbāna directly. [He takes refuge in] the Saṅgha by way of its unity through commonality of view and virtue.

Thus, when the Blessed One had explained the procedure for going for refuge along with the demonstration of the qualities of the refuges by means of these three verses, the young brahmin, through the recollection of the respective qualities of each refuge, established within his own heart the fact that he had performed the procedure for going for refuge.
As he was elucidating each verse, immediately following it, he recited that respective verse in response, beginning with the words, "He who is the most excellent among those who speak.

Having thus recited them in response, and having explained to him who stood there the five training rules (sikkhāpada) both in their literal form and in terms of their fruits and benefits, he described the procedure for undertaking them.
He, too, having reflected upon this thoroughly, with a mind full of serene confidence—
Saying, “Come now, Blessed One, I shall go,” he set out on that very same path, recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem.
The Blessed One, thinking, “Enough; this much merit is sufficient for his rebirth in the world of the gods,” returned to the Jeta Grove.
However, as the young man’s mind was filled with faith, through the act of discerning the virtues of the Triple Gem, he thought, “I go for refuge.”
Because his mind was active with the thought of the refuges, and because he was established in the five precepts according to the method taught by the Blessed One,
he proceeded while recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem in that very same manner;
thus, even though bandits encountered him on the road, he disregarded them and continued on his way, recollecting only the qualities of the Triple Gem.
Then a certain thief, stationed near a thicket, suddenly pierced him with a poisoned arrow, bringing him to the end of his life;

he took the bundle of coins and departed with his companions. But the young man, having passed away, appeared in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven within a golden celestial mansion thirty yojanas in size, surrounded by a thousand nymphs as if waking from sleep.
He was reborn with a body adorned with ornaments weighing sixty cartloads;
the radiance of that celestial mansion remained pervading more than twenty yojanas.
Then, seeing that the young man had passed away, the people living in the village of Setavyā went to Setavyā and [informed] his parents.
The inhabitants of Ukkatthā village went to Ukkatthā and told the brahmin Pokkharasāti.
Upon hearing this, his parents, his kinsmen and friends, and the brahmin Pokkharasāti along with his retinue went to that place weeping with tearful faces;
and for the most part, so did the inhabitants of Setavyā, the inhabitants of Ukkatthā, and the inhabitants of Icchānaṅgala.
They gathered together, and there was a great assembly. Then the young man’s parents, having prepared a funeral pyre not far from the road, began to perform the rites for the body.
Then the Blessed One thought: "When I have gone, the youth Chattapāṇi will come to pay homage to me; and when he has arrived..."
Thinking, “By recounting his past deeds and making the fruit of that karma manifest before his eyes, I shall teach him the Dhamma;

in this way, there will be a realization of the Dhamma for the great multitude,” he approached that place together with a large community of monks and sat down at the foot of a certain tree, emitting the six-colored rays of a Buddha. Then—
The young brahmin deity Chattamāṇava, too, having reflected upon his own prosperity and investigating its cause, saw that it was due to his taking refuge and his undertaking of moral discipline.
Filled with wonder and having conceived great faith and reverence for the Blessed One, he thought:
"Right now I shall go and pay homage to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and [reflect upon] the qualities of the Triple Gem."
Thinking, “I shall make it known to the great multitude,” out of gratitude he illuminated that entire forest region with a single light;
then, arriving together with his celestial mansion, descending from the mansion, and appearing in visible form along with a vast retinue,
he approached, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, paid homage, and raising his joined palms, stood to one side.
He stood there. Seeing him, the great multitude, struck with wonder and amazement, asked, "Who might this be?
Is he a deva or a Brahmā? Having approached, they surrounded the Blessed One. The Blessed One, wishing to make manifest the meritorious deed performed by him, said:
"The sun does not so scorch in the sky, nor does the moon shine, nor even Phussa; [the radiance of this man outshines them all]."
“Since this incomparable, great radiance has come from the triple heaven to the earth, who indeed are you?
The rays of the light-maker cut through more than twenty-four leagues of darkness;
even by night he makes it as if by day, with his perfectly pure, stainless, and beautiful celestial mansion.”
“Variegated with many lotuses and white lilies, strewn with various flowers of many colors, covered by a net of stainless, dustless gold,
it shines in the sky like the sun. With women clad in red and yellow garments,
who are richly perfumed with aloe-wood, yellow sandalwood, and sandalwood paste;”
With skin resembling the color of gold, they fill the sky like stars.
"There, many men and women of various complexions, adorned with flowers and ornaments, are joyful;
fragrant breezes are released by the wind and blow there, spread over with refined gold and covered in gold."
“Of what self-restraint is this the result? By what fruit of karma have you been reborn here?
And how was this celestial mansion attained by you? Answer me now, as you are questioned.
Thus he questioned that son of the gods.
886. *Tapatī* means it shines. *Nabhe* means in the sky. *Phusso* refers to the constellation Puṣya. *Atulaṃ* means incomparable, or immeasurable.

This is what is meant: just as this palace of yours, being incomparable and immeasurable, shines in the sky because of its radiant nature and thus possesses great splendor, so too do the forms of the stars not shine, nor does the moon; they [do not shine] in that way.
"Let that be for now; even the sun does not shine. Who are you, appearing thus, who have come from the world of the gods to this region of the earth?
Make yourself known and speak to this great multitude.
*Chindati* means "he cuts off"; the meaning is that he obstructs, not allowing [them] to proceed. *Raṃsī* means "rays."
“Of Pabhaṅkara” means of the sun. The radiance of that celestial mansion remains pervading twenty-five *yojanas* all around;
therefore he said, “the light extends for more than twenty-five *yojanas*.
“Even at night it makes [it] as if by day” means that by dispelling the darkness with its own radiance, it makes even the portion of night like a portion of day. All around...
It is "pure" because of its purity both inside and out. It is "stainless" (vimala) due to the total absence of impurities. It is "beautiful" (subha) because of its loveliness.

Regarding the phrase "abounding in various lotuses and white water-lilies" (*bahupadumavicitrapuṇḍarīka*): it refers to many kinds of red lotuses (*raktakamala*) as well as multicolored and white lotuses.
They say that the white lotus is the *paduma*, while the red lotus is the *puṇḍarīka*. It is "strewn with flowers" by means of other [blossoms].
And it was strewn with various kinds of flowers. "Variegated by many designs" (*nekacitta*) means variegated by various patterns such as floral and scrollwork.
"Covered by a dustless, stainless golden lattice" (*arajavirajahemajālachanna*) means it was itself free from dust and covered by a stainless, faultless golden net.
(892) "By those wearing red and yellow garments" (*rattambarapītavāsasāhi*) means by those wearing both red and yellow clothes; for one [of them] wore a divine red garment.
One puts on a yellow upper garment after having dressed in [a yellow lower robe], while another, having dressed in yellow, makes a red upper garment.

It is with reference to this that it is said: “Those clad in red and yellow garments. “Abounding in aloe-wood, priyaṅgu, and sandalwood” means abounding in the fragrance of aloe-wood, in priyaṅgu garlands, and in the scents of sandalwood;
the meaning is that they possess an abundance of divine aloe-wood fragrance and so forth.
"With skins resembling golden bodies" means with skins as delicate as gold.
"Filled" means it is full of those who wander here and there, intent on musical performance.
"Many here" means many are present here. "Of manifold colors" means of various forms. "Adorned with flower-ornaments" means specifically...
Adorned with divine flowers and celestial ornaments for the purpose of diffusing fragrance. "Therein" means in this celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
"Sumanā" means those of beautiful mind, with hearts full of joy. "They waft a sweet fragrance released by the wind":
they diffuse a pleasant scent from flowers whose fragrance is released by the wind, like a leaf-cup opened by the breeze, due to their lack of obstruction and their blossoming state.
They also read it as “anilapadhūpitā,” meaning golden flowers being gently wafted by the wind.

They are “spread with refined gold” because they are draped over braids and the like with golden cloths and such. They are “covered in gold” because their bodies are mostly concealed by golden ornaments.
By the phrase “men and women,” he shows that there are many sons of gods and daughters of gods here in your celestial mansion.
894. *Iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation. *Puṭṭho* means "asked"; the intention is: "for the sake of making this great multitude directly perceive the fruit of karma.
Thereupon, the son of the gods answered with these verses:
"The Teacher himself, having encountered me here on the road, instructed me out of compassion, O young brahmin;..."
“Having heard the Dhamma from you, the most excellent jewel, I shall do so,” said Chatta.
“Go for refuge to the supreme Victor, and likewise to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha of monks.
“I did not say ‘yes’ first, venerable sir, but afterwards I acted exactly according to your word.”
“Do not practice various kinds of impure killing of living beings,
for the wise have not praised lack of restraint toward living beings.
“So be it,” I said first, venerable sir, and afterwards I acted exactly according to your word.
“Do not think that what is guarded by another person may be taken as your own without it being given;
thus, O Venerable One, I first spoke ‘No,’ and afterwards I acted exactly according to those words.
Do not go to those who are guarded by another, who are the wives of others; this is ignoble.”
“I did not say ‘No’ first, venerable sir; afterwards I acted exactly according to your word.
Do not speak falsely or otherwise, for the wise do not praise lying.
I did not say ‘No’ first, venerable sir; afterwards I acted exactly according to your word.”
“Whatever causes a person’s perception to depart—avoid all such intoxicants entirely.
‘No,’ I said first, venerable sir, and afterwards I acted exactly according to your word.
Having observed the five training rules here and practiced in accordance with the Dhamma of the Tathāgata,”
“I went along a forked path in the midst of thieves, and they killed me there for the sake of my wealth.
‘I remember this much merit; beyond that, no other [deed] is known to me.
By virtue of that well-performed action, I have been reborn among the Thirty-three Gods, enjoying all desires.’”
“Behold the fruit of practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, even for a mere moment or instant:
they look upon me with fame as if I were a blazing fire, and those of inferior deeds long for my many desires.
Behold how, through this brief instruction, I have gone to a happy destination and attained bliss.”
And those who constantly hear the Dhamma, I think they touch the deathless security.
"Even a small deed has great fruition; it becomes vast in the Dhamma of the Tathāgata.
Behold, through his merit, the Chatta tree illuminates the earth just like the sun."
“What is this that is wholesome? What should we practice?”—thus some, having come together, deliberate.
Having once again obtained human birth, let us dwell practicing with virtue.
“The Teacher is most helpful and compassionate”—with this mindfulness, day after day, I went forth.
“Svāha, I have come here under my true name; have compassion on me and let me hear the Dhamma once more.
“Those who here abandon sensual lust, having abandoned the underlying tendency to existence and delusion, do not enter a womb again;
for they have attained final Nibbāna and become cooled.”
895. Regarding the phrase "having approached there himself on this path":
here, on this path—the great highway—he was approached and met by a young brahmin, a *māṇava*, who had come of his own accord.

Because he instructs beings according to their capacity through the ultimate truths concerning both the present life and the future life, he is the Teacher, the Blessed One; you, O *māṇava*, have instructed him in accordance with the Dhamma.

The construction of the words is as follows: "Chatta," the young brahmin named Chatta, spoke—that is, he said—out of compassion and favor toward you, the most excellent jewel, the supreme jewel, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
having heard that Dhamma, [he thought], "I shall do thus: I will practice exactly as instructed."

896. Having thus shown the action as it was asked about by way of its cause, he now speaks the verse beginning with “The excellent, supreme Victor” in order to show both how he was exhorted by the Teacher and how he himself subsequently established himself therein.
In that context, the phrase “No, Bhante, I did not say so first” means: “Bhante, Blessed One.”
When you asked me, “Do you know how to go for refuge? I first said, “No,” meaning “I do not know.
Later, when you said, “I will act exactly according to your word,” I acted and practiced accordingly by repeating your words;
the meaning is that I went for all three refuges.
897. *Vividhanti* means various, both high and low, including both minor and major offenses. *Mā carassūti* means do not perform.
*Asucinti* means impure because of being mixed with the impurity of the defilements (*kilesa*). *Pāṇesu asaññatanti* means unrestrained toward living beings, that is, not abstaining from killing.
*Na hi avaṇṇayiṃsūti* means they do not praise it; for this expression in the past tense refers to the present time.
Alternatively, the phrase “they censured” (*avaṇṇayiṃsu*) is a partial characterization of the entire period of time;
therefore, what is meant is that just as they did not praise it in the past, so too they do not praise it now, and they will not praise it in the future.
898–900. “Guarded by another person” refers to property belonging to another. Hence he said, “what is not given” (*adinnam*). “Do not go” (*mā agamāsi*).
"Do not transgress. "False" (*vitatha*) means that which is not so; "untrue" (*musa*) is the meaning. "Otherwise" (*aññathā*) means in a different way; the meaning is:
"Knowing it to be false, thinking 'it is false,' do not speak thus. (901) "By which" (*yena*) means by which liquor;

"having drunk" is the intended sense. "Departs" (*apeti*) means it vanishes. "Perception" (*saññā*) refers to the perception of phenomena (*dhammasaññā*) or simply the perception of the world. "All" (*sabba*) means without remainder; the meaning is "starting from the seed."
902. "Svāhā!"—thus I spoke then, having been the young brahmin Chatta. "Here," meaning in this very spot on the road, or within this teaching of yours.
Therefore he said, "In the Dhamma of the Tathāgata. "The five trainings" refers to the five precepts (*sīla*).
"Having performed" means having undertaken; the sense is "having resolved. "A two-path" refers to a road situated between the boundaries of two villages.

The meaning is "the path between the boundaries. "Those" refers to those thieves. "Therein" means on the path between the boundaries. "For the sake of wealth" means for the purpose of some material thing. 903.

"Than that" means beyond or above the aforementioned wholesome state, there exists no other wholesome state that I might recollect—this is the meaning. "One who desires sensual pleasures" means one who possesses the strands of sensual pleasure as they are desired. 904.

"Of one who perceives [only] moments and instants" means of one whose virtue lasts for only a moment or an instant. "In accordance with the Dhamma" means through practice in conformity with the Dhamma.

The meaning is: for one who practices the Dhamma in accordance with the fruit already attained—whether it be the Dhamma of the Blessed One’s instruction or the practice of Dhamma corresponding to that—the Blessed One beholds [them] through the very method described, namely, by means of going for refuge and undertaking the precepts.
"Shining like fire" means blazing as it were with success (*iddhi*) and the excellence of a retinue. "Beholding" means...
*Passantā*: observing. *Bahukā*: many. *Pihayanti*: they long for, meaning they aspire, thinking, "How might we ourselves become like this?
*Hīnakammā*: those whose wealth is inferior compared to my own prosperity.

905. *Katipayāya*: with only a little. *Ye*: those who, namely both the monks and the lay followers (*upāsaka*) and so forth. The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of distinction. *Te*: your. *Satataṃ*: day after day.
906. *Vipulaṃ* means having sublime fruit and great power. The construction is: "having stood upon the Dhamma—that is, the instruction and advice—of the Tathāgata.
Having thus explained the meaning by way of reference to others (*anuddesika*), he says "Behold" (*passa*) and so forth to show that same meaning by way of reference to himself (*attuddesika*).
Therein, "Behold" (*passa*) he addresses the Blessed One, or perhaps himself or another.
And having acted as if [in doubt], he says:
"What is this 'wholesome' (kusala)? What should we practice?"—meaning, "Of what nature is this so-called wholesome? Of what kind is it?
Or how indeed should we practice it? Thus, some, having come together and deliberated, [addressed] the earth.
They deliberate and investigate, performing what is extremely difficult as if they were turning Mount Sineru over or lifting it up;
however, their intention is: "May we, moreover, practice wholesome deeds without any difficulty. For this very reason, he says "we," and so forth.
(908) *Bahukāro* means one who provides much assistance, or one who is of great benefit. *Anukampako* means compassionate. The letter *ma* is used for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).
*Iti* means "thus"; he speaks with reference to the manner in which the Blessed One had practiced within himself.

*Me sati* means "when I am present" or "while I exist," the sense being that [the thieves] were not slain by the robbers. *Divā divassa* means "even during the day," the sense being "at the very time.
*Svāhaṃ* means "I, who was that young brahmin named Chatta. *Saccanāmaṃ* means by such names as "the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One," and so forth.
"True by name" means its name corresponds to reality. "Be compassionate" means: show favor. "And again" means: may we hear even more; the sense is, "may we hear your Dhamma.
Thus the devaputta, standing in gratitude for all this, [spoke] regarding attendance upon the Teacher and listening to the Dhamma.

And he spoke while indicating that [the assembly] was indeed not yet satisfied. The Blessed One, having observed the disposition of the son of the gods and the assembly gathered there, delivered a gradual discourse (*anupubbikathā*).
Then, knowing their hearts were moistened with faith, he proclaimed the Dhamma teaching that brings out the excellence of the goal (*sāmukkaṃsikā dhammadesanā*).
At the conclusion of the teaching, both the son of the gods and his parents attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*).
They were established [in the fruits], and there was a realization of the Dhamma for the great multitude of people.

Having been established in the first fruit, the son of the gods, demonstrating his own profound reverence for the higher paths and the great benefits of their attainment, spoke the final verse: "Those here who abandon sensual lust... (Sn 236).

The meaning of this is as follows: Those who, established here in this teaching, abandon sensual lust without remainder and utterly eradicate it, do not enter a womb again because the lower fetters have been eradicated.
And those who, having abandoned delusion and having completely uprooted it, also abandon the underlying tendency to lust for existence—they [likewise] do not...
It cannot even be said that they enter a womb. Why? Because they have attained final Nibbāna and become cooled;
for those supreme persons have indeed gone to final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue, having thus become cooled here and now through the exhaustion of all sensations and all fevers.
Thus, the son of the gods, announcing his own attainment of the noble stream, having reached the climax of the teaching on the element of Nibbāna without residue,
paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him to the right, showed reverence to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
took leave of his parents, and departed for the world of the gods; the Teacher also rose from his seat and departed together with [the assembly].
[He stayed] with the community of monks. As for the young brahmin’s parents—the brahmin Pokkharasāti and the entire great multitude—they followed the Blessed One and then turned back.
The Blessed One, having gone to Jetavana, spoke on this celestial mansion in detail to the assembled assembly.
That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The commentary on the *Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna* is finished.
4. The commentary on the *Kakkaṭakarasadāyaka-vimāna*:
"This lofty mansion with jeweled pillars" refers to the mansion of the giver of crab-meat. What was its origin? The Blessed One... [text continues]
The Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. At that time, a certain bhikkhu who was practicing insight (vipassanā) was afflicted by an earache;
because his body was unwell, he was unable to advance in his insight practice. Although the physicians administered medicine according to their prescribed methods, the illness did not subside.
He reported this matter to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One said to him, "The consumption of crab broth..."
Knowing it was suitable, he said, "Go, monk, and wander for alms in the Magadha country.
That monk, thinking, "Surely something has been seen by the One of Long Vision," replied to the Blessed One,
"Very well, Bhante," and having paid homage to the Blessed One, took his bowl and robes and went to the Magadha country.
He stood at the door of a certain field-guard’s hut for alms.
That field-guard, having prepared crab soup and cooked rice, sat down thinking, "I will eat after resting for a little while.
Seeing the Elder, he took his bowl, had him sit inside the hut, and gave him the crab-soup rice. For that Elder, that meal—
As soon as he had eaten a little, his earache subsided; it was as if he had been bathed with a hundred jars of water.
Having attained mental ease through suitable food, he directed his mind toward insight (*vipassanā*).
Even before his meal was finished, he exhausted the taints (*āsava*) without remainder and established himself in *arahantship*. Then he said to the field-guardian: "Upāsaka,..."
"By your gift of alms-food, my illness has been pacified and my body and mind have become healthy;
you too, through the fruit of this merit, shall be free from suffering of body and mind," he said, and having offered this expression of thanks, he departed.
Later, at another time, the field-guardian passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven upon a jeweled pillar twelve yojanas in height.
He was reborn in a golden celestial mansion adorned with seven hundred gabled chambers, within a chamber made of beryl.
At its door hung a golden crab, fashioned from pearls, which remained suspended as an indicator of his previously accumulated kamma.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having gone there by the method previously described, saw him and questioned him with these verses:
“High indeed is this celestial mansion with its jeweled pillars, twelve yojanas on all sides;
seven hundred magnificent gabled chambers, beautiful with pillars of beryl set upon silver bases.
There you eat, drink, and feast, while divine lutes play their sweet melodies.”
“Here are divine flavors and the five strands of sensual pleasure, and women adorned in gold dance.
By what means do you have such a complexion? By what means is it fulfilled for you here?
And from where do those riches arise that are dear to the mind?”
“I ask you, O god of great power: while a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?
To show him that, he explained it to him as follows:
“Thus the deva-son, being questioned by Moggallāna, was pleased;
having been asked the question, he explained it—the fruit of which karma this is. So it was said:
“A crab stands at the gate, causing mindfulness to arise.”
“The ten-fold ornament of gold, when finished, shines brilliantly.
‘Because of that, my complexion is thus; because of that, I prosper here;
and whatever wealth is dear to my heart arises for me.’”
“I declare to you, O monk of great power, that while a human being, I performed meritorious deeds;
therefore, my majesty blazes forth in this way, and my complexion shines toward all directions.

(910) In this context, *ucca* means risen high. *Maṇithūṇa* means a pillar made of gems such as ruby (*padumarāga*) and the like. *Samantato* means on all four sides. *Rucakatthatā* means spread with golden plates upon each respective floor.
"911. 'You drink and you eat'—this is said with reference to the fragrant drinks and ambrosial food being consumed from time to time.

'They praise' means they extol. 'Divine tastes, the five strands of sensual pleasure are here'—the meaning is that abundant divine tastes, the five strands of sensual pleasure, are found here in this palace of yours. 'Covered in gold' means adorned with golden ornaments."

915. *Satisamuppādakaro* means one who causes the arising of mindfulness; that is, he is the one who causes the arising of mindfulness regarding the meritorious deed by which this divine attainment was obtained by me.
The meaning is that he causes the arising of mindfulness [with the thought]: "This attainment was obtained by you through the gift of a crab's claw.
*Niṭṭhito jātarūpassa* means "completed by means of gold" (*jātarūpa*); thus it is "made of gold" (*jātarūpamaya*).
Having placed five [claws] on each side, there are ten feet belonging to this [crab]; thus, a crab stands at the door and shines.
This very thing reveals my meritorious deed to such great queens; the intention is that there is nothing further for me to say in this matter.
Therefore he said, "By that, my complexion is such as this," and so forth. The rest is exactly according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the *Kakkaṭakarasadāyaka-vimāna* is finished.
5. The commentary on the *Dvārapālaka-vimāna*:
"This lofty pillar of jewels" refers to the *Dvārapālaka-vimāna*. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha.
In the Bamboo Grove. At that time, a certain lay follower in Rājagaha was providing four regular meals for the Saṅgha.
However, because his house was situated on the outskirts, it mostly had its doors closed due to the fear of thieves.
When the bhikkhus went there, they sometimes returned empty-handed, having failed to receive the meal because the door was shut. The lay follower...
He said to his wife, "My dear lady, is almsfood being given to the noble ones with due respect? She replied, "On some days the noble ones did not come.
"For what reason? "I suppose it was because the gate was closed. Upon hearing this, the lay follower was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency;
he appointed a man as gatekeeper and stationed him there, saying, "From today onwards, you must [keep the gate open]..."
“Sit guarding [the door], and when the masters arrive, admit them; once they have entered, attend to everything for them properly, such as receiving their bowls and preparing seats.
He replied, “Very well,” and acting accordingly, he heard the Dhamma from the presence of the bhikkhus.
Having developed faith and believing in the fruit of kamma, he established himself in the refuges and the precepts, and he attended upon the bhikkhus with great care.
In a later time, the lay follower who provided the regular meal passed away and was reborn among the Yāma devas.

However, the gatekeeper, having served the monks with diligence and having rejoiced in the generosity of others by performing services and offering words of appreciation, was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
His twelve-league golden mansion and all else [described] are as in the case of the Kakkaṭaka-vimāna.
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The verses for the questions and answers are thus handed down:
“This celestial mansion with its jeweled pillars is lofty, extending twelve yojanas on all sides;
it has seven hundred magnificent gabled chambers, beautiful with pillars of beryl and adorned with golden ornaments.”
“There you bathe, drink, and eat, while divine lutes play their sweet melodies.
Here are the five divine strands of sensual pleasure and women adorned in gold who dance.
By what means do you possess such a complexion... [and] why does your complexion illuminate all directions?”
922. “Thus the son of the gods was delighted... [as before] ...the fruit of which deed this is.
“My lifespan is a divine thousand years; it is sustained by speech and set in motion by the mind.
For so long shall one who has performed meritorious deeds remain, endowed with divine sensual pleasures.”
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this...
[and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.
(923) Therein, “my divine lifespan is a thousand years” refers to the specific class of deities in which one has been reborn; of those [deities], it is a thousand years.
He speaks of the lifespan of the gods of the Thirty-three as being exactly that. For them, one hundred human years is a single night and day;
thirty such nights make a month, twelve such months make a year, and their lifespan is one thousand such years.
By human calculation, that is three hundred million years.
And it lasts for sixty hundred thousand years. "Chanted with speech" means chanted by means of speech;
that is, merely spoken by way of conversation such as, "Come, noble sirs, this seat has been prepared, sit here," or, "Is there health for the bodies of the noble ones?
Is the dwelling place comfortable? and so forth. By mind...
“Produced” means a mere state of confidence produced by the thought, “These noble ones are amiable, practitioners of the holy life, and practitioners of the Dhamma,” and so forth;
it shows that nothing belonging to him has been relinquished.
“By this much alone” means by merely speaking thus, even by a mere measure of confidence. “Merit-making karma will stand” means that one is called a “doer of merit.”
"Having offered [the sacrifice], he will stand long in the world of the gods; it will endure.

And while standing there, being endowed with divine sensual pleasures, he dwells enjoying his faculties, having become possessed of and provided with the fivefold divine strands of sensual pleasure as an object of enjoyment for the gods in that divine assembly—this is the meaning. The rest is exactly as previously stated."
The commentary on the Mansion of the Gatekeepers is finished.
6. Commentary on the First Mansion of What Should Be Done (*Karaṇīya-vimāna*):
"This lofty mansion with jeweled pillars" is the Mansion of What Should Be Done. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī.

At Jetavana. At that time, a certain lay follower living in Sāvatthī, having taken his bathing requisites and gone to the Aciravatī River to bathe, was returning when he saw the Blessed One entering Sāvatthī for alms.
Approaching and paying homage, he said, "Venerable sir, by whom have you been invited? The Blessed One remained silent. [The lay follower, perceiving] that he had not been invited by anyone...
Having understood this, he said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal out of compassion.

The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. He led the Blessed One to his own home, prepared a seat worthy of a Buddha, and having seated the Blessed One there, satisfied him with excellent food and drink. When the Blessed One had finished his meal,
Having offered his expression of appreciation, he departed. The remainder is similar to the immediately preceding *vimāna*.
Therefore it was said: 926. “This lofty mansion with its jeweled pillars... [and] women dance, adorned in gold. 928.
“By what means do you have such a complexion... [and] your complexion illuminates all directions?”
930. “Thus the son of a god was satisfied... [as before] ...the fruit of which deed this is.
“Virtuous deeds should be performed by the wise person who understands, for what is given to Buddhas who have reached the right path yields great fruit.”
“Truly for my benefit has the Buddha come from the forest to the village!
Having gladdened my mind where, have I gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven?
(933) Because of that, such is my complexion... [and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.”

931. Therein, "by the wise" means by one possessing discernment (*sappañña*). "By the knowing one" means by one who knows what is beneficial and what is harmful for oneself. "Among those who have gone rightly" means among those who have entered upon the right practice; "among the Buddhas" means among the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddha*). 932.
"For the sake of" means for the sake of welfare (*hita*) or for growth (*vuḍḍhi*). "From the forest" means from the monastery; he speaks with reference to Jetavana.

"One who has approached the Thirty-three" means one who has approached the host of the Thirty-three gods (*tāvatiṃsa-devakāya*), or the abode of the Thirty-three (*tāvatiṃsa-bhavana*), by way of rebirth.
The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Karaṇīya-vimāna is finished.
7. The commentary on the second Karaṇīya-vimāna.

The seventh mansion is similar to the sixth. The only difference is that in the former case the alms-food was given to the Blessed One by a lay follower (*upāsaka*), whereas here it was given to a certain elder (*thera*). The description of these is exactly according to the method already stated. Therefore it is said:
“High is this mansion with its jeweled pillars, twelve leagues in every direction;
seven hundred lofty gabled chambers, beautiful, with pillars of beryl and adorned with golden ornaments.”
“There you bathe, drink, and eat; divine lutes play their sweet melodies;
here are the five celestial qualities of sensual pleasure and women adorned in gold who dance. 937.
‘By what means do you have such a complexion... [and] why does your complexion illuminate all directions?’”
“Thus the son of the gods was delighted... [as before] ...the fruit of which action this is.
“Virtuous deeds should be performed by the wise person who understands:
where gifts are given to monks who have attained the right path, there they bear great fruit.”
“Truly, O bhikkhu, it was for my benefit that you came from the forest to the village.
Having gained confidence there, I have gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
(942) Because of that, such is my complexion... [as before] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.”
The commentary on the Second Karaṇīya-vimāna is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Sūci-vimāna:
"This lofty mansion with jeweled pillars" refers to the Sūci-vimāna. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha.
In the Bamboo Grove. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta had some work to do on a robe and was in need of a needle.
While wandering for alms in Rājagaha, he stood at the door of a smith’s house.
Seeing him, the smith asked, "What do you need, venerable sir? "I have some work to do on a robe; I am in need of a needle."
The smith, with a mind full of faith, gave him two finished needles and said, "Venerable sir, if you have need of more needles in the future, please let me know.
Having spoken thus, he paid homage by prostrating himself on his five limbs. The Elder, having offered him words of thanksgiving, departed.
Later, having passed away, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—
While wandering on his journey among the gods, he questioned that son of the gods with these verses:
“This lofty celestial mansion with its jeweled pillars...
[and so forth] ...and your radiance illuminates all directions.”
948. “Thus the son of the gods was satisfied... [as before] ...the fruit of which action this is.
“What one gives does not remain as that; rather, what one would give is better.
A needle given is better than a needle [not given].”
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this...
[and so on] ...and my complexion shines in all directions.
(949) In this context, “whatever he gives” means whatever kind of gift he gives; “that does not remain for him” means that for him, it remains exactly like that.
There is no fruit. Rather, through both the excellence of the field and the excellence of the mind, there is a fruit that is even more extensive and more sublime.
Therefore, "whatever one gives, that indeed is better" means that whatever exists, one should give it;
one should bestow it. Of any blameless thing fit to be given, the act of giving itself is better.

Why is it better? For I gave a needle; indeed, the needle itself is better, and the gift of the needle alone has become better for me, since such prosperity as this has been obtained—this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the *Sūcivimāna* is finished.
9. Commentary on the Second *Sūcivimāna* (The Needle Mansion):
"This lofty pillar of jewels" refers to the second *Sūcivimāna*. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove (*Veḷuvana*).
At that time, a certain tailor living in Rājagaha, while looking for a monastery, [entered] Veḷuvana.
He went there. There, seeing a certain bhikkhu sewing a robe with a needle in Veḷuvana, he gave him needles together with a needle-case. The rest is all exactly as previously described.
"This lofty palace with its jeweled pillars... [and so on].
"And your complexion shines in all directions," he asked.
"That son of the gods was pleased... [the rest of the verse] ...of what deed is this the fruit?
"In my previous birth, I was a human being among humans in the world of men."
“I saw a stainless bhikkhu, serene and untroubled;
with my own hands, full of faith, I gave him a needle.
Because of that, such is my complexion... [and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.”
All of that is exactly according to the method explained below.
The commentary on the Second Needle Mansion is finished.
10. Commentary on the First Ox Mansion.
Having mounted the elephant-like celestial mansion called Susukka-khandha, what was its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wandering on a tour of the deva realms in the manner previously described, arrived at the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There he saw a certain son of the gods who was entirely white.
Having seen him mounted upon a great divine elephant, traveling through the air with a vast retinue and great divine majesty,
illuminating all directions like the moon or the sun, he approached that son of the gods.
Then that son of the gods descended from there, paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and...
He stood with palms joined in reverence. Then the Elder said:
"Having mounted the elephant Susukkakhandha—unscarred, tusked, powerful, and of great speed;
having mounted that noble, well-equipped elephant, you have come here through the air, across the sky."
“Upon the two tusks of the elephant are fashioned lotus ponds of clear water, in full bloom.
Amidst the lotuses, groups of musical instruments resound, and these enchanting women dance.
You have attained the sovereign power of a god, O one of great majesty; while still a human being, what merit did you perform?”
“By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?”—thus he asked about the deeds performed by way of praising his attainments. 961.
In that context, “susukkakhandhaṃ” means a very white trunk. Although that nāga had four...
Except for the feet, the sheath of the trunk, the region of the face, both ears, and the tail—leaving these parts aside—the entire body is white;
however, because the region of the neck is exceptionally more brilliant, it is described as "having a very bright neck" (*susukkakhandha*).
"Nāga" refers to a divine elephant-king. "Akācina" means faultless, being free from skin defects such as spots, freckles, and *tilaka* marks.

The meaning is as follows. There is also a reading, “ājānīyaṃ,” which means “endowed with the characteristics of a thoroughbred. “Dantaṃ” means possessing large and beautiful tusks. “Balaṃ” means powerful, one of great strength.
“Mahājavan” means exceedingly swift, one who moves quickly. Regarding the phrase “puna abhiruyha,” the elision of the nasal vowel (anunāsikalopa) should be understood here;
it is said that “abhiruyhaṃ” means “to be mounted. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
Thus questioned by the Elder, the son of the gods, recounting the deed he himself had performed,
said: “Eight handfuls of jasmine flowers, with my own hands, I offered with faith upon the stupa of Kassapa, the Great Sage.”
“By that [merit], such is my complexion… [and so on] … ‘And my complexion shines in all directions’”—with these verses he explained it.
The meaning of this is: formerly, when the golden stupa one yojana in height belonging to the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa was being dismantled from its base, I released [a brick].
Having obtained eight *mutta*-flowers that had fallen at the foot of a tree, I took them and, with a mind full of serene faith,
offered and honored them as an act of worship. It is said that in the past,
after the Parinibbāna of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, when a golden stupa one *yojana* in height had been constructed, [I did so] together with my retinue.
Kikī, the King of Kāsi, the city-dwellers, the merchants, and the country-folk performed flower-offerings day after day.

As they did so, the flowers became expensive and difficult to obtain. Then, a certain lay follower, having wandered through the street of the florists and being unable to obtain even a single flower for a single kahāpaṇa, took eight kahāpaṇas.
Having gone to the flower garden, he said to the gardener, "Give me eight flowers for these eight kahāpaṇas.
"Venerable sir, there are no flowers; they were given to you after I had carefully inspected and plucked them myself. "I take them only after inspecting them," he replied.
"If that is so, enter the garden and search for them yourself. Having entered and searched, he found eight fallen flowers.
Having obtained [the flowers], he said to the garland-maker, "Take them, dear father, for these coins. He replied, "These were obtained through your merit;

I do not take coins. The other thought, "I will not perform an offering to the Blessed One by taking flowers for nothing," and placing the coins before him, he took the flowers, went to the courtyard of the shrine, and with a devout heart—
He performed an act of worship. Later, having passed away, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas;

having remained there for the full span of his lifespan, he was reborn again in the world of the gods, and again in the world of the gods—in this way, wandering from one to another solely among the devas, and by the remaining ripening of that very same karma, he was reborn even during this current appearance of a Buddha among the Tāvatiṃsa devas themselves. It is with reference to him [that this was said].
Regarding what was stated below, beginning with "There he saw a certain son of the gods," the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna returned to the human world and reported this occurrence to the Blessed One.
Taking that matter as the occasion for a discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*), the Blessed One taught the Dhamma in detail to the assembled assembly.
That teaching was beneficial to the great multitude.
The commentary on the *Nāgavimāna* is concluded.
11. Commentary on the Second *Nāgavimāna*.
"Mounting a great elephant" refers to the second Nāga-vimāna. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove.

At that time, a certain lay follower (upāsaka) in Rājagaha—faithful, confident, and established in the five precepts—having undertaken the Uposatha vows on Uposatha days, [spent] the morning in accordance with his own means...
Having given gifts to the monks and eaten himself, dressed in clean lower garments and a clean upper robe,
he would take mostly eight kinds of drinks after the meal, go to the monastery, offer them to the Saṅgha of monks,
approach the Blessed One, and listen to the Dhamma. In this way, he performed much good conduct consisting of both giving and virtue with due care.
Having accumulated merit, when he passed away from here, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods. Through the power of his merit, a great, divine, all-white elephant appeared before him.
Mounting it, accompanied by a vast retinue and endowed with great divine majesty, he would go from time to time for pleasure excursions in the parks.
Then one day, urged by his sense of gratitude, he mounted that divine elephant at the hour of midnight and,
accompanied by a great retinue, came from the world of the gods with the thought, "I shall pay homage to the Blessed One. He illuminated the entire Veḷuvana grove,
dismounted from the back of the elephant, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and, raising his joined palms, stood to one side.
He stood there. Standing near the Blessed One, the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having received the Blessed One’s permission, questioned him with these verses:
“Having mounted a great elephant, all-white, the best of tuskers, you wander from forest to forest, preceded by a host of women.”
Illumining all directions like a star among the herbs:
“By what means is your complexion such as this… [etc. …and your complexion illuminates all directions?”
Being questioned there, he too answered him with verses:
“Delighted, that son of the gods, being questioned by Vaṅgīsa,
Answered the question asked, [concerning] the fruit of which karma this is.”
“Among humans, having become a human, I was a lay follower of the One with Vision;
I abstained from taking life and avoided what was not given in the world.
I did not drink intoxicants, nor did I speak falsehoods; I was content with my own wife.”
"With a mind full of serene confidence, I gave a vast gift of food and drink with due respect.
Because of that, such is my complexion...
[as before] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions."
In this regard, there is nothing new; the remainder is exactly according to the method explained below.
The commentary on the second Nāga-vimāna is finished.
12. Commentary on the third Nāga-vimāna.
"Who indeed [traveled] by means of a divine vehicle?"—this is the third *Nāga-vimāna*. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
At that time, three elder monks whose taints were exhausted entered the rains retreat at a village monastery.
Having completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, they set out for Rājagaha with the intention of "paying homage to the Blessed One," while on the way between...

In the evening, having gone near a sugar-cane field belonging to a certain brahmin of wrong view in a certain village, they asked the sugar-cane guard, "Friend, is it possible to reach Rājagaha today?
He replied, "It is not possible, venerable sirs; Rājagaha is half a yojana from here.
Stay right here and go tomorrow. They asked, "Is there any dwelling suitable for staying here?"
“There is no [place], venerable sirs, but I shall know a place for you to dwell. The elders consented.
He, while the sugarcane remained exactly as it was, tied stakes together in the shape of a bower of branches, covered them with sugarcane leaves, spread straw underneath, and gave it to one elder;
to the second elder, he gave three stalks of sugarcane.
Having bound him with a bundle of sticks, covered him with grass, and spread a layer of straw underneath, he gave him [the shelter].
To the other, he brought out two or three sticks and branches from his own hut, and having constructed a robe-hut by concealing them with his robes, he gave it to him.
They dwelt there. Then, when the night had turned to dawn, at the very early hour, they took their meal.
Having cooked it, he gave them tooth-sticks and water for rinsing the mouth, and served the meal together with sugarcane juice.
After they had eaten and he had offered words of thanksgiving, as they were departing, he gave each of them a stalk of sugarcane, thinking, "This shall be my portion.
He followed the Elders for a short distance on the road, and as he was turning back, he reflected upon his own service and his act of giving, and felt a sublime...
Experiencing joy and gladness, he turned back.
Meanwhile, as the field-owner was coming along the path toward the departing monks, he asked them, "Where did you get these sugarcane stalks?
"They were given by the sugarcane guard," they replied. Upon hearing this, the brahmin became angry and displeased.
Overcome by rage, he rushed after him with a crashing sound and, striking him with a club, deprived him of life in a single blow.
As he was passing away, he recollected only the meritorious deeds he had performed himself and was reborn in the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods.
By the power of his merit, he was reborn as a great, divine, and excellent white elephant.

Upon hearing of Ucchupālaka’s death, his parents, kinsmen, and friends went to that place with tearful faces and weeping, and all the villagers gathered together. There, his parents began to perform the funeral rites for the body.
At that moment, that son of the gods, having mounted his celestial elephant and surrounded by all kinds of musical instruments, [arrived].
Accompanied by a great retinue and accompanied by the sounding of a vast five-fold musical ensemble, he came from the world of the gods with great divine splendor;
appearing visibly to that assembly, he stood in the air.
Then, a man of wise nature there questioned him regarding the meritorious deeds he had performed with these verses:
“Who indeed, on a divine vehicle, with an all-white elephant,
honored in the sky to the sound of musical instruments and cymbals—
is it you, a deity, or a gandhabba, or perhaps Sakka, the first-born lord?”
“Not knowing it, we ask you; how may we come to know it?
He explained this matter to him with these verses:
“I am neither a deva nor a gandhabba, nor am I Sakka Purindada;”
“I am one among those gods called the Sudhammas.
“Having joined our palms together in reverence, we ask the god Sudhamma:
‘By performing what kind of human deed does one arise in the Sudhamma realm?’”—thus he asked again.
“He who gives a cowshed, a grass-hut, or a cloth-hut—having given one of these three, he is reborn in Sudhammā. Thus he answered again.
Therein, “the sound of musical instruments being struck” refers to the sound of celestial five-piece musical ensembles being struck specifically for oneself.
"The sound of divine musical instruments being played resounds in the sky" means that standing in the sky, he is honored by a great retinue while remaining in the celestial realm itself.
"Are you perhaps a deity? means "Are you indeed a deity? What, are you a god? "A *gandhabba*" refers to a deity belonging to the *gandhabba* class.
The meaning is "were you? Is it that you are Sakka Purindada—meaning, are you the one renowned as "Purindada" because he gives in the city—or is it that you are Sakka, the king of the gods?

And here, although both Sakkas and Gandhabbas possess the status of devas, since they have been mentioned separately, the word *deva* should be understood as referring to other gods, according to the principle of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalibaddha-nyāya*).

978. Then the son of the gods, thinking that "an answer must correspond to the nature of the question," rejected their inquiries regarding his being a deva, a gandhabba, or Sakka, and identifying himself, he said, "I am neither a deva nor a gandhabba," and so forth. In this context, "I am not a deva" means:
I am not any deva whatsoever whom you might suspect; nor am I a gandhabba, nor Sakka; rather, [I am from] Sudhammā...
Among those gods, I am one; I am a deity named Sudhammā. There is a certain divine realm called the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
It is said that some say Ucchupāla, having heard of the prosperity of those gods, had already established his mind upon that realm long ago.
979. "Puthuṃ" means having made it great and complete; this was said for the purpose of illustrating thorough performance (*sakkacca-kiriyā*).

980. Questioned by the goddess Sudhammā, the young deva, like one speaking of the *kakaṇṭaka* bird while grasping only what was seen, declared his own performed merit by reciting the verse beginning with "ucchāgāraṃ.
Therein, [he refers to] one of the three [types of huts].
"Having given"—even if three houses were given by me, the meaning "by one of the three" is also established;
thus the son of the gods spoke in this way by grasping the underlying method (*nayaggāha*). The rest is easily understood.
Having thus questioned him and answered that matter, he, while proclaiming the virtues of the Triple Gem, [spoke] together with his mother and father.

Having exchanged greetings, he departed for the world of the gods. When the people heard the words of the son of the gods, they conceived great faith and reverence toward the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
they prepared many requisites for giving, filled their carts, and went to Veḷuvana.
There, having offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, they [reported] that news to the Teacher.

They reported this. The Teacher, having given his response by answering that very question, and having used that same incident as the occasion for a discourse, taught the Dhamma in detail and established them in the Refuges and the Precepts.
Having gained faith and paid homage to the Blessed One, they returned to their own village and had a monastery built on the spot where the sugarcane guard had died.
The commentary on the Third Nāga-Vimāna is finished.
13. Commentary on the Cūḷaratha-Vimāna:
"For one of firm virtue who is free from deceit..."—this is the Cūḷaratha-Vimāna. What is its origin? It arose after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.
When the distribution of the relics had been made and they were being enshrined in various stupas for the Teacher,

and when the disciples— headed by the Elder Mahākassapa— had been selected and gathered to recite the Dhamma, they remained in their respective locations together with their own retinues until the commencement of the rains retreat,
out of regard for those yet to be converted; meanwhile, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana was in a border region.
He was dwelling in a certain forest region. At that time, in the city of Potali in the kingdom of Assaka, King Assaka reigned;

his eldest queen’s son, a prince named Sujāta, sixteen years of age, had been exiled from the kingdom by his father due to the attachment of the younger queen. Having entered the forest, he lived among the forest-dwellers.

He lived in the forest depending [on that tree]. It is said that after going forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa and remaining established in mere virtue, he passed away as an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.

Having remained there for the full span of his lifespan and wandering successively through the happy realms, during this current appearance of a Buddha, thirty years after the Blessed One’s full enlightenment—
He was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Assaka and was named Sujāta.
He grew up with a great retinue.
However, when his mother passed away, the king appointed another princess to the position of chief queen. She too—

At a later time, she gave birth to a son. When the king saw his son, he was filled with joy and granted her a boon, saying, "Bhadde, take whatever boon you desire. She set it aside after accepting it.
Later, when Prince Sujāta reached the age of sixteen, she said to the king, "Your Majesty, when you saw my son and were pleased in heart, you granted me a boon."
“Give him that now! “Take it, O Queen. “Give the kingdom to my son! “Begone, you low-born woman!
While my eldest son, who resembles a young god and is of noble birth, stands here, why do you speak thus? She refused.
The queen, persisting again and again but failing to gain her way, said one day: “Your Majesty, if it be true...”

“Wait! Give it to her! The king, feeling remorseful at the thought, “I gave this boon to her without due consideration, yet she speaks thus,” summoned Prince Sujāta, informed him of the matter, and shed tears.
Seeing his father grieving, the prince was overcome with sorrow; shedding tears himself, he said, “Grant me leave, Your Majesty, for I—”
“I shall go elsewhere,” he said. Upon hearing this, the king replied, “I will have another city built for you;
