you may dwell there. But the prince did not wish for that. When the king further said, “I will send you into the presence of my friends, the kings,” he still did not grant permission.
He simply said, “Your Majesty, I shall go to the forest. The king embraced his son and kissed him on the head.
Having said, "Come here after my passing and establish yourself in the kingdom," he dismissed him.
He entered the forest and lived depending on the forest-dwellers;

one day, while out hunting, a certain son of the gods—who had been his best friend during his time as a recluse—ran toward him in the form of a deer, seeking to entice him for his own benefit. [He did so] before the Venerable Mahākaccāyana...
Having reached the vicinity of the Elder’s dwelling, he vanished. Thinking, "I shall catch this deer now," he ran after it;
but upon reaching the Elder’s dwelling and not seeing him, he saw the Elder sitting outside the leaf-hut.
Leaning the tip of his bow against him, he stood near him. The Elder looked at him and [recounted] everything from the beginning.
Knowing his conduct and desiring to favor him, yet acting as if he did not know, he offered him this greeting:
"Firmly holding your bow, you stand there like a reed;
are you a khattiya, a prince, or perhaps a hunter wandering in the forest?"
He asked. In that context, "daḷhadhamma" means a strong bow. A "strong bow" is said to have a strength of two thousand [units].

And "a strength of two thousand" refers to one whose string, when strung and fastened, releases from the ground a load of iron balls and so forth—weighed by holding the handle—as far as the length of an arrow. "Nisāra" means of unsurpassed essence, of distinguished essence.
"A bow of wood" means a bow made of a very strong kind of wood. "Olubbha" means having firmly grasped.
"Rājanna" means a prince. "Vanecara" means a forest-dweller.
Then, making himself known—
“I am the son of the Lord of Assaka, O Bhante, a forest-dweller;
I tell you my name, Bhikkhu: I am known as Sujāta.
While searching for deer, I entered this great forest.”
"I did not see that deer, but having seen it, I stood still," he said.
Therein, "of the lord of Assaka" means of the king of Assaka, the ruler of the Assaka country. "Monks" is how he addresses the Elder. "Searching for a deer" means seeking deer, boars, and so forth;
the sense is that he was out hunting. Having heard this, the Elder, exchanging greetings with him, said:
“Welcome to you, O one of great merit; indeed, you have come from afar.
Taking water from here, wash your feet.
This cool drinking water too has been brought from within the mountain caves.”
“Then, Prince, having drunk from it, sit down upon the prepared seat,” he said.
(984) Regarding this, “not ill-come” (*adurāgata*) means free from the fault of coming poorly. “O one of great merit, your arrival here is welcome;
there is not even the slightest ‘ill-coming’ on your part, for it produces joy and gladness for both you and me”—this is the intended meaning.
“*Adhunāgatan*” is also a reading, meaning “having just now arrived.
“He sat down upon the prepared [seat]” means: do not sit on the bare ground, but sit on such-and-such a grass mat.
Then the prince, accepting the elder’s hospitality, said:
“Truly auspicious is your speech, worthy of being heard, O Great Sage!
It is faultless, meaningful, and beautiful; you speak having considered the matter.
What is your delight while dwelling in the forest? Tell me, O bull among seers, when you are asked.”
“Having listened to the path of your words, may we practice the steps of the Dhamma that lead to the goal.
(986) In this context: *Kalyāṇī* means beautiful and lovely. *Savanīyā* means worthy of being heard. *Nela* means faultless.
*Atthavatī* means endowed with meaning, possessed of benefit pertaining to the present life and so forth. *Vaggū* means sweet. *Mantvā* means having understood through wisdom.
"Having discerned. "Meaningful" (*attha*) means not departing from the true purpose, bringing about exclusively what is beneficial.
(Verse 987) "A bull among sages" (*isinisabha*) means one who is like a well-bred bull among sages. "Path of speech" (*vacanapatha*) means speech.

For speech itself is called the "path of speech" because it serves as the means for the realization of meaning. "One should practice the path of the Dharma that leads to the goal" (*atthadhammapadaṃ samācarema se*): [the commentary continues:]...
"Let us practice those portions of the Dhamma beginning with virtue which bring benefit both in this world and in the life to come.
Now, the Elder, speaking of his own right practice as being appropriate for that [purpose], says:
"Non-violence toward all living beings—this is pleasing to us, O Prince."
“Abstention from theft, from transgressions, and from the drinking of intoxicants;
abstention, even conduct, great learning, and gratitude—
these qualities are praised and should be commended in this very life,” he said.
989. Therein, "abstinence and even conduct" refers to abstinence from the aforementioned evil states as well as the even conduct of bodily equanimity and so forth.
"Great learning" means great learning in the scriptures (*pariyatti*). "Gratitude" is the recognition of the assistance rendered to oneself by others.
"Praiseworthy" means worthy of being esteemed in various ways by sons of good family who desire their welfare. "These are the qualities" means these [qualities] belong to them.
The qualities such as non-violence and so forth, as previously described. "Praiseworthy" means they are to be praised by the wise.
Thus the Elder, having explained the appropriate right practice for him, surveyed the formations of his life-span with knowledge of the future;
seeing that it would last for only about five months, he stirred him to a sense of urgency and firmly established him in that right practice.
To establish him [in the Dhamma], he spoke this verse:
“Death is near for you, within five months;
O prince, understand this, and liberate yourself.”
Therein, "liberate yourself" means: free yourself from the suffering of the states of misery.
Then the prince, asking for the means to his own liberation, said:
"To which country shall I go, and what work or what human endeavor [must I undertake]?"
"Or perhaps through knowledge, I might become free from old age and death.

In this context, what is the meaning of *svāhaṃ*? It means "I indeed. What is the meaning of *nū*? It means "perhaps. What is the action (*kiṃ kammaṃ*) and what is the human effort (*kiñca porisaṃ*)? This is the implied remainder of the statement. "Human effort" (*porisaṃ*) refers to the duty of a man.
Then, in order to teach him the Dhamma, the Elder spoke these verses:
“O princes, there is no place found— neither by action, nor by knowledge,
nor by human effort— where a mortal, having gone, would become free from old age and death.
Even those Kṣatriyas who possess great wealth, vast enjoyments, and sovereign kingdoms [are not exempt].”
Though they possessed abundant wealth and grain, even they were not exempt from aging and death.
“If those sons of Andhakaveṇḍu whom you have heard of— those heroes, warriors who struck with great prowess—
even they reached the end of their lifespan, shattered, despite being regarded as eternal.”
“Khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas—
these and others by birth, even they are not exempt from old age and death.
Those who recite the mantra consisting of six limbs, as contemplated by Brahmā;”
These and others through their knowledge are likewise not subject to old age or death.
And those seers who are peaceful, self-restrained, and ascetic— even they,
the ascetics, eventually abandon their bodies in due time.
“Because they have developed themselves, the Arahants, having done what was to be done and being free from taints, lay down this body through the exhaustion of merit and demerit.

(992) In that context, “having gone where” means: having gone to whatever place, and having approached and reached [the goal] through physical exertion and other forms of exertion—both action and knowledge—one might become ageless and immortal; such is the meaning.
993. "Those who possess great wealth" (*mahaddhana*) are those who have accumulated and set aside a vast amount of riches, measuring hundreds of millions at the very least.
"Those who possess great fortune" (*mahābhoga*) are those whose assets consist of a great abundance of property, such as three jars [of gold] or the price of a *kahāpaṇa* coin.

"Possessing a kingdom" (*raṭṭhavanta*) means being the lords of a kingdom; the intended meaning is that they rule over a kingdom extending for many *yojanas*. "Kṣatriyas" (*khattiya*) refers to those belonging to the *kṣatriya* caste.
"Possessing abundant wealth and grain" means having great accumulations of wealth and grain;
"possessing enough wealth and grain for seven or eight years for their own retinues" means they too are subject to aging and death.
The meaning is that even great wealth and such cannot turn back the aging and death that falls upon them.
"994. *Andhakaveṇḍuputtā* means those known as the sons of Andhakaveṇḍu. *Sūrā* means possessed of spears. *Vīrā* means possessed of heroism.
*Vikkantappahārino* means those whose habit is to strike by overcoming and crushing the strength of their enemies precisely through their state of being brave heroes.
*Viddhastā* means ruined. *Sassatīsāmā* means together with the eternal [deities] such as the moon and the sun, who endure through the succession of generations."
"Of equal standing" (*samānā*): the meaning is that they too belong to clans whose lineages have existed for only a short time.
995. "By birth" (*jātiyā*): by one's own birth; the meaning is that even a more distinguished birth is unable to turn back their aging and death.

996. "Mantra" (*manta*): the Veda. "Six-limbed" (*chaḷaṅga*): [by means of] what are reckoned as the treatises on ritual procedure (*kalpa*), etymology (*vyākaraṇa*), grammar (*nirukti*), phonology (*śikṣā*), prosody (*chandas*), and astronomy (*jyotiḥ*).
It has six factors because it possesses six limbs. "Contemplated by the Brahmās" means contemplated by the Brahmās, such as Aṭṭhaka and others, and seen with the eye of wisdom.
"Peaceful" means those whose bodily and verbal actions are tranquilized. "Self-restrained" means those whose minds are restrained. "Austere" means those devoted to asceticism.
Now, the youth, speaking of what he himself must do—
“O Great Sage, your verses are well-spoken and full of meaning;
I am won over by their excellence, so please be my refuge,” he said.

In this context, *nijjhatto* means that I have been won over (*nijjhāpito*) by the perception of the essence of the Dhamma, having reached a state of being thoroughly convinced (*saññatti*). *Subhaṭṭhena* means by what is well-spoken (*suṭṭhu bhāsitena*).
Then the Elder, instructing him, spoke this verse:
"Do not go to me for refuge; go instead to that very refuge, To the Great Hero, the Son of the Sakyas, to whom I have gone for refuge."
Then the prince said:
"In which country, dear sir, is that Teacher of yours?
I too shall go to see the Jina, the peerless one."
Again the Elder said:
“In the eastern province, born of the Okkāka clan, there was a noble steed among men; he has indeed attained final Nibbāna.”
In this context, because the Middle Country lies to the eastern direction from the place where the Elder was seated, it is said: “in the eastern province.
Thus, having heard the Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma, that prince, with a mind full of confidence, established himself in the Refuges and the Precepts. Therefore it is said:
“If, dear sir, the Buddha were still living, he would be your Teacher.”
“I would travel thousands of yojanas to attend upon you.
“But since the Teacher has attained final nibbāna, O venerable sir,
I go for refuge even to the Great Hero who has attained nibbāna.”
“I go for refuge to the Buddha, and also to the unsurpassed Dhamma;
and to the Sangha of the God among Men, I go for refuge.
I shall quickly abstain from taking life, and I shall avoid what is not given in this world.”
“I do not drink intoxicants, nor do I speak falsehood; I am content with my own wife.
But when he was thus established in the refuges and the precepts, the Elder said to him:
“Prince, you have no need for dwelling here in the forest; your life will not last long; within five months, you will pass away.”
“You must do so; therefore, go to your father’s presence, perform meritorious deeds such as giving, and become one destined for heaven,” he said.
Having given him relics from his own possession, he dismissed him. As he was departing, [the prince] said:
“Venerable sir, I shall go from here according to your word; out of compassion for me, you too should come there.”
Having spoken thus, and perceiving the elder’s consent, he paid homage, circumambulated him, and went to his father’s city.
Entering the park, he informed the king of his arrival.
Upon hearing this, the king, accompanied by his retinue, went to the park, embraced the prince, and led him to the inner palace, desiring to consecrate him.
The prince said, "Your Majesty, my life is short; four months from now my death will come.
What use have I for kingship? Relying on you, I shall perform only meritorious deeds. Having spoken thus, he proclaimed the virtues of the Elder and the power of the Triple Gem.
Hearing this, the king was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and became filled with serene faith toward the Triple Gem and the Elder.
Having had a great monastery built, he sent a messenger to the presence of the Elder Mahākaccāyana.
The Elder also came, out of compassion for the king and the great multitude. The king, together with his retinue, went out from afar to meet him;
having ushered the Elder into the monastery, he attended upon him with the four requisites with great care, and [established him] in the Refuges and the Precepts.

And he was established [in the Dhamma]. Having undertaken the precepts and diligently attending upon the Elder and the monks, making offerings and listening to the Dhamma, the prince passed away at the end of four months and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
By the power of his merit, a chariot seven yojanas in measure, adorned with the seven precious gems, appeared for him.
He had a retinue of many thousands of celestial nymphs.
After the king had performed the funeral honors for the prince’s body and offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks, he made offerings at the stupa;
there a great multitude gathered, and the Elder also went to that place together with his followers.
Then the young god, reflecting upon the wholesome kamma he had performed, thought with gratitude: "I shall go and pay homage to the Elder, and I will make the virtues of the Dispensation manifest.
Having thought thus, he mounted his celestial chariot and approached with a great retinue, his form visible to all.
Alighting from the chariot, he paid homage at the feet of the Elder and, having exchanged greetings with his father, [addressed] the Elder.
As he stood there paying homage with palms joined, the Elder questioned him with these verses:
“Like the thousand-rayed sun of great splendor, shining through the sky in its successive course,
such is this appearance of yours, O Great Charioteer, extending for seven yojanas in every direction.”
“Covered all around with golden bands, its breast variegated with pearls and gems;
lines of gold and silver shine forth, well-fashioned from beryl.
This head is fashioned of beryl, and this yoke is variegated with red gems.”
“Yoked with gold and silver, these horses, swift as thought, are resplendent.
You stand there, established upon a golden chariot, like the Lord of the Devas with his thousand steeds.
I ask you, O illustrious one, skilled in all things: how was this magnificent [chariot] obtained by you?”
1007. In this context, "the thousand-rayed one" refers to the sun.
For he is called "the thousand-rayed one" because he possesses many thousands of rays. "According to his great splendor" means possessing a radiance befitting his own greatness.
Just as there is no circle of light equal to the sun’s disk in terms of its magnitude, so too is it with its radiance. For in a single moment, it [illuminates] the three great continents.
"He stands radiating light" means: just as it shines toward a direction in the sky, moving through the sky and space;
just as it moves and proceeds while shining, gleaming, and glowing—so too is its manner, that is, its such-like form.
"This is yours" means: this belongs to you.
"1008. With golden bands (suvaṇṇapaṭṭehi) means with bands made of gold. 'Covered all around' (samantamotthaṭo) means covered on every side.
'Of the chest' (urassāti) refers to its chest; it also refers to the base of the pole of the chariot. 'Inlaid designs' (lekhāti) refers to designs such as floral wreaths and creepers made of beryl.
Because these were visible upon both the golden bands and the silver bands, it is said: 'of gold and silver'..."
"And they beautify" means they adorn the chariot.
"The crest" refers to the top of the chariot's pole. "Fashioned from beryl" means made of beryl; the sense is that it is composed of beryl gems.
"Red" means by a red gem, or by any kind of red gem. "Yoked" means harnessed. Now...
"Or cords of gold and silver" means cords made of gold and cords made of silver; the meaning is "chains.
(1010) "Established" means standing having overcome this entire place by means of his own divine majesty. "Having a thousand vehicles" means having a vehicle yoked with a thousand [horses];
the intention is that he is like Devānaminda (the Lord of the Gods) with a chariot yoked with a thousand thoroughbreds. "Possessing glory..."
"Ālapanaṃ" means "renowned. "Kovidaṃ" means one possessed of skillful knowledge, or one expert in mounting a chariot.
"Ayaṃ uḷāro" means this great fame; such is the intended meaning.
Thus questioned by the Elder, the son of the gods replied with these verses:
“Venerable sir, formerly I was a prince named Sujāta;
out of compassion for me, you established me in self-restraint.
Knowing that my life span was exhausted, you gave my body to the Teacher.”
“Worship this well-born one; it will be for your benefit.
Having diligently worshipped him with perfumes and garlands, I have abandoned my human body and been reborn in the Nandana grove.
“In the delightful Nandana grove, filled with flocks of various birds, I delight in dancing and singing, honored by the apsarases.

(1012–3) In this context, *sarīranti* means the constituent elements of the body (*sarīradhātu*). *Hehiti* means it will come to be. *Samuyyuto* means thoroughly exerted; the meaning is one who is properly and diligently engaged.

Thus the young god, having explained the matter asked by the Elder, paid homage to the Elder, circumambulated him, took leave of his father, mounted his chariot, and departed for the world of the gods.
The Elder, taking that event as the occasion for instruction, delivered a detailed discourse on the Dhamma to the assembled multitude. That discourse [was beneficial] to the great multitude.

It was purposeful. Then, at the time of the Council, the Elder reported all of that to the compilers of the Dhamma exactly according to the sequence spoken by himself and by him; and they recorded it accordingly.
The commentary on the Cūḷarathavimāna is finished.

14. Description of the Mahāratha Vimāna The Mahāratha Vimāna is beautiful, with a horse-drawn chariot yoked to a thousand [beings]. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, in the manner described below, was on a tour of the deva realms.
While he was wandering in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, he appeared not far from a son of the gods named Gopāla, who had emerged from his own palace,
mounted a great divine chariot yoked with a thousand [horses], and was proceeding with a vast retinue and great divine splendor for the purpose of a pleasure excursion to the park.
Upon seeing him, the son of the gods conceived feelings of reverence and deep respect.
Quickly alighting from his chariot, he approached, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and stood with his hands joined in reverence over his head.
This was his former deed: it is said that after he had honored the Blessed One Vipassī with a golden garland, he made this aspiration:
"By the power of this merit, may a golden breastplate-garland manifest for me in birth after birth."
Having wandered through many eons solely in happy realms, she was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa as the daughter of King Kiki of Kāsī, the chief queen’s womb-born child.
Having obtained a golden garland in accordance with her aspiration, she was given the name “Uracchadamālā” (The Chest-Garland).
Resembling a celestial maiden, while she was [a princess], he became a brahmin teacher named Gopāla and [served] the Buddha together with his community of disciples.
Having performed great acts of giving, such as the peerless gifts for the Blessed One Kassapa, yet being unable to produce any spiritual distinction because his faculties were not yet mature—
even though he had heard the Dhamma taught by the Teacher concerning himself and the princess—
he passed away as a worldling (puthujjana). By the power of the merit thus accumulated, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas at a distance of one hundred yojanas.
He was reborn in a golden celestial mansion, accompanied by a retinue of many tens of millions of nymphs. For him, a divine chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses appeared;
it was composed of the seven precious gems, yoked to a thousand steeds, with its walls beautifully divided and variegated, and emitting a smooth and sweet sound.
By the mass of its own radiance, it seemed to mock the orb of the sun.

Thus, having experienced divine prosperity there for the duration of his lifespan and wandering from one celestial realm to another among the gods, in this present arising of a Buddha, by the remaining ripening of that very same karma, he was reborn as a son of the gods named Gopāla within the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, possessing the wealth and glory of the aforementioned prosperity. It is with reference to him that it was said: "And at that time..."
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna... [as before] ...stood with his hands joined in reverence at his head.
Having thus approached and stood there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned that son of the gods with these verses:
“Mounted upon this beautiful chariot yoked with a thousand horses, which possesses many colors;”
He proceeded step by step toward the park grounds, like Vāsava, the lord of beings and first-giver.
“Both the golden hubs of your chariot are perfectly joined with the felloes;
fashioned by a hero among men, they shine like the moon on the fifteenth day, its clusters of blossoms well-formed.”
“This chariot is covered with a golden net and adorned with many various jewels;
it possesses a beautiful sound and a lovely resonance, and it shines with arms holding chowries.
And these wheels, fashioned by the mind, are beautifully ornamented between the feet of the chariot.”
And these naves, adorned with a hundred royal lines, are radiant like shimmering lightning.
This chariot has many-colored seats, and its broad felloes possess a thousand spokes;
the sound of them is heard like a sweet melody, resonating like a five-fold musical ensemble.
“In my head, the mind is fashioned like a jeweled moon—ever pure, beautiful, and radiant;
exceedingly well-composed with streaks of gold, it shines intensely like a row of beryl.
And these horses, adorned with jeweled moons, swift and noble as the best of elephants, are many in number.”
"Great, powerful, and of great speed, they turn back exactly as they know your mind.
And all these together in groups of four, knowing your mind, turn back exactly as you intend;
they carry you evenly, gently, and without pride—these supreme steeds who are full of joy."
“They shake, they brandish, they fall in the air, tossing up their well-fashioned ornaments;
the sound of their arrows is heard like a clamor, like the sounding of a fivefold musical ensemble.
The rattle of the chariot and the clatter of the ornaments, the roar of the hooves, and the noise of the assault—”
The lovely sound of the Samita is heard, like the music of Gandhabbas in a wondrous grove:
"There stand upon chariots those with eyes like a deer's, with broad, long-lashed eyes, smiling and sweet-spoken;
their skin is fine, draped in nets of beryl, and they are worshipped by gods, Gandhabbas, and the foremost of heroes."
“Clad in garments of deep red and yellow, with wide eyes and lovely glances;
well-born in noble families, slender-limbed and of pure conduct, they stood upon the chariot with palms joined in reverence.
Wearing shell necklaces and armlets, beautifully dressed, they were of moderate build, endowed with shapely thighs.”
"With rounded fingers, beautiful faces, and lovely to behold, they stand upon the chariot, waiting with palms joined in reverence.
Others have well-braided hair, with locks beautifully interwoven, evenly parted and radiant;
devoted to you and delighted in your mind, they stand upon the chariot, waiting with palms joined in reverence."
“Adorned with garlands, shaded by lotuses and water-lilies, decorated and scented with the essence of sandalwood, they follow you, delighting in your mind;
standing upon the chariot, they wait upon you with palms joined in reverence.
Adorned with garlands, shaded by lotuses and water-lilies, decorated and scented with the essence of sandalwood—”
Attentive and devoted to your mind, they stood upon the chariot with palms joined in reverence.
“The ornaments upon your necks, as well as those on your hands, feet, and head,
illuminate all ten directions in every way, like the autumnal sun risen from the clouds.”
“Shaken by the force of the wind, the garlands and ornaments on their arms released a sound that was lovely,
pure, and beautiful, a form fit to be heard by all who are wise.
And from the park grounds, standing at a distance, came the sound of chariots, elephants, and musical instruments.”
They delight the Lord of Devas with their lutes,
as if with lotus-leaf arms. Amidst these many lutes, melodious and pleasing to the heart,
as the Apsarases play them exceedingly well, those skilled maidens whirl about like lotuses.
“When songs and instrumental music, and these dances, come together as one;
then there they dance, and there the celestial nymphs, those women of exquisite form, illuminate both sides.
Thus you rejoice, awakened by the ensemble of musical instruments, being honored like Vajirāvudha himself.”
“Among these many lutes, sweet-toned and pleasing to the heart, they produce a joy stirred within the mind.
What deed did you perform for yourself in the past, when you were a human being in a former birth?
Which Uposatha did you observe, or what practice of the Dhamma and vow did you delight in?”
“This is not the result of a small deed performed, nor of merit previously well-accrued through the observance of the Uposatha;
this vast power and majesty of yours, by which you shine so intensely upon the host of gods—
this is the fruit of your giving, or else of your virtue.”
“And also regarding the act of joining the palms in reverence—explain that to me when asked.
(1015) In this context, *sahassayuttaṃ* means “yoked with a thousand,” or “that to which a thousand is yoked or joined”; thus it is *sahassayuttaṃ*. To what does this “thousand” belong?
It belongs to “horses,” because of the phrase “having horses as its vehicle” (*hayavāhanaṃ*) which is stated immediately thereafter.
This meaning is indeed understood. *Hayavāhanaṃ* means "that which has horses as its vehicle.

Some, however, explain it by treating *sahassayuttahayavāhanaṃ* as a single compound word with the elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*), stating that in this alternative, the sense "a vehicle like a horse-vehicle" is appropriate.
For the meaning is: "yoked to a thousand horse-vehicles," that is, "a thousand yoked horse-vehicles."
Others, however, say: "Yoked with a thousand" means "yoked with a thousand divine, noble steeds. "Chariot" (*sandana*) means a chariot.
"Possessing manifold thoughts" (*nekacitta*) means having many kinds of diverse thoughts. "Near the park grounds" (*uyyānabhūmiṃ abhito*):
this accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*), depending on the word *abhito*. Some, however, read it as "uyyānabhūmiyā" (in the locative).
They recite [this], yet they recite it without even considering the method of grammar (*saddanaya*).
The connection is: "As Purindada, Bhūtapati, and Vāsava advance and go, you shine forth.
(1016) *Sovaṇṇamayā* means "made of gold. *Teti* means "your. *Rathakubbarā ubho* means "on both sides of the chariot."
The *vedikā*. That specific part of a chariot which is constructed as a railing on both sides for the sake of its beauty and for the protection of those seated above,
extending from the front part of the chariot to the two side-poles (*rathīsā*) and being graspable by the hands—
this very thing is intended here by the term *kubbara*.
For this very reason it says, “both. In other contexts, however, the term *rathīsā* refers to the felloes.
By “wheels” (*phalehi*) is meant the two wheels, distinguished as right and left, belonging to the chariot’s axle-tree; here they are called “wheels” because they form the boundary.
By “shoulders” (*aṃsehi*) is meant the lower shoulders that rest upon the felloes. “Extremely well-fitted” means exceedingly well-joined, well-adjusted, and without gaps.
And this was stated by attributing to it a specific quality found in the case of a monument fashioned by a craftsman.

However, that [monument] is beyond comparison because it is not fashioned by anyone; it is self-arisen and unconstructed. "Well-formed clusters" (*sujātagumbā*) refers to collections of pillars that are well-proportioned.
For those collections of pillars which stand continuously along the railing, possessing specific well-formed parts such as capitals and so forth—
It is on account of them that it is said, “clusters of well-grown [trees]. “Completed by heroes among men” means they are like those finished by masters of crafts.
For masters of crafts, disregarding the exhaustion of their own bodies, thoroughly investigate the craft through the power of their vigor;
thus, because they possess vigor among men, they are here called “heroes among men” (*naravīra*). Alternatively, “heroes among men” is an address to the son of a god.
“Completed” means finished, possessing an excellence of perfect beauty. Alternatively, there is the reading “naravīranimmitā,” which means fashioned by men endowed with fortitude among men.
Because of such craftsmanship, this chariot of yours shines forth.
Like what? Like the moon on the fifteenth day; like the moon when it is full during the bright fortnight on the fifteenth day.
1017. *Suvaṇṇajālāvatata* means covered or overspread with golden nets. There is also a reading, *suvaṇṇajālāvitata*, which has the same meaning:
"interlaced. *Bahūhi* means by many. *Nānāratanehi* means by various kinds of jewels, such as ruby (*padumarāga*) and topaz (*phussarāga*).
*Sunandighosa* means a sound that is truly delightful to hear; the meaning is a sweet and melodious resonance. *Sunandighosa*.
"Or 'well-made joyful sound' (suṭṭhu-kata-nandi-ghoso)" means a cry of delight produced by such things as seeing dancing and so forth, or sounds such as cries of "well done!
uttered during those activities; they also say it means "a well-employed joyful sound consisting of blessings from time to time.
"Of beautiful luster" (subhassaro) means having a nature that shines very brightly, or [it refers to] those qualities occurring therein...
*Subhassara*: possessing a beautiful voice due to the lovely sound of the singing and instrumental music of the deities. *Cāmarahatthabāhubhi*:
by means of the arms of the deities joined with chowries in their hands—that is, by the arms of the deities fanning [him] here and there with bundles of chowries;
or [it means] he shines because of such deities. *1018. Nābhiyo*: the hubs of the chariot wheels. *Manasābhinimmitā*: "created by mind" means [fashioned] by the thought, "May these be like this."

"Resembling a creation. "Adorned with the intervals between the spokes of the chariot" means it was decorated by the rims (*nemi*)—which shine with various jewels—of the wheels of the chariot, as well as by the middle of the spokes (*ara*).

"Variegated with a hundred royal stripes" means it has attained a state of diversity, being variegated with many hundreds of lines and streaks of manifold colors. "Radiant like lightning" refers to the lightning known as *sateratā*.
They shine forth, radiant as if [with light]. 1019. *Anekacittāvatato* means covered and strewn with many designs such as those for garlands and the like.
They also read it as *anekacittāvitato*, which has the same meaning; however, the lengthening of the vowel is for the sake of the meter (*gāthāsukha*). *Puthū ca nemī ca* means having broad rims.
And, the single *ca*-kāra is merely a particle. “*Sahassaraṃsiko*” means possessing many thousands of rays.
There is also a textual reading (*pāḷi*) as “*sahassaraṃsiyo*. Others, however, read it as “*natā raṃsiyo*”;
therein, “*natā*” refers to the rim-regions being bent down like the staff of the Ajiya bow. “*Sahassaraṃsiyo*” means having a mass of radiating rays like the solar disk. Of them...
Of the regions of the rims [of the wheels] which have networks of hanging tinkling bells.
1020. "On the head" means on the top; the meaning is "on the head of the chariot. Or, "the head" (sira) is that which is in this chariot.
"Variegated" (citta) means diverse. "Adorned with jeweled circles" means pierced by jeweled discs, [specifically] pierced by a jewel resembling the lunar disc.
By the phrase "beautiful and radiant," he clarifies that it resembles the lunar disc;
by the phrase "always pure," however, he shows its distinction even from the lunar disc.
"With golden streaks" means with lines of gold arranged in a circular pattern here and there. "Joined together" means contiguous. "With beryl streaks" refers to those between the golden streaks.
It shines like rows of beryl because it is inlaid with circles of gems. They also read "veḷuriyarājīhi" (by rows of beryl). 1021.
"Vāḷī" means possessing tails, those endowed with fine tails; he says this referring to horses. Or the reading is "vājī.
"Maṇicandakappitā" means threaded with gem-studded crescents at the places where yak-tail whisks are suspended. "Ārohakambū" means tall.
"And likewise with a corresponding circumference" means they are endowed with both height and girth. "With beautiful speed" means having lovely speed, possessing speed, or great speed;
the meaning is that their gait is beautiful. "Measurable like giants" means they should be measured as if they were giants;
the meaning is that they appear as if exceeding their own [actual] proportions. "Giants" (*brahā*) means grown, with all limbs and members fully developed. "Great" (*mahantā*)...

"Of great majesty" means of great psychic power (*mahiddhika*). "Powerful" means strong both by virtue of physical strength and by virtue of the strength of effort. "Of great speed" means possessing swift velocity.
"Having known your mind" means having understood your consciousness (*citta*). "In that very way" means exactly according to the mind.
"He wanders" (*siṃsare*) means he moves about; the sense is that he proceeds.
1022. This is said with reference to the horses just described. "All" means even as many as a thousand.

"In harmony" (*sahitā*) means they are united in their movement by virtue of having equal speed and equal gait; the meaning is that their progress is neither deficient nor excessive relative to one another. "Moving on four feet" (*catukkamā*) means they walk or go upon four legs. "Carrying evenly" clarifies the same meaning already expressed by the word "in harmony."
It acts. "Gentle" means having a gentle nature; the sense is that they are noble thoroughbreds. Therefore he said "unagitated," meaning free from agitation and not causing disturbance.
"Rejoicing" means being delighted; the sense is that, because they are not unbroken (wild), they proclaim their mutual satisfaction as well as that of the charioteers and others.
They "shake" (dhunanti) means they shake their bundles of chowries, their manes, or their tails.
They "gallop" (vagganti) means that sometimes, placing one foot after another, they go with a galloping gait. They "fall" (patanti) means they move forward;
the meaning is that they leap. Some read "plavanti," which has the same meaning. "They toss upward" (abbhuddhunanti) refers to those skilled in the craft of horsemanship.
"Excellently made" means well-constructed; "small bells and other horse ornaments" refers to those [ornaments] shaking and shaking excessively.
"Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to those ornaments.

Regarding the phrase "the sound of the chariot" (*rathassa ghoso*), it is the aforementioned roar of the chariot. In the expression "and of the ornaments" (*apiḷandhanāna ca*), the syllable *a-* is merely a particle (*nipātamattaṃ*).
"Of ornaments" means of jewelry. Some say that "not an ornament" (*apiḷandhana*) is a synonym for jewelry; thus the meaning is "the sound of the chariot's ornaments.
"The noise of the hooves" is the sound produced by the striking of the horses' hooves.
Although the horses travel through the air, it is due to the karma that serves as the cause for perceiving the sweet sound of the striking of their hooves.
They say that with every placement of their hooves, a rebounding echo is obtained.
And "by means of excessive violence" (*abhihiṃsanāya*) means by the excessive harming of the horses, and by the neighing produced by the horses from time to time;
some read it as "by means of excessive neighing" (*abhihesanāya*). And the sound of the assembled host of celestial beings is lovely and very sweet.
It is being heard. To the question "What is it like?", he says: "Like the musical instruments of the Gandhabbas in the Vicitrasaṃvana grove.

This means it is like the fivefold musical ensembles of the Gandhabba devaputtas in the Vicitralatāvana grove. For the sound dependent upon musical instruments is called "musical instruments" by way of metonymy (*nissayavohāra*).
There is also the reading "gandhabbatūriyānañca vicitrasaṃvane," where the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) has been added to "tūriyānañca."
It should be joined [to the previous verse]. Others read: "The musical instruments of the gandhabbas in the variegated grove.
(1025) "Standing on chariots" means these women are standing upon chariots. "With eyes like those of a deer" means their glances are soft, smooth, and moist like those of a female deer.
"With broad eyelashes" means having thick and closely set lashes; the meaning is "cow-lashed" (*gopakhuma*). "Laughing" means laughing aloud; "with smiling faces."
The meaning is as follows: *piyavadā* means those who speak kindly. *Veḷuriyajālāvatatā* means whose bodies are covered by a net made of beryl gems.
*Tanucchavā* means having delicate skin. *Sadevā* means always, indeed, at all times.
*Gandhabbasūraggapūjitā* means honored by the gandhabba deities and other supreme deities.
1026. "Clad in garments of deep red and yellow" means they possess forms that are lovely to behold and are dressed in red and yellow clothes.

"With eyes full of passion" means their eyes are especially adorned with red streaks. "Well-born in a noble family" means well-born in the Sindhu lineage, having originated from a distinguished class of deities.
"Slender-limbed" means possessing a beautiful body. "Purely smiling" means having a pure, bright countenance.
1027. "Wearing shell-bracelets" means wearing golden armlets. "Well-proportioned" means having a slender waist. "Endowed with thighs and breasts" means possessing excellent thighs and breasts;
that is, thighs like the trunk of a plantain tree and breasts like a casket. "Round-fingered" means fingers that are rounded from top to bottom.
"Fair-faced" means having a beautiful face or a joyful countenance. "Pleasant to behold" means lovely to look upon.
1028. *Aññā* means certain others. *Suveṇī* means those with beautiful braided hair. *Susū* means young girls.
*Missakesīyo* means rows of hair interspersed with red garlands and the like. How so?

"Evenly distributed and radiant"—that is, evenly distributed in a manner similar to one another through various arrangements, and radiant like sapphire gems and the like, being inlaid with gold, cloth, and other materials.
The construction is: "one whose hair is mixed with locks of hair like those of Keśava. *Anubbatā* means compliant action. *Tā* refers to the nymphs (*accharā*). 1029.
*Candanasāravositā* means smeared and sprinkled with divine sandalwood that is of the essence (*sāra*). 1031.
By the words beginning with *kaṇṭhesu*, he shows the ornaments for the neck, the hands, the feet, the head, and so forth. *Obhāsayanti* means illuminating.
The construction is: "They illuminate with those ornaments which are worn upon their necks. The same applies to the remaining [verses]. "Abbhuddayanti" means rising up;
there is also a reading "abbhuddasaṃ," which has the same meaning. "Sāradiko" means pertaining to the autumn season. "Bhānumā" refers to the sun;
for he, being free from defects such as clouds and the like, thoroughly illuminates the ten directions.
1032. "By the force of the wind" means by the blowing of the wind as if it were offering and presenting a pleasing gift of fragrance and a gift of sound.
"And by the speed of the chariot-horses. "They release" means they let go.
"Delightful" (rucira) means, like the fivefold musical instruments, that which bestows delight one after another. "Pure" (suci) means clean and unmixed. "Beautiful" (subha).

"Charming. The construction is as follows: "It emits a sound of supreme nature, which is fit to be heard by all wise ones"—that is, it is to be heard (*savaniya*) and worthy of being listened to by all those of the class of the wise who are conversant with the conventions of the Gandhabbas. 1033.
"In the park grounds" means in the park grounds. "From both sides" means from two half-sides. "And from both... [text fragment]
They also read “ṭhitā,” which has the same meaning. *Rathe* means “in the chariot. *Nāge* means “in the elephant.

This is a nominative plural used in the sense of the accusative. *Sara* refers to the sound produced in dependence upon the chariots, elephants, and musical instruments. *Devinda* is an address to a son of the gods (*devaputta*).
*Vīṇā yathā pokkharapattabāhubhī* means just as a lute [resounds] when its sounding-board, skin, and arm-sticks are properly joined together.
Just as a lute, played by the hands of a lute-player who have attained a state of excellence and beauty through thorough training,
delights the people who hear it when it is sounded with strings tuned according to their respective notes,
so too do those chariots and other vehicles delight [beings] with their own sounds. Just as that lute delights the great multitude, so too do those chariots and others.
"Delighting with her own voice.
(1034) The summary meaning of this verse beginning with "Among these lutes" is as follows:

Among these many lutes—distinguished by types such as the *ujukoṭi*, *vaṅka*, *brahatī*, *nandinī*, and *tisara*—which are warbling due to their smooth and sweet tone, and are therefore of pleasing form, [the sound] stirred the heart.
As the celestial nymphs, the daughters of the gods, sang songs that were heart-stirring and captivating, inducing rapture and the signs of joy,
they wandered about, dancing and displaying their well-trained skills, tossed by the force of their rapture upon divine lotuses.
1035. “These” (imāni) should be applied to each respectively: “these songs, these instrumental performances, and these dances.
“They harmonize as one” (samenti ekato) means they become of a single flavor (ekarasa) together. Alternatively, “they harmonize as one” means they make them equal and of a single flavor together;
that is, the sound of the strings merges with the sound of the song, and the sound of the song merges with the sound of the strings.
The meaning is that by means of dancing, they do not allow the flavors of laughter and so forth—already attained—to decline; they "unite" and "bring together.

Here, "they dance" means that the *accharās* (nymphs) illuminate [the scene]; thus, while making the songs and other arts harmonious, some other *accharās* here, on this chariot of yours, dance; and then other excellent women, the most sublime of women.

The meaning is that those watching the dance, by means of the radiance of their own bodies as well as the radiance of their garments and ornaments, illuminate and flash forth light throughout the ten directions on both sides—on this very spot. (1036) *So* means you, being such as described.

*Tūriyagaṇappabodhano* means one awakened by the joy produced by a multitude of celestial musical instruments. *Mahīyamāno* means being honored. *Vajirāvudhoriva* means like Indra, who possesses the thunderbolt as his weapon.
1037. "Whose *uposatha* do you observe?"—he asks this because the *uposatha* is observed by others as well;
he asks, "Whose, or of what kind, is the *uposatha* that you observe? "Dhammacariya" means the practice of merit such as giving and so forth.
"Vata" means the undertaking of a vow. "Abhirocayī" means he delighted in it; the sense is that, having taken pleasure in it, he fulfilled it. It is also read as "abhirādhayī."
*Pāṭho* means he accomplished or brought to completion.
*Idaṃ* is a mere particle, or its intended meaning is "this fruit. *Abhirocasi* means you shine forth having overcome [all things].
Thus, being questioned by the Great Elder, the son of the gods explained that matter. Therefore it was said:
“Thus the son of the gods, being asked by Moggallāna, was delighted;
having been questioned, he explained the answer as to which karma this is the fruit.
“The Buddha who has conquered the senses, whose mind is free from conceit, the supreme among men, Kassapa, the foremost person—”
I saw him opening the door to the Deathless, the God beyond gods, who possesses the marks of a hundred merits.
I saw that elephant who has crossed over the flood, resembling gold, emerald, the *nada* reed, and the *bimba* fruit.
Having seen him, my mind immediately became pure; having seen him, whose banner is well-spoken truth.
“Whether it was food and drink, or even a robe, pure, excellent, and endowed with delicious flavors—
I established that in my own dwelling strewn with flowers,
with a mind free from attachment. With that food and drink, and with robes, hard food, soft food, and refreshments;”
Having satisfied the Supreme among Bipeds, I rejoice in the city of the gods in heaven.
“By this means, having performed this unbarred sacrifice— threefold and pure—
I cast off this human body and, like the Moon, I rejoice in the city of the gods.”
“Desiring longer life, beauty, happiness, strength, and a more sublime form, O Sage,
one with a mind free from attachment should provide abundant, well-prepared food and drink.
Neither in this world nor in the next is there found anyone equal to or superior to the Buddha.”
"He has reached the supreme offering among those worthy of offerings, for those seeking merit who desire abundant fruit.

(1041) Therein, "one with conquered faculties" (*jitindriya*) means that because the six faculties, including the mind, were conquered by the supreme path right at the foot of the Bodhi tree, and because the state of being free from defilement was achieved, he is one with conquered faculties.
Because things such as the knowable have been known in their entirety, without remainder, [he is so called].

"Buddha" because of his perfect awakening. "Of sublime stride" means through the fulfillment of energy that is perfectly complete, namely, the energy endowed with four factors and the fourfold right exertion (*samyakprahāṇa*).
"Supreme among men" means the highest among humans, the supreme among bipeds. "Kassapa" he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name. "Opening up the deathless..."

"The gate" refers to the Noble Path, which opens the door to the great city of Nibbāna that has been closed since the disappearance of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana’s teaching. "God beyond gods" means the supreme god among all gods.
"One possessing the marks of a hundred merits" refers to the marks of a Great Man produced by means of many hundreds of merits.
1042. "Like an elephant" means like an elephant because of his crushing of the enemies that are the defilements; the meaning is "a great tusker.

"One who has crossed the flood" means he has crossed over the great flood of saṃsāra consisting of the four floods. "Resembling gold, *siṅgī* gold, and *jambunada* gold" means resembling the form of *siṅgī* gold, *suvaṇṇa* gold, and *jambunada* gold;
the meaning is "one whose skin is like refined gold. "Having seen him, I quickly became pure-minded"—that is, having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa.

Upon seeing him, at that very moment, through the influence of serene confidence (*pasāda*) toward the Blessed One as the "Perfectly Enlightened One," my mind became pure and purified by the removal of the stains of defilement;
and this occurred precisely upon seeing him, as soon as I saw him. "The banner of well-spoken words" refers to the banner of the Dhamma.
"Food and drink for him" means food and drink for that Blessed One. Alternatively, "or even a robe" (*cīvara*) means a robe as well.
“Endowed with flavor” means possessed of taste, having a sweet flavor; the meaning is “excellent.
“Strewn with flowers” means strewn by way of hanging down and spreading out with both woven and unwoven flowers. “I placed” means I set down or gave.
“With an unattached mind” should be construed as: he was one whose mind was not clinging to anything whatsoever.
1044. “In every heaven” means in each successive heaven through rebirth after rebirth; and there too, in the great city of Sudassana, the city of the gods. “I delight” means I play and rejoice. 1045.
“By this method” means by the same method as when, during my time as the brahmin Gopāla, I gave an incomparable gift to the Blessed One Kassapa together with his community of disciples.
“Having performed this ‘boltless’ sacrifice, [my merit] is purified in three ways” means by virtue of having left the gates unbarred.
Having performed a sacrifice— a *yañña* that is "unobstructed" because it is free from the shedding of blood, and "threefold" because it is perfected through the three times,
the three doors, and the three modes of performance, namely doing, causing to be done, and recollecting— and which is "pure" therein due to the absence of defilement,

and "greatly unobstructed" (*mahācāgatā*) by virtue of the relinquishing of immeasurable wealth— having thus performed the sacrifice and given the great gift; and furthermore, even though that gift was given long ago...
Because of the excellence of his fields, lands, and mind, by recollecting them from time to time, he took that which was manifest to himself,
present, and as if directly perceived, and said, "This. (1046) Thus the deva-son, having told the Elder the deed he had performed, [now spoke] regarding such an attainment.
Desiring to establish others [in this faith] as well, and proclaiming his own supreme confidence and great respect for the Tathāgata, he spoke these two verses beginning with “Long life and beauty.
Therein, *abhikaṅkhatā* means “by one who desires. *Munī* is an address to the Elder.
Regarding the phrase “not in this world,” the son of the gods speaks of the world as it is directly perceived by himself; *parasmim* [means “in the other world”].
"Then another. By this, he shows [him to be superior] to everyone in the world including the devas.
"An equal is not found"—let alone a superior, the meaning is that even an equal is not found.

"He has gone to the supreme offering among those worthy of offerings": whatever are called "worthy of offerings" in this world, among all of them, he has reached the supreme offering, the state of being supremely worthy of offerings. "Among those worthy of gifts..."
Or there is the reading “paramaggataṃ gato”; therein, “paramaggaṃ” means the supreme state of being the foremost, that is to say, the state of being the most worthy of offerings.
To the question “Of whom? he says: “Of those seeking merit who desire abundant fruit.
This shows that the Tathāgata alone is the field of merit for the world, for those who need merit and who seek the vast and great fruit of merit.
Some, however, read: "He has reached the supreme state among those worthy of offerings," which conveys the same meaning.
While he was speaking thus, the Elder, perceiving that his mind was ready, pliant, free from hindrances, uplifted, and serene, proclaimed the Truths to him.
At the conclusion of the Truths, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Then the Elder, having returned to the world of men, reported that matter to the Blessed One exactly according to what had been told by himself and the son of the gods.
The Teacher, taking that matter as the occasion for instruction, taught the Dhamma appropriate to the assembly.
That teaching was of great benefit to the multitude.
The commentary on the Mahāratha Vimāna is finished.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Mahāratha Vagga, adorned with fourteen stories, within the *Vimānavatthu* of the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.
The commentary on the meaning is finished.
6. The Chapter on Pāyāsi. 1.
Commentary on the First Mansion of the Householder.
Just as the forest shines with its variegated creepers, so it is with the Householder’s Mansion (*Agāriya-vimāna*). What is its origin?

The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove (*Veḷuvana*). At that time, there was a certain family in Rājagaha who were devoted on both sides, endowed with virtue and good conduct, and served as a wellspring for the monks and nuns.
Those two husband and wife, for as long as they lived, dedicated themselves to the Three Jewels...
Having performed meritorious deeds, they passed away from there and were reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas; for them, a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in extent appeared.
There they enjoyed divine splendor. Then, the venerable Mahāmoggallāna—this and more should be understood according to the method already explained below.
"Just as the forest of Cittalatā shines forth—the most excellent garden of the Thirty-Three Gods—so too does this celestial mansion of yours stand illuminating the sky.
You have attained the power of a deva, O one of great majesty; while you were a human being, what merit did you perform?"
“By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?
Thus the Elder asked.
“That son of the gods, being questioned by Moggallāna, was delighted.”
“Being asked a question, he explained: ‘Of what karma is this the fruit?
‘My husband and I, while living as a household in the world of men, dwelt as a well for others;
with a confident heart, we respectfully gave abundant gifts of food and drink.’”
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this… [and so on] …and my complexion shines in all directions.
Thus he explained his own prosperity. There is nothing new even in these verses.
The commentary on the First Householder’s Mansion is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Householder’s Mansion:
"Just as a forest is a creeper-grove"—this is the Second Householder’s Mansion. Here too, the origin story (aṭṭhuppatti) is exactly the same as the preceding one.
“Just as the forest of Citra shines forth, the best of gardens and supreme among the Thirty-three gods,
even so does this celestial mansion of yours stand, illuminating the sky.
You have attained the power of a deva, O one of great majesty.”
"What merit did you perform while being a human being?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?"— thus he asked.
“Thus the son of a deva was delighted… [as before] …the fruit of which deed is this.
“In the world of humans, my wife and I lived in our home as a well for all;
with a mind full of faith, we respectfully gave abundant gifts of food and drink.
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this...
[and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.
Thus he explained his own prosperity. There is nothing new even in these verses.
The commentary on the *Dutiya-agāriya-vimāna* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Phaladāyaka-vimāna*:
"This lofty palace with jeweled pillars" is the *Phaladāyaka-vimāna*. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha.
In the Bamboo Grove. At that time, King Bimbisāra felt a desire to enjoy mango fruits out of season.
He said to the park-keeper: "My good man, a desire for mango fruits has arisen in me;
therefore, bring some mangoes and give them to me. "Your Majesty, there are no mango fruits at present, but nevertheless, I shall do as you ask."
“If Your Majesty will wait for a short time, just as my mother does not take fruit for long,” he said.

“Very well, my man, do so,” [the king replied]. The park-keeper went to the park, cleared away the soil at the roots of the mango trees, and scattered soil of that same kind and watered them with water of that same kind, so that before long the mango trees were stripped of their leaves.
Then, having removed that sand and having scattered ordinary soil mixed with *phārusaka* and *kasaṭa*, he gave it plenty of water.
At that time, the mango trees did not take long to become covered in buds, then sprouted leaves, then developed flower-buds, and finally blossomed;
then, having produced young fruit, they bore fruit. There, upon one mango tree—
First of all, four mangoes—yellowish-brown like powdered sapphires, endowed with excellent fragrance and flavor, and fully ripened—became ready.

Taking them, he set out thinking, "I will give these to the King. While on his way, seeing the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna walking for alms, he thought: "These mangoes are the very best fruit; I shall give them to this noble sir."

“Let the king kill me or let him ordain me; for when a gift is given to a king, the fruit in this very life is merely a small measure of honor, but when given to a noble one, there will be immeasurable fruit both in this present life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, she gave those fruits to the Elder and, approaching the king, [reported] that matter to the king.
He reported this. Having heard it, the king commanded his royal officers: "Go, men, investigate whether he spoke as he did.
But the Elder presented those fruits to the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave one to the Elder Sāriputta, one to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, and one to the Elder Mahākassapa, and ate one himself.
The men reported that occurrence to the king.
Having heard it, the king thought, "Truly, this man is wise, who, having even renounced his own life, was devoted to merit and made his own exhaustion merely a matter of passing through a place.
With a joyful heart, he granted him an excellent village.
Having given him garments, ornaments, and other gifts, he said, "O man, from whatever merit you have acquired by giving this mango fruit, give me a share of it.
He replied, "I give it, Your Majesty; take the share as you please.
Later, the park-keeper passed away and was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, where a golden celestial mansion sixteen yojanas in extent appeared for him.
It was adorned with seven hundred gabled chambers. Having seen it, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna asked:
"This lofty celestial mansion has jeweled pillars extending sixteen yojanas all around;
its seven hundred magnificent gabled chambers are beautiful, with pillars of beryl and inlaid with gold."
“There you bathe, drink, and eat, while celestial lutes play their lovely strains;
there the well-trained, beautiful maidens of the Thirty-three,
divine and noble, dance, sing, and bring you delight.”
“You have attained divine power, O one of great majesty… your radiance illuminates all directions.
The son of the gods, being delighted… [said: “…this is the fruit of that karma.”
“One who gives with a mind full of faith to those of upright conduct obtains abundant fruit;
for having gone to heaven, he rejoices among the Thirty-three gods and experiences the vast fruit of his merit.
To you alone, O Great Sage, did I give four fruits.”

“Therefore, indeed, a person who constantly desires happiness, whether aspiring for celestial joys or seeking the highest excellence among humans, ought surely to give the fruit [of their merit]. Because of that,
my complexion is such as this…” [and so forth].
"And my radiance shines in all directions"—thus he also explained it to him.
In that context, "eight by eight" means that in each gabled chamber there were sixty-four, measured at eight by eight.
"Of noble form" means they were of beautiful nature due to the perfection of their physical form, the perfection of their virtue and conduct, and the perfection of their training. "Divine..."

"Kaññā" refers to celestial nymphs (*devaccharā*). "Tidasacarā" means those who move in happiness among the Thirty-three gods (*tīvasa*), dwelling in bliss. "Uḷārā" means those of magnificent splendor. (Verse 1064) "Phaladāyī" (the giver of fruit):
he speaks with reference to himself because he himself gave mango fruit;
"phalaṃ" refers to the fruit of merit. "Vipulaṃ" means great; the intention is that he obtains it, having been established in the world of humans. "Dadanti" (they give).
"By giving, for the sake of generosity. "Among those who have entered the straight path" means among those who have practiced the straight way.

"Gone to heaven" means having gone to heaven by way of rebirth; even there, in the triple heaven, in the abode of the Thirty-three, he experiences abundant fruit of merit just as I do—the meaning is that it is so for others as well.
1066. Therefore, since such prosperity is attained by the mere giving of the four fruits, for that reason it is "sufficient" (alam) and indeed "fitting" (yuttam).
"Constantly" (niccam) means at all times. "Divine" (dibbāni) means belonging to the celestial realms.
"Human excellence" (manussasobhaggatam) means the state of being fortunate among humans. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the *Phaladāyaka-vimāna* is finished.
4. The commentary on the *Paṭhama-upassaya-dāyaka-vimāna*:
"Like the moon in a cloudless sky," is the *Upassaya-dāyaka-vimāna*. How did it originate? The Blessed One—

The Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. At that time, a certain bhikkhu, having spent the rains retreat in a village monastery and having completed the retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā*, was traveling toward Rājagaha to pay homage to the Blessed One.
On the way, he entered a certain village in the evening and, while searching for a place to stay, saw a lay follower and questioned him.
“Lay follower, is there any place in this village suitable for those who have gone forth to dwell?
With a mind full of faith, the lay follower went home, consulted with his wife, and designated a place suitable for the elder to stay.
There he prepared a seat, set out water for washing the feet and a footstool, and [invited] the elder.
Having had him enter, while he was washing his feet, he lit a lamp, spread out coverlets on the couch, and gave them to him.
Having invited him for the following day, he fed the Elder on the second day, gave him a lump of sugar for drink, and followed the Elder as he departed before turning back.
At a later time, he passed away together with his wife.
Having done so, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden celestial palace twelve *yojanas* in extent.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned him with two verses:
"Just as the moon, when the clouds have vanished, moves through the sky illuminating the firmament;..."
“Your celestial mansion is just like that; it stands illuminating the mid-air.
You have attained the power of a deva and possess great majesty. While you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means do you possess such blazing majesty, and why does your complexion radiate light in all directions?”
Thus that son of the gods answered with these verses:
“That son of the gods was pleased... [the rest of the verse] ...the fruit of which action this is.
“In the world of humans, my wife and I gave lodging to an Arahant;”
“With a mind full of faith, we gave abundant gifts of food and drink with due respect.
Because of that, my complexion is such as this... [and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.
Regarding this, whatever is to be said concerning the verses follows the same method already explained above.
The commentary on the First Mansion of the Provider of a Dwelling is finished.
5. The commentary on the Second Mansion of the Provider of a Dwelling:
"Like the sun in a cloudless sky"—this is the Second Mansion of the Provider of a Dwelling. How did it come to be?

The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. At that time, a number of bhikkhus, having spent the rains retreat in a village residence, were traveling toward Rājagaha to see the Blessed One when they arrived at a certain village in the evening.
The rest is exactly as in the immediately preceding Vimāna story.
“As the sun in a cloudless sky...
[as in the previous mansion, so it should be expanded] ...
‘And my radiance illuminates all directions.’”
In this regard, there is nothing new even in the verses.
The commentary on the second *Vimāna* of the donor of the dwelling place is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Vimāna* of the Donor of Alms-food.
"This lofty jeweled-pillared mansion" refers to the mansion of the almsgiver. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove.

At that time, a certain bhikkhu, while traveling along a highway, entered a certain village for alms and stood at the door of a house. There, a certain man—having washed his hands and feet—[approached him].
Sitting down with the thought, “I shall eat,” he had food brought to him. When it was placed in his bowl, he saw that monk;
as he was pouring the rice from his bowl into the monk’s alms-bowl, even though the monk said, “Give me only a portion,” he poured in all of it.
After the monk had recited a blessing of thanksgiving, he departed. That man [thought], “To the monk whose belly is empty of hunger...”
Recalling, "I gave almsfood without having eaten myself," he obtained sublime joy and gladness.
Later, having passed away, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods in a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in size.
When the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera, while wandering on his tour of the devas, saw him shining with great divine majesty, [he spoke] these verses:
He questioned him with verses:
“This lofty celestial mansion with its jeweled pillars extends for twelve yojanas all around;
it has seven hundred magnificent gabled chambers, beautiful with pillars of beryl and adorned with golden ornaments.”
“You have attained divine power,
O one of great majesty… your radiance illuminates all directions.
He too answered him with these verses:
“Thus the son of a deva was delighted... [as before] ...the fruit of which deed is this.
“When I was a human being among humans, I saw a bhikkhu who was thirsty and exhausted;
for one day I provided him with almsfood, and at that time I made him well-provided with a meal.”
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this… [and so on] …and my complexion shines in all directions.
(1084) Therein, *ekāhaṃ bhikkhaṃ* means one day’s portion of alms-food; the meaning is, “one increased meal.
*Paṭipādayissanti* means “I bestowed,” or “I gave. *Samaṅgi bhattena* means “endowed with a meal.”
The meaning is "alms that have been obtained. Thus, when the Great Elder had thus explained his own deeds of good conduct to that son of the gods, he taught the Dhamma to him and his retinue;
having returned to the human world, he related that occurrence to the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Teacher, taking that as the occasion for instruction, taught the Dhamma to the great assembly that had gathered. That teaching...
"It was of great benefit to the multitude.
The commentary on the *Bhikkhādāyaka-vimāna* is finished.
7. The commentary on the *Yavapālaka-vimāna*.
"This lofty palace with jeweled pillars" refers to the Yavapālaka-vimāna. What is its origin?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. At that time, a certain poor boy in Rājagaha was guarding a barley field.
One day, having obtained some boiled rice for his morning meal, he thought, "I will go to the field and eat it," and so—
Taking the gruel, he went to a barley field and sat down at the foot of a tree.

At that moment, a certain elder who had destroyed the taints (khīṇāsavatthera), traveling along the road, arrived at that place as evening approached and approached the spot where the barley-keeper was sitting at the foot of the tree.
The barley-keeper, looking at the time, said, "Venerable sir, have you obtained food? The elder—
He remained silent. Realizing that he could not obtain [the meal], he said, "Venerable sir, the time is drawing near; it will not be possible to wander for alms and eat.
Out of compassion for me, please partake of this sour gruel," and he gave the sour gruel to the Elder.
Out of compassion for him, the Elder consumed it while the man was looking on, and after giving his blessing, he departed.

He departed. That boy also, having gladdened his heart with the thought, "I have indeed given a very good gift of sour gruel to one such as this," passed away later on and was reborn in a celestial mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, in the manner already described.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera questioned him with these verses:
“This celestial mansion with its lofty jeweled pillars...
[and so forth] ...and your radiance shines in all directions.
He too answered him with these verses:
1089. “Thus the young god was delighted… [as above] …the fruit of which deed this is.
“When I was among humans, having become a human being, I was a keeper of barley fields.
There I saw a stainless monk, serene and unperturbed.”
“With a mind full of faith, I gave him a portion with my own hands;
having given that ball of boiled rice, I rejoice in the Nandana Grove.
Because of that, such is my complexion…” [and so on].
"And my radiance shines in all directions.
Therein, there is nothing new even in the verses.
The commentary on the *Yavapālaka-vimāna* is finished.
8. Explanation of the First Kuṇḍalī-Vimāna:
"Adorned, wearing garlands, and well-robed"—this is the Kuṇḍalī-Vimāna. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, the two Chief Disciples, together with their retinues, were wandering on tour among the Kāsī people.
At the time of sunset, they arrived at a certain monastery.

Having heard of this occurrence, a certain lay follower (*upāsaka*) from the village where that monastery was located approached the elders, paid homage to them, and provided them with water for washing their feet, oil for anointing their feet, a bed, a bench, a coverlet, and a lamp.
He then invited them for the following day. On the second day, [he served them].
He gave a great gift, and after the elders had recited the words of thanksgiving, they departed.
At a later time, having passed away, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas in a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in size.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned him with these verses:
“Adorned with garlands, well-clothed, wearing fine earrings and having his hair and beard trimmed,
with hand-ornaments fastened on, glorious as the moon in a celestial mansion.
And divine lutes, beautiful and well-trained, playing in unison with eight strings each, resound melodiously.”
And divine maidens, moving among the Thirty-three gods, lofty ones, dance, sing,
and bring delight. “You have attained the power of a god,
O one of great majesty… Your radiance illuminates all directions.”
He too answered him with these verses:
1097. “That son of the gods was pleased... [as before] ...the fruit of which deed this is.
“When I was among humans, having become a human being, I saw recluses endowed with virtue;”

To one who was accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, renowned, learned, and established in the destruction of craving, I gave abundant gifts of food and drink with a devout heart, offering them with due respect.
"Because of that, my complexion is such as this... [and so on].
"And my radiance shines in all directions.
(1094) Therein, *sukuṇḍalī* means one whose ears are adorned with beautiful earrings. There is also the reading *sakuṇḍalī*;
*sakuṇḍalaṃ* means a matching pair of earrings, and one who possesses that is *sakuṇḍalī*, meaning one who wears a fitting pair of earrings. Furthermore, they are mutually [harmonious].

"And you are worthy of earrings" is the meaning. "With hair and beard trimmed" means with hair and beard properly trimmed. "With hand-ornaments put on" means with finger-rings and other ornaments for the hands fastened.
1098. "Endowed with the destruction of craving":
the meaning is that he has arrived at, or attained, the destruction of craving, which is Arahantship, or indeed Nibbāna itself. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the First Kuṇḍalī-vimāna is finished.
9. The commentary on the Second Kuṇḍalī-vimāna:
"Adorned, wearing garlands, and well-clothed"—this is the Second Kuṇḍalī-vimāna. How did it originate? The Blessed One was at Sāvatthī.
He was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove. At that time, the two chief disciples were wandering on a tour of the Kāsī country, and so forth—all [the details] are exactly as in the preceding account.
“Adorned, wearing garlands, well-clothed, with fine earrings and trimmed hair and beard;”
Renowned, with hand-ornaments fastened, he dwells in a celestial mansion like the moon.
And divine lutes, played by eightfold groups of well-trained and beautiful women, sound forth sweetly.
And divine maidens, noble wanderers of the Thirty-three, danced, sang,
and delighted him. “You have attained the power of a god,
O one of great majesty… your radiance illuminates all directions,” she asked.
“Thus the young deva was delighted... [as before] ...the fruit of which action this is.
“When I was among humans, being a human myself, I saw ascetics of noble form, renowned for their perfected knowledge and conduct, learned, virtuous, and inspiring confidence;”
"With a mind full of faith, I gave abundant gifts of food and drink with due respect.
Because of that, such is my complexion...
[and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions."
There is nothing new even in the verses.
The commentary on the second Kuṇḍalī-vimāna is finished.
10. (Uttara) Commentary on the Pāyāsi-vimāna.
The assembly hall of the king of the gods is called Sudhamma; it is the Uttaravimāna. How did its origin come about?

After the Blessed One had attained final nibbāna and the distribution of his relics had been performed, while the stūpas were being established here and there and the Great Elders headed by Mahākassapa had been selected and gathered to recite the Dhamma and Vinaya, [this occurred] until the time they entered the rains retreat, as well as during other times.
While those [other teachers] were dwelling here and there with their respective retinues,
the Venerable Kumārakassapa went to the city of Setavyā with five hundred bhikkhus and stayed in the Siṃsapā Grove.
Then, having heard that the Elder was staying there, Prince Pāyāsi, surrounded by a great multitude of people, approached him.
Having offered a hospitable welcome, he sat down and declared his own speculative views. Then the Elder,
demonstrating the existence of the next world through similes such as those of the moon and the sun, taught him the Pāyāsi Sutta— adorned with various causes and parables,
a disentangling of the knots of speculative views, and variegated by manifold methods— and established him in the perfection of right view.
Having thus become one of purified view, he gave alms to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, and others;
yet, because of his lack of noble aspiration, he gave only coarse offerings—mere food and clothing, broken rice with sour gruel as the second course, and garments of hemp.
Having given such careless gifts, at the breaking up of the body, he was reborn in a lowly state, into the company of the Cātumahārājika devas.
Among those engaged in what was to be done and what was not to be done, there was a young brahmin named Uttara who was occupied with giving alms.
Having given gifts with due care, he was reborn in the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods (*Tāvatiṃsa-kāya*), where a celestial mansion (*vimāna*) twelve *yojanas* in extent manifested for him.
Manifesting his gratitude, he approached the Elder Kumāra Kassapa together with his mansion; descending from the mansion, he prostrated himself on his five limbs.
Having paid homage and raising his hands in reverential salutation, he stood there. The Elder said to him:
“Just as the Sudhamma assembly hall of the king of the gods, where the entire host of devas gathers together—so too is this celestial mansion of yours, standing in the sky and illuminating it.”
“You have attained divine power,
O one of great majesty… your radiance illuminates all directions”— with these verses he questioned him;
“That son of the gods was delighted… [he spoke] of that deed of which this is the fruit.”
“Among humans, having become a human, I was a young brahmin in the service of King Pāyāsi.
Having acquired wealth, I shared it out; those who were virtuous were dear to me.
With a confident heart, I gave abundant gifts of food and drink with due respect.”
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this… [and so on] …and my complexion shines forth in all directions.
Thus that son of the gods answered him with these verses.
1108. *Tattha devarājassa* means of Sakka. *Sabhā Sudhammā* is the assembly hall (santhāgāra) bearing that name.
*Yattha* means in which assembly hall. *Acchati* means he sits. *Devasaṅgho* means the host of Tāvatiṃsa devas. *Samaggo* means together, assembled. 1111.
*Pāyāsissa ahosiṃ māṇavo* means he was a young man (*māṇava*) in his youth who performed the duties and services for King Pāyāsi.

By name, however, I was called Uttara. "I practiced sharing" means that I myself, without consuming it, practiced the distribution of whatever wealth I obtained by way of relinquishing it through the gateway of giving (*dānamukha*). There is an ellipsis [to be supplied] as "relinquishing food and drink.
Alternatively, "I gave abundant gifts. How so? "Respectfully. Of what kind? It should be construed as "food and drink."
The commentary on the *Pāyāsi-vimāna* is finished.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the *Pāyāsi-vagga*, adorned with ten stories, within the *Vimānavatthu* of the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the commentary on the *Khuddaka-nikāya*.
The commentary on the meanings is finished.
7. The Chapter on the Well-Placed Mansion (Sunikkhittavimānavagga).
1. Commentary on the Cittalatā Mansion.
