Because it shines like a forest of mind-creepers, it is called the *Cittalatā-vimāna*. What was its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, there was a certain lay follower in Sāvatthī who was poor and of little means, living by performing work for others.
He was faithful and devoted, supporting his aged and elderly parents, [thinking]: "Women, indeed..."
"Women established in their husbands' families exercise authority, yet those who behave agreeably toward their mothers-in-law and fathers-in-law are rare.
Avoiding such mental suffering for his parents, he did not take a wife but instead attended upon them himself;
he guarded his moral precepts, observed the Uposatha, and gave gifts according to his means. Later, having passed away, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.

He was reborn in a celestial mansion twelve yojanas in extent. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having gone there by the manner previously described, questioned him regarding his past deeds with these verses:
"Just as this forest, variegated with creepers, shines forth—the most excellent garden of the Thirty-three, supreme among them—"
“Just like that, this celestial mansion of yours stands illuminating the sky.
‘You have attained the power of a deva,
O one of great majesty… your radiance shines forth in all directions.’”
“Thus the young deva was delighted... [as before] ...the fruit of which action is this.
“When I was among humans, being a human, I was poor, without protection, wretched, and a laborer;
I supported my aged mother and father, and they were dear to me and possessed of virtue.”
“With a confident heart, I gave abundant gifts of food and drink with due respect.
Because of that, such is my complexion... [as before] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.
He too explained it to him. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Cittalatā Vimāna is finished.
2. Commentary on the Nandana Vimāna:
It is called the Nandana Vimāna because it shines like the Nandana grove. What is its origin? The Blessed One was at Sāvatthī.
He dwelt in Jeta’s Grove. At that time, in Sāvatthī, there was a certain lay follower (*upāsaka*), and so forth—all of which is similar to the immediately preceding *vimāna* [story].
However, the distinction here is this: having taken a wife, he supported his parents.
Just as the Nandana grove shines, the best of gardens, supreme among the Thirty-three gods;
“Just like that, this celestial mansion of yours stands illuminating the sky.
‘You have attained the power of a god, O one of great majesty… your beauty shines forth in all directions.
That son of the gods, being delighted… [said: ‘Of what karma is this the fruit?’”
“Among humans, having become a human being, I was poor, without protection, wretched, and a laborer;
yet I supported my aged mother and father, and my beloved parents were virtuous.
With a mind full of serene confidence, I respectfully gave abundant gifts of food and drink.”
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this... [and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.
Thus he explained it with verses. In those verses, moreover, there is nothing new.
The commentary on the Nandana-vimāna is finished.
3. Description of the Maṇithūṇa Mansion:
This is called the Maṇithūṇa Mansion because it is a lofty mansion with jeweled pillars. How did its origin come about?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove. At that time, a number of elder bhikkhus were dwelling in a forest region.
On the path leading to that village for alms, a certain lay follower levels the uneven ground,
removes thorns, clears away thickets of shrubs, builds embankments on irrigation channels during the rainy season, plants shade trees in barren spots, and at water sources,
he removes loose soil to make them wide and deep, and establishes landing-stairs.
He gave gifts according to his means and guarded his virtue. Later, having passed away, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas in a golden celestial mansion twelve *yojanas* in extent.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera approached him and questioned him with these verses:
“This lofty celestial mansion with its jeweled pillars extends for twelve *yojanas* all around.”
Seven hundred magnificent gabled palaces, with pillars of beryl and beautiful golden railings—
there you drink, eat, and enjoy yourself; divine lutes play sweet melodies,
there are divine flavors and the five strands of sensual pleasure, and women adorned in gold dance.
“By what means do you have such a complexion... [as before] ...and your complexion illuminates all directions?
He too answered him with verses:
“That son of the gods is delighted... [as before] ...this is the fruit of that karma.”
“Among humans, having become a human being, I made a journey along a path in the wilderness;
I planted groves and trees, and those who were virtuous became dear to me;
with a confident heart, I gave abundant gifts of food and drink with due respect.”
“Because of that, my complexion is such as this... [and so on] ...and my complexion shines forth in all directions.

(1131) Herein, *vivaneti* means in the forest (*araññe*). Regarding *ārāmarukkhāni*: it refers to trees that have become groves; the meaning is that they planted trees there after having made them into a grove.
All the rest is exactly as previously stated. The commentary on the Mansion with Jewel Pillars is finished.
4. The Description of the Golden Mansion (*Suvaṇṇavimānavanṇanā*).
"In a mountain made of gold" refers to the golden mansion. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Andhakavinda.
At that time, a certain lay follower—faithful, confident, and endowed with great wealth—[lived] in that village.
Not far away, on a certain Muṇḍaka Mountain, he had a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) constructed for the Blessed One, endowed with every excellence and suitable for the Blessed One’s dwelling.
Having caused the Blessed One to reside there, he attended upon him with great care.

He himself was established in the constant observance of moral discipline, and having become one whose restraint of virtue was perfectly pure, at the time of his death he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Of him—
Upon the summit of that golden mountain, there arose a celestial mansion, radiant with a network of rays from various jewels indicative of the power of karma;
it was surrounded by variegated railings, adorned with diverse and abundant ornaments, and featured well-proportioned walls, pillars, and stairways, as delightful as a pleasure garden.
While wandering on his journey through the deva realms, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw it and questioned him with these verses:
“Upon a mountain made of gold, there is a celestial palace radiant on all sides;
it is covered with a network of gold and adorned with a lattice of tinkling bells.
The well-fashioned pillars are eight-sided, and all are made of beryl.”
Upon each single beam, seven jewels were fashioned:
of beryl and gold, crystal and silver,
of emerald and pearls, and of ruby gems.
“The ground is variegated and delightful, where no dust rises;
the rafters are yellow, and the gables are fashioned with carvings.
There are four staircases, constructed toward the four directions.”
With its inner chambers of various jewels, it shines like the sun.
Therein are four altars, divided and measured in their proportions;
dazzling, they radiate light toward the four directions all around.
“In that most excellent celestial mansion, you, a son of the gods of great radiance,
outshine all with your beauty, like the sun as it rises.
Is this the fruit of your generosity, or perhaps of your virtue?”
“And furthermore, regarding the act of joining the palms in reverence—explain that to me when asked.
He answered him with these verses: 1142.
“That son of the gods was delighted... [as before] ...the fruit of which deed this is.”
“In Andhakavinda, with my own hands, I, full of faith, had a monastery built for the Teacher, the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
There, I offered perfumes, garlands, requisites, and ointments;”
With a mind full of serene confidence, I gave a monastery to the Teacher;
by that merit, this has been obtained by me, and I dwell at ease in the Nandana Grove.
In the delightful Nandana forest, filled with various flocks of birds, I abide.
“I delight in dance and song, honored by the celestial nymphs.
(1134) In this context, *sabbatopabham* means shining forth from all sides, emitting radiance. *Kiṅkiṇijālakappitam* means fashioned with a network of tinkling bells.
(1135) *Sabbe veḷuriyāmayā* means that all the pillars are made of beryl gems. Furthermore, there, for each individual...
"On each shoulder" means on each individual shoulder-section among the eight pillar-like shoulders. "The seven jewels fashioned" means fashioned by the work of the seven jewels;
the meaning is that each individual shoulder is made of the seven jewels.
With the words "Of beryl and gold," etc., he shows the various jewels. Therein, "of beryl and gold" means...
"Adorned with beryl and gold," or alternatively, "variegated by means of"—for here the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
This same principle applies to the phrases "crystal and silver. "With emeralds and pearls" refers to *kabara* gems. "And with rubies" refers to red gems.
(1137) "No dust rises there" means that because the floor is made of jewels, no dust arises in that celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
“Gopānasīgaṇā” means a multitude of rafters. “Pītā” means yellow-colored; the meaning is that they are made of gold as well as of gems such as topaz (phussa-rāga) and so forth.
“Dhārenti kūṭaṃ” means they support a pinnacle made of the seven precious gems. 1138–9. “Nānāratanagabbhehi” means by means of inner chambers made of various gems.
“Vediyā” means a railing. “Catasso” means four in the four directions. Therefore he said: “all around in the four directions.”
1140. *Mahappabho* means possessing great radiance. *Udayanto* means rising. *Bhānumā* refers to the sun.

1143. Regarding *sehi pāṇibhi*: the construction is that, producing merit which is the essence of the body and performing various tasks with his own hands, he caused a monastery to be built for the Teacher.
Alternatively, *sehi pāṇibhi* [refers to] there, in Andhakavinda, both fragrance and...

[He gave] garlands, requisites, and ointments by way of worship. How so? "With a serene mind, I gave a monastery to the Teacher; I worshipped it; I dedicated it"—thus should the construction be understood here.

(1144) *Tenā* means by that aforementioned meritorious deed acting as the cause. *Mayhaṃ* means by me. *Idaṃ* refers to this fruit of merit, or this divine sovereignty. Therefore he said, "I exercise mastery."
1145. "In Nandana" means in this divine world, the place where the celestial prosperity called "Nandi" arises;
specifically, in that delightful Nandana Grove. The construction is: "I delight in this delightful Nandana Grove.
The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
When the deity had thus revealed her own meritorious deed, the Elder taught the Dhamma to that son of the gods and his retinue, and then reported the matter to the Blessed One.
Taking that as the occasion, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the assembled company.
That teaching was of great benefit to the multitude.
The commentary on the Suvaṇṇavimāna is finished.
5. Commentary on the Ambavimāna:
"This lofty palace with jeweled pillars" refers to the Ambavimāna. What is its origin? The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, a certain poor man in Rājagaha, having been hired by others for food and wages,
was guarding a mango grove. One day, during the summer season, as the Venerable Sāriputta was traveling along a road not far from that mango grove—
on a stretch of ground heated by the sun’s rays, scorched by hot sand, and overspread with shimmering webs of heat-rays— he [encountered him].
Seeing him walking with limbs covered in sweat, he conceived a sense of reverence and high esteem; approaching him, he said this:
"Venerable sir, this heat is great; you appear exceedingly exhausted.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the noble one were to enter this mango grove, rest for a moment, and dispel the fatigue of the journey."
“Go, out of compassion. Desiring especially to increase his confidence of mind, the Elder entered the monastery and sat down at the foot of a certain mango tree.
Again that man said, “Venerable sir, if you wish to bathe, I shall draw water from this well.”
“I will bathe you and give you water to drink. The Elder consented by remaining silent.
He drew water from the well, strained it, and bathed the Elder; having bathed him and washed his hands and feet, he offered water to the seated Elder.
After the Elder had drunk the water and his fatigue was allayed, [the Elder spoke] regarding that man’s gift of water.
Having performed the bathing and expressed his appreciation, he departed.
Then that man, thinking, "I have indeed quenched the heat of the elder who was tormented by the summer heat; I have surely produced much merit," experienced a sublime sense of joy and gladness.
Later, having passed away, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna [saw him there].
Having approached, he asked about the merit performed with these verses:
“This lofty celestial mansion with jeweled pillars extends twelve yojanas all around;
it has seven hundred magnificent gabled chambers, beautiful with pillars of beryl and adorned with gold.”
“There you bathe, drink, and eat; celestial lutes play their sweet melodies;
here are the five celestial strands of sensual pleasure, and women adorned in gold dance.
By what means do you possess such a complexion? … [and so forth] …
"And your radiance illuminates all directions.
"That son of the gods was delighted...
[as before] ...of what deed is this the fruit?"
“In the last month of summer, when the sun was scorching the day,
a man working for hire watered another’s mango grove.
Then a monk arrived there, renowned as Sāriputta.”
Exhausted in body, yet untiring in mind,
I saw him approaching and said to the water-sprinkler:
"It would be well, venerable sir, if you would bathe me, which would bring me happiness."
“Out of compassion for me, he set aside his bowl and robes;
clad in a single robe, he sat at the foot of a tree in the shade.
And a man, with a serene mind, [honored him] with clear water.”
At the foot of a tree, beneath the shade, he bathed while wearing a single robe.
"The mango tree has been watered and the ascetic has been bathed;
by me, no small merit has been sown."
Thus, he pervades his entire body with rapture.
“In this very life, I performed only this much work;
having abandoned my human body, I have been reborn in the Nandana grove.”
“In the delightful Nandana grove, filled with flocks of various birds,
I delight in dance and song, honored by the apsarases.
He too answered him with these verses.
1151. Therein, "in the last month of summer" means in the month of Āsāḷhi. "Blazing forth" means shining exceedingly;
the meaning is that they emit heat in every way. "Divāṅkare" means the maker of day (the sun); or this very reading [divākare] is correct.
"Asiñcati" means he sprinkles—the syllable "-a-" is merely a particle—meaning he surely sprinkles water at the roots of the mango trees. "Asiñcatha" [is the imperative].

And the reading is *siñcittha*, meaning "he sprinkled. Some read *asiñcaha*; the meaning is: "Having become a servant for others, I then sprinkled that mango grove (*ambārāma*). (Verse 1152) *Tenā* means:
he went, he proceeded, toward that direction in which that mango grove was located. *Akilanto va cetasā* means: without being weary in mind.
The construction is as follows: because it was abandoned by that very path of mental suffering, although he was not weary in mind, he appeared weary in body as he went along that path.
(1153–4) "At that time I spoke, having been a mango-waterer"—this is the construction. "Wearing a single robe" means with the intention of wishing to bathe.
1156. Regarding the word *iti*: "The mango tree has been watered, the ascetic has been bathed, and no small merit has been performed by me;

by this single effort, all three purposes have been accomplished. In this manner, through the joy (*pīti*) that arises, the man pervades his entire body and makes it completely suffused—this is the construction.
Furthermore, this verb in the present tense is used in the sense of the past; thus, the meaning is "he pervaded" (*pharī*).

1157. "Tadeva ettakaṃ kammaṃ" means: "I performed only this much karma—namely, the mere act of giving water—and in that birth, I do not recall any other [deed]. This is the intended meaning. Their [explanations] follow the same method as stated above.
The commentary on the Ambavimāna is finished.
6. Commentary on the Gopālavimāna.
"Having seen [him], the monks questioned the god"—this is the *Gopāla-vimāna*. What is its origin?

The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. At that time, a certain cowherd living in Rājagaha, taking a bundle of boiled rice tied in a ragged cloth for his morning meal, departed from the city and went to the grazing ground where the cows roamed.
He arrived there. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, perceiving that "he will die this very moment and, having given me some sour gruel, will be reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas," went to his side.
Looking at the time, he wished to give the elder the sour gruel. At that time, cows were entering the bean field.
Then that cowherd thought, "Should I give the elder some rice gruel, or should I take out the cows from their month-long pen?
Then it occurred to him, "Let my masters do whatever they wish; however, once the elders have departed, there might be an obstacle to my giving the rice gruel.
Come now, I shall first give the rice gruel to the noble one."
He offered it to the Elder. Out of compassion, the Elder accepted it.
Then, as he was running forward with speed—failing to look out for danger in order to turn back the cows—a venomous snake that had been touched by his foot bit him.
The Elder, feeling compassion for him, began to eat the rice gruel. The cowherd also...
Having turned back the cows, he returned and saw the Elder consuming the sour gruel;
with a serene mind, experiencing sublime joy and gladness, he sat down. At that very moment, poison overwhelmed his entire body.
In a mere instant, as the venom reached the peak of its intensity, he passed away. Having died, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas in a palace twelve yojanas in extent.
He was reborn in a golden celestial mansion. Seeing him, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna questioned him with these verses:
“Having seen the god dwelling for a long time in a lofty, enduring celestial mansion—glorious, with hand-ornaments fastened, like the moon in a divine chariot—the monk questioned him.”
“Adorned with garlands, well-clothed, wearing beautiful earrings and having his hair and beard trimmed, with hand-ornaments fastened on,
he was illustrious like the moon in a celestial mansion. And divine lutes,
played by eightfold groups of skilled and handsome women, sounded sweetly.”
And sublime celestial maidens, moving among the thirty-three gods, dance, sing,
and bring delight: “You have attained the power of a deva,
O one of great majesty… Your radiance illuminates all directions.”
He too explained it to him:
“That son of the gods was pleased... [as before] ...the fruit of which deed is this.
“When I was a human being among humans, I would gather together and protect the cows of others;”
Then a monk came into my presence, and the cattle arrived to eat the grass.
"Today there are two tasks, both of which must be done"—thus, venerable sir, I reflected at that time.
Then, having regained right mindfulness through proper reflection, I quickly offered the infinite [gift], saying, "I give, venerable sir."
“In haste, I passed through the field of coins before this man could destroy it, whose wealth it was.
Then the black, highly venomous serpent bit my foot as I was hurrying.
Thus, I am afflicted with pain and tormented by distress, while the bhikkhu has himself released that endless one.”
“Out of compassion for me, he took my gruel; having passed away from there, I am now a deity.
‘That very wholesome deed was performed by me, and I myself experience the happiness resulting from that deed.
For you have shown me great compassion, O Venerable One; out of gratitude, I pay homage to you.”
“In this world with its devas and Māras, there is no other sage more compassionate than you.
For you, O Blessed One, have shown me great compassion; out of gratitude, I pay homage to you.
In this world or in the next, there is no other sage more compassionate than you.”
"Indeed, Venerable Sir, I have been greatly favored by her; out of gratitude, I pay homage to you.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reported to the Blessed One exactly what had been said by himself and the deity.
The Teacher, having restated that matter and made it the occasion for a discourse, taught the Dhamma to the assembled multitude.
In order to instruct [him], the Teacher said, "Having seen the god, the monks asked," and so forth.
Therein, "the god" refers to Gopāladevaputta. "The monks" refers to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna;
the Teacher speaks thus because he is a *bhikkhu* (one who has utterly broken the defilements). Because the celestial mansion had stood for a very long time...
Or rather, it is said to be "long-lasting" (*ciraṭṭhitika*) precisely because it endures for an eon (*kappa*). Some read it as "long-enduring" (*ciraṭṭhitika*);

that [term] should be connected with the word "divine" (*deva*). For that [divine life-span] also receives the designation "long-lasting" because it remains there for three hundred and sixty million years. Just as in the phrase "just as the moon," so too...
The young god Candima shines in his own divine mansion, radiant with a web of lovely, cool, and enchanting rays;
“shining thus” is the ellipsis of the statement. 1160.
“Adorned,” and so forth, is the Elder’s demonstration of the manner in which that young god was questioned; its meaning has already been explained above.

1164. *Saṅgamma*: having come together; or alternatively, *saṅgamma* means having gathered. For here the sense of the causal suffix (*hetu*) is also included; the meaning is "having become many in one place.
*Āga*: he came. *Māse*: the crops of the month. 1165. *Dvayajja*: two things today, now, must be done. *Ubhayañca kāriyaṃ* is a synonymous expression for the very same meaning already stated.
*Saññaṃ*: the perception of phenomena (*dhamma-saññā*). Therefore he said: "having wisely acquired" means having obtained.
"Threw" means he threw it into his hand by way of making him take hold of it.
"Anantaka" refers to a rag (*pilotika*) that had been tied up after stuffing it with scraps of food; here, the vowel *a* is merely a particle.
"He" refers to me. "Hurriedly" means in a state of haste or agitation. "He approached" or "he entered" the place where there was no room.
"Before this [herd] destroys that which is his wealth": the meaning is that before this herd of cattle destroys the wealth of the field-owner—namely, the crop of beans—it should be done;
that is, even prior to its destruction or trampling. "From there" means in that place.
"While I am in haste" means while I am in a state of agitation; on the path, due to my traveling with haste.
The intention is: "having gone without looking at the black snake.
(Verse 1167) "I am distressed, oppressed by suffering" means: by that bite of the venomous serpent, I am distressed (*aṭṭo*), afflicted (*aṭṭito*), tormented, and beset by the suffering of death.
"He swallowed" (*ahāsī*) means he ingested; the meaning is that he consumed it. "Fallen from there, I am dead, O deity."

Then, having passed away from the human state upon reaching the time of death, or because the time characterized by the exhaustion of the life-formations (*āyu-saṅkhāra*) had been reached there, I have "passed away" (*kālakato*).
And immediately thereafter, I am a deity (*devatā*), meaning that through the attainment of the state of a deity, I am a deity. 1169. "Than you" (*tayo*):

there is no other sage (*muni*) like you, one endowed with the qualities of sagehood (*moneyya*). Or, "than you" (*tayo*) is used here as an instrumental expression in the sense of the ablative. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Gopāla-vimāna is finished.
7. The commentary on the Kaṇḍaka-vimāna:
"Like the moon on the full-moon day" refers to the Kaṇḍaka-vimāna. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
At Jetavana. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wandering on a tour of the deva realms in the manner previously described, had gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
At that moment, the deva-son Kaṇḍaka emerged from his own abode, mounted his celestial vehicle, and was proceeding to the park with a great retinue and magnificent divine splendor.

Seeing the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, his heart filled with reverence and great esteem, he quickly descended from his vehicle, approached the Elder, and having paid homage with the fivefold prostration, stood with palms joined above his head. Then the Elder said to him:
“Like the full moon surrounded by the stars...”
“The moon, the lord of stars, travels all around it.
This celestial mansion is just like that, even in the city of the gods;
it outshines [all else] in beauty, like the sun rising with its rays.”
“With beryl and gold, crystal and silver,
with emeralds and pearls, and with rubies;
the variegated and delightful ground was spread with beryl.”
“Your gabled halls are beautiful and delightful; your palace has been well-constructed.
And your lotus pond is charming, frequented by water-fowl;
its waters are clear and serene, with a bed of golden sand.”
“Covered with various lotuses and strewn with white lilies,
they waft a fragrant scent, delightful when stirred by the breeze.
On both sides of that [river], groves of forest trees are beautifully arranged.”
It was filled with both flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees.
Seated upon a couch with golden legs, covered with soft woolen rugs,
they waited upon him like the king of the gods attended by celestial nymphs.
“Adorned with every ornament and decorated with various garlands, they delight that one of great psychic power; you rejoice like Vasavatti.
With kettledrums, conchs, mridangas, lutes, and cymbals—”
You take delight, fully possessed of pleasure, in dancing, singing, and well-played music.
Various divine forms are yours, as are divine sounds and tastes;
fragrances are desired by you, as are delightful tactile sensations.
“In that most excellent celestial mansion, O son of the gods of great radiance,
you outshine all with your beauty, like the sun rising.
Is this the fruit of your giving, or perhaps of your virtue?”
“And also regarding the act of joining the palms in reverence—explain that to me when asked.
Thus he asked about the deed performed by way of proclaiming the attainment of success.
“That son of the gods, being questioned by Moggallāna, was delighted;”
“Being asked a question, he explained it: ‘Of what karma is this the fruit?
‘In Kapilavatthu, among the foremost of the Sakyans, I was Kaṇḍaka, born at the same time as the son of Suddhodana.’”
“When he went forth for enlightenment at the hour of midnight,
he struck me with his soft hands,
whose copper-colored nails were glowing, and said, ‘Carry me!’”
“I shall deliver the world, having attained supreme enlightenment.
As I heard those words of his, a great joy arose within me;
with an uplifted heart and a happy mind, I was then consecrated.
“Knowing that I had mounted [the chariot], the Sakyaputta of great renown,
with a joyful and uplifted heart, I would have carried that Supreme among Men.
Having gone to the conquered territory of others while the sun was high,”
Leaving me and Channa behind, he departed without looking back.
"I would have licked his copper-nailed feet with my tongue;
as the Great Hero walked away, I would have gazed after him while weeping."
“Because I did not see that glorious son of the Sakyans,
I contracted a grievous illness, and my death came quickly.
By his very power alone, we now dwell in this celestial mansion.”
Endowed with every quality of sensual pleasure, like a god in the city of the gods.
"And whatever laughter I had upon hearing the sound of the Bodhi tree—
by that very root of merit, may I touch the destruction of the taints."
“If, venerable sir, you should go into the presence of the Teacher, the Buddha,
you should pay homage on my behalf by bowing your head at his feet.
I too shall go to see the Jina, the peerless one.”
“Rare is the sight of those Tathāgatas, the Lords of the World.
He too related the deed he had performed. For in his immediately preceding existence, he had been Kaṇḍaka, the king of horses, born at the same time as our Bodhisatta.
He was mounted at the time of the Great Departure, and by the remainder of that very night, [he traveled] three...
Having caused the great man to pass beyond the boundary ropes, he brought him to the bank of the Anomā River.

Then, when the sun had risen, the Great Being took the bowl and robes offered by the Great Brahmā Ghaṭīkāra, went forth into homelessness, and was sent with Channa toward Kapilavatthu. With a heart heavy with affection for the Great Man...
Licking his own foot with his tongue and opening his eyes, which were gentle with faith, he gazed as far as the range of his vision;
but when the Lord of the World had passed beyond the vicinity of sight, he became filled with a serene mind, thinking: "I have carried such a Great Being, the supreme leader of the world!
Truly, my body has become fruitful," and so he remained for a long time.

Unable to endure the suffering of separation due to his affection for her who was with him, and being urged by the natural law (*dhammatā*) through the prospect of divine prosperity in the future, he passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. With reference to him, it was said:
“Like the moon on the full-moon day... [I am now] in Kapilavatthu,” and so forth.
1171. Regarding the phrase *tattha puṇṇamāse*: it refers to the full moon day (*puṇṇamāsiyaṃ*) on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight (*sukkapa-kkhe*).
*Tārakādhipatī* means the lord of the stars. *Sasī* means he who bears the mark of the hare (*sasalañchanavā*). Some read the text as *tārakādhipo dissatī*;

for them, *tārakādhipa* is a nominative form lacking a case-ending (*avibhattikaniddeso*), and the construction should be understood as: "He is seen as the lord of the stars, and he moves around [the world]."
1172. "And divine in the city of the gods" means it is divine even within the city of the gods.
Just as the city of the gods is superior to the place of humans, he shows that this palace of yours is likewise superior even to the city of the gods. Therefore he said:
"It outshines [all] in color, like the sun rising with its rays," the meaning of which is "like the sun as it ascends."
1173. *Veḷūriyasuvaṇṇassa*: the construction is to be understood through ellipsis as "this mansion was fashioned with beryl and gold. *Phalika*: with crystal gems (*phalikamaṇi*).
1175. *Pokkharaṇī*: lotus ponds. 1177–8. *Tassā*: of that lotus pond. *Vanagumbā*:
he speaks with reference to the well-flowered trees in the park. *Devarājaṃva*: like Sakka. *Upatiṭṭhantī*: they wait upon [him].
1179. *Sabbābharaṇasañchannā* means covered with all the ornaments of women; the meaning is that her body was adorned in every way. *Vasavattīvā* means like the divine king Vasavatti (Indra). 1180.
*Bherisaṅkhamudiṅgāhī* is stated with a change of grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*); the construction is "with kettledrums (*bherī*), conchs (*saṅkha*), and drums (*mudiṅga*).
*Ratisampanno* means endowed with celestial delight. *Naccagīte suvādite* [refers to] dancing... [and well-sounded music].

And in beautiful singing and instrumental music, and in dancing, singing, and beautiful instrumental music, [it is] as the cause. For this locative case is used in the sense of "on account of" (*nimitta*), or there is an ellipsis of the word "occurred" (*pavattita*). 1181.
"Various divine forms" means various kinds of forms cognizable by the eye included within the world of the gods.
The phrase should be construed by supplying the verb "exist" (*vijjanti*), as in: "The delightful things you desire exist, just as you have desired them.
This same method applies to the expressions "divine sounds" (*dibbā saddā*) and so forth.

Regarding the line "Kaṇḍaka was my co-born," the word *ahu* here is merely a particle. Some read it as *ahū*; the meaning is that the horse-king named Kaṇḍaka was "co-born" (*sahaja*) because he was born on the very same day as the Great Being.
1186. *Aḍḍharattāyam* means "at midnight"; the meaning is "at the time of the middle watch. *Bodhāya ma-abhinikkhamī*:
the syllable *ma-* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*); the meaning is that he went forth on the Great Renunciation for the sake of perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
*Mudūhi pāṇīhi*: this refers to the Great Man’s mark (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*) of having soft hands. *Jālitambanakhehi*: [meaning] with webbed [fingers] and copper-colored nails.
With his nails being slightly copper-colored, he thereby displays the Great Man’s mark of webbed hands (*jālahatthatā*) and the secondary characteristic (*anubyañjana*) of copper-colored nails.
1187. *Satthi* means the shank; here, however, the part of the thigh situated near the shanks is called "the shank.
*Ākoṭayitvāna* means having tapped. And he said, "Carry me well," meaning, "Good Kaṇḍaka, for this one night..."

He said, "Carry me; let me be your vehicle. Regarding the purpose for carrying him, the Great Being then explained it by saying, "I shall ferry the world across, having attained supreme and perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-sammāsambodhi*). By this he meant:
"Having reached and realized the supreme, unsurpassed, and perfect enlightenment, I shall [rescue] the world, including the devas, from the great flood of *saṃsāra*..."
“I shall cause you to cross over; therefore, you should not think that this journey is of no consequence. Thus he shows that the purpose of the journey is unsurpassed.
(1188–9) *Hāsa* means joy. *Vipula* means vast and extensive. *Abhisīsiṃ* means I hoped, I desired, I accepted.
“And knowing me as one who has embarked, the Son of the Sakyas of great fame”—that is, the Son of the Sakya King, whose fame is spread wide and vast.
Knowing that I, the Great Being, was seated having mounted [the elephant], they would carry me;
thus it says "they will carry. 1190–91. "Of others" means of other kings. "Conquered" refers to a region or a foreign kingdom.
"Having abandoned" means having relinquished. "He departed" means he began to depart. They also read "he went forth" (*paribbajī*). "Scratched all around" means he scratched on every side.
“Udikkhisanti” means they looked upon [me]. 1192–3.
“Garukābādhaṃ” means a heavy, severe affliction; the meaning is a suffering that ends in death. Therefore he said, “My death was swift.
For he had been one of firm devotion toward the Mahāsatta throughout many births.
Because he had come [to see the Buddha], he was unable to endure the suffering of separation;
however, upon hearing that [the Buddha] had set out to attain supreme perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), a sublime, spiritual joy and gladness arose within him.
Consequently, immediately after death, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, and magnificent divine fortunes appeared for him. Therefore it is said: "By his very power."
By the power of the merit consisting of serene confidence (*pasāda*) attained at that place—like Sakka, the king of the gods, in the city of the gods, namely the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

(1194) "And whatever laughter there was for me upon hearing the word 'Bodhi'" means that when I first heard the sound of the word "Bodhi" [proclaiming], "He has attained supreme perfect enlightenment," laughter arose within me;
by that very root of skillfulness (*kusalamūla*), which was the dwelling-place of that laughter, [I attained this state].
"By that very same wholesome seed, they will touch it; I shall touch it; I shall attain it.

(1195) Thus, while the son of the gods was speaking of his own wholesome karma as the cause for the future attainment of existence he had realized, even though he now desired to go into the presence of the Blessed One, [he waited] for the Elder to come first.
Sending his salutation to the Teacher, he spoke the verse beginning with “If. Therein, “if you should go” (*sace gaccheyyāsi*) means if you will go.
Some read “if you go” (*sace gacchasi*), which has the same meaning.

“By my word as well” (*mamāpi naṃ vacanena*) means not only by your own nature, but also by my word—to the Blessed One. “You should speak” (*vajjāsi*) means you should say; the construction is: “you should offer salutation to me as well with your head.”
1196. Even if I were now to send a salutation, he said, "I too shall go to see the Jina, the peerless one," showing that once sent, he would not remain [without going].
Furthermore, to demonstrate a more compelling reason for his journey, he said, "The sight of such Lords of the World is difficult to obtain."
“Thus grateful and mindful of what had been done for him, he approached the Teacher;
having heard the words of the One with Vision, he purified his eye of Dhamma.
Having purified his course of views, his doubt, and his vows;”
“Having paid homage at the Teacher’s feet, he vanished right there.
These two verses were placed [in the canon] by the compilers of the collection.
Regarding the phrase “having heard the speech of the One with Vision”: it refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One with Vision, who possesses the five kinds of vision.
Having heard these words, he purified the "eye of Dhamma"—that is, the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
For its purification is indeed its attainment.
Having purified his "course of views"—that is, having utterly eradicated his adherence to views—and [having abandoned] doubt and [wrong] practices...

The construction is as follows: he purified both doubt based on the sixteen grounds and the eight grounds, as well as the adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) that occurs [in the form] "purification comes through rules and observances.
For in that context, the adherences (*parāmāsa*) occurring in such a manner along with their synonyms are called "vows" (*vatāni*).
The rest is exactly according to the method already stated.
The commentary on the Kaṇḍaka-vimāna is finished.
8. Commentary on the Anekavaṇṇa-vimāna:
"Anekavaṇṇa" means "of manifold colors"; it is the Anekavaṇṇa-vimāna. What is its origin? The Blessed One was at Sāvatthī.
He was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wandering on a tour of the devas in the manner described above, went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Then a deva-son of manifold colors, seeing him, conceived a sense of reverence and great esteem;
approaching him, he stood with palms joined in homage. The Elder—
“Mounted upon a celestial mansion of many colors and manifold designs, which dispels fear and sorrow,
you rejoice like Sunimmita, the Lord of Beings, surrounded by a host of nymphs.
There is no one equal to you in glory, merit, and psychic power, much less anyone superior.”
All the gods of the Thirty-three hosts have gathered together and pay homage to you, as the gods do to the moon;
and these nymphs all around you dance, sing, and delight you.
"You have attained the power of a god, O one of great majesty!"
"What merit did you perform while being a human being?
By what means have you come to possess such blazing majesty, and why does your complexion illuminate all directions?"
He asked about the deed performed by way of proclaiming the attainment of success he had achieved. To show that, it was said:
“That son of the gods, being delighted... [omitted] ...the fruit of which action is this. He too—
“Venerable sir, formerly I was a disciple of the Conqueror named Sumedha;
being an ordinary person lacking realization, I wandered as a mendicant for seven years.
Then, after the Teacher, the Conqueror Sumedha—the one who had crossed over the flood and was poised in equanimity—had attained final Nibbāna...”
Having paid homage at the stupa, which was covered with a net of gold and a collection of jewels, I gladdened my mind:
“I have no gift, nor do I have anything to give; yet I have encouraged others there, saying:
‘Worship this relic of one worthy of worship; thus, it is said, you shall go from here to heaven.’”
“That very same wholesome deed was performed by me,
and thus I myself experience celestial happiness;
I rejoice in the midst of the hosts of the Thirty-three.”
"He never reached the exhaustion of that merit," he related.
"It is said that thirty thousand aeons ago, a Perfectly Enlightened One named Sumedha appeared in the world.
Having brought illumination to the world including the devas and having fulfilled the duties of a Buddha, he attained Parinibbāna. And by humans, the relics of the Blessed One..."
After the Jewel Stupa had been built, a certain man who had gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation,
having practiced the holy life for seven years, became remorseful due to his lack of mental stability and left the order. Having left the order,
because of his great sense of spiritual urgency and his longing for the Dhamma, he performed such tasks as sweeping and plastering the courtyard of the stupa.
Practicing the constant precepts and the Uposatha precepts, guarding them, listening to the Dhamma, and exhorting others to perform meritorious deeds, he lived his life.
At the end of his lifespan, having passed away, he was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa gods.
Due to the loftiness of his meritorious karma, he became one of great influence and great power, honored and worshipped by deities such as Sakka, and remained there for the duration of his lifespan.
Having remained there, when he passed away from that state, he wandered from one existence to another among gods and humans.

During this current dispensation of a Buddha, by the remaining ripening of that very same karma, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; the deities perceived him as "Anekavaṇṇa" (the Multicolored One).
With reference to him, it was said: "Then the divine son Anekavaṇṇa... [and so on] ...there is no exhaustion of that merit."
"...they have attained," he said. 1199.

Therein, "of many colors" means having various colors by way of blue, yellow, and so forth, and possessing diverse forms due to the various shapes of the adjacent celestial mansions (*vimāna*) and other such things.
"Dispelling distress and sorrow" means [dispelling] the fever of affliction through its coolness.
Because it provides diversion through its charm and beauty, and because there is no room for sorrow, it is the destroyer of intense grief. "Anekacitta" means manifold forms of mind.

"Like the well-fashioned lord of beings"—even though he belongs to the Tāvatiṃsa host, because of his magnificent divine enjoyments, he rejoices, is satisfied, and delights like the god-king Sunimmita.
1200. *Samassamo*: Being equal, he is indeed equal; there is no one like you by way of excellence (*nibbaryāya*).
From what cause, then, could anyone be superior or more distinguished? To explain by what [qualities] this equality and superiority exist, he says:
"By glory, by merit, and by power. Therein, "by glory" means by retinue; "by power" means by majesty (*ānubhāva*).
"By glory" means by sovereignty; "by success" means by divine power (*deviddhi*). Alternatively, "by glory" means by the attainment of wealth;
"by success" means by the fulfillment of whatever sensory pleasures he desires. Or, "by glory" means by the sound of his fame; "by success" means by complete accomplishment.
"By merit" means by the fruit of the remaining merit accumulated here and there, or simply by meritorious action itself.
The phrase “all the gods” refers to the meaning taken in a general sense, which is then specified by the term “the hosts of the Thirty-three.
While some perform respectful homage individually yet do not do so with joy, this is not the case for him.
To show that he performs it even with joy, the word “approaching” (*samecca*) is used. “That” (*taṃ*) means “you” (*taṃ*). Like the moon...

"Deva" means that just as humans and gods, filled with reverence, pay homage to the moon—the "lord" (deva)—when it is seen on the first day of the bright fortnight, so too do all the hosts of the Thirty-three pay homage to him; this is the meaning.
(1203) "Bhadanta" is a term used to address the Elder with great respect and esteem. "Ahuvāsi" means "you were. "Pubbe" means...

"In a previous birth... as a disciple of the Victor named Sumedha": this means that by virtue of having gone forth in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One who was widely known by the name Sumedha, he was a disciple.
"An ordinary person" (*puthujjana*) means one who is not noble. Furthermore, because he lacked even the mere awakening to the Truths, he was "one who has not awakened.
"He will wander for seven years" means that I, he, [shall wander] for seven years.
The intention is that he wandered about merely for the sake of the virtues of the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), yet did not attain any superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
1204. *Ratanuccaya* means a shrine (*cetiya*) piled high with jewels such as gems and gold.
*Channaṃ hemajālena* means covered on all sides and above by a golden net. *Vanditvā* means having paid homage by prostrating oneself with the five points of the body.
Having paid homage here and there, [he says]: "I gladdened my mind toward the stupa. Regarding the phrase "I gladdened my mind toward the stupa," he means:
"Oh, this stupa is indeed the repository for the relics that are the foundation of the qualities of the Omniscient One!
Regarding "My gift did not perish": the gift performed by me did not perish; it did not fail to exist. But why? Because "there was nothing left for me to give."
"I have no gift belonging to my own possession to give; not a single thing fit for giving exists [for me].
However, I incited other beings to that act of giving. They also read "paresañca tattha samādapesī" (and he incited others therein);

in this context, the genitive case in "paresaṃ" should be understood as having the sense of the accusative. The passage beginning with "pūjetha naṃ" (worship him) is a demonstration of the manner in which he incited them.
The construction is: "that relic. *Evaṃ kira*—the word *kira* here signifies tradition.
"They did not reach the exhaustion of that merit": they did not attain the complete destruction of that meritorious deed performed at that time in honor of the Blessed One Sumedha;
rather, [he thought], "I am experiencing the remaining result of that very same karma."
This is shown. Furthermore, whatever has not been stated here should be understood as being easily comprehensible because it follows the method already explained below.
The commentary on the *Anekavaṇṇa-vimāna* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī-vimāna*.
“Adorned with polished earrings” refers to the *Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī-vimāna*. How did it originate? The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, there was a certain brahmin living in Sāvatthī who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments;
yet he was faithless, lacking confidence, and held wrong views. He gave nothing to anyone, and because of his refusal to give, he was known as “One Who Has Never Given Before.”
He was thus characterized. Because of his state of wrong view and his cruelty, he did not even wish to see the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata.
He instructed his own son, named Maṭṭhakuṇḍala, saying:
"Dear son, you must not approach nor see the ascetic Gotama or his disciples. And he acted accordingly.
Then his son fell ill; out of fear that his wealth would be exhausted, the brahmin did not have him treated with medicine.
But when the disease had increased, he summoned physicians and showed [the boy] to them. The physicians, having examined his body and realized that he was "incurable," departed.
The brahmin, thinking, "When a son has died within the house, the removal [of the corpse] is painful," [prepared to take his son out].
He had him laid down outside the gatehouse.
At the time of dawn during the night, the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of great compassion,
surveyed the world and saw that the young man Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī’s life span was exhausted, that he was subject to death on that very day, and that his destiny was hell.

The opportunity for my work has been created. "If I go there, he will gain confidence in me, be reborn in the world of the gods, and then approach his father as he is weeping at the funeral pyre and cause him to be moved by spiritual urgency.
Thus, both he and his father will come into my presence, and a great multitude of people will assemble there when I preach the Dhamma."
“there will be a great realization of the Dhamma. Having understood this, he dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms together with a large community of monks.
Standing near the house of the young brahmin Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī’s father, he emitted the six-colored rays of a Buddha. Seeing them, the young brahmin asked, “What is this?”

Looking here and there, he saw the Blessed One—tamed, guarded, with senses at peace, radiant with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, a fathom-wide halo, and a crest of light, shining with the incomparable glory of a Buddha and the inconceivable majesty of a Buddha.
Upon seeing him, this thought occurred to him: "Is the Blessed One a Buddha?"
"Having arrived here, he whose perfection of form by his own majesty surpasses even the sun,
by his loveliness the moon, and by his state of tranquility all recluses and brahmins— tranquility indeed must exist only here—
and who, I think, is the foremost person in this world, has surely come here out of compassion for me alone. Thus, with the Buddha as her object...
With his body continuously suffused with rapture, experiencing no small measure of joy and gladness, he lay down with a serene mind, having raised his hands in reverential salutation.
Seeing him, the Blessed One thought, "Enough for him with this much; he shall attain rebirth in heaven," and departed.
He too, without abandoning that joy and gladness, passed away and was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas in a celestial mansion twelve yojanas in extent.
...was reborn. His father, having performed the funeral rites for his body, went to the cremation ground at dawn on the following day;
lamenting, "Alas, alas, Maṭṭhakuṇḍali! Alas, alas, Maṭṭhakuṇḍali! he walked around the pyre weeping.
The deva-son, looking upon his own magnificent splendor, thought: "From where have I come here, and what..."

Reflecting thus, "Having performed this deed," he recognized his own previous existence; and seeing there, at the time of death, the serene confidence of mind directed toward the Blessed One and that heart-stealing mere gesture of joining his palms, he thought, "Oh, how great is the power of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones!
With an especially intense faith and reverence for the Tathāgata born within him, [he wondered], "Am I perhaps the Brahmin Adinnapubbaka?"

While reflecting, "What is he doing?", he saw him weeping at the cremation ground. Thinking, "In the past, this man did not provide even a measure of medicine for me, yet now he weeps fruitlessly at the cremation ground;

come, I shall stir his spiritual urgency and establish him in wholesome states," he descended from the world of the gods and, in the form of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, weeping and raising his arms, cried out, "Alas, alas, O Moon! Alas, alas, O Sun!"
Taking [the child] and weeping, he stood near his father. Then the brahmin, thinking, "This Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī has arrived," addressed him with a verse:
"Adorned, wearing polished earrings, bearing garlands, and anointed with yellow sandalwood paste—"
“Raising your arms you weep; why are you distressed in the middle of the forest?

Here, “adorned” means decorated. “Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī” means one who wears earrings in a polished manner, without displaying garlands, creepers, and so forth, for the purpose of not touching certain parts of the body.
Alternatively, “maṭṭhakuṇḍalī” means one with pure earrings, having [the gold] heated...
"Having been rubbed with *jātihiṅgulikā* and washed, he is one whose earrings have been rubbed with boar-hair"—this is the meaning.

"Wearing a garland" (*māladhārī*) means wearing a garland; the sense is that he has a garland fastened upon him. "Abounding in yellow sandalwood" (*haricandanussada*) means his limbs are entirely anointed with red sandalwood.
"What? (*kiṃ*) is an interrogative expression. "Afflicted" (*dukkhita*) means one who has reached a state of suffering. Or, "afflicted by what? (*kiṃdukkhita*) is a single compound.
"Foot"—the meaning is, "by what suffering am I afflicted?
Then the son of the gods said to him:
"A radiant chariot-fender made of gold has appeared for me."
“I do not find a pair of wheels for it; because of that suffering, I am losing my life.
Then the brahmin said to him:
“Whether made of gold, or made of gems, or made of red stone, or made of silver;”
"Tell me, noble youth, and I shall provide you with a pair of wheels.

Having heard this, the youth thought: "This man, instead of providing medicine for his son, sees me as a substitute for his son and, weeping, says, 'I will make a chariot wheel made of gold and other precious materials. Very well, I shall rebuke him. Having reflected thus—
Having said, "How large will you make my wheel-axle?
and being told, "As large as you desire," he requested, "I have need of the moon and sun; give them to me.
To him, that youth replied: "The moon and sun are both seen here."
“My chariot is made of gold; it shines with its wheels and yoke.
Then the brahmin said to him:
“You are a fool, young man, you who desire that which is undesired.”
“I think you will die, for you shall not see the moon and sun.
Then the young man said to him, “But is one a fool for weeping over that which is still visible, or over that which is no longer visible? And he replied:
“Going and coming are seen, and the element of color is present on both sides of the road.”
“One who has passed away and died is no longer seen; who here is more foolish than those who weep?
Hearing this, the brahmin reflected, “What he says is fitting,” and said:
“You speak the truth, young man; I alone am more foolish than those who weep.”
“Like a child crying for the moon, he yearned for a deceased peta.
Having said this, and being freed from sorrow by his words, he spoke these verses in praise of the young man:
“Alas! While I am burning like a fire fed with ghee, you have come to me as one who brings cool water.”
Like sprinkling with water, he extinguished all my distress.
"Truly, you have extracted the arrow that was lodged in my heart—
the grief for my son which you dispelled for me as I was overcome by sorrow."
“O young man, having heard you, I have extracted the dart; I have become cooled and attained Nibbāna. I do not grieve, nor do I weep.
In this context, *rathapañjara* means the frame of the chariot. *Na vindāmi* means I do not obtain. *Bhadda-māṇava* means O auspicious young man.
"Addressing. "I shall provide," meaning I give after having prepared it; the intention is: "May you not lose your life due to the lack of a pair of wheels.
"Both are seen here": both the moon and the sun are seen here in the sky. The letter *ya* serves to join the words (*padasaṃdhikara*);
or alternatively, the word-analysis is "both [of them] are here."
1212. "Going and coming" (*gamanāgamana*) refers to the visible going and coming of the moon and sun by way of their rising and setting day after day.
There is also a textual reading of "going and returning" (*gamanogamana*), which has the same meaning: rising and setting.

"Color-element" (*vaṇṇadhātu*) refers to the appearance of color characterized by coolness and radiant with beauty, and the appearance of color characterized by heat and radiant with sharpness. "In both cases" means...
It should be connected thus: "In both the moon and the sun, color-elements are seen. "In the path" means in the path of occurrence in the sky, or in paths such as the Nāga-path and so forth.
There is also a reading, "ubhayettha," which is a sandhi of words meaning "both here.
"Bālyatara" means more foolish, excessively foolish.
Having heard these words, he stood in reflection, thinking: "Alas! Having sought after an unattainable object, I am being consumed solely by the fire of grief; what is the use of this my futile ruin?
Then the son of the gods withdrew his form as Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī and stood there in his own divine form. But the brahmin—
Having observed this, while speaking in the very manner of a young brahmin, he said, "Is it true, young man, that you speak the truth? and so forth.
In this context, "like a child crying for the moon" means crying like a child who cries longing for the moon.
"I longed for the deceased" (*kālakatābhipatthayin*) means I longed for one who had passed away. There is also a reading: "longing" (*abhipatthayan*).
1214–5. "Set on fire" means set ablaze by the fire of sorrow. "He extinguished the distress" means he extinguished the fever of grief (*sokaparilāha*).

"He drew it out" means he extracted it. Then the brahmin, having dispelled his sorrow and seeing the one who had given him the instruction standing there in a divine form, asked, "Who are you?"— "Are you a deity, or a *gandhabba*, or perhaps Sakka Purindada?"
“Who are you, or whose son are you? How may we know you? he asked.
And he [the son] said to him:
“What you wail and what you lament, having yourself burned your son upon the funeral pyre;”
“Having performed wholesome deeds, I have gone to the company of the Thirty-three gods.
Thus he spoke of himself. In that regard, “whatever you weep and whatever you wail” means: whatever you weep and shed tears for your son Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī.
Then the brahmin said to him:
“We have seen neither little nor much given by you as a gift in your own home, nor have we seen such an observance of the Uposatha ceremony;
by what deed have you gone to the world of the gods?
In this context, the construction is: “We have not seen such an observance of the Uposatha ceremony.”
Then the young man said to him:
“I am afflicted, suffering, and sick; I am in a state of distress in my own home.
Yet I have seen the Buddha, free from dust, who has crossed over doubt—the Sugata of peerless wisdom.”
“With a joyful mind and a clear heart, I paid homage with joined palms to the Tathāgata;
having performed that wholesome deed, I have gone to the company of the Thirty-three gods.

(1220–21) In this context, *ābādhiko* means one who possesses an affliction (*ābādha*). *Dukkhito* means one who has experienced suffering (*dukkha*) precisely because of that state of being afflicted.
“Gilāno” means “one who is ill. “Āturarūpo” means one whose body is struck by painful sensations. “Vigatarajo” means one from whom the dust of passion (rāga) and so forth has departed.
“Vitiṇṇakaṅkhaṃ” means one who has crossed over doubt because all uncertainties have been completely eradicated.
“Anomapaññaṃ” means one of perfect wisdom; the meaning is “the Omniscient One. “Akarin” means “I performed. “Tāhaṃ” means “that I.”
Even as he was speaking thus, the entire body of the brahmin was filled with rapture. Proclaiming that rapture, he said:
“It is wonderful, truly marvelous!
Such is the fruit of this act of joining the palms!”
“I too, with a joyful mind and a serene heart,
go this very day for refuge to the Buddha,” he said.
In that context, it is called *acchariya* (marvelous) because it is worthy of a clap of the hands due to its not having occurred frequently, and because of its unprecedented nature.
“It is wonderful! Having shown that both [of these] are indeed causes for amazement, he said: ‘I too, with a joyful mind and a clear heart, this very day go for refuge to the Buddha.
Then the son of the gods, enjoining him to go for refuge and to undertake the precepts, said—”
“Go this very day for refuge to the Buddha, and with a confident heart, to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha;
likewise, undertake the five precepts of training, keeping them unbroken and flawless.
Quickly refrain from taking life, and avoid what is not given in the world.”
"Do not drink intoxicants; do not speak falsehood; and be content with your own wife"—thus he spoke these two verses.
Regarding that, "in the same way" means just as one with a clear mind takes refuge in the Buddha, thinking, "The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One."
Just as you went for refuge with a confident heart, saying, "The Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha has practiced well," go likewise for refuge to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha with a confident heart.

Or, just as you went for refuge to the Triple Gem with a confident heart, go likewise for refuge to the training with a confident heart, thinking, "This brings benefit and happiness unilaterally both in this very life and in the future."

The five precepts are the constituent parts of the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), or they serve as the means for the trainings in higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*).
You should undertake them so that they remain unbroken and untarnished, neither shattered nor defiled; the meaning is that, having undertaken them, you should practice them.
Thus, having been exhorted by the son of the gods regarding going for refuge and the undertaking of virtue, the brahmin, accepting his words with his head bowed, said:
“O Yakkha, you desire my welfare; O deity, you desire my benefit.
I shall do as you say, for you are my teacher.
Having spoken this verse, he stood firm there.
“I go for refuge to the Buddha, and also to the Dhamma, unsurpassed;
and to the Sangha of the God among Men, I go for refuge.
I quickly abstain from taking life; I avoid what is not given in the world.”
“I drink no intoxicants, nor do I speak falsehood; I am content with my own wife. Thus he spoke these two verses.
These too are indeed easy to understand.
Then the deva-son thought, “I have done what was appropriate for me to do for the brahmin; now [I shall approach] the Blessed One myself.”

“I shall go to visit him,” and right there he vanished. The brahmin too, having conceived faith and great reverence for the Blessed One and being urged by the deity, set out toward the monastery, thinking, “I will go to visit the ascetic Gotama.
Seeing him, the great crowd said, “This brahmin has not visited the Tathāgata for so long, yet today, because of grief for his son—”
He followed after him, thinking, "What kind of Dhamma teaching will there be?
Having approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings, the brahmin said this:
"Is it possible, Master Gotama, by giving no gift at all, or by not guarding one's virtue, but merely through faith in you alone, to [be reborn] in heaven?"
“...to be reborn. “Did not the young deva Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, Brahmin, explain to you this very morning at the hour of dawn the cause for his own rebirth in the deva-world?
the Blessed One said. At that moment, the young deva Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī arrived together with his celestial mansion, appearing in visible form;
descending from the mansion, he paid homage to the Blessed One and, with palms joined—

Having taken it, he stood to one side. Then the Blessed One, having recounted the wholesome conduct performed by that son of the gods in that assembly and perceiving the mental readiness of the gathering, delivered a discourse on the Dhamma that was exalted and supreme.
At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a penetration of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings, including the son of the gods, the brahmin, and the assembled company.
The commentary on the Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī-vimāna is finished.
10. Commentary on the Serīsaka-vimāna:
"Listen to [the account] of the yakkha and the merchants"—this is the Serīsaka-vimāna. What is its origin? It occurred after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.
The Venerable Kumārakassapa arrived at the city of Setavyā together with five hundred bhikkhus.
There, he led Prince Pāyāsi away from his erroneous grasp and established him in right vision.
From that time forward, having become devoted to merit and giving alms to ascetics and brahmins, [he proceeded] because of his lack of familiarity with that place.
Having given a gift without due respect, he passed away at a later time and was reborn in an empty Serīsaka mansion in the realm of the Four Great Kings.

It is said that in the past, during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, a certain elder whose taints were exhausted went for alms in a certain village and, every day, performed his meal duties in a particular spot outside the village. Seeing him, a certain cowherd...
Thinking, “The venerable one is suffering from the heat of the sun,” he, with a devout mind, constructed a bower of branches using four *siris* pillars and gave it to him;
they also say that he planted a *sirisa* tree near the bower. Having passed away, by virtue of that very meritorious deed, he was reborn among the Cātumahārājika devas.
At the door of his celestial mansion, there appeared a sign indicating his former karma.
A grove of *sirīsa* trees arose there, beautifying it at all times with flowers endowed with exquisite color and fragrance;

therefore, that celestial mansion became known as "Serīsaka. That son of the gods, wandering through the realms of devas and humans for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, [was reborn] during this current appearance of a Buddha among the four lay companions of Venerable Yasa, beginning with Vimala.
Having become known as Gavampati, he was established in Arahatship through the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma;
yet, by virtue of his former habit, he would frequently go to that empty vimāna for his midday rest.
Later on, seeing the devaputta Pāyāsi there, he asked him, “Who are you, friend? and he replied, “I am...”
When it was said, "Venerable sir, the royal sage Pāyāsi has been reborn here," he replied, "Are you not one of wrong view and perverted perception? How could you have been reborn here?
Then the deva-son Pāyāsi said to him, "Noble sir, I have been diverted from wrong views by the Elder Kumāra Kassapa;
however, because I performed meritorious deeds without full diligence, I have been reborn in this empty mansion."
“It would be well, venerable sir, if when you have gone to the human world, you would inform my attendants:

‘King Pāyāsi, having given a gift without due respect, has been reborn in an empty Serīsaka mansion; but you, having performed meritorious deeds with due respect, should set your hearts on being reborn there.
Out of compassion for her, the elder did so. And they too, having heard the elder’s words...
Having thus directed their minds and performed meritorious deeds, they were reborn in the Serīsaka mansion.

Furthermore, the Great King Vessavaṇa appointed the divine youth Serīsaka as a guardian of the road in the Marubhūmi wilderness to protect humans traveling on paths devoid of shade and water from the obstacles posed by non-human beings.
Then, on another occasion, merchants dwelling in Aṅga and Magadha, having filled a thousand carts with merchandise, were traveling toward the country of Sindhuvīradeśa.
Fearing the heat of the day in the desert wilderness, they did not set out by day; instead, they set out by night, guided by the signs of the constellations.
Having lost their way, they proceeded in the wrong direction. Among them was one lay follower (upāsaka).
There was a man who was faithful and confident, endowed with virtue, and possessed of the necessary support for attaining arahantship;
he had gone on a trading journey for the purpose of attending upon his parents. Out of compassion for him, the deity Serīsaka revealed himself together with his celestial mansion.
Having shown himself, he asked: "Why have you entered this desert of sand, devoid of shade and water?"
He questioned them. They then told him there how they had come about; the verses consisting of the questions and answers between the son of the gods and the merchants serve to illuminate that matter.
However, the first two verses were placed by the compilers of the Dhamma (the *Dhammasaṅgāhakas*) for the purpose of showing the connection between them.
“Listen to how the meeting between the yakkha and the merchants took place, and how they conversed with one another;
listen to all of that well-spoken discourse.
He who was the king named Pāyāsi, glorious, has gone to the company of the earth-dwellers.”
“Thus, rejoicing in his own celestial mansion, the non-human being addressed the human being.
(1228–9) In this context, “listen” is a command to hear. It means: “Listen to what we are now saying.
“Of the yakkha” refers to the deity; for a deity is called a “yakkha” because he is worthy of worship by certain humans and some gods.
...is so called. Furthermore, Sakka, the Four Great Kings, the retinues of Vessavaṇa, and even ordinary men are called "yakkhas.
For instance, in such passages as, "This yakkha indeed dwells far too negligently;

what if I were to stir this yakkha to a sense of urgency? and so forth, Sakka is referred to as a "yakkha. Likewise, in such passages as, "Four yakkhas with swords in hand... and so forth, [the Four Great Kings are so called].
“Great kings. In passages such as, “Venerable sir, there are indeed sublime *yakkhas* who have no faith in the Blessed One,” they refer to the attendants of Vessavaṇa.
In passages such as, “To this extent is the purification of a *yakkha*,” they refer to a male spirit. But here, the attendant of Vessavaṇa is intended.
The phrase “and of the merchants” is stated with the elision of the nasal vowel for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition. “Meeting” (*samāgama*) means a coming together.
"Where" means in which sandy desert (*vaṇṇupatha*). "Then" means at that time when they were lost on the road and traveling.
"And also by this or that" means *itarītarañcāpi*; this should be connected with the word "how" (*yathā*). This is the meaning here:
listen to where the meeting between the deva-son Serīsaka and the merchants took place at that time, and also how they spoke well to one another.
"Listen all with attentive minds to how this was well-spoken and set forth. "Of the earth-dwellers" means of the terrestrial devas.
Now follow the verses of the Yakkha’s inquiry:
"In the crooked forest, a place uninhabited by humans, in the wilderness devoid of water and lacking food;"
In the midst of a forest path so difficult to traverse, people lost their minds through fear of the crooked ways:
"There are no fruits here, nor any produced from roots; there is no sustenance, so from where could food come? There is nothing here but hot, burning, and dreadful sand and gravel."
“This arid place is like a heated skull, resembling the world beyond;
it is an ancient dwelling of hunters, a region of the earth that appears utterly desolate.
Now, for what reason and with what purpose have you come to this place?”
“Having entered suddenly and encountered [it], they are either overcome by greed, fear, or utter delusion.
(1230) Therein, *vaṅke* means in a place of uncertainty.

In such a forest where those who have entered it have uncertainty regarding life, thinking, “Shall we live, or shall we die? *Amanussaṭṭhāne* means in a place of non-human beings, such as *pisācas* and the like.
In a place frequented by people, or in a place that is not the range of human activity. A *kantāra* is a waterless desert;
for it is called *kantāra* because they cross (*tārenti*) or lead (*nayanti*) through it. It is a place where one must cross after taking up water. Therefore he said, "in a place with little water.

Here, the word *appa-* has the sense of absence, as in such expressions as "one of few desires" (*appiccha*) or "of little noise" (*appanigghosa*). "In the middle of a path through a forest thicket" (*vaṇṇupatha*):
The meaning is: "they are in the midst of a desert of sand. "Terrified by crooked things" (*vaṅkaṃbhayā*): they are afraid because of crooked things.
Although it should be said "those for whom there is fear from crooked things" (*vaṅkabhayā*), it is stated as "vaṅkaṃbhayā" with a nasalized vowel for the sake of metrical ease in the verse.
And this was said with reference to the fear that arose in them prior to entering the desert of sand. "Lost their minds" (*naṭṭhamanā*):...
"Those whose minds are lost through separation from the path of mindfulness" means they are "lost on the path. "O people! is an address to them.
"Here" refers to this desert wilderness (*marukantāra*). The construction is: "There are no fruits," meaning there are no fruits such as those of the mango, rose-apple, palmyra, or coconut trees.
"And consisting of roots": "roots themselves" are what is meant by "consisting of roots"; he says this with reference to creepers, tubers, and so forth. "Grasping" (*upādāna*)...
“There is nothing” means that although there is no food whatsoever, nor fuel for grasping, nor even so much as fuel for fire, how and by what cause could there be food here in this desert wilderness?
To show what *does* exist there, it is said: “Except for dust,” and so forth.

1232. *Ujjaṅgala* means that which is called *jaṅgala*, a region of land that is parched, dusty, and devoid of water; yet because that place is even more intensely parched than a mere *jaṅgala*, it is called "ujjaṅgala.
Therefore he said, "like a heated skull-bowl," meaning it is like a red-hot iron bowl. And here, for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukha*), it is stated with the nasalized vowel.
It should be understood as being just like heated [iron]. "Anāya" means there is no *āya*—that is, happiness—therein;

for that very reason, it consumes (*sīyati*) and destroys life, thus it is "anāyasa. Alternatively, it is "anāyasa" because it does not bring about prosperity (*āyasa*). "By the other world" means equal to hell.
For hell is specifically called the "other world" (*paraloka*) because, due to its absolute lack of benefit, it is a world that stands opposed to beings as their adversary.
It is called "the other world" (*paraloka*) because it is made entirely of iron; however, this [place] is "not of iron" (*anāyasa*) because of the absence of that [iron].
It is shown to be like the other world because it is a place where great suffering arises.
Some read it as "without refuge" (*anassaya*), meaning it is a place where happiness finds no footing. "This ancient abode of the cruel ones"—this...
This place has long been the dwelling of cruel hunters and of fierce spirits such as *pisācas*.

"One who has taken a vow" (*abhisattarūpo*) means one who resembles those ancient seers (*isī*) who had taken a solemn oath, thinking, "May I become so wretched and of such a terrible appearance"; the meaning is that he was like one to whom a curse (*sapa*) had been given.
"For what reason" (*kena vaṇṇena*) means for what cause. "Expecting what" (*kimāsamānā*) means desiring what in return. "Hi" is merely a particle.
They also read "padesampi," meaning "even this much of a place. "Sahasā samecca" means having entered together by chance, without having reflected upon the danger or the benefit.

"Lobhā bhayā" means either tempted by someone wishing them harm out of greed, or fallen away from greed due to being struck down by some non-human spirit or the like out of fear. Alternatively, "sampamūḷhā" means those who have lost their way.
The construction is: "They have entered this place.
Now the merchants said:
"Caravan leaders from Magadha and Aṅga, having loaded various kinds of merchandise..."
We are hastening toward the land of Sindhu-Sovīra, seeking wealth and longing for gain.
"Enduring thirst even by day, looking out with compassion for our draft animals, let us all proceed with this speed;
we have set out on the road at night, at an improper hour."
“Traveling on foot, we have strayed from the path, blind and bewildered, lost in the forest;
in the midst of this impenetrable thicket, our minds are utterly confused and we do not know the direction.
Having seen this, O Yakkha—this celestial mansion never seen before and this excellence of yours—”
“Expecting a life even longer than that, they were joyful, glad, and elated upon seeing him.
(1234) In this context, “caravan leaders in Magadha and Aṅga” refers to those born and raised in the kingdom of Magadha and the kingdom of Aṅga,
residents of those places who are both carriers of caravans and owners of caravans.
"Merchandise" means goods. "We" means we ourselves. "Let us go" means let us travel. "The land of Sindhu and Sovīra" refers to the country of Sindhu and the country of Sovīra.
"Advantage" means benefit or extra profit.
"Unable to endure" means being incapable of putting up with it. "Compassion for the draft animals" refers to living beings such as oxen and the like.
"Anuggahaṃ. By this phrase "with speed," it means with that velocity by which we have come from before your sight.
"Having set out on the road at night" means having entered upon the path during the night. "At the wrong time" means at an improper time, at a non-seasonable hour.
"Ill-traversed" means poorly traversed, having gone onto a wrong path, and for that very reason, having missed the way. "Blinded and confused."
"Blinded like the blind": they were as if blind due to the absence of the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu), which is capable of knowing the path;

for that very reason, they were bewildered, and they were lost because of their confusion regarding the path. "They looked toward the direction" means the direction in which the region of Sindhu-Sovīra lay—that direction.
"With minds utterly perplexed" means with minds completely confused by doubt concerning the direction.

“Tavañca” means “you too. “Yakkha” is a form of address. “Tatuttariṃ jīvitamāsamānā” means those who, having developed a doubt regarding their lives—thinking, “Beyond this point, there is no life for us”—are now hoping for life even beyond that.
“Disvā” means because of seeing. “Patītā” means delighted. “Sumanā” means having attained mental joy (*somanassa*). “Udaggā” means with uplifted minds through uplifted rapture (*pīti*).
When the merchants had thus explained their own circumstances, the son of the gods questioned them again with two verses:
“You travel across the ocean and this land, through the cane forest and along the path of thorns;
you go toward rivers and mountain passes, and into many directions for the sake of wealth.”

“Having invaded the victory of our enemies, while looking upon the men of the hostile kingdom—whatever you have heard or even seen that is wonderful, tell us that, dear ones. Its meaning is as follows:
“To the further shore of the ocean” means to the opposite bank of the sea; and such as this, a stretch of forest and a path through the forest.
Having bound yourselves with cane-creepers, go along the path of cane-conduct (*vetthācara*) because it must be traversed thus;
