having struck [your way] through the forked stumps, go along the path of the forked-stumps (*saṅkupatha*);

and as for rivers such as the Candabhāgā and other mountains’ uneven regions—go toward these various difficult directions that serve as signs of wealth. And while going thus, having leaped over the precipices, leap forth.
"Having entered, as you go through the territories of other kings, observing the people there who are natives of the realm or dwellers from abroad,
whatever wonderful or marvelous thing you have heard or seen while in such a state—
dear ones, merchants, we wish to hear that from you. Thus he asks, desiring to have them describe the marvelous nature of his own celestial mansion.
Thus questioned by the son of the gods, the merchants said:
"O Prince, even more wonderful than this have we neither heard nor seen.
Having beheld all that is beyond the human realm, we are not satiated by your peerless beauty."
“Lotus ponds flow through the air, abounding in garlands and many white lotuses;
these trees are ever laden with fruit, and their fragrance wafts forth most sweetly.
Columns of beryl stand a hundred high, and there are long beams of crystal and coral.”
“Masāragalla and red lohitanga—these pillars are composed of radiant *jotirasa*.
Upon them stands this excellent celestial palace (*vimāna*), with a thousand pillars and incomparable majesty;
it is interspersed with various jewels and golden pedestals, and is beautifully covered with cloths of refined gold.”
“This Jambonada tree is well-established, endowed with a palace-like trunk and steps;
it is firm, lovely, well-proportioned, exceedingly worthy of contemplation, and charming.
Amidst its various jewels are abundant food and drink, and it is surrounded by a throng of celestial nymphs.”
Resounded by the music of muraja-drums, ālambara-cymbals, and trumpets, you were saluted with hymns of praise and veneration.
"Awakened by throngs of women, you rejoice in that most delightful and excellent palace on the celestial mansion—
unthinkable, endowed with every virtue, like King Vessavaṇa in the Nalini grove."
“Were you a water-dwelling spirit,
or perhaps a lord of the gods who had become human?
The merchants and caravan leaders ask you this.”
"Tell us, who indeed are you, O yakkha? (1240–2).
Therein, "O youth," he addresses the son of the gods because he stands in the first stage of life.
"All," he says with reference to the son of the gods and that which is connected to his celestial mansion. "Lotus-pools" means lotus ponds. "A hundred fathoms high" means...
"One hundred ratanas in height. "Of stone and coral" means of stone and of coral; the sense is that they are made of stone and made of coral. "With broad shoulders" means with long shoulders.
Alternatively, having broad [shoulders], they possess eight, sixteen, thirty-two, and so forth, shoulders.
1242. "Upon them" means upon those pillars. "This is excellent for you" means this celestial mansion (*vimāna*) of yours is beautiful.
"Ratanantaraṃ" means possessing various jewels; it is joined with diverse other gems such as those on the walls, pillars, staircases, and so forth.
"Kañcanavedimissaṃ" means accompanied by, or surrounded by, a golden railing (*vedikā*).
"Tapanīyapaṭṭehi ca sādhuchannaṃ" means well-covered here and there with roofs made of refined gold (*tapanīya*) and various kinds of gems.
"Made of refined gold" means this celestial mansion (*vimāna*) of yours is for the most part radiant with refined gold (*jambunada*).
"Well-constructed, provided with palaces, stairs, and floors" means that each respective part of it is well-constructed and thoroughly polished;
it is endowed with various adjacent palaces, specific staircases, and delightful floor-boards. "Firm" means...
*Thiro*: firm. *Vaggū*: beautiful, well-formed, and elevated. *Susaṅgato*: having well-joined parts; its components, such as the pillars, are perfectly suited to one another. *Atīva nijjhānakhamo*:
even in its radiant brilliance, it is exceedingly worthy of being gazed upon. *Manuñño*: pleasing and delightful. 1245. *Ratanantarasmim*:
within that which is made of jewels, or within that which consists of jewels—the essential core—of the celestial mansion (*vimāna*).
“Abundant food and drink” means that excellent and plentiful food and drink exist; the intended sense is that they are available.
“Resounding with the music of murajas, ālambaras, and other instruments” means it is constantly filled with the sounds of mudiṅgas, ālambaras, and all remaining musical instruments.
“You were worshipped” means you were honored or praised. Therefore he said: “By the praise and worship.”
1246. *Acintiya* means "of inconceivable power. *Naḷinī*: the construction is that just as the Great King Vessavaṇa rejoices in a pleasure-grove named Naḷinī, so do you rejoice.

1247. *Āsi* means "you were" (*asi bhavasi*). *Devinda* refers to Sakka, the king of the gods. *Manussabhūta* means "born among humans," one of human birth. Regarding *yakkha*, even after asking about his status as a god or other being, some say this because they suspect he might be a *yakkha*.
Now, that son of the gods, making himself known—
“I am a yakkha named Serīsaka, stationed in the wilderness to guard the path through the forest;
I protect this region, acting according to the word of King Vessavaṇa,” he said.

Therein, “I am a yakkha” means I am a yakkha. “Stationed in the wilderness” (kantāriya) means appointed to the wilderness for the purpose of guarding. “Guardian” (gutta) means a protector. Therefore he said, “I protect.”
Now the merchants, inquiring about his work and other matters, said:
"Was this obtained by chance, or born of transformation, was it made by yourself, or was it given by the gods?
O caravan leader, the merchants ask you: how was this delightful thing obtained by you?"
In this context, "obtained by chance" (*adhiccaladdha*) means produced by accident; the meaning is "obtained according to one's whim.

"Produced by transformation" (*pariṇāmaja*) refers to that which has been transformed by destiny, conjunction, or state, or else transformed by time. "Made by oneself" (*sayaṃkata*) means made by you yourself;
the meaning is "produced by you yourself through your own supernatural power. Or, "given by the gods" (*devehi dinna*) means [given] by the gods whom you have propitiated.
It was bestowed by the gods out of their favor.
Now, the son of the gods, having rejected all four modes [of acquisition], points only to merit, saying:
"It was not obtained by chance, nor born of transformation; it was not made by myself, nor indeed given by the gods."
“By means of blameless deeds, by meritorious acts, this delightful thing has been obtained by me,” he said,

reciting this verse. Having heard it, the merchants again added those four modes of excellence to his merit, thinking, “It was not obtained by chance,” and asked for the specific nature of that merit with another verse:
“What was your vow, and what was your holy life? Of what well-practiced deed is this the result?
The merchant caravan leaders ask you: how was this celestial mansion obtained by you?
In this context, *vata* means the undertaking of a vow; *brahmacariya* means the supreme conduct.
Again, the son of the gods, having rejected those [offerings], showed himself as he was according to his accumulated merit:
“When I ruled the kingdom of the Kosalans, I had the name ‘Pāyāsi.
At that time, I held the view of nihilism, I was miserly, evil-natured, and an advocate of annihilationism.”
“The ascetic Kumārakassapa was indeed one who had heard much, a sublime speaker with a brilliant mind;
he then delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to me and dispelled my doubts regarding various views.
Having heard that discourse on the Dhamma from him, I shall declare myself a lay follower.”
I abstained from taking life, and I avoided what was not given in the world;
I drank no intoxicants, nor did I speak falsehoods, and I was content with my own wife.
"That indeed was my vow, that was my holy life (brahmacariya); this is the fruit of that well-practiced conduct."
"By those very same blameless deeds, by merits, this celestial mansion was obtained by me," he said. This is indeed easy to understand.

Then, having seen the son of the gods and his celestial mansion directly before their eyes, the merchants, having gained faith in the fruit of karma, proclaimed their own faith in the fruit of their own actions:
“Truly, wise men have said this: the word of the learned is not otherwise.
Wherever one who has performed meritorious deeds goes, there he rejoices, seeking his desires.
Wherever there is sorrow and lamentation, killing, bondage, and affliction—”
“Wherever he goes, the one of evil karma is never released from the miserable states”—thus they spoke these two verses.
Therein, “sorrow and lamentation” means both sorrow (*śoka*) and lamentation (*parideva*). “Affliction” refers to the arising of misfortune.

While they were thus speaking, at the very gate of the celestial mansion, a ripe *sipāṭikā* fruit, its stalk having loosened through ripening, fell from a *sirīsa* tree; because of that, the son of the gods, together with his retinue, became overcome with dejection. Seeing this, the merchants—
“The people were as if utterly bewildered; in this very moment, they were as if turned to a mass of froth.
O Prince, by what cause has this lack of composure come upon these people and upon you?”—thus they spoke in verse.
Therein, “as if utterly bewildered” means as if their entire nature had become deluded due to grief. “The people” refers to...
"Devajana. "In this very moment" means in just this brief instant. "Made into a *kalala*" means made like a *kalala* (embryonic mass);
the intended meaning is that it has become turbid, as if turned into water dependent upon a *kalala*. "'Of this person and of you' means of your retinue and of yourself.
'Appaccaya' means mental distress (*domanassa*)."
Having heard that, the son of the gods said:
“O dear ones, these blossoming *siris* trees emit divine, fragrant, and sweet scents;
they waft through this celestial mansion, dispelling the darkness both by day and by night.”
“After the passing of these hundred years, each single seed-pod will burst open;
when a human century has elapsed, that is the time since I was reborn here in this body.
Having seen five such centuries pass, I—”
"O dear ones, having stood in this celestial mansion,
I shall pass away through the exhaustion of my lifespan and the exhaustion of my merit;
it is because of that very sorrow that I am distraught," he said.
1256. Therein, "sirīsasavanā" means from the *sirīsa* tree. "Tāta" is how he addresses the merchants.
"These divine fragrances, belonging both to you and to me, being directly perceptible, blow and waft about, exceedingly sweet-smelling and most fragrant on all sides.
As those divine fragrances waft in this manner, they pervade this celestial mansion (*vimāna*), causing its fragrance to be fully grasped.
It is not only the blossoming itself; rather, it also dispels darkness by its own radiance. Therefore, he said:
"Having dispelled the darkness both by day and by night.
(1260–61) "Of these" refers to the *sirisā* trees. "A pod" (*sipāṭikā*) is a small case formed from the fruit. "It bears fruit" means that after ripening, [the fruit] detaches from the stalk.

It is released, or it will burst open upon reaching its maturity. "A human century has passed" means that since the pod of this *siris* tree bursts open after the lapse of a hundred years, and this one has burst open, therefore a human century has passed for me.
"From which point on" (*yadagge*) means from the time when I was reborn here in this divine realm.
He has been reborn. My lifespan, by the calculation of the gods, is five hundred years; therefore, he shows that he is utterly bewildered by the power of grief, thinking, "My life is wasting away.
Thus he said: "Having seen [the world] for five hundred years... [and so on]... I am utterly distraught by that very grief.
Then the merchants, comforting him—
“How could such a one as he grieve, having obtained an incomparable mansion after a long time?
But those who have been reborn for only a short duration, being of meager merit, would surely grieve.
Thus they spoke. In this regard, while one might grieve over death due to such short-lived beings, such a person [as the one described] is thus...
"Endowed with divine power and possessing a lifespan of ninety-one million years, how could he grieve? Indeed, there is no reason to grieve"—this is the intended meaning.
Having comforted them with those very words, the son of the gods, accepting their speech and giving them instruction, said:
"It is fitting and worthy of me that you speak such kind words to me."
"And you, dear ones, being protected by me, may you go wherever you wish in safety"—this he said in verse.
Therein, *anucchaviṃ* means suitable; that is indeed appropriate for you. *Ovadiyañca me taṃ*:
"And this should be spoken to me by you" means it should be addressed to me (*me*) by you (*tumhehi*) as an exhortation (*ovādavasena*). Because (*yaṃ yasmā*), to me (*maṃ mayhaṃ*)...
"You should speak pleasant words and endearing speech," beginning with "How indeed should one grieve?"—this is the construction:
that speaking and conversing with pleasant words is appropriate for you alone. Or alternatively, since you speak pleasant words, therefore it is appropriate;
and what should be advised, what ought to be advised, and what should be done in accordance with such advice.
“I have done this; but what then? he asks with the words, “But you yourselves, dear ones,” and so forth.
Therein, “protected by me” means that in this desert infested by non-human beings, until we had crossed the wilderness, you were protected and guarded by me;
the meaning is: “Go safely and securely wherever you desire, according to your pleasure.”
Then the merchants, demonstrating their gratitude, said:
"Having gone to the land of Sindh and Sovīra, seeking wealth and aspiring for profit, we—
having applied our efforts and fulfilled our generosity— shall hold a magnificent festival of freedom."

They spoke this verse. Therein, "according to their application" means according to the application consistent with the promises they have now made. "Perfect in generosity" means complete in giving, having relinquished sufficient wealth for the sake of a great festival. "A great festival" refers to a festival of celebration.
Again, the son of the gods, rejecting the performance of the festival while enjoining them to what ought to be done, said:
"Do not hold a *serīsa* festival; whatever you say shall be fulfilled for you all."
"Abandon evil deeds and resolve upon devotion to the Dhamma"—thus he spoke this verse.

Therein, "that which you say" refers to what you say while longing for safety and expecting abundant gain and profit from reaching the regions of Sindhu and Sovīra, saying, "Having gone there, we shall... and so forth. All that of yours—
"It shall be exactly so for you; be free from doubt in this regard. But from now on, you must avoid and shun evil deeds such as the taking of life.
'Devotion to the Dhamma' means applying oneself to wholesome qualities such as giving and the like.
'Be resolute' shows that you should train yourselves in this way: 'This is our foremost task.'"
But wishing to favor that lay follower and desiring to provide protection and shelter for them, he praised his virtues and, pointing him out to them, spoke these verses:
“There is a lay follower in this Saṅgha, learned, endowed with virtue and conduct;
faithful, generous, and very kind, discerning, contented, and wise.”
“Knowing the truth, one should not speak falsely; one should not intend harm to others;
one should not engage in divisive speech for the sake of creating discord; rather, one should speak words that are gentle and friendly.
Being respectful, deferential, and disciplined, one should be free from evil and purified in higher virtue.”
Thus a person, living with noble conduct, supports both mother and father in accordance with the Dhamma.
"I think that for the sake of his parents, he seeks wealth and not for his own sake;
and after the passing of his parents, he will live the holy life, inclining toward renunciation."
“Straight, unbent, without guile, and without deceit, one should not speak with a hint of artifice;
such a person, who has performed deeds well done and stands firm in the Dhamma—how could they experience suffering?
It is for that reason that I have revealed myself; therefore, O merchants, behold the Dhamma!”
"Otherwise, one would here be reduced to ashes, blind, bewildered, and lost in the forest;
therefore, it is better to be quickly driven away by another, for indeed, association with a true person is blissful.

(1266) In this context, "saṅgha" means a collection of beings. "Vicakkhaṇo" means skillful in what ought to be done in various circumstances. "Santusito" means contented. "Mutīmā" means wise, so called because of discerning the welfare of this world and the next through such knowledge as that of one's own karma being one's own property.

1267. “Knowing, one should not speak falsely” means one should not utter conscious falsehood (*sampajānamusā*). “Divisive speech” (*vebhūtika*) is so named because it causes the separation of those who are united; such slanderous speech one should not perform—that is, one should not speak it. 1268. “Possessing deference” (*sappatissa*):

*Patissaya* is gentleness (*soracca*), which arises from behaving with humility toward those worthy of respect; thus, one who possesses this is *sappatissa*. Regarding the “higher training in virtue” (*adhisīla*), this refers to the training in the higher precepts that must be observed by a lay follower (*upāsaka*). “Noble conduct” (*ariyavutti*) means conduct that is completely pure.
1269. *Nekkhammapoṇo* means inclined toward *nibbāna*. *Carissati brahmacariyaṃ* means he will practice the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the renunciant’s teaching (*sāsana*).
1270. *Lesakappenā* means by means of what is permissible (*kappiya*). *Na ca vohareyyā* means he should not utter speech through deceit or guile.
*Dhamme ṭhito kinti labhetha dukkhaṃ*—standing thus in the Dhamma according to the manner described.
"How could one who walks according to the Dhamma (*dhammacārī*) and walks with equanimity (*samacārī*) come to experience or encounter suffering? In what manner (*kena pakārena*) might this happen?

"For that reason" (*taṃkāraṇā*) means for that purpose, for the sake of that lay follower (*upāsaka*). "I have appeared of my own accord" (*pātukatomhi attanā*) means that I myself have manifested before you.
There is also a reading, "my self" (*attananti*); [in this case] it means: "I have made my self manifest to you."

The meaning is as follows: Therefore, because I, while honoring the Dhamma and protecting it, also protect you, for that reason you should "behold the Dhamma"—that is, look upon it by making the Dhamma alone your conduct.
"Otherwise, you would be reduced to ashes here" means that if you have come without that lay follower, you will, being helpless and without refuge in this desert wilderness, be turned to ashes.
"You should go. "By one who is quickly [hurled]" means by one who is thus hurled, reviled, and oppressed.
"Lightly" means easily. "By another" means by someone else, or in addition. Therefore: "Truly, meeting with a superior person is happy. For he is established in patience and gentleness;
even when addressed by anyone with anything, he does not oppose them—this is the intended meaning.
Thus he had been praised in general terms. Then the merchants, desiring to know him in detail, asked:
"What is his name, and what work does he do?
What is his personal name, and what is his clan?"
“We too wish to see him, O yakkha, for whose sake you have come here out of compassion;
it is indeed a gain for him whom you hold in such regard.
Thus they spoke this verse. Therein, “Who indeed is he? means: by name, who is that person, that being? And what does he do as his karma?
What kind of work does he do among farming, trading, and so forth? What is his name?
Regarding names such as "Tissa" or "Phussa" given by his parents, what is his name? Or regarding [names like] "Bhaggava" or "Bhāradvāja," what is his clan (gotta)?
"Whom you hold dear" means the one whom you love.
Now the deva-son, pointing him out by way of his name,
clan, and so forth, said: “The barber named Sambhava,
a lay follower who subsisted on the fruit of the *koccha* tree;”
"Know him to be your own son;

do not despise him, for he is very dear," he said. In that context, *kappaka* means a barber. *Sambhavanāmadheyyo* means one whose name is Sambhava. *Kocchaphalūpajīvī* means one who subsists on the fruit of the *koccha* tree.
One who lives depending on a brush and a fruit. In this context, a "brush" (koccha) is an instrument for scraping hair and so forth, used for the purpose of arranging the hair in curls and the like.
A "messenger" (pesiyo) is one who performs services as a messenger or attendant.
Now, having recognized him, the merchants said:
“We know what you say, O Yakkha, yet we do not know him to be such as that;
we too shall worship him, O Yakkha, having heard your sublime words.

In this context, “we know” means that we know him in his physical form according to what you say. But as for “such as that,” we do not know him by way of his qualities to be exactly as he has been described by you; the intention is that we do not know him as one who is so ignorant.
Now the young god, having caused them to board his own celestial palace,
spoke for the sake of instruction: "Whosoever among the people in this caravan— whether young, old, or middle-aged—
let them all take hold of the palace and let even the stingy behold the fruit of meritorious deeds."
He spoke this verse. In it, "great" means grown old. "Let them climb up" means let them ascend. "Misers" means those who are stingy and of a nature not to give.
Now, at the conclusion, six verses were spoken by the compilers of the Dhamma:
"All those there, 'I was before'—having placed that barber at their head there..."
They all took hold of that celestial mansion, just as [the gods] do for Vāsava at Masakkasāra.
There, they all declared, "I am first," and they announced their status as lay followers (*upāsaka*).
They abstained from taking life and avoided what was not given in the world.
“They drank no intoxicants and spoke no falsehoods, and they were content with their own wives.
“I was the very first among them all there, having declared my status as a lay follower (upāsaka);
the caravan departed, offering thanks, repeatedly permitted by the power of the yakkha.”
“Having gone to the lands of Sindhu and Sovīra, seeking wealth and hoping for gain,
they returned safely to Pāṭaliputta with their efforts fully rewarded.
Having traveled through the wilderness in safety, they were reunited with their children and wives.”
Joyful, elated, well-disposed, and thrilled, they performed a magnificent festival for the *serīsa* tree;
they had a monastery cell (*pariveṇa*) built there for the *serīsaka* [tree].
"Such is the service of true men: the service of the qualities of the Dhamma brings great benefit."
“For the sake of one lay follower, all beings indeed became happy.
(1276) Therein, “I was before” means “I was first, I was first,” that is, “I was the ‘I-maker’.
Having said “all of them there,” the further statement “all of them indeed” is for the purpose of [showing] how they all [ascended] into the celestial mansion.
This was said for the purpose of showing that they became eager, and thus everyone ascended it, and there was no obstacle for anyone in ascending.
Or, as in the phrase "like Masakkasāra to Vāsava": "Masakkasāra" refers to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, or indeed to all the celestial abodes;
however, here it should be understood as the abode of Sakka. Therefore he said, "like Masakkasāra to Vāsava."
1277–8. Then those merchants, having seen the celestial mansion, with hearts full of faith, abided by the exhortation of that son of the gods;
and having established themselves in the refuges and the precepts, they reached their desired destination in safety through his power.
Thus it is said: “There, all of them... and so forth. In that context, the caravan departed with his permission through the supernatural power of the *yakkha*.
The construction is: “rejoicing again and again. By whom, then, was it approved? By the *yakkha*—this meaning is evident.

(1279) “According to their application” means applications performed according to their respective inclinations. “With full gains” means with successful gains. “Unharmed” refers to Pāṭaliputta being free from affliction; or, “unharmed” means free from disease and oppression—the sense being that there is no obstacle.
(1280) “They gather” means they go to their own homes. “Secure” means endowed with security, being safe. By the words beginning with “joyful,” etc. [the following is expressed].
With these four lines, he speaks precisely of a state of joy. "They had a *pariveṇa* built for you, called Serīsaka"—this was said out of gratitude and for the purpose of releasing his promise;

it refers to a courtyard (*pariveṇa*) so named after the deity’s name, which was to be regarded as a grove (*serīsaka*) by way of its enclosure, and which was endowed with palaces, gabled chambers, night-quarters, and so forth, and surrounded by a wall.
They made a dwelling provided with gate-towers.
(1281) "Of such a kind" means of this sort; thus, it wards off harm and accomplishes welfare. "Of great benefit" means having a great purpose and a great advantage.
"Of the qualities of the Dhamma" means of the unerring qualities. For the sake of the welfare of even a single being, all [of them...]
All those beings included within the Teacher’s dispensation became happy, attained happiness, and attained security.

However, the lay follower Sambhava, having learned the verses exchanged between the divine son Pāyāsi and the merchants according to the sequence of the suttas, recited them to the elders. [Thus spoke] the divine son Pāyāsi.
Others say that he related it to the Venerable Sambhava Thera. The great elders, headed by the Venerable Yasa, included it in the compilation during the Second Council.
As for the lay follower Sambhava, after the passing away of his parents, he went forth into homelessness and established himself in Arahantship.
The commentary on the Serīsaka Vimāna is concluded.
11. Commentary on the *Sunikkhittavimāna*:
"This celestial mansion (*vimāna*) with its well-placed jeweled pillars" is thus called the *Sunikkhittavimāna*. How did it originate?
The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, in the manner described above, went on a tour of the devas.
While wandering, he arrived at the realm of the Thirty-three. At that moment, a certain son of the gods, standing at the door of his own celestial mansion, saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna;
filled with reverence and great esteem, he approached, paid homage by prostrating himself at the five points, and stood with palms joined in reverential salutation.
It is said that in the past, after the Parinibbāna of the Sammāsambuddha Kassapa, his bodily relics were enshrined and a golden stupa one *yojana* in height was constructed.

From time to time, the four assemblies would approach it and perform worship at the cetiya with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth. Seeing flowers that had been poorly arranged at the place of worship, he properly rearranged them right there;
thus, by way of their placement, he performed a flower-offering that was beautiful to behold, inspiring, and characterized by a specific artistic arrangement.
Having done this, he took hold of that object as a mental focus, recollected the virtues of the Teacher with a mind full of serene confidence, and established that merit within his heart.
Thus, at a later time, having passed away, by the power of that very same karma, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in size;
he possessed great majesty and a vast retinue. It was with reference to him that it was said:
"And at that moment, a certain son of the gods... stood there. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—
By way of praising the prosperity he had obtained, he asked about the deeds of good conduct performed [in the past] with these verses:
“This lofty celestial mansion has jeweled pillars extending twelve yojanas all around;
it contains seven hundred magnificent gabled chambers, beautiful with pillars of beryl and adorned with golden ornaments.”
“There you bathe, drink, and eat, while celestial lutes play their sweet melodies;
here are divine flavors and the five strands of sensual pleasure, and women adorned in gold dance for you.
By what means is your complexion so radiant, and by what means do you prosper here?”
“And those riches arise for you, whatever is dear to the mind.
‘I ask you, O god of great majesty: when you were a human being, what merit did you perform?
By what means do you possess such blazing majesty, and your complexion shines forth in all directions?’”
He too explained his own past deed with these verses. To show this, the compilers of the collection said:
"The son of the gods, being questioned by Moggallāna, was delighted;
having been asked the question, he answered concerning the fruit of that karma."
“Having carefully replaced the poorly placed garland and having established it upon the stupa of the Sugata,
I have become one of great psychic power and great majesty, endowed with celestial sensual pleasures.
Because of that, my complexion is such as this, and because of that, I prosper here.”
“Riches arise for me, whatever is dear to my heart.
‘I declare to you, O monk of great power, what I did while I was a human being;
because of that, I am thus blazing with majesty, and my complexion shines in all directions.’”

1287. Regarding that, "badly placed garland" means that it was not well-placed because it was set down without the specific arrangement of continuous placement and so forth at the site of worship at a cetiya; or, it is a flower badly placed because it has been struck by the wind.
"Having well-placed" means having placed it well so that it is beautiful to behold through a specific arrangement.
"Having made it beautiful and having set it down. "Having established" means having placed the flower by way of its specific arrangement and so forth.
Alternatively, while setting that flower down, one should understand the meaning here as: "having established wholesome states within my own continuum for the sake of the Teacher’s shrine (cetiya).
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
When the son of the gods had thus declared his own deeds of good conduct, the Elder taught him the Dhamma.
Having returned, he reported the matter to the Blessed One. Taking that as the occasion for instruction, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the great assembly that had gathered.
The teaching was of great benefit to the multitude.
The commentary on the *Sunikkhittavimāna* is finished.
Thus ends the seventh [chapter] of the *Vimānavatthu*, adorned with eleven stories, within the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya.
The commentary on the Sunikkhittavagga is finished.
The commentary on the Purisavimāna is also finished.
The concluding remarks.
And to this extent—
manifesting to beings the splendor of the celestial mansions and so forth of the deities, as well as their cause—
it brings about the welfare of the entire world.
The teaching which reveals that even small deeds bear magnificent fruit is due to the excellence of the field of the mind;
for those skilled in the subject matter of discourse have thoroughly understood the nature of that field.
The great seers have thus compiled [this work] as the *Vimānavatthu*.
Relying upon the method of the ancient commentaries, I have undertaken this commentary on its meaning in order to elucidate that meaning.
That which elucidates the ultimate meanings (paramattha) therein, in their respective places as appropriate,
is called by name the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
Having reached completion through unconfused analysis, it stands finished.
From this recitation section of the seventeen-fold text—
whatever merit has been gained by me while compiling it—
by the power of that merit, [may there be success for] the teaching of the Lord of the World.
May all embodied beings, having plunged into the practice of virtue and the other perfections that lead to purity, partake of the essence of liberation.
May the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One endure for a long time in the world.
May all living beings always be full of reverence toward him.
May the Lord of the World, the deity, also rain down in due season;
and may he, devoted to the True Dhamma, govern the world through the Dhamma alone.
Thus ends the Commentary on the Minor Works (*Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*),
titled *Paramatthadīpanī*, composed by the teacher Dhammapāla, a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery.
The commentary on the Vimānavatthu is finished.
The *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā* is completed.
